In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm, then set out in detail, from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

First issue: Know that His saying ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ is the name of the surah and is a subject (mubtada'). His saying ﴿A Book﴾ is its predicate (khabar), and His saying ﴿whose verses have been made firm, then set out in detail﴾ is an attribute (sifa) of the Book.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is not permissible to say that ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ is the subject and ﴿A Book whose verses have been made firm, then set out in detail﴾ is the predicate, because ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ alone is not the one described by this attribute. This objection is corrupt, because it is not a condition of a thing being a subject that its predicate be restricted to it. I do not know how this question came to al-Zajjaj. Then al-Zajjaj chose another opinion, namely that the implied meaning is: "Alif, Lam, Ra, this is a Book whose verses have been made firm." In my view this opinion is weak, for two reasons:

The first: on this reading, His saying ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ becomes a meaningless statement with no benefit.

The second: when you say "this is a Book", the word "this" refers to the nearest mentioned item, which is ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾. Thus ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ becomes what is reported about as being a Book whose verses have been made firm, and so on this opinion there follows what he did not accept in the first opinion. It is therefore established that the correct view is what we have mentioned.

Second issue: Regarding His saying ﴿whose verses have been made firm﴾ there are several interpretations:

The first: ﴿whose verses have been made firm﴾ means they were arranged in a solid, firmly joined order, in which no defect or flaw occurs, like a well-built, tightly fitted structure.

The second: firmness (ihkam) is an expression for preventing corruption in a thing. So His saying ﴿whose verses have been made firm﴾ means that they were not abrogated by another Book, as earlier books and laws were abrogated by it.

Know that on this interpretation not every part of the Book is firm, since there are abrogated verses in it. Nevertheless, since the majority is like this, it is correct to apply this description to the whole, treating the ruling that holds for the majority as the ruling that holds for the whole.

The third: the author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿uhkimat﴾ may be a causative form with the hamza, from ḥakuma with a damma on the kaf, when it became wise (ḥakīm), i.e. "it was made wise," as in His saying: ﴿the verses of the Wise Book﴾ [Yunus: 1].

The fourth: its verses were made firm in several respects:

One: the meanings of this Book are tawhid (divine oneness), justice, prophethood and the Return, and these meanings do not accept abrogation, so they are in the utmost firmness.

Two: the verses revealed in it are not contradictory, and contradiction is the opposite of firmness. Since its verses are free of contradiction, firmness has been achieved.

Three: the wording of these verses reached such eloquence and power that they do not admit of being matched, and this too indicates strength and firmness.

Four: religious sciences are either theoretical or practical. The theoretical is the knowledge of God Most High, the knowledge of the angels, the books, the messengers and the Last Day, and this Book includes the noblest and subtlest of these sciences. The practical is either the refinement of outward deeds, which is jurisprudence (fiqh), or the refinement of inward states, which is the science of purification and the discipline of the soul. We find no book in the world that equals this Book in these subjects. It is thus established that this Book contains the most exalted spiritual subjects and the highest divine inquiries, and so it is a firm Book that cannot be undone or demolished. The full discussion of the meaning of "firm" we have given in the commentary on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are firm verses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7].

Third issue: Regarding His saying ﴿set out in detail﴾ there are several interpretations:

One: this Book was set out in detail as proofs are set out with spiritual benefits, namely proofs of tawhid, prophethood, rulings, admonitions and narratives.

Two: its parts were made into sections, surah by surah and verse by verse.

Three: ﴿set out in detail﴾ means that it was divided in its sending down and was not sent down all at once. A parallel is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood as distinct signs﴾ [Al A'raf: 133], meaning that these signs came separate and successive.

Four: the separation of what the servants need, that is, it was made explanatory and summarized.

Five: it was made into sections of the lawful and the unlawful, parables and encouragement, warning and admonition, command and prohibition, and each meaning in it has a section devoted to it, not mixed with anything else, so that the benefits of each one are completed and one can attain understanding of each chapter in its most complete form.

Fourth issue: The meaning of "then" (thumma) in His saying ﴿then set out in detail﴾ is not sequence in time but sequence in rank, as when you say: "It is firmly made in the best firmness, then set out in the best detail," and as when you say: "So-and-so is noble of origin, then noble in deeds."

Fifth issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: It was read as "uhkimat ayatuhu thumma fassaltu" (I made its verses firm, then I set them out in detail), meaning I made them firm, then I set them out in detail. And it is reported from 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak: "thumma fasaltu," meaning I distinguished between truth and falsehood.

Sixth issue: Al-Jubba'i argued by this verse that the Qur'an is originated and created, in three ways:

The first: he said: "The firm (muhkam) is that which its maker has perfected. Were it not that God Most High originates this Qur'an, this would not be valid, because firmness applies only to acts. It is not permissible to say: it existed unfirm, then God made it firm, because this would require that the part which He made firm be originated, and no one has said that part of the Qur'an is eternal and part is originated."

The second: His saying ﴿then set out in detail﴾ indicates that separation and division occurred in it, and it indicates that this separation and division came about through the making of a maker and the forming of one who forms, and this too indicates the point at issue.

The third: His saying ﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾.

The meaning is "from His presence." Something eternal cannot be said to have come from another eternal, because if both were eternal, it would not be more appropriate to say that one came from the other than the reverse.
Our companions answered that these attributes return to these letters and sounds, and we acknowledge that they are originated and created; what we claim to be eternal is something other than these letters and sounds.

Seventh issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: His saying ﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ may carry several meanings:

The first: we have stated that His saying ﴿A Book﴾ is the predicate and ﴿made firm﴾ is an attribute of this predicate, and His saying ﴿from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ is a second attribute, the sense being: "Alif, Lam, Ra, a Book from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware."

The second: that it is a predicate after a predicate, the sense being: "Alif, Lam, Ra, from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware."

The third: that it is an attribute of His saying ﴿made firm﴾ and ﴿set out in detail﴾, meaning: it was made firm and set out in detail from One who is All-Wise, All-Aware. On this reading, a subtle point arises between the beginning of this verse and its end, as if He were saying: its verses were made firm by One who is All-Wise, and set out in detail by One who is All-Aware of the realities of affairs.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 2–4 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That you worship none but Allah. Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ ﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord and then turn to Him in repentance; He will let you enjoy a good provision until a specified term, and will give every person of virtue his virtue. But if you turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ ﴿To Allah is your return, and He is over all things competent﴾.

Know that in this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that concerning His saying, ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾, there are several aspects.

The first: that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, object of purpose), and the estimation is: "a Book whose verses were made firm, then detailed, for the sake of ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾." And I say: this interpretation indicates that there is no purpose of this noble Book except this single phrase, so whoever spends his life on the rest of the aims has failed and lost.

The second: that "an" (أن) be explanatory (mufassirah, explanatory), because in the detailing of the verses there is the meaning of saying, and taking it this way is more preferable, because His saying, ﴿And that you seek forgiveness﴾, is conjoined to His saying, ﴿That you worship none﴾, so its meaning must be: i.e., "do not worship," so that the command is conjoined to the prohibition; for its being in the sense of "lest you worship" would prevent the conjunction of the command to it.

The third: that the estimation be: "Alif Lam Ra, a Book whose verses were made firm, then detailed, from the presence of One Wise, Aware, that He may command the people that they not worship but Allah, and say to them: Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings." And Allah knows best.

The second issue: Know that this verse includes obligation in several respects.

The first: that He, exalted, commanded that they not worship but Allah. And when we say that an exception from a negation is an affirmation, the meaning of this statement is the prohibition of worshipping other than Allah, exalted, and the command to worship Allah, exalted. That is the truth, because we have clarified that whatever is other than Allah is originated, created, nurtured, and came into being only through the making and bringing-into-existence of Allah. Worship is an expression for manifesting submission, humility, the utmost lowliness and abasement, and this befits none but the Creator, the Governor, the Merciful, the Benefactor. So it is established that worshipping other than Allah is reprehensible, and turning away from worshipping Allah is reprehensible.

Page 145

Know that the worship of Allah is conditioned upon attaining knowledge of Allah, exalted, before the worship; for whoever does not know his object of worship does not benefit by his worship. So the command to worship Allah is a command to attain knowledge first. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted, at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿O people, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21], then He followed it with the proofs indicating the existence of the Maker, which is His saying: ﴿Who created you and those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21]. And this was good because the command to worship includes the command to attain knowledge, so inevitably He mentioned what indicates the attainment of knowledge.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾, and concerning it there are discussions:

The first discussion: the pronoun in His saying "from Him" (minhu) refers to the One Wise, Aware, and the meaning is: "Indeed I am to you a warner and a bringer of good tidings from His direction."

The second discussion: His saying, ﴿That you worship none but Allah﴾, includes the prohibition of worshipping other than Allah and the encouragement toward worshipping Allah, exalted. So he (ﷺ) is a warner regarding the first by inflicting severe punishment on whoever does not do it, and a bringer of good tidings regarding the second by bestowing great reward on whoever does it.

Know that he (ﷺ) was sent only for these two matters: warning against doing what is not fitting, and good tidings for doing what is fitting.

The second rank among the matters mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾.

The third rank is His saying: ﴿Then turn to Him in repentance﴾. And they differed in explaining the distinction between these two ranks in several respects:

The first aspect: the meaning of His saying, ﴿And that you seek forgiveness﴾, is: ask your Lord for forgiveness of your sins; then He explained the thing by which that is sought, which is repentance, so He said: ﴿Then turn to Him in repentance﴾; for the motive toward repentance and the urging upon it is seeking forgiveness, which is an expression for asking for forgiveness. This indicates that there is no way to ask for forgiveness from Allah except by manifesting repentance. In reality the matter is so, because the sinner turns away from the path of truth, and one who turns away and persists in distance, as long as he has not returned from that aversion, cannot direct himself to the object in itself. The object in itself is turning toward the sought thing, but that is not possible except by turning away from its opposite. So it is established that seeking forgiveness is sought in itself, and repentance is sought because it is among the completions of seeking forgiveness; and what is last in attainment is first in seeking. For this reason He mentioned seeking forgiveness before repentance.

The second aspect regarding the benefit of this ordering: that the meaning is: seek forgiveness for past sins, then turn to Him in repentance for the future.

The third aspect: "And that you seek forgiveness" from polytheism and sins, "then turn in repentance" from the false deeds.

The fourth aspect: seeking forgiveness is a request from Allah for the removal of what is not fitting, and repentance is the striving of the human being in removing what is not fitting. So He placed seeking forgiveness first, to show that a person must ask for nothing except from his Master, for He is the one who is able to bring it about; then after seeking forgiveness He mentioned repentance, because it is a deed the human being performs and by which he seeks means to ward off what is hateful; and seeking help through the grace of Allah, exalted, takes precedence over seeking help through the striving of the self.

Page 146

Know that when He, exalted, mentioned these three ranks, He mentioned after them what follows from them of beneficial effects and desired results. It is known that objectives are confined to two kinds: either their attainment is in this world or in the Hereafter. As for worldly benefits, they are what is meant by His saying: ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision until a specified term﴾. This indicates that one who devotes himself to the worship of Allah and occupies himself with it remains in this world with well-ordered circumstances and a comfortable mind.

* * *

In the verse there are questions:

The first question: Did not the Prophet (ﷺ) say: "The world is the prison of the believer and the paradise of the disbeliever," and also say: "Affliction is reserved for the prophets, then the friends of Allah, then the best, and then the next best"? And Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And were it not that people would become one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 33]. These texts indicate that the share of one occupied with acts of obedience in this world is hardship and calamity. The implication of this verse is that the share of one occupied with acts of obedience is comfort in this world. So how is the combination of these two?

The answer: from several aspects:

The first: the meaning is that He does not punish them with the punishment of extirpation as He extirpated the people of the towns who disbelieved.

The second: that He conveys provision to them however it may be, and to this points His saying: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you﴾ [Taha: 132].

The third, and it is the strongest in my view, is that it may be said: the one occupied with the worship of Allah and with the love of Allah is occupied with loving something whose change, cessation, and annihilation are impossible. So whoever's persistence in that path is greater and whose immersion in it is more complete, his detachment from creation is more complete and perfect; and whenever perfection in this domain is greater, joy and delight are more complete, because he is secure from the change of his object of desire and secure from the cessation of his beloved. But whoever is occupied with love of other than Allah is always in the pain of fear of losing the beloved and of its cessation, so his life is clouded and his heart is agitated. For this reason Allah, exalted, said in describing those occupied with His service: ﴿So We will surely give him a good life﴾ [an-Nahl: 97].

The second question: Does His saying, ﴿until a specified term﴾, indicate that the servant has two terms, and that advancement and delay occur in that?

The answer: No. The meaning of the verse is that He, exalted, decreed that if this servant were occupied with worship his term would be at such-and-such time, and if he turned away from it his term would be at another time. But He, exalted, knows that whether he is occupied with worship or not, his term is only at that specified time. So it is established that every person has only one term.

The third question: Why did He call the benefits of this world "provision" (matā')?

The answer: to draw attention to its lowliness and scantiness, and He alerted to its being finite by His saying, ﴿until a specified term﴾. So this verse indicates that it is lowly, base, and finite. Then, after Allah, exalted, made this clear, He said: ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾, and what is meant by it is the happinesses of the Hereafter, and in it there are subtleties and benefits.

The first benefit: His saying, ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾, means: and will give every person of virtue the cause of his virtue and its consequence. The matter is so, because when a person is at the furthest distance from occupation with other than Allah, and is at the utmost desire to attain the means of knowing Allah, exalted, then his heart becomes a gem for the engraving of the Dominion, and a mirror by which the holiness of the Divinity is manifested. However, fleshly, dark attachments cloud those spiritual lights; but when these attachments vanish, those lights shine forth and those radiances gleam, and the causes of happiness follow in succession. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾.

Page 147

The second benefit: this is an alert that the ranks of happiness in the Hereafter are varied; because they are measured by the degrees attained in this world. Since turning away from what is other than the Truth and turning toward the servitude of the Truth are unlimited degrees, likewise the ranks of the happinesses of the Hereafter are unlimited. For this reason He said: ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾.

The third benefit: He, exalted, said regarding the benefits of this world: ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision﴾, and said regarding the happinesses of the Hereafter: ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾; and this indicates that all the goods of this world and the Hereafter are only from Him, and are only by His bringing-into-being, His making, His giving, and His bounty. My father, the Imam Shaykh, may Allah, exalted, have mercy on him, used to say: "Were it not for the intermediaries, no doubter would doubt. Most people's intellects are weak, and their minds' occupation with these perishable intermediaries blinds them from witnessing that everything is from Him. But as for those who have plunged deeply into the divine knowledges and immersed themselves in the seas of the lights of Reality, they know that whatever is other than Him is possible in its essence, existent by His bringing-into-being; so their gaze is cut off from whatever is other than Him, and they know that He, glorified and exalted, is the one who harms and benefits, and gives and withholds."

Then, when He, exalted, had explained these states, He said: ﴿But if you turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾, and the matter is so; because whoever occupies himself with the worship of other than Allah becomes blind in this world, and whoever is blind in this world is blind in the Hereafter and further astray in the way. What makes this clear is that whoever turns to seeking the world and its pleasures and its good things, his love for them grows strong, his nature inclines to them, and his desire for them becomes great; then when he dies, that intense love and complete inclination remain with him, and he becomes incapable of reaching his beloved. At that point the affliction greatly increases and wretchedness is complete. This is the known measure for us of the punishment of that day; as for the details of those states, they are hidden from us as long as we are in this worldly life. Then He explained that a return to Allah, exalted, is inevitable, by His saying: ﴿To Allah is your return, and He is over all things competent﴾.

Know that His saying, ﴿To Allah is your return﴾, contains a subtle point: this wording expresses restriction (al-hasr), meaning that our return is to Allah and not to anyone else. This indicates that there is no manager (mudabbir) or disposer of affairs (mutasarrif) there except Him. The same holds true in this worldly life as well, except that some people have occupied themselves with looking at intermediaries (al-wasa'it), so they failed to reach the Causer of causes (musabbib al-asbab). Thus they thought that in the abode of this world they had power over something. As for the abode of the Hereafter, this corrupt state also disappears. For this reason, He expressed this restriction with His saying: ﴿To Allah is your return﴾.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾. I say: this is, in some respects, a great threat, and in all other respects, a great good tiding. As for it being a great threat: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To Allah is your return﴾, indicates that our return is only to Him, and His saying ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾ indicates that He is capable of all that is possible, with no one to repel His decree and no one to prevent His will. And returning to a Judge described with this attribute, together with many defects and great sins, is troubling. As for it being a great good tiding: this indicates a dominant power and a tremendous majesty of this Judge, and a complete weakness and great incapacity of this servant. A king who is dominant, exalted and overpowering, when he sees a helpless person on the brink of destruction, rescues him from destruction. From this comes the well-known proverb: "You have power, so be lenient" (malakta fa-asjah).
The author of this book says: I have spent my life in serving knowledge and studying books, and I have no hope in anything except that I am in the utmost state of humility and shortcoming. The generous, when able, forgives. I ask You, O Most Generous of the generous, O Most Merciful of the merciful, O Concealer of the faults of the faulty, O Answerer of the call of the distressed, to pour out the abundance of Your mercy upon my son and the fruit of my liver, and to deliver us by Your grace, forgiveness, bounty and generosity.

The first: the meaning is that He does not punish them with the punishment of extirpation as He extirpated the people of the towns who disbelieved.

The second: that He conveys provision to them however it may be, and to this points His saying: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you﴾ [Taha: 132].

The third, and it is the strongest in my view, is that it may be said: the one occupied with the worship of Allah and with the love of Allah is occupied with loving something whose change, cessation, and annihilation are impossible. So whoever's persistence in that path is greater and whose immersion in it is more complete, his detachment from creation is more complete and perfect; and whenever perfection in this domain is greater, joy and delight are more complete, because he is secure from the change of his object of desire and secure from the cessation of his beloved. But whoever is occupied with love of other than Allah is always in the pain of fear of losing the beloved and of its cessation, so his life is clouded and his heart is agitated. For this reason Allah, exalted, said in describing those occupied with His service: ﴿So We will surely give him a good life﴾ [an-Nahl: 97].

The second question: Does His saying, ﴿until a specified term﴾, indicate that the servant has two terms, and that advancement and delay occur in that?

The answer: No. The meaning of the verse is that He, exalted, decreed that if this servant were occupied with worship his term would be at such-and-such time, and if he turned away from it his term would be at another time. But He, exalted, knows that whether he is occupied with worship or not, his term is only at that specified time. So it is established that every person has only one term.

The third question: Why did He call the benefits of this world "provision" (matā')?

The answer: to draw attention to its lowliness and scantiness, and He alerted to its being finite by His saying, ﴿until a specified term﴾. So this verse indicates that it is lowly, base, and finite. Then, after Allah, exalted, made this clear, He said: ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾, and what is meant by it is the happinesses of the Hereafter, and in it there are subtleties and benefits.

The first benefit: His saying, ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾, means: and will give every person of virtue the cause of his virtue and its consequence. The matter is so, because when a person is at the furthest distance from occupation with other than Allah, and is at the utmost desire to attain the means of knowing Allah, exalted, then his heart becomes a gem for the engraving of the Dominion, and a mirror by which the holiness of the Divinity is manifested. However, fleshly, dark attachments cloud those spiritual lights; but when these attachments vanish, those lights shine forth and those radiances gleam, and the causes of happiness follow in succession. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾.

For this reason He said: ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾.

What makes this clear is that whoever turns to seeking the world and its pleasures and its good things, his love for them grows strong, his nature inclines to them, and his desire for them becomes great; then when he dies, that intense love and complete inclination remain with him, and he becomes incapable of reaching his beloved. At that point the affliction greatly increases and wretchedness is complete. This is the known measure for us of the punishment of that day; as for the details of those states, they are hidden from us as long as we are in this worldly life. Know that His saying, ﴿To Allah is your return﴾, contains a subtle point: this wording expresses restriction (al-hasr), meaning that our return is to Allah and not to anyone else. This indicates that there is no manager (mudabbir) or disposer of affairs (mutasarrif) there except Him. The same holds true in this worldly life as well, except that some people have occupied themselves with looking at intermediaries (al-wasa'it), so they failed to reach the Causer of causes (musabbib al-asbab). Thus they thought that in the abode of this world they had power over something. As for the abode of the Hereafter, this corrupt state also disappears. For this reason, He expressed this restriction with His saying: ﴿To Allah is your return﴾.

Then He said: ﴿And He is Able over all things﴾. I say: this is, in some respects, a great threat, and in all other respects, a great good tiding. And returning to a Judge described with this attribute, together with many defects and great sins, is troubling. As for it being a great good tiding: this indicates a dominant power and a tremendous majesty of this Judge, and a complete weakness and great incapacity of this servant. A king who is dominant, exalted and overpowering, when he sees a helpless person on the brink of destruction, rescues him from destruction. From this comes the well-known proverb: "You have power, so be lenient" (malakta fa-asjah).
The author of this book says: I have spent my life in serving knowledge and studying books, and I have no hope in anything except that I am in the utmost state of humility and shortcoming. The generous, when able, forgives. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Verily they fold their breasts to hide from Him. Yet when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you turn away﴾, meaning from His worship and obedience, ﴿then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾, He afterward explained that turning away inwardly is like turning away outwardly. So He said: ﴿Verily they﴾, meaning the disbelievers among the people of Muhammad ﷺ, ﴿fold their breasts to hide from Him.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, related two things about these disbelievers:

The first: that they fold their breasts. It is said: "thanaytu al-shay'" (I folded the thing) when you bend it and fold it over. In the verse there are two interpretations:

The first interpretation: It is narrated that a group of the polytheists said: "When we close our doors, let down our curtains, cover ourselves with our garments, and fold our breasts in enmity toward Muhammad, how would He know about us?" On this interpretation, His saying ﴿they fold their breasts﴾ is a metaphor for hypocrisy, as if it were said: they conceal the opposite of what they display, so as to hide from God, exalted is He. Then by His saying ﴿Yet when they cover themselves with their garments﴾ He alerted that they hide from Him when they cover their garments.

The second interpretation: It is narrated that when some of the disbelievers passed by the Messenger of God, he would fold his chest, turn his back, and cover himself with his garment. The meaning is as if it were said: they turn away from him so as to hide from him when they cover themselves with their garments; lest they hear the speech of the Messenger of God and what he recites of the Qur'an, and so that they might say in themselves what they desire of slander. His saying ﴿Ala (Indeed/Verily)﴾ is for alerting. He first alerted that they turn away from him to hide, then repeated the word ﴿ala﴾ for alerting, to draw attention to the mention of hiding, so as to point out the time of their hiding, which is when they cover themselves with their garments. As if it were said: Verily they turn away from him to hide from God; verily they hide when they cover themselves with their garments. Then he mentioned that there is no benefit for them in their hiding, by His saying: ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾

The passage is the exegesis of Qur'an 11:6 in al-Razi's *Mafatih al-Ghayb*.

**Allah's words: ﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah, and He knows its place of settlement and its place of storage. All of it is in a clear Book.﴾**

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned in the previous verse that He ﴿knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾, He followed it with what indicates that He is knowing of all that is known. Thus it is established that the provision of every living creature reaches it only from Allah, exalted is He. Had He not known all that is known, these great matters would not have been accomplished. There are several issues concerning the verse:

**First issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: *dabba* (creature) is a term for every animal, because *dabba* is a word derived from *dabib* (crawling), and this word was formed with the feminine *ha'* (ة). It is applied to every living animal, whether male or female. However, by the usage of the Arabs it became specifically restricted to the horse. The intended meaning of the word in this verse is its original linguistic sense, so it includes all animals. This is agreed upon among the exegetes. There is no doubt that the categories and kinds of animals are many: they are the species that exist on land, in the sea, and in the mountains. Allah alone enumerates them, and He, exalted is He, knows the nature of their constitutions, their organs, their conditions, their foods, their poisons, their dwellings, what suits them and what opposes them. So how could the God who governs the layers of the heavens and the earths, and the natures of animals and plants, not know their conditions?

It is narrated that when revelation came to Moses, peace be upon him, his heart became attached to the affairs of his family. So Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to strike a rock with his staff, and it split and a second rock came out. Then he struck it with his staff and it split and a third rock came out. Then he struck it with his staff, and it split, and from it came out a worm like a mote, and in its mouth was something that served as its food. The veil was lifted from Moses' hearing, and he heard the worm saying: "Glory be to the One who sees me, hears my speech, knows my place, remembers me, and does not forget me."

**Second issue:** Some people argued from this verse that certain things are obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, and said: the word ﴿upon﴾ (ʿalā, عَلَى) indicates obligation, and this shows that delivering provision to the creature is obligatory upon Allah.

Their answer: it is obligatory by way of His promise, His bounty and His beneficence.

**Third issue:** Our companions (the Ash'aris) relied on this verse to establish that provision may be unlawful. They said: it has been established that delivering provision to every living creature is obligatory upon Allah, exalted is He, both by way of His promise and by way of entitlement, and Allah, exalted is He, does not neglect what is obligatory. Yet we see a person who does not eat from lawful means all his life. If unlawful things were not provision, then Allah, exalted is He, would not have delivered his provision to him, and so He would have failed in an obligation, and that is impossible. We therefore know that the unlawful may be provision.

As for His words ﴿and He knows its place of settlement and its place of storage﴾: the *mustaqarr* (place of settlement) is its place on the earth, and the *mustawda'* (place of storage) is where it was deposited before settling, in a loin, a womb or an egg. Al-Farra' said: its *mustaqarr* is where it takes refuge at night or by day, and its *mustawda'* is the place where it dies. The detailed explanation of *mustaqarr* and *mustawda'* has already passed in surah (chapter) al-An'am.

Then He said: ﴿All of it is in a clear Book.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that this is established in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. Others said: it is in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). We have already mentioned this in His words: ﴿Nor anything fresh or dry, but it is in a clear Book﴾ [al-An'am: 59].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water—that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed. But if you, [O Muhammad], say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾

Know that when Exalted God proved, by the argument mentioned earlier, that He is Knowing of all that is known, He then proved by this argument that He, exalted is He, is Capable over all that is capable. In reality, each of these two arguments indicates the perfection of God's knowledge and the perfection of His power.

Page 150

Know that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾ has already had its interpretation explained comprehensively in Surah Yunus. What remains here is that we mention ﴿and His Throne was upon the water﴾. Ka'b said: God, exalted is He, created an emerald green jewel, then He looked at it with awe, and it became water that trembled. Then He created the wind and made the water upon its back. Then He placed the Throne upon the water. Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: The meaning of His saying, ﴿and His Throne was upon the water﴾ is like their saying: "The sky is upon the earth." This does not mean that one of them is attached to the other. And however the situation was, this indicates that the Throne and the water existed before the heavens and the earth. The Mu'tazilah said: In the verse there is an indication of the existence of the angels before the creation of the two, because it is not permissible that He would create that and no one benefits from the Throne and the water. For when He created them, either He created them for a benefit or not for a benefit. The second is pointless, so the first remains, namely that He created them for a benefit, and that benefit either returns to God, which is impossible because He is exalted above benefit and harm, or it returns to another, so that other must be living, because what is not living does not benefit. Everyone who said this said: that living being was of the kind of the angels. As for Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, he said: The meaning of His saying, ﴿and His Throne was upon the water﴾, that is, His building of the heavens was upon the water. The explanation of this has passed in Surah Yunus, and he clarified that when God, exalted is He, builds the heavens upon the water, they are more wondrous and more marvelous, for a weak building, if it is not founded upon solid ground, does not stand; how then with this great matter when it is spread out upon the water? Here there are questions:

The first question: What is the benefit in mentioning that His Throne was upon the water before the creation of the heavens and the earth?

The answer: In it there is an indication of the perfection of power from several aspects:

The first: That the Throne, despite being greater than the heavens and the earth, was upon the water. Had He not been capable of holding up the heavy without pillars, this would not have been valid.

The second: That He, exalted is He, held the water not upon a base; otherwise it would necessarily follow that the parts of the world are infinite, and that indicates what we have mentioned.

The third: That the Throne, which is the greatest of created things, God, exalted is He, has held it above seven heavens without a prop beneath it or a suspension above it, and that also indicates what we have mentioned.

The second question: Is what is narrated correct, that it was said: "O Messenger of God, where was our Lord before the creation of the heavens and the earth? He said: He was in 'amaa' (a cloud), above Him was air and below Him was air"?

The answer: This report is weak, and the more appropriate position is that the well-known report is more deserving of acceptance, namely his saying ﷺ: "God was, and nothing was with Him; then His Throne was upon the water."

The third question: The lam in His saying, ﴿that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ requires that He, exalted is He, created the heavens and the earth for the testing of the accountable. So what is the situation regarding this?

The answer: The apparent meaning of this statement requires that God, exalted is He, created this vast world for the benefit of the accountable, and groups of intellectuals have said this, and each group has another aspect beyond the aspect that the others said, and explaining those doctrines does not befit this book. Those who said that His acts and judgments are not caused by considerations of benefit said: the lam of causation came according to the outward appearance of the matter, and its meaning is that God, exalted is He, performed an act which, if one who is permitted to observe benefits were to perform it, he would not have done it except for this purpose.

The fourth question: Testing is only valid regarding one ignorant of the outcomes of affairs, and that is impossible for Him, exalted is He; so how can the realization of the meaning of testing be conceived in relation to Him?

Page 151

The answer: This discussion, in comprehensive form, we have mentioned in the explanation of His saying, exalted is He, at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿so that you may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21].

Know that when He, exalted is He, made clear that He created this world for the sake of testing and examining the accountable, this necessitates the certainty of the occurrence of resurrection and gathering; for testing and examination necessitate singling out the good-doer with mercy and reward, and singling out the evildoer with punishment, and that is not complete except with acknowledgment of the return and the Resurrection. At this point He addressed Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, and said: ﴿But if you say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ Its meaning is that they deny this statement and judge the notion of resurrection to be corrupt.

If it is said: That which can be described as magic is a specific act; how can this statement be described as magic?

We say: The answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: Al-Qaffal said: its meaning is that this statement is a deception from you, which you devised to prevent people from the pleasures of the worldly life, and to entice them to submit to you and enter under your obedience.

The second: The meaning of His saying, ﴿This is nothing but obvious magic﴾ is that magic is a false matter. God, exalted is He, said, relating from Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿What you have brought is magic; indeed, God will nullify it﴾ [Yunus: 81]. So His saying, ﴿This is nothing but obvious magic﴾ means: manifest falsehood.

The third: The Qur'an is what establishes the occurrence of resurrection, and they attacked the Qur'an by calling it magic, because an attack on the root entails an attack on the branch.

The fourth: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "In this is nothing but a sorcerer" (inna hadha illa sahir), meaning the Prophet ﷺ, and the sorcerer is a liar.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a countable community, they will surely say, "What is it that holds it back?" Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be turned away from them, and what they used to mock will encompass them.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, related about the disbelievers that they denied the Messenger ﷺ by their saying: ﴿This is nothing but clear magic﴾. Then in this verse He related another kind of their falsehoods, which is that whenever the punishment that the Messenger ﷺ threatened them with is delayed, they began to mock and say: "What is the reason that has held it back from us?"

So Allah, exalted is He, answered that when the time that Allah appointed for the descent of that punishment, which they used to mock, arrives, that punishment will not be turned away from them, and that punishment will encompass them.

Here there remain some questions:

The first question: Is the meant punishment the punishment of this world or the punishment of the Hereafter?

The answer: The exegetes have several opinions on this:

The first: al-Hasan said: the meaning of Allah's ruling in this verse is that He does not punish any of them with the punishment of annihilation, and He postponed that until the Day of Resurrection. So when Allah deferred that punishment from them, they said, by way of mockery: "What is it that has held it back from us?"

The second: that the meant matter is the command to fight (jihad) and what descended upon them on the Day of Badr, and according to this view they interpreted His saying: ﴿and what they used to mock encompassed them﴾, meaning that this punishment descended upon them on the Day of Badr.

Page 152

The second question: What is meant by His saying: ﴿until a countable community﴾?

The answer is in two respects:

The first: that the basic meaning of ummah (community) is people or a group. So when you say, "A community of people came to me," the meaning is a gathered group. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and he found upon it a community of people watering﴾ [al-Qasas: 23], and His saying: ﴿and he recalled after a community﴾ [Yusuf: 45], meaning after the passing and extinction of a community. Likewise here His saying: ﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a countable community﴾ means: until the time when a community of people passes away after this verbal threat, they would say: "What has held it back from us, when the people who were threatened with this threat have already passed away?" And naming a thing by the name of what occurs in it is like your saying: "I was with so-and-so at the time of the afternoon prayer," meaning at that time.

The second: that the derivation of ummah is from umm, which means intention, as if it refers to the appointed time in which this promised matter is to be carried out.

The third question: Why did He say ﴿and encompassed﴾ in the past tense, although that had not yet occurred?

The answer: Many verses of this kind have passed in this book, and the governing principle in them is that He, exalted is He, informs about the states of the Resurrection using the past tense, for emphasis and affirmation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 9–11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us and then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing and ungrateful.﴾ ﴿And if We let him taste comfort after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, "The evils have gone away from me." Indeed he is exultant and boastful.﴾ ﴿Except for those who are patient and do righteous deeds; those will have forgiveness and great reward.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that the punishment of those disbelievers, even if delayed, will inevitably befall them, He mentioned after it what indicates their disbelief and that they deserve that punishment, so He said: ﴿And if We let man taste...﴾ and in this there are several issues:

The first issue: the word "al-insan" (man) in this verse has two opinions:

The first opinion: that what is meant by it is man in general, and several things indicate this:

The first: that He, exalted is He, made an exception from it with His saying: ﴿except for those who are patient and do righteous deeds﴾, and an exception removes from the statement what would otherwise have been included. So it is established that the man mentioned in this verse includes both the believer and the disbeliever, and this indicates what we have said.

The second: that this verse, on this interpretation, agrees with His saying: ﴿By time, indeed man is in loss, except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Asr: 1-3], and it also agrees with His saying: ﴿Indeed, man was created anxious; when evil touches him, he is distressed; and when good touches him, he is withholding﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 19-21].

The third: that the temperament of man is created upon weakness and incapacity. Ibn Jurayj said regarding this verse: "O son of Adam, when a blessing from Allah descends upon you, you are ungrateful; and when it is taken from you, you are despairing and hopeless."

The second opinion: that what is meant by it is the disbeliever, and several things indicate this:

The first: that the basic principle for a singular noun with the definite article (al-) is that it is taken to refer to a previously known referent, unless there is an obstacle, and here there is no obstacle, so it must be taken to refer to that. The previously known referent is the disbeliever mentioned in the preceding verse.

The second: that the attributes mentioned for man in this verse are fitting only for the disbeliever, since He described him as "yaʾus" (despairing), and that is among the attributes of the disbeliever, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾ [Yusuf: 87]. He also described him as "kafur" (ungrateful), which is an explicit statement of disbelief. He also described him as saying, when he finds ease: "The evils have gone away from me," and that is audacity toward Allah, exalted is He. He also described him as "farih" (exultant), and Allah does not love the exultant. He also described him as "fakhur" (boastful), and that is not among the attributes of the people of religion. Then those who hold this view said: it is necessary that the exception mentioned in this verse be taken as a disjunctive (munqati') exception, so that these objectionable implications do not apply to us.

The second issue: the words "idhaqa" (to let taste) and "dhawq" (tasting) convey the least amount by which taste is perceived. So the meaning is that man, by attaining even the least of the immediate goods, falls into rebellion and transgression, and by experiencing even the least of trial and affliction, falls into despair, hopelessness and ingratitude. The worldly life in itself is small, what a single person obtains from it is small, and the tasting from that amount is a small good; then, in its swift passing, it resembles the dreams of sleepers and the imaginings of the whisperers. So this tasting is a little of a little, yet man has no capacity to bear it and no patience to act well with it. As for "al-na'ma'" (comfort), al-Wahidi said: it is a favour whose effect appears upon its possessor, and "al-darra'" (hardship) is a harm whose effect appears upon its possessor; for they came in the form of visible states, as in "hamra'" and "awra'", and this is the difference between "ni'mah" (blessing) and "na'ma'", and between "madarrah" (harm) and "darra'".

The third issue: know that the states of this world do not remain; rather they are always in change, decline, transformation and transition. The governing principle is that a person either passes from blessing to trial, and from pleasures to calamities, or the reverse, passing from what is disliked to what is loved, and from prohibited things to good things.

As for the first category, it is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us and then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing and ungrateful.﴾ The sum of the statement is that He, exalted is He, judged this man to be despairing and ungrateful. Its explanation: when that blessing is removed, he becomes despairing; this is because the disbeliever believes that the cause of obtaining that blessing was a chance cause, and then he finds it unlikely that such a chance will occur again, so he deems the return of that blessing unlikely, and falls into despair. As for the Muslim who believes that that blessing came only from Allah by His grace, bounty and favour, he does not fall into despair, but says: perhaps He, exalted is He, will return it to me afterward more complete, better and more excellent than it was. As for the state when that blessing is present, he is ungrateful; for since he believes that its attainment was by way of chance, or because man obtained it through his own effort and striving, then at that time he does not occupy himself with thanking Allah, exalted is He, for that blessing.

The sum, then, is that the disbeliever, when that blessing is removed, is despairing, and when it is present, is ungrateful.

As for the second category: that a person passes from what is disliked to what is loved, and from trial to blessing, here the disbeliever becomes exultant and boastful. As for the intensity of the exultation, it is because the ultimate aim of the disbeliever is to gain these worldly felicities, and he denies the spiritual, otherworldly felicities; so when he finds the world, it is as if he has won the utmost felicity, and therefore his joy in it greatly increases. As for his being boastful, it is because, since attaining all that is sought is the utmost felicity, he therefore takes pride in it.

The sum of the statement is that He, exalted is He, clarified that the disbeliever, in the face of affliction, is not among the patient, and in attaining comfort, is not among the grateful.

Then, having established this, He said: ﴿Except for those who are patient and do righteous deeds﴾, and what is meant by it is the opposite of what preceded; so His saying: ﴿except for those who are patient﴾ means that they are among the patient in the face of affliction, and His saying: ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ means that they are among the thankful in ease and good. Then He clarified their state, saying: ﴿those will have forgiveness and great reward﴾, combining for them these two goals:

One of them: the removal of punishment and deliverance from it, which is what is meant by His saying: ﴿they will have forgiveness﴾.

The second: attaining reward, which is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and great reward﴾. Whoever comprehends this detailed explanation that we have mentioned will know that this noble Book, just as it is inimitable in its wording, is also inimitable in its meanings.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps you will leave out some of what is revealed to you, and your breast will be constrained by it, because they say, "Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or an angel not come with him?" You are only a warner, and Allah is Guardian over all things.﴾

Know that this is another kind of the words of the disbelievers. Allah, exalted is He, explained that the heart of the Messenger was constrained because of it, then He, exalted is He, strengthened and supported him with honour and support. In this are several issues:

The first issue: It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that "the leaders of Makkah said: 'O Muhammad, make the mountains of Makkah gold for us if you are a messenger.' Others said: 'Bring us the angels to testify to your prophethood.' He said: 'I am not able to do that.' So this verse was revealed." They differed concerning the meaning of His saying: ﴿leave out some of what is revealed to you﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Bring us a book in which there is no insulting of our gods, so that we may follow you and believe in you.'" Al-Hasan said: "They asked him not to say: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15]." Others said: the meaning is attributing to them ignorance, blind following, and persistence in falsehood.

The second issue: The Muslims are agreed that it is not permissible for the Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, to betray the revelation and the sending down, or to leave out some of what is revealed to him; because permitting it leads to doubt concerning all the laws and obligations, and that undermines prophethood. Also, the purpose of the mission is conveying the commands and rulings of Allah, exalted is He; if this benefit is not achieved, the mission has departed from achieving its intended benefit. Since this is established, the meaning of His saying: ﴿Perhaps you will leave out some of what is revealed to you﴾ must be something other than that he, peace be upon him, did that. People have several views on it:

The first: It is not impossible that it is known to Allah, exalted is He, that he only leaves off falling short in conveying the revelation and the sending down because of a cause that comes to him from Allah, exalted is He, of such strong preparations.

The second: They did not believe in the Qur'an and treated it lightly, so the Messenger's breast would be constrained at delivering to them what they would not accept and would laugh at. So Allah, exalted is He, stirred him up to convey the mission and cast aside concern for their corrupt words and to disregard their mockery. The purpose of this is to alert that if he conveys that revelation, he falls into their ridicule and foolishness, and if he does not convey that revelation to them, he falls into leaving off the revelation of Allah, exalted is He, and into committing betrayal in it. So there must be bearing one of the two harms. Bearing their foolishness is easier than bearing committing betrayal in the revelation of Allah, exalted is He. The purpose of mentioning this statement is to alert to this subtle point, because when a person knows that each of the two sides of doing and not doing contains great harm, then knows that the harm on the side of leaving off is greater and stronger, that act becomes easy for him and light. So the purpose of mentioning this statement is what we have mentioned.

If it is said: His saying ﴿perhaps﴾ is a word of doubt, so what is the benefit in it?

We say: What is meant by it is restraint (zajr). The Arabs say to a man, when they want to keep him away from a matter: "Perhaps you are able to do such-and-such," although there is no doubt about it; and a father says to his son, if he orders him: "Perhaps you will fall short in what I have ordered you," intending to emphasise the command; its meaning is: do not leave it.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and your breast is constrained by it﴾, "ḍāʾiq" means "ḍayyiq" (constrained). Al-Wahidi said: The difference between them is that "ḍāʾiq" is constraint that is accidental and not permanent, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was the most spacious of people in breast; and similar to it is your saying: "Zayd is a sayyid, a jawād" (a lord, a generous one), intending the lordship and generosity that are established and fixed; but when you intend occurrence, you say: sāʾid and jāʾid. The meaning: your breast is constrained for the sake of their saying: ﴿Why has he not been sent a treasure?﴾

If it is said: How can a treasure be sent down?

We say: What is meant is that which is hoarded, and it is customary that abundant wealth is called by this name. It is as if the people said: "If you are truthful that you are the messenger of the God whom you describe as capable of everything, and that you are honoured with Him, then why has He not sent down to you what makes you independent and enables you to enrich your loved ones from hardship and toil, and to be helped by it in your affairs and to aid your supporters? And if you are truthful, why has Allah not sent with you an angel to testify for you to the truth of your words and to help you attain your aim, so that doubt about your matter would be removed? Since your God has not done that, you are not truthful." So Allah, exalted is He, made clear that he is a messenger who warns of punishment and gives glad tidings of reward, and he has no power to bring about these things. The One who sent him is the One capable of that; if He wills He does, and if He wills He does not, and no one has any objection to His action or His judgement.

The meaning of ﴿Guardian (wakīl)﴾ is "protector" (ḥafīẓ), i.e., He preserves their deeds for them, that is, He will recompense them for them. A parallel to this verse is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He will give you palaces﴾ [al-Furqan: 10], and His saying: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you"﴾ [al-Isra: 90] up to His saying: ﴿Say, "Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra: 93].

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: "Then bring ten surahs like it, invented, and call upon whomever you can besides God, if you are truthful."﴾

Know that when the people asked him for a miracle (mu'jiz), he said: "My miracle is this Qur'an." When the one miracle had been established, seeking more was transgression and ignorance. Then he confirmed that it is a miracle by challenging them to produce its equal (mu'aradah). A detailed account of this argument has already been given in al-Baqarah and in Surah Yunus. The verse raises several issues:

**First issue:** The pronoun in ﴿افْتَراهُ﴾ ("he has invented it") refers to what precedes it, namely ﴿يُوحى إلَيْكَ﴾ ("that which is revealed to you"). The meaning is: if they say that what is revealed to you is invented, then say to them, "Bring ten surahs like it, invented." The phrase ﴿مِثْلِهِ﴾ ("like it," singular) is taken to mean "like its counterparts" (i.e., each of those surahs). It is also not far-fetched that the intended meaning is the whole collection, since the ten surahs together form one thing.

**Second issue:** Ibn 'Abbas said: the surahs in which this challenge occurred are specific, namely al-Baqarah, Ali 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, al-Anfal, al-Tawbah, Yunus, and Hud, peace be upon them both. The words ﴿فَأْتُوا بِعَشْرِ سُوَرٍ مِثْلِهِ مُفْتَرَياتٍ﴾ ("then bring ten surahs like it, invented") refer to the surahs that came before this one. This raises a difficulty, because this surah is Meccan while some of the surahs that precede it are Medinan. How, then, can these ten surahs be those that had not yet been revealed at the time of this statement? It is therefore better to say that the challenge was made with any surahs in which the strength of the composition and its arrangement is evident.

Know that a challenge with ten surahs must necessarily come before a challenge with a single surah. This is like a man saying to another, "Write ten lines like the ones I write." When the other proves unable to do so, he says, "I have reduced it to one line like it."

Given this, we say: the challenge with a single surah appears in al-Baqarah and in Yunus, as already mentioned. As for this surah preceding al-Baqarah, it is clear, since this surah is Meccan and al-Baqarah is Medinan. As for Yunus, the difficulty is also resolved, since both of these surahs are Meccan. The argument we have given requires that Hud be earlier in revelation than Yunus, so that what we have said holds together.

**Third issue:** People have differed about the aspect because of which the Qur'an is a miracle. Some said it is eloquence (fasahah). Some said it is style (uslub). A third said it is the absence of contradiction. A fourth said it is its inclusion of many branches of knowledge. A fifth said it is the turning away (sarfah) of people from producing its like. A sixth said it is its inclusion of reports of the unseen. My chosen view, and that of the majority, is that it is a miracle by virtue of its eloquence. They supported the correctness of their position with this verse, because if the aspect of its inimitability were the abundance of knowledge, or reports of the unseen, or the absence of contradiction, the phrase ﴿مُفْتَرَياتٍ﴾ ("invented") would have no meaning. But if the aspect of its inimitability is eloquence, then this is valid, since the eloquence of an eloquent speaker shows itself in speech, whether the speech is true or false. Also, if the reason it is a miracle were the turning away of people, then the evidence of a base, inferior speech for this purpose would be stronger than the evidence of a lofty, eloquent speech.

Then, after He had established the aspect of the challenge, God said: ﴿وادْعُوا مَنِ اسْتَطَعْتُمْ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾ ("and call upon whomever you can besides God, if you are truthful"). The meaning is: if you are truthful in claiming that it is invented, as He said: ﴿أمْ يَقُولُونَ افْتَراهُ﴾ ("Or do they say, 'He has invented it'?").

**Fourth issue:** Know that this passage indicates that establishing the religion requires the setting out of proofs and demonstrations. This is because God presented this proof and this argument in establishing the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him. And if religion were not complete without proof, there would be no benefit in mentioning it.

[p. 156]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So if they do not respond to you, then know that it was revealed with the knowledge of Allah, and that there is no god except Him. So will you submit?﴾

Know that the preceding verse contains two addresses:

The first: the address to the Messenger, which is His saying: ﴿Say: bring ten surahs like it, forged﴾.

The second: the address to the disbelievers, which is His saying: ﴿and call upon whomever you can besides Allah﴾. When He followed it with His saying: ﴿So if they do not respond to you﴾, it may mean that the disbelievers did not respond in producing a counter-challenge, since it was impossible for them. It may also mean that those whom they call upon besides Allah did not respond. For this reason the exegetes differed on two views.

Some of them said: this is an address to the Messenger ﷺ and to the believers, and the meaning is that if the disbelievers do not respond to you in bringing a counter-challenge, then know that it was revealed with the knowledge of Allah. The meaning is: remain steadfast upon the knowledge you hold, and increase in certainty and firmness of footing that it is sent down from Allah.

The meaning of His saying: ﴿So will you submit?﴾ is: so will you be sincere?

Among them are those who said: there is an ellipsis here, and the implied sense is: so say, O Muslims, to the disbelievers: know that it was revealed with the knowledge of Allah.

The second view: this is an address to the disbelievers, and the meaning is that those whom you call upon besides Allah, if they do not respond to you in aiding you to produce a counter-challenge, then know, O disbelievers, that this Qur'an was only revealed with the knowledge of Allah. So will you submit after the proof has been established against you? Those who held this view said: this is better than the first view, because in the first view you needed to take His saying "know" as an command to remain steadfast or to assume an implied saying. In this reading there is no need for any ellipsis, so this is preferable. Also, the return of a pronoun to the nearest of the mentioned referents is obligatory, and the nearest of the mentioned referents in this verse is this second possibility. Also, the first address was with the Messenger alone, peace be upon him, by His saying: ﴿Say: bring ten surahs﴾, while the second address was with the group of disbelievers by His saying: ﴿and call upon whomever you can besides Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿So if they do not respond to you﴾ is an address with the group. So it is better to take it according to what we have said.

Remaining in the verse are questions:

First question: What is the thing in which they did not respond?

Answer: The meaning: if they do not respond to you regarding the challenge of the Qur'an. Some said: if they do not respond to you regarding the whole of faith, but this is far-fetched.

Second question: Who is referred to by His saying: ﴿to you﴾?

Answer: If we take His saying: ﴿So if they do not respond to you﴾ as addressed to the believers, then that is clear. If we take it as addressed to the Messenger, then there are two answers regarding it:

The first: the meaning is: if they do not respond to you and to the believers, because the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the believers were challenging them, and in another place He said: "So if they do not respond to you, then know."

The second: it is possible that the plural is used to honor the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Third question: What connection is there between the condition mentioned in this verse and the consequence it contains?

Answer: The people claimed that the Qur'an was a forgery against Allah, so He said: if it were a forgery against Allah, it would necessarily be that creation could produce its like, and since they could not produce it, it is established that it is from Allah. So His saying: ﴿that it was revealed with the knowledge of Allah﴾ is a metonymy for its being from Allah and from His side, just as a judge says: this ruling was issued with my knowledge.

Fourth question: What connection does His saying: ﴿and that there is no god except Him﴾ have with their inability to produce a counter-challenge?

The answer to this has several aspects:

The first: when Allah commanded Muhammad ﷺ to ask the disbelievers to seek help from idols in achieving the counter-challenge, and then their inability to do so became evident, then it became clear that the idols neither benefit nor harm in any matter whatsoever. Once that is the case, the claim that they are gods is refuted. Thus the people's inability to produce a counter-challenge after seeking help from the idols became a refutation of the divinity of the idols and a proof of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. So His saying: ﴿and that there is no god except Him﴾ is an allusion to the corruption that became evident in the claim of the divinity of the idols.

The second: it is established in the science of principles (usul) that the affirmation of the absence of a partner with Allah is among the matters that can be established by the saying of the Messenger, peace be upon him. On this basis, it is as if it were said: once the inability of the opponents to produce a counter-challenge is established, the truth of the Qur'an is established, and the truth of Muhammad ﷺ in his claim of prophethood is established. Then he used to report that there is no god but Allah, so once his veracity in the claim of prophethood is established, His saying: ﴿and that there is no god except Him﴾ is established.

The third: the mention of His saying: ﴿and that there is no god except Him﴾ operates as a warning, as if it were said: once it is established by this proof that Muhammad, peace be upon him, is truthful in his claim of the message, and you know that there is no god but Allah, then be fearful of His subjugation and His punishment, abandon persistence in disbelief, and accept Islam. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Baqarah at the mention of the verse of challenge: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it, then fear the Fire whose fuel is people and stones, prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 24].

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿So will you submit?﴾
If we say it is an address to the believers, its meaning is encouragement to increase in sincerity.
If we say it is an address to the disbelievers, its meaning is encouragement toward the very basis of Islam.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 15-16:

﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire, and what they did therein will come to nothing, and what they used to do is void.﴾

Know that the disbelievers used to dispute with Muhammad (ﷺ) in most circumstances. They would show themselves as saying that Muhammad was in the wrong and they were in the right, and that they only pushed hard in opposing him to establish the truth and nullify falsehood. In this they were lying. Rather, their aim was purely envy and refusal to follow him. So God Most High revealed this verse to confirm this meaning.

A parallel to this verse is God Most High's saying: ﴿Whoever desires the hastened [good of this world], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We wish﴾ [al-Isra: 18], and His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We increase for him his tilth, and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We give him of it, but he has no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Shura: 20]. There are issues concerning the verse:

[Page 159]

The first issue: Know that there are two views concerning the verse.

The first view: it is specific to the disbelievers, because His saying ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world﴾ includes the believer, the disbeliever, the sincere person and the heretic, since everyone desires to enjoy the pleasures of this world, its good things, and benefiting from its goods and desires. However, the end of the verse indicates that what is meant by this general wording is the specific: the disbeliever. This is because His saying ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire, and what they did therein will come to nothing, and what they used to do is void﴾ is fitting only for disbelievers. So the sense of the verse becomes: whoever desires only the life of this world and its adornment, meaning that his intention is confined to loving this world and its adornment and he does not seek the felicities of the Hereafter, his ruling is such and such. Then those who hold this view differ about it. Some of them said: what is meant is those who deny resurrection, for they deny the Hereafter and desire only the felicities of this world. This is the view of al-Asamm, and his statement is clear.

The second view: the verse was revealed about the hypocrites, who, by their participation in campaigns with the Messenger (peace be upon him), sought the spoils without believing in the Hereafter and its reward.

The third view: what is meant is the Jews and the Christians, and this is transmitted from Anas.

The fourth view, which al-Qadi chose: what is meant is whoever, by doing good, desires the life of this world and its adornment.

Doing good is of two kinds: acts of worship, and conveying benefit to living beings. Within this second kind fall righteousness, maintaining ties of kinship, charity, building bridges, paving roads, striving to avert harms, and digging rivers. So when a disbeliever does these things for the sake of praise in this world, through them good things and benefits reach the needy, so all of them are among the acts of good, and therefore these deeds are acts of obedience, whether they come from a disbeliever or a Muslim. As for acts of worship, they are acts of obedience only with specific intentions. So if the doer does not perform them with that intention, but performs them in pursuit of the adornment of this world and of gaining ostentation (riya', showing off to people) and reputation (sum'a, seeking a name) in it, their existence becomes like their non-existence, and they are not among the category of acts of obedience.

Once you know this, we say: His saying ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment﴾ means the acts of obedience that can validly proceed from a disbeliever.

The second view: that the verse be taken in its apparent generality, and we say that it includes the believer who performs acts of obedience for the sake of ostentation and reputation, and it includes the disbeliever who has this attribute. This view is problematic, because His saying ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire﴾ fits the believer only if we say that what is meant by ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire﴾ is because of these corrupt deeds and void actions joined with ostentation.

Then those who hold this view have related many reports on this subject:

It is narrated that the Messenger (peace be upon him) said: "Seek refuge with God from the well of grief." It was said: "What is the well of grief?" He (peace be upon him) said: "A valley in Hell into which the reciters who show off are cast."

He (peace be upon him) also said: "The most severely punished of people on the Day of Resurrection is the one whom people think has good in him, but there is no good in him."

On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "On the Day of Resurrection a man who had memorized the Qur'an will be summoned, and he will be asked: 'What did you do with it?' He will say: 'O Lord, I stood with it through the night and the day.' God Most High will say: 'You lie. Rather, you wanted it to be said: "So-and-so is a reciter." And that has been said.' Then the owner of wealth will be brought, and God will say to him: 'Did I not make your provision abundant? What did you do with what I gave you?' He will say: 'I maintained ties of kinship and gave charity.' God Most High will say: 'You lie. Rather, you wanted it to be said: "So-and-so is generous." And that has been said.' Then one who was killed in the way of God will be brought, and he will say: 'I fought in jihad until I was killed.' God Most High will say: 'You lie. Rather, you wanted it to be said: "So-and-so is brave." And that has been said.'" Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck my knee and said: 'O Abu Hurayrah, these three are the first creatures by whom the Fire will be kindled on the Day of Resurrection.'"

It is also narrated that Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) mentioned this hadith in the presence of Mu'awiyah. The narrator said: "He wept until we thought he would die. Then he recovered and said: 'God and His Messenger have spoken truly: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾.'"

The second issue: What is meant by paying in full the wages for those deeds is that whatever reward they deserve through them reaches them while they are in the abode of this world. When they depart from this world, no trace of the good of those deeds remains with them; rather, nothing awaits them of them but the Fire.

Know that reason definitively indicates this. This is because whoever performs deeds in order to seek praise in this world and for the sake of ostentation, this is because the love of this world has overcome his heart and the love of the Hereafter has not taken root in his heart. For if he knew the reality of the Hereafter and the felicities it contains, he would refrain from performing good deeds for the sake of this world and forgetting the matter of the Hereafter. Thus it is established that one who performs deeds of righteousness for the sake of this world must necessarily be of intense desire for this world and devoid of seeking the Hereafter. Whoever is like this, when he dies, all the benefits of this world escape him, and he remains unable to find them, incapable of obtaining them. And whoever loves something and then is prevented from reaching what he desires will inevitably have the fires of regret kindled in his heart. Thus by this rational proof it is established that everyone who performs any deed to seek worldly aims will find that worldly benefit suited to that deed. Then, when he dies, nothing from it reaches him except the Fire, and that deed becomes, in the Hereafter, nullified, void, and without effect.
