Then one who was killed in the way of God will be brought, and he will say: 'I fought in jihad until I was killed.' God Most High will say: 'You lie. Rather, you wanted it to be said: "So-and-so is brave." And that has been said.'" Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) struck my knee and said: 'O Abu Hurayrah, these three are the first creatures by whom the Fire will be kindled on the Day of Resurrection.'"

It is also narrated that Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) mentioned this hadith in the presence of Mu'awiyah. The narrator said: "He wept until we thought he would die. Then he recovered and said: 'God and His Messenger have spoken truly: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾.'"

The second issue: What is meant by paying in full the wages for those deeds is that whatever reward they deserve through them reaches them while they are in the abode of this world. When they depart from this world, no trace of the good of those deeds remains with them; rather, nothing awaits them of them but the Fire.

Know that reason definitively indicates this. This is because whoever performs deeds in order to seek praise in this world and for the sake of ostentation, this is because the love of this world has overcome his heart and the love of the Hereafter has not taken root in his heart. For if he knew the reality of the Hereafter and the felicities it contains, he would refrain from performing good deeds for the sake of this world and forgetting the matter of the Hereafter. Thus it is established that one who performs deeds of righteousness for the sake of this world must necessarily be of intense desire for this world and devoid of seeking the Hereafter. Whoever is like this, when he dies, all the benefits of this world escape him, and he remains unable to find them, incapable of obtaining them. And whoever loves something and then is prevented from reaching what he desires will inevitably have the fires of regret kindled in his heart. Thus by this rational proof it is established that everyone who performs any deed to seek worldly aims will find that worldly benefit suited to that deed. Then, when he dies, nothing from it reaches him except the Fire, and that deed becomes, in the Hereafter, nullified, void, and without effect.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 17:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is he who stands upon clear evidence from his Lord, and a witness from Him recites it, and before it the Book of Moses as a leader and a mercy? Those believe in it. And whoever disbelieves in it among the factions, the Fire is his promised place. So do not be in doubt about it; indeed it is the truth from your Lord, but most of the people do not believe.﴾

Know that the connection of this verse with what precedes it is evident, and the implied meaning is: ﴿Is he who stands upon clear evidence from his Lord like one who desires the worldly life and its adornment, and for whom in the Hereafter there is nothing but the Fire?﴾ However, the response has been omitted because it is evident, and there are many similar instances in the Qur'an, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him so that he sees it as good [equal to one guided]? For indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills﴾ [Fatir: 8], and His saying: ﴿Or is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing﴾ [az-Zumar: 9], and His saying: ﴿Say, "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ [az-Zumar: 9].

Know that the beginning of this verse contains four terms, each of which is open to more than one interpretation.

The first: who is the one that God, exalted is He, described as standing upon clear evidence from his Lord?

The second: what is meant by this clear evidence?

The third: what is meant by His saying ﴿and recites it﴾: the Qur'an, or its being present immediately after something else?

The fourth: what is this witness? These four terms are ambiguous, and therefore the exegetes differed greatly concerning this verse.

As for the first, namely: who is the one that God, exalted is He, described as standing upon clear evidence from his Lord? It has been said: it refers to the Prophet, upon whom be blessings and peace. It has also been said: it refers to those among the Jews who believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and others, and this is the more apparent view, because of His saying, exalted is He, at the end of the verse: ﴿Those believe in it﴾, and this is a plural form, so it cannot be returned to Muhammad ﷺ. The clear evidence is the explanation and the proof by which the correctness of the true religion is known. The pronoun in ﴿and recites it﴾ refers to the meaning of "clear evidence", which is explanation and proof, and the witness is the Qur'an; ﴿from Him﴾ means from God; and ﴿before it the Book of Moses﴾ means: and that proof is recited, before the coming of the Qur'an, by the Book of Moses.

Know that the Book of Moses being a follower of the Qur'an is not in existence, but in its indication of this matter. ﴿A leader﴾ is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl). The summary is that he says: three matters have combined in establishing the correctness of this religion:

The first of them: the indication of the rational proofs of its correctness.

The second: the testimony of the Qur'an to its correctness.

The third: the testimony of the Torah to its correctness. When these three combine, no doubt or suspicion remains regarding its correctness. This view is the best of the opinions concerning this verse and the closest to the wording. There are other opinions:

The first of these other opinions: the one whom God, exalted is He, described as standing upon clear evidence from his Lord is Muhammad, peace be upon him; the clear evidence is the Qur'an; and what is meant by His saying ﴿and recites it﴾ is recitation in the sense of reading. On this interpretation, they have mentioned several views concerning the witness:

One of them: it is Gabriel, peace be upon him, and the meaning is that Gabriel, peace be upon him, recites the Qur'an to Muhammad, peace be upon him.

The second: that witness is the tongue of Muhammad, peace be upon him. This is the saying of al-Hasan and a report from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah from Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I said to my father: "You are the reciter (al-tālī)." He said: "What is the meaning of al-tālī?" I said: "His saying: ﴿and recites it, a witness from Him﴾." He said: "I wished I were he, but he is the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Since a person only reads the Qur'an and recites it with his tongue, the tongue is therefore called a reciter (tālī) by way of metaphor, as one says: "a seeing eye, a hearing ear, and an eloquent tongue."

The third: the intended one is Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and the meaning is that he recites that clear evidence.

His saying ﴿from Him﴾ means: this witness is from Muhammad and a part of him, and what is meant by "from him" is to honour this witness by saying that he is a part of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

The fourth: the intended meaning of His saying ﴿and recites it﴾ is not the Qur'an, but the occurrence of this witness immediately after that clear evidence. On this view they said: the meaning is that the form of the Prophet, peace be upon him, his face and his features, all of these bear witness to his truthfulness, because whoever looks at him with his intellect knows that he is not a madman, nor a soothsayer, nor a sorcerer, nor a liar. And what is meant by this witness being "from him" is that these circumstances are attached to the very person of the Prophet ﷺ.

The second opinion: the one whom God, exalted is He, described as standing upon clear evidence are the believers, who are the companions of the Prophet ﷺ; the clear evidence is the Qur'an; ﴿and recites it﴾ means: and follows the Book which is the proof, meaning: a witness from God, exalted is He, follows it. On this opinion they differed concerning that witness. Some said: it is Muhammad, peace be upon him. Others said: rather, that witness is the Qur'an being in a form by which everyone who considers it knows that it is a miracle, and that form is its containing perfect eloquence and complete rhetoric, and its being such that no human can produce its like. His saying ﴿a witness from Him﴾ means: from that clear evidence, because the states and attributes of the Qur'an, including its recitations, are connected to it.

The third: al-Farra' said: ﴿and recites it, a witness from Him﴾ means: the Gospel follows the Qur'an, although it was revealed before it, and the meaning is that it follows it in confirmation. Its explanation: God, exalted is He, mentioned Muhammad ﷺ in the Gospel and commanded belief in him.

Know that although these two opinions are possible, the first opinion is stronger and more complete.

Know that God, exalted is He, described the Book of Moses, peace be upon him, as being a leader and a mercy. The meaning of its being a leader is that it was the one followed by the worlds, and a leader for them to whom they return concerning knowledge of the religion and the laws. As for its being a mercy, it is because it guides to the truth in this world and in religion, and that is a cause of attaining mercy and reward; so since it was a cause of mercy, the name of mercy was applied to it, applying the name of the effect to the cause.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those believe in it﴾. The meaning is: those whom God described as standing upon clear evidence from their Lord concerning the correctness of this religion believe.

Know that matters are of two kinds: some of them are known to be correct by immediate perception, and some of them require seeking and effort to attain knowledge of them. This second kind is of two kinds, because the means of attaining knowledge is either argument and proof deduced by reason, or benefit from revelation and inspiration. These two means are the two that can be returned to in defining unknown things. When they combine, and each of them is reinforced by the other, they reach the utmost in strength and certainty. Moreover, among the prophets of God, exalted is He, there is a multitude; so when the words of the prophets agree on its correctness, and the certain proof stands on its correctness, this level has reached such strength that no increase is possible. So His saying ﴿Is he who stands upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾: the clear evidence means the certain rational proofs. His saying ﴿and recites it, a witness from Him﴾ is an indication of the revelation that came to Muhammad, peace be upon him. His saying ﴿and before it the Book of Moses, as a leader and a mercy﴾ is an indication of the revelation that came to Moses, peace be upon him. When these three combine, this certainty has reached such strength, clarity and manifestness that no increase upon it is possible.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it among the factions, the Fire is his promised place.﴾ What is meant by "the factions" are the categories of disbelievers, so Jews, Christians and Magians are included among them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Abu Musa that the Prophet ﷺ said: "No Jew or Christian hears of me and then does not believe in me, except that he will be among the people of the Fire." Abu Musa said: I said to myself: the Prophet ﷺ would not say such a thing except from the Qur'an, and I found that God, exalted is He, says: (﴿And whoever disbelieves in it among the factions, the Fire is his promised place﴾). Some said: since the verse indicates that whoever disbelieves in it, the Fire is his promised place, it indicates that whoever does not disbelieve in it, the Fire is not his promised place.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not be in doubt about it; indeed it is the truth from your Lord﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

The first: "So do not be in doubt about the correctness of this religion, and about the Qur'an being sent down from God, exalted is He." This connects with what came before, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾

The second: "So do not be in doubt that the promised place of the disbeliever is the Fire." It was also read as "miryah" with a dammah on the mim.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿But most of the people do not believe﴾. The implied meaning is: since the truth has become manifest to the utmost, so be a follower of it and do not care about the ignorant, whether they believe or do not believe. The closer view is that what is meant is: they do not believe in what has been mentioned of the description of the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 18–22 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, "These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers,﴾ ﴿who avert [people] from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and they, of the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾

Know that the disbelievers had many customs and various ways. Among them was their intense greed for this world and their desire to acquire it, and Allah nullified this practice with His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the worldly life and its adornment…﴾ to the end of the verse. Among them was that they denied the prophethood of the Messenger (ﷺ) and disparaged his miracles, and Allah the Exalted nullified that with His saying: ﴿Is one who has clear evidence from his Lord…﴾. Among them was that they claimed about the idols that they were their intercessors with Allah, and Allah the Exalted nullified that with this verse. That is because this claim is a fabrication against Allah the Exalted. So when He explained the threat for those who fabricate against Allah, this claim was included within it.

Know that His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah﴾ is stated only in the context of hyperbole (mubalagha, emphatic exaggeration). It indicates that fabricating against Allah the Exalted is the greatest kind of wrongdoing.

Then He the Exalted explained the threat against them with His saying: ﴿Those will be presented before their Lord.﴾ He described them with this because they are particularly singled out for that presentation, since the presentation is general for all servants, as He said: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾ [al-Kahf: 48]. He only meant that they will be presented and thus be disgraced, for when they are presented the witnesses will say: ﴿These are the ones who lied against their Lord.﴾ Thus they receive a degree of humiliation and punishment beyond which there is no more. And there are questions on this:

The first question: If it is impossible for Allah the Exalted to be in a place, how can He say: ﴿they will be presented before their Lord﴾? The answer: They will be presented at the places prepared for reckoning and questioning. It is also possible that this is a presentation before whomever Allah wills among the creation, by the command of Allah, from among the angels, the prophets and the believers.

The second question: Who are the witnesses (al-ashhad) to whom this statement is attributed?
The answer: Mujahid said: They are the angels who used to record their deeds against them in the world. Qatada and Muqatil said: The witnesses are the people, as it is said: "before the heads of the witnesses," meaning before the heads of the people. Others said: They are the prophets, peace be upon them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6]. The benefit of mentioning the statement of the witnesses is the intensification of the exposure of disgrace.

The third question: "Ashhad" is a plural; what is its singular?
The answer: It may be the plural of shahid (witness), like ṣāḥib (companion) and ṣaḥāb, and nāṣir (helper) and anṣār; and it may be the plural of shahid (in the sense of "martyr/witness" in the form fa'īl), like sharīf and ashrāf. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: This seems more likely, because what came of this in revelation came in the pattern fa'il, such as His saying: ﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], and ﴿And We will bring you as a witness over these﴾ [al-Nisa': 41].
Then, after He informed about their state in the punishment of the Resurrection, He informed about their state in the present, saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers,﴾ and He made clear that they are, at present, cursed by Allah. Then He mentioned among their attributes that they avert [people] from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked. He means that just as they wronged themselves by adhering to disbelief and misguidance, they also added to that the prevention from the true religion, the casting of doubts, and the distortion of the straight proofs. This is because one does not say of a sinner that he "seeks crookedness"; rather, that is said only of one who knows how straightness is achieved and how crookedness is achieved, through casting doubts and establishing errors.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and they, of the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: The word "hum" (they) is repeated for the sake of emphasis, to affirm their steadfastness in disbelief.

* * *

(﴿They could not escape [Allah] in the earth, and they had no protectors other than Allah. The punishment will be doubled for them. They were not able to hear, and they were not seeing.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones who have lost themselves, and what they used to invent has strayed from them.﴾ ﴿Certainly, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers.﴾)

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They could not escape [Allah] in the earth, and they had no protectors other than Allah. The punishment will be doubled for them. They were not able to hear, and they were not seeing.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones who have lost themselves, and what they used to invent has strayed from them.﴾ ﴿Certainly, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers.﴾

Know that Allah the Exalted described these deniers and rejecters with many attributes, in the context of censure.

The first attribute: that they are fabricators against Allah, and this is His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah.﴾

The second attribute: that they are presented before Allah in a state of humiliation, abasement, disgrace and punishment, and this is His saying: ﴿Those will be presented before their Lord.﴾

The third attribute: the occurrence of disgrace, punishment and great exposure, and this is His saying: ﴿And the witnesses will say, "These are the ones who lied against their Lord."﴾

The fourth attribute: that they are cursed by Allah, and this is His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers.﴾

The fifth attribute: that they are those who bar [others] from the way of Allah, preventing [people] from following the truth, and this is His saying: ﴿who avert [people] from the way of Allah.﴾

The sixth attribute: their striving in casting doubts and distorting the straight proofs, and this is His saying: ﴿and seek to make it crooked.﴾

The seventh attribute: that they are disbelievers, and this is His saying: ﴿and they, of the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾

The eighth attribute: that they are unable to escape the punishment of Allah, and this is His saying: ﴿They could not escape [Allah] in the earth.﴾ Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of i'jaz (escaping/frustrating) is preventing the attainment of what is intended. It is said: "So-and-so frustrated me," meaning he prevented me from my aim. The meaning of "mu'jizin fi al-ard" is: they cannot flee from Our punishment, for a servant's fleeing from the punishment of Allah is impossible, because He, glory be to Him and exalted, is capable of all possible things, and His power does not vary by distance or nearness, or by strength or weakness.

The ninth attribute: that they have no protectors who can repel the punishment of Allah from them. What is meant by this is a refutation of them in their describing the idols as their intercessors with Allah. The intended meaning of His saying: ﴿They could not escape [Allah] in the earth﴾ is that they have no power to flee. And His saying: ﴿and they had no protectors other than Allah﴾ means that no one can rescue them from that punishment. Thus Allah the Exalted combined what relates to them with what relates to others, and by this He made clear the cutting off of their means of escape from the punishment of this world and the Hereafter. Then they differed. Some said: What is meant is that the non-descent of the punishment is not because they were able to prevent Allah from sending down the punishment, nor because they had a helper who would prevent that punishment from them; rather, that respite occurred because He the Exalted gave them respite so that they might repent and turn away from their disbelief. If they refuse anything but persistence in it, then the punishment must be doubled in the Hereafter. Others said: Rather, what is meant is that they will be unable to frustrate Allah in what He wills to send down upon them of punishment, in the Hereafter or in this world, and they will find no ally to help them and repel that from them.

The tenth attribute: His saying the Exalted: ﴿The punishment will be doubled for them.﴾ It was said: The cause of the doubling of the punishment for them is that they disbelieved in Allah, in the Resurrection and in the Rising. Their disbelief in the origin and the return became the cause of doubling the punishment. The more correct view is to say: Together with their intense misguidance, they strove to misguide others and to prevent people from the true religion, and for this reason this doubling was imposed upon them.

The eleventh attribute: His saying: ﴿They were not able to hear, and they were not seeing.﴾ What is meant is their state in this world: the deafness of the heart and the blindness of the soul. Our companions (the Ash'aris) cited this verse as evidence that Allah the Exalted may create in the one who is obligated (mukallaf) that which prevents him from belief. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: Allah prevented the disbeliever from belief in this world and in the Hereafter. As for this world, it is in His saying: ﴿They were not able to hear, and they were not seeing﴾; and as for the Hereafter, it is His saying: ﴿And they are called to prostration, but they will not be able﴾ [al-Qalam: 42]. The essence of the argument in this reasoning is that Allah the Exalted informed about them that they are not able to hear. Either what is meant is that they were not able to hear sounds and letters, or what is meant is that they were incapable of standing upon the proofs of Allah the Exalted. The first view is false, because necessity indicates that they used to hear sounds and letters, so the wording must be taken in the second sense. Al-Jubba'i answered this by saying: Hearing is either an expression for the specific sense organ, or for a meaning that Allah creates in the ear canal, and neither of these is within the servant's power, for if he were to strive to do it or to leave it, it would be impossible for him. Once this is established, affirming the ability regarding it is impossible, and when affirming it is impossible, negating the ability regarding it is the truth. Thus it is established that the apparent meaning of the verse does not undermine our position. Then he said: What is meant by His saying: ﴿They were not able to hear﴾ is their neglect of it and their aversion from it, as a speaker says: "This is speech that I cannot bear to hear, and this is something my hearing rejects." Someone other than al-Jubba'i offered another excuse, saying: Allah the Exalted denied that they have any protectors, and what is meant are the idols; then He made clear the denial of their being protectors by His saying: ﴿They were not able to hear, and they were not seeing﴾, so how could they be fit for guardianship?

The answer: As for interpreting the verse to mean that they had no power to create the sense organ and to create the meaning in it, that is false, because this verse came in the context of a threat, so this meaning must be specific to them, whereas the meaning they mentioned is present in the angels and the prophets, so how can the wording be taken to mean it?

As for his statement that this is to be understood as meaning that they found it burdensome to hear the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to look at his form, the answer is that He the Exalted negated the ability, and he took it to mean something else contrary to the apparent meaning. Moreover, that burdensomeness either prevents understanding and reaching the aim, or it does not. If it prevents it, then that is what is intended; and if it does not prevent it, then it is a foreign cause unrelated to the meanings that count in understanding and perception, and the states of the heart in knowledge and recognition do not vary because of it, so how can it be made a censure of them in this context? Also, we have explained many times in this book that the occurrence of an act together with the presence of a preventing factor (ṣārif) is impossible. So when He the Exalted made clear that this meaning is a barrier against accepting the true religion, and made clear that it came about in such a way as to be inevitable, not disappearing at all at that time, the one obligated was, at that time, prevented from belief, and then the objective is achieved. As for his statement that "we make this attribute one of the attributes of the idols," it is far-fetched, because He the Exalted said: ﴿The punishment will be doubled for them﴾, then He said: ﴿They were not able to hear﴾; so the pronoun in this later verse must necessarily refer to the very same thing to which the pronoun in the first verse refers.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and they were not seeing﴾, it was said: What is meant by it is insight (basirah). And it was said: What is meant by it is that they turned away from seeing what would have served as proof for them.

The twelfth attribute: His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾. Its meaning is that they exchanged the worship of Allah the Exalted for the worship of gods, so this loss was the greatest aspect of loss.

Part 2 of 2 of the commentary is translated below.

The thirteenth attribute: His saying, ﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾. The meaning is that when they sold the religion for the worldly life, they incurred loss, because they gave away the noble and accepted the base in exchange. This is the very essence of loss, in this world and then in the Hereafter. This base thing perishes and is destroyed, and no trace of it remains. This is what is meant by His saying, ﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾.

The fourteenth attribute: His saying, ﴿Without doubt, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers﴾. Its explanation is what preceded: since they gave up the lofty and noble and were content with the lowly and base, they lost in the transaction. Then, since this base thing is of such a nature that it does not remain, but must inevitably be destroyed and perish, that trade turned into the utmost degree of loss. Therefore He said: ﴿Without doubt, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers﴾. As for His saying ﴿Without doubt (la jaram)﴾, al-Farra' said: it is equivalent to our saying "la budda" (there is no escaping) and "la mahalata" (without fail). Then its use became frequent until it came to have the sense of "haqqan" (truly). The Arabs say: "la jarama annaka muhsin" (undoubtedly you are a good person), meaning "haqqan innaka muhsin" (truly you are good). As for the grammarians, they have several interpretations concerning it:

The first: "la" is a particle of negation and "jazm," meaning "qat'" (decisive cutting-off). So when we say "la jarama," its meaning is that there is no decisive cutting-off that prevents them from being, in the Hereafter, the greatest losers.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: the word "la" negates what they supposed would benefit them, and "jarama" means "kasaba" (to earn, to bring about). The meaning is: that will not benefit them, and that action earned for them loss in this world and the Hereafter. We have mentioned "jarama" in the sense of "kasaba" in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And let not the enmity of a people prompt you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. Al-Azhari said: this is among the best of what has been said on this subject.

The third: Sibawayh and al-Akhfash said: "la" is a rebuttal to the people of disbelief, as we have mentioned, and "jarama" means "haqqa" (was due) and "sahha" (was established). The interpretation is that it is due, for their disbelief, that punishment and loss befall them. Sibawayh cited as evidence the words of the poet:

*Indeed I struck Abu 'Uyayna with a thrust that made Fazara deserve, after it, that they should be angry.*

He meant: the thrust was due to Fazara, that they should be angry.

It is said: "So-and-so frustrated me," meaning he prevented me from my aim. What is meant by this is a refutation of them in their describing the idols as their intercessors with Allah. And His saying: ﴿and they had no protectors other than Allah﴾ means that no one can rescue them from that punishment. Thus Allah the Exalted combined what relates to them with what relates to others, and by this He made clear the cutting off of their means of escape from the punishment of this world and the Hereafter. Then they differed. Some said: What is meant is that the non-descent of the punishment is not because they were able to prevent Allah from sending down the punishment, nor because they had a helper who would prevent that punishment from them; rather, that respite occurred because He the Exalted gave them respite so that they might repent and turn away from their disbelief. If they refuse anything but persistence in it, then the punishment must be doubled in the Hereafter. Others said: Rather, what is meant is that they will be unable to frustrate Allah in what He wills to send down upon them of punishment, in the Hereafter or in this world, and they will find no ally to help them and repel that from them.

Their disbelief in the origin and the return became the cause of doubling the punishment. The more correct view is to say: Together with their intense misguidance, they strove to misguide others and to prevent people from the true religion, and for this reason this doubling was imposed upon them.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: Allah prevented the disbeliever from belief in this world and in the Hereafter. The meaning is that when they sold the religion for the worldly life, they incurred loss, because they gave away the noble and accepted the base in exchange. This is what is meant by His saying, ﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾.

The interpretation is that it is due, for their disbelief, that punishment and loss befall them. Sibawayh cited as evidence the words of the poet:

He meant: the thrust was due to Fazara, that they should be angry.

He only meant that they will be presented and thus be disgraced, for when they are presented the witnesses will say: ﴿These are the ones who lied against their Lord.﴾ Thus they receive a degree of humiliation and punishment beyond which there is no more. And there are questions on this:

The first question: If it is impossible for Allah the Exalted to be in a place, how can He say: ﴿they will be presented before their Lord﴾? The answer: They will be presented at the places prepared for reckoning and questioning. It is also possible that this is a presentation before whomever Allah wills among the creation, by the command of Allah, from among the angels, the prophets and the believers.

The second question: Who are the witnesses (al-ashhad) to whom this statement is attributed?

Qatada and Muqatil said: The witnesses are the people, as it is said: "before the heads of the witnesses," meaning before the heads of the people. Others said: They are the prophets, peace be upon them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6]. Then He said: ﴿and they, of the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: The word "hum" (they) is repeated for the sake of emphasis, to affirm their steadfastness in disbelief.

(﴿They could not escape [Allah] in the earth, and they had no protectors other than Allah. The punishment will be doubled for them. The second attribute: that they are presented before Allah in a state of humiliation, abasement, disgrace and punishment, and this is His saying: ﴿Those will be presented before their Lord.﴾

The third attribute: the occurrence of disgrace, punishment and great exposure, and this is His saying: ﴿And the witnesses will say, "These are the ones who lied against their Lord."﴾

The fourth attribute: that they are cursed by Allah, and this is His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers.﴾

The fifth attribute: that they are those who bar [others] from the way of Allah, preventing [people] from following the truth, and this is His saying: ﴿who avert [people] from the way of Allah.﴾

The sixth attribute: their striving in casting doubts and distorting the straight proofs, and this is His saying: ﴿and seek to make it crooked.﴾

The seventh attribute: that they are disbelievers, and this is His saying: ﴿and they, of the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾

The eighth attribute: that they are unable to escape the punishment of Allah, and this is His saying: ﴿They could not escape [Allah] in the earth.﴾ Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of i'jaz (escaping/frustrating) is preventing the attainment of what is intended. It is said: "So-and-so frustrated me," meaning he prevented me from my aim. The meaning of "mu'jizin fi al-ard" is: they cannot flee from Our punishment, for a servant's fleeing from the punishment of Allah is impossible, because He, glory be to Him and exalted, is capable of all possible things, and His power does not vary by distance or nearness, or by strength or weakness.

The ninth attribute: that they have no protectors who can repel the punishment of Allah from them. What is meant by this is a refutation of them in their describing the idols as their intercessors with Allah. The intended meaning of His saying: ﴿They could not escape [Allah] in the earth﴾ is that they have no power to flee. And His saying: ﴿and they had no protectors other than Allah﴾ means that no one can rescue them from that punishment. Thus Allah the Exalted combined what relates to them with what relates to others, and by this He made clear the cutting off of their means of escape from the punishment of this world and the Hereafter. Then they differed. Some said: What is meant is that the non-descent of the punishment is not because they were able to prevent Allah from sending down the punishment, nor because they had a helper who would prevent that punishment from them; rather, that respite occurred because He the Exalted gave them respite so that they might repent and turn away from their disbelief. If they refuse anything but persistence in it, then the punishment must be doubled in the Hereafter. Others said: Rather, what is meant is that they will be unable to frustrate Allah in what He wills to send down upon them of punishment, in the Hereafter or in this world, and they will find no ally to help them and repel that from them.

The tenth attribute: His saying the Exalted: ﴿The punishment will be doubled for them.﴾ It was said: The cause of the doubling of the punishment for them is that they disbelieved in Allah, in the Resurrection and in the Rising. Their disbelief in the origin and the return became the cause of doubling the punishment. The more correct view is to say: Together with their intense misguidance, they strove to misguide others and to prevent people from the true religion, and for this reason this doubling was imposed upon them.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: Allah prevented the disbeliever from belief in this world and in the Hereafter. Also, we have explained many times in this book that the occurrence of an act together with the presence of a preventing factor (ṣārif) is impossible. So when He the Exalted made clear that this meaning is a barrier against accepting the true religion, and made clear that it came about in such a way as to be inevitable, not disappearing at all at that time, the one obligated was, at that time, prevented from belief, and then the objective is achieved. As for His saying: ﴿and they were not seeing﴾, it was said: What is meant by it is insight (basirah). And it was said: What is meant by it is that they turned away from seeing what would have served as proof for them.

The meaning is that when they sold the religion for the worldly life, they incurred loss, because they gave away the noble and accepted the base in exchange. This is the very essence of loss, in this world and then in the Hereafter. This base thing perishes and is destroyed, and no trace of it remains. This is what is meant by His saying, ﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾.

The fourteenth attribute: His saying, ﴿Without doubt, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers﴾. Its explanation is what preceded: since they gave up the lofty and noble and were content with the lowly and base, they lost in the transaction. The meaning is: that will not benefit them, and that action earned for them loss in this world and the Hereafter. This is the very essence of loss, in this world and then in the Hereafter. This base thing perishes and is destroyed, and no trace of it remains. This is what is meant by His saying, ﴿And what they used to fabricate has vanished from them﴾.

The fourteenth attribute: His saying, ﴿Without doubt, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers﴾. Its explanation is what preceded: since they gave up the lofty and noble and were content with the lowly and base, they lost in the transaction. Then, since this base thing is of such a nature that it does not remain, but must inevitably be destroyed and perish, that trade turned into the utmost degree of loss. Therefore He said: ﴿Without doubt, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers﴾. As for His saying ﴿Without doubt (la jaram)﴾, al-Farra' said: it is equivalent to our saying "la budda" (there is no escaping) and "la mahalata" (without fail). Then its use became frequent until it came to have the sense of "haqqan" (truly). The Arabs say: "la jarama annaka muhsin" (undoubtedly you are a good person), meaning "haqqan innaka muhsin" (truly you are good). As for the grammarians, they have several interpretations concerning it:

The first: "la" is a particle of negation and "jazm," meaning "qat'" (decisive cutting-off). So when we say "la jarama," its meaning is that there is no decisive cutting-off that prevents them from being, in the Hereafter, the greatest losers.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: the word "la" negates what they supposed would benefit them, and "jarama" means "kasaba" (to earn, to bring about). The meaning is: that will not benefit them, and that action earned for them loss in this world and the Hereafter. We have mentioned "jarama" in the sense of "kasaba" in the commentary on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And let not the enmity of a people prompt you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2]. Al-Azhari said: this is among the best of what has been said on this subject.

The third: Sibawayh and al-Akhfash said: "la" is a rebuttal to the people of disbelief, as we have mentioned, and "jarama" means "haqqa" (was due) and "sahha" (was established). The interpretation is that it is due, for their disbelief, that punishment and loss befall them. Sibawayh cited as evidence the words of the poet:

*Indeed I struck Abu 'Uyayna with a thrust that made Fazara deserve, after it, that they should be angry.*

He meant: the thrust was due to Fazara, that they should be angry.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 23:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds and humbled themselves before their Lord — those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide eternally.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the punishment of the disbelievers and their loss, He followed it with mention of the states of the believers. Ikhbat (humbling oneself, submission) is khushu' (humble reverence) and khudu' (lowliness), and it is derived from al-khabt (khabt), which is low, level ground (al-ard al-mutma'innah). Khabata dhikruhu means his mention became hidden (khafiya). So his saying akhbata means he entered the khabt, just as it is said of one who reaches Najd: anjada, and of one who reaches Tihamah: atrama. From this comes al-mukhbit among people, the one who has humbled himself to his Lord, i.e., who has become tranquil (ita'mann) in Him. The word ikhbat is construed with ila (to) and with al-lam (for). When we say akhbata fulan ila kadha, its meaning is that he became tranquil in it; and when we say akhbata lahu, its meaning is that he humbled himself before him (khasha'a lahu).

Having understood this, we say: His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds﴾, is a reference to all righteous deeds. His saying ﴿and humbled themselves﴾ is a reference to the fact that these deeds do not benefit in the Hereafter except together with the states of the heart. Then, if we interpret ikhbat as tranquility (tuma'nina), the meaning is that they worship Allah, and their hearts, at the performance of the acts of worship, are tranquil in the remembrance of Allah, free from turning toward anything other than Allah, exalted is He. Or it may be said: their hearts have become tranquil in the truthfulness of Allah regarding all that He promised them of reward and punishment. But if we interpret ikhbat as khushu', its meaning is that they perform the righteous deeds fearful and anxious lest they have performed them with deficiency and shortcoming. Then He made clear that whoever has these three attributes, they are the companions of Paradise, and for them there will be eternal abiding in Paradise.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of the two groups is like the blind and the deaf versus the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not then remember?﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the two groups, He mentioned for them a matching likeness. Then the scholars differed. It was said: it refers to those mentioned last among the believers and the disbelievers before it. Others said: rather, it refers back to His saying: ﴿Is one who is upon clear evidence from his Lord﴾ [Hud: 17]. Then, after it, He mentioned the disbelievers and described them as being unable to hear or to see, while the hearing and the seeing are those whom Allah described as being upon clear evidence from their Lord.

Know that the aspect of the comparison is that He, glorified is He, created the human being composed of a body and a soul. Just as the body has sight and hearing, so too the essence of the spirit has hearing and sight. And just as the body, when it is blind and deaf, remains bewildered, unable to be guided to any of its benefits, rather it becomes like one lost in the depths of darkness, not seeing any light by which to be guided, nor hearing any sound, so too the ignorant, misguided one who misguides others is blind and deaf of heart, and so he remains in the darkness of misguidance, bewildered and lost.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾, drawing attention to the fact that it is possible to treat this blindness and this deafness. And when the treatment is possible, the harm arising from the occurrence of this blindness and this deafness obliges the intelligent person to strive for that treatment to the extent possible.

Know that it has been the custom that when He, exalted is He, presents to the disbeliever various kinds of proofs, He follows them with narratives, so that their mention reinforces those proofs, as we have established this meaning in many places. In this surah He mentioned kinds of narratives.

THE FIRST STORY

The Story of Noah (peace be upon him)

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people: "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner, that you not worship except Allah. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a painful day."﴾

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people: "Indeed, I am to you a clear warner, that you not worship except Allah. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a painful day."﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, began mentioning this story in Surah Yunus, and He has repeated it in this surah as well, because of the additional benefits and wondrous wisdoms it contains. There are two issues here:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i recited "anni" (أنِّي) with a fatha on the hamza, and the meaning is: We sent Noah with (the message) that "I am to you a clear warner," meaning We sent him while accompanied by this speech, which is his saying, "I am to you a clear warner." When the preposition bi (the letter ba', meaning "with") attached to it, it was given a fatha, just as it is given a fatha in kana (in the phrase "kana..."). As for the rest of the readers, they recited ﴿inni﴾ with a kasra, according to the meaning: he said, ﴿Indeed, I am to you a clear warner﴾.

The second issue: Some said: what is meant by "warner" (nadhir) is that he threatens the disobedient with punishment, and by "clear" (mubin) is that he makes clear what Allah has prepared for the obedient of reward. The more appropriate meaning is that he is a warner to the disobedient of punishment, and that he is "clear" in the sense that he made that warning in the most perfect manner and the most powerful, most manifest clarity. Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear that this warning occurred in the prohibition of worshipping other than Allah and in the command to worship Allah; because His saying, ﴿that you not worship except Allah﴾ is an exception from a negation, which necessitates the negation of what is excluded.

Know that the construction of the verse is as if He, exalted is He, said: And We certainly sent Noah to his people with this speech, which is His saying, ﴿Indeed, I am to you a clear warner﴾.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿that you not worship except Allah﴾. So His saying, ﴿that you not worship except Allah﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying, ﴿Indeed, I am to you a warner﴾. Then He emphasized that with His saying, ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a painful day﴾. The meaning is that, since the great pain occurs on that day, that pain is attributed to the day, like the saying of people: "Your day is fasting, and your night is standing."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 27:

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the chiefs (al-mala') among those of his people who disbelieved said, "We see you only as a human being like us, and we see none following you except those who are the lowest among us, hasty in judgment. And we see no virtue for you over us. Rather, we think you are liars."﴾**

Know that when He, exalted is He, related about Noah, peace be upon him, that he invited his people to worship God, exalted is He, He related about them that they attacked his prophethood with three kinds of doubts.

The first doubt: he is a human being like them, and the difference that exists between individual human beings cannot reach the point where one of them becomes someone whose obedience is obligatory for all the worlds.

The second doubt: that only the lowly people of the community followed him, such as weavers and people of base trades. They said: "If you were truthful, the shrewd among the people and their nobles would have followed you." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿Shall we believe you, when the lowest have followed you?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 111].

The third doubt: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And we see no virtue for you over us.﴾ The meaning is: we see no virtue for you over us, neither in intellect, nor in managing immediate interests, nor in strength of argument. So if we do not witness your superiority over us in any of these apparent conditions, how can we acknowledge your superiority over us in the highest ranks and loftiest stations? This is the essence of the discussion in establishing these doubts.

Know that the first doubt befits only the Barahima (Brahmins), who deny the prophethood of human beings absolutely. As for the remaining two doubts, they can be held by one who affirms the prophethood of the other prophets. In the wording of the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** al-mala' are the nobles. Concerning its derivation there are several views:

The first: it is derived from their saying: *maliʾa bi-kadha* (he is full of such-and-such) when he fills it completely, and *qad mulʾiʾu bil-amr* (they have been filled with the matter). The reason this term is applied to them is that they are filled with the ordering of important affairs and excel in managing them.

The second: they are described thus because they *yatamālaʾūn* (act in concert), i.e., they support one another against him.

The third: they are described thus because they fill hearts with awe and gatherings with dignity.

The fourth: they are described thus because they fill minds with sound reasoning and correct opinions.

Then God, exalted is He, related their first doubt, which is their saying: ﴿We see you only as a human being like us.﴾ This is similar to what God, exalted is He, related about some Arabs who said: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am: 8]. This is ignorance, because it is the right of the Messenger to address the community with proof, evidence, clarity and argument, not with appearance and physical form. Indeed, we say: if God had sent an angel to human beings, the doubt against his messengership would be stronger, because it would occur to the mind that the miracles that appeared might have been produced by that angel himself, owing to his more perfect power and greater ability. For this reason, God has sent no messenger to human beings except from among human beings.

[page 170]

Then He related the second doubt, which is their saying: ﴿and we see none following you except those who are the lowest among us, hasty in judgment.﴾ What is meant by it is the paucity of their wealth, the paucity of their standing, and the baseness of their crafts and trades. This too is ignorance, because elevation in religion is not by lineage, wealth, or lofty positions. Rather, poverty is easier for religion than riches. Indeed, we say: the prophets were sent only to abandon this world and turn toward the Hereafter, so how can scarcity of wealth in this world be made a criticism of prophethood and messengership?

Then God, exalted is He, related the third doubt, which is their saying: ﴿And we see no virtue for you over us.﴾ This too is ignorance, because the virtue that is considered by God is only through knowledge and action. So how could they have gained access to the inner states of creation until they knew the negation of this virtue? Then, after mentioning these doubts to Noah, peace be upon him, and to those who followed him, they said: ﴿Rather, we think you are liars.﴾ In this there are two views:

The first: this is an address to Noah and to his people, and what is meant by it is the denial of Noah's claim to messengership.

The second: this is an address to the lowly ones, so they attributed to them that they lied in believing in him and following him.

**The second issue:** al-Wahidi said: *al-arhal* (the lowest) is the plural of *radhl*, which is the basest of everything in its appearance and conditions, and a man who is *radhl* in clothing and deed. *Al-aradhil* is the plural of *al-arhal*, like their saying *akabir mujrimiha* (the greatest of its criminals), and His saying, peace be upon him: "*Ahasinukum akhlaqan*" ("the best of you in character"). According to this, *al-aradhil* is a plural of a plural. Some have said: the original form of it is to say: *huwa arhal min kadha* (he is more base than such-and-such), then it became common until they said *huwa al-arhal* (he is the lowest), so the *alif* and *lam* became a substitute for the annexed genitive construction. As for His saying: ﴿hasty in judgment (badiya al-ra'y)﴾: *al-badi* is the apparent, from your saying: *bada al-shay'* when a thing appeared, and from it one says *badiya* (a desert dweller) because of their appearance and exposure to the viewer. They differed concerning *badiya al-ra'y* and mentioned several views concerning it:

The first: they followed you outwardly, while inwardly they were otherwise.

The second: it may be that what is meant is that they followed you at the very beginning of the emergence of the opinion, and they did not take precaution in that opinion, nor did they give it its due of correct thought and complete reflection.

The third: when they described the people with baseness, they said: their being thus is an evident matter to everyone who sees them. The *ra'y* in this sense is from *ra'y al-ayn* (seeing with the eye), not from *ra'y al-qalb* (opinion of the heart). This interpretation is reinforced by what is related from Mujahid, that he used to recite: "*illa al-ladhina hum arazilana badiya al-ra'y al-ayn*" ("except those who are our lowest, hasty in the judgment of the eye").

**The third issue:** Abu 'Amr and Nusayr, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, read *badi'* with a *hamza*, and the others read it with *ya'* without *hamza*. Whoever reads *badi'* with *hamza*, the meaning is the first of the opinion and its beginning. Whoever reads with *ya'* without *hamza* it is from *bada yabdu*, i.e., appeared. And *badiya* is in the accusative as a verbal noun (*masdar*), like your saying: *darabtu awwala al-darb* (I struck the first of the striking).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 28–30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my people, tell me, if I should be upon clear evidence from my Lord and He has given me mercy from Himself, but it has been obscured from you, should we compel you to accept it while you are averse to it?﴾

In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when Exalted God related the doubts of those who denied the prophethood of Noah, peace be upon him, He then related what would serve as a reply to those doubts.

The first doubt was their saying: ﴿You are only a human being like us﴾. Noah said: The sharing of humanity does not prevent the occurrence of distinction in the attribute of prophethood and messengership. Then he mentioned the path that proves its possibility, saying: ﴿Tell me, if I should be upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾, from knowledge of the essence of God and His attributes, and what is necessary, impossible and permissible for Him. Then Exalted God has given me mercy from Himself. By that mercy is meant either prophethood, or the miracle that indicates prophethood. ﴿But it has been obscured from you﴾, that is, it has become a doubtful and ambiguous matter in your minds. So am I able to make you reach its knowledge, whether you wish or refuse? What is meant is that I am absolutely unable to do that. Qatadah said: By God, if the Prophet of God could have compelled it, he would have compelled it, but he was not able to do so. The sum of the discourse is that when they said: ﴿And we do not see that you have any merit over us﴾, Noah, peace be upon him, stated that this is because the proof has been obscured from you and has become confused. But if you were to abandon obstinacy and contentiousness and look into the evidence, the intended meaning would become apparent, and it would be clear that God Exalted has given me a great favour over you.

The second issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿fa-ʿummiyat ʿalaykum﴾ with a damma on the ʿayn and a shadda on the mim, in the passive form, meaning "was made obscure" and "was made to appear dubious". The rest read it with a fatha on the ʿayn and a light mim, meaning "became confused and ambiguous".

Know that when a thing remains wholly unknown, it resembles something concealed (muʿammā, a riddle), because knowledge is the light of the inner insight and sight is the light of the outer vision, so it is fitting to use each of them metaphorically for the other. The verification of this is that evidence (bayyina) is described by sight, as He, Exalted, says: ﴿And when Our signs came to them as perceptible (mubṣira)﴾ [al-Naml: 13], and likewise it is described by blindness, as He, Exalted, says: ﴿So the reports became obscure to them (fa-ʿamiyat ʿalayhimu al-anbāʾ)﴾ [al-Qasas: 66], and He said in this verse: ﴿fa-ʿummiyat ʿalaykum﴾.

The third issue: In ﴿anulzimukumuha﴾ there are three hidden pronouns: the pronoun of the speaker, the pronoun of the absent party, and the pronoun of the addressee. Al-Farra' permitted the sukūn (quiescence) of the first mim, and it is related from Abu ʿAmr. He said: This is because the vowels followed one another, so the mim was made quiescent, while it is also in the nominative case and preceded by a kasra, and the vowel after it is a heavy damma. Al-Zajjaj said: All the Basran grammarians do not permit making the case-ending letter quiescent except in cases of poetic necessity, and what is related from Abu ʿAmr, al-Farra' did not report it accurately from him. It is related from Sibawayh that he used to lighten the vowel and make it brief (yakhtalisuhā), and this is the correct view. Quiescence is permitted only in poetry, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Today I drink, not one who is held to account (fa-al-yawma ushrab ghayra mustahqibin)

The verification of this is that evidence (bayyina) is described by sight, as He, Exalted, says: ﴿And when Our signs came to them as perceptible (mubṣira)﴾ [al-Naml: 13], and likewise it is described by blindness, as He, Exalted, says: ﴿So the reports became obscure to them (fa-ʿamiyat ʿalayhimu al-anbāʾ)﴾ [al-Qasas: 66], and He said in this verse: ﴿fa-ʿummiyat ʿalaykum﴾.

The third issue: In ﴿anulzimukumuha﴾ there are three hidden pronouns: the pronoun of the speaker, the pronoun of the absent party, and the pronoun of the addressee. Al-Farra' permitted the sukūn (quiescence) of the first mim, and it is related from Abu ʿAmr. He said: This is because the vowels followed one another, so the mim was made quiescent, while it is also in the nominative case and preceded by a kasra, and the vowel after it is a heavy damma. Al-Zajjaj said: All the Basran grammarians do not permit making the case-ending letter quiescent except in cases of poetic necessity, and what is related from Abu ʿAmr, al-Farra' did not report it accurately from him. It is related from Sibawayh that he used to lighten the vowel and make it brief (yakhtalisuhā), and this is the correct view. Quiescence is permitted only in poetry, like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Today I drink, not one who is held to account (fa-al-yawma ushrab ghayra mustahqibin)

[Page 172]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, I do not ask you for wealth in return for it. My reward is only from Allah. And I will not drive away those who have believed; indeed, they are going to meet their Lord. But I see you as a people who are ignorant.﴾ ﴿And O my people, who would protect me from Allah if I drove them away? Will you not then be mindful?﴾ ﴿And I do not tell you that I have the treasuries of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say that I am an angel, nor do I say about those whom your eyes look down upon that Allah will never give them any good. Allah knows best what is within their souls. Indeed, if I did so, I would be among the wrongdoers.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that this is the answer to the second doubt, which is their saying: "None follow you except the lowest of the people." The explanation of this answer has several aspects.

The first aspect: He (peace be upon him) said: "I do not seek any wealth from you for conveying the message of the Call, so that the situation would vary according to whether the one who responds is poor or rich. My reward for this arduous obedience is only from the Lord of the worlds." If this is the case, then whether they are poor or rich makes no difference in this matter.

The second aspect: It is as if he (peace be upon him) said to them: "When you looked at the outward appearances of affairs, you found me to be poor, and you thought that I had taken up this craft only to use it as a means of seizing your wealth. This assumption of yours is an error. I do not ask you for any reward for conveying the message; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds. So do not deprive yourselves of the happiness of the religion because of this corrupt assumption."

The third aspect in explaining this answer is that they said: ﴿We see you only as a human like ourselves﴾ up to His saying: ﴿nor do we see in you any merit over us﴾. So he (peace be upon him) explained that Allah had given him many kinds of favor that make him superior to them. For this reason, he did not strive in pursuit of this world, but strove in pursuit of the religion. Turning away from this world is among the foremost virtues by the consensus of all. So perhaps the purpose is to establish the attainment of virtue from this aspect.

As for His saying: ﴿Nor am I one who drives away those who have believed﴾, this is like evidence that the people had asked him to drive them away in order to elevate themselves above sharing with those poor people. Ibn Jurayj narrated that they said: "If you wish, O Noah, that we follow you, then drive them away, for we do not accept sharing with them." So he (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Nor am I one who drives away those who have believed.﴾ And His saying, Exalted is He, quoting them: ﴿We do not see those who follow you except the ones who are the lowest among us, at first glance﴾ is like evidence that they asked him to drive them away, because it indicates that they used to say: "If the nobles of the people followed you, we would agree with you." Then He, Exalted is He, related that he did not drive them away. In explaining what necessitates refraining from this driving away, He mentioned several matters:

The first: that they are going to meet their Lord. This statement admits several meanings:

Among them: that they (the disbelievers) said: "They are hypocrites in what they show, so do not be deceived by them." He answered that this matter will be revealed at the meeting with their Lord in the Hereafter.

Among them: that he made it a cause for refraining from driving them away, and he meant that they are going to meet what their Lord has promised them. If I drove them away, they would dispute with me in the Hereafter.

Among them: that by this matter he alerted that we will be gathered together in the Hereafter, and I would then be punished for driving them away, and I would find no one to help me.

Then he explained that they base their matter on ignorance of the outcomes and on being deceived by appearances, so he said: ﴿But I see you as a people who are ignorant.﴾

Then he said after this: ﴿And O my people, who would protect me from Allah if I drove them away? Will you not then be mindful?﴾ The meaning is that reason and the Law agree that it is necessary to honor the believer who is righteous and pious, and to humiliate the sinful disbeliever. So if you reversed the story, inverted the matter, brought near the disbelieving sinner as a sign of honor, and drove away the pious believer as a sign of humiliation, you would be acting contrary to the command of Allah, Exalted is He, and against His ruling, and in this ruling you would be opposing what Allah, Exalted is He, has commanded regarding giving reward to the righteous and punishment to the wrongdoers. In that case, I would become deserving of a great punishment. So who is it that would help me against Allah, Exalted is He, and who would deliver me from the punishment of Allah? Will you not then be mindful, so that you would know that this is not valid?

Then he confirmed this explanation with a third aspect, so he said: ﴿And I do not tell you that I have the treasuries of Allah.﴾ That is: just as I do not ask you for anything, likewise I do not claim that I possess wealth, nor do I have any desire for wealth, neither to take it nor to give it. Nor do I know the unseen so that I could reach through it what I want for myself or for my followers. Nor do I say, "I am an angel," so that I would exalt myself over you by that. Rather, my way is humility and modesty. Whoever has this as his condition and way does not disdain mixing with the poor and the needy, and does not seek the company of rulers and sultans. His concern is the pursuit of the religion, and his conduct is mixing with the humble and the submissive. Since my way requires mixing with the poor, how do you make that a fault for me?

Then he confirmed this explanation with a fourth way, so he said: ﴿Nor do I say about those whom your eyes look down upon that Allah will never give them any good. Allah knows best what is within their souls.﴾ This is like an indication that they used to attribute hypocrisy to his followers because of their poverty and humiliation. So he said: "I do not say that, because it belongs to the matter of the unseen, and the unseen is known only to Allah. Perhaps their inner state is like their outer state, and Allah will grant them the kingdom of the Hereafter. Then I would be lying in what I reported. If I did that, I would be among the wrongdoers toward myself and toward them, in describing them as having no good, while Allah, Exalted is He, has given them good in the Hereafter."

The second issue: Some people used this verse as evidence for the superiority of the angels over the prophets. They said: when a person says, "I do not claim such and such," this is only appropriate if that thing is more noble than the state of that speaker. Since the one who said this statement was Noah (peace be upon him), it must be that the rank of the angels is higher and more noble than the ranks of the prophets. Then they said: And how could it not be so, when the angels have persisted in worshiping Allah, Exalted is He, throughout the world since they were created until the Hour arrives? The complete explanation is that the true spiritual virtues are only three things:

The first of them: absolute self-sufficiency. It is the custom in this world that whoever possesses much wealth is described as rich. So His saying: ﴿And I do not tell you that I have the treasuries of Allah﴾ is an indication that I do not claim absolute self-sufficiency.

The second of them: complete knowledge, and to this refers His saying: ﴿Nor do I know the unseen.﴾

The third of them: complete and perfect power. It has been established in the common understanding that the most perfect of created beings in power and strength are the angels, and to this refers His saying: ﴿Nor do I say that I am an angel.﴾ The purpose of mentioning these three matters is to show that what I possess of these three ranks is only what befits human power and human capacity. As for absolute perfection, I do not claim it. If this is the case, it becomes clear that His saying: ﴿Nor do I say that I am an angel﴾ indicates that they are more perfect than humans. Also, it is possible to take this statement as an answer to the doubt they raised. They criticized his followers for their poverty, so he said: ﴿And I do not tell you that I have the treasuries of Allah﴾ so that I could make them rich. They also criticized them by saying they were hypocrites, so he said: ﴿Nor do I know the unseen﴾ so that I could know the reality of their inner states; rather, I judge matters by outward appearances. They also criticized them by saying that they might commit actions not as they should be, so he said: ﴿Nor do I say that I am an angel﴾ so that I would be free from all sensual desires and psychological impulses.

The third issue: Some people used this verse as evidence that the prophets may commit sin. They said: this verse indicates that driving away the believers in order to seek the pleasure of the disbelievers is among the roots of disobedience. Then Muhammad (ﷺ) drove away the poor believers in order to seek the pleasure of the disbelievers, to the point that Allah, Exalted is He, rebuked him in His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face﴾ [al-An'am: 52].

[Page 174]

This indicates that Muhammad (ﷺ) undertook a sin.
The answer: The driving away mentioned in this verse is to be understood as absolute driving away in a permanent sense, while the driving away mentioned in the event concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) was a reduction for specific times, for the sake of preserving benefits.

The fourth issue: al-Jubba'i (a Mu'tazili theologian) argued that intercession before Allah to ward off punishment is not permissible, using the saying of Noah (peace be upon him): ﴿who would protect me from Allah if I drove them away?﴾ Its meaning is: if this driving away were forbidden, then who would protect me from Allah? That is, who would deliver me from His punishment? And if intercession were permissible, it would be permissible for Noah (peace be upon him) as well, and then his statement ﴿who would protect me from Allah﴾ would be invalid. Know that this argument resembles their argument on this issue by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], up to His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48]. The answer given there is the answer to this statement.
