Then Muhammad (ﷺ) drove away the poor believers in order to seek the pleasure of the disbelievers, to the point that Allah, Exalted is He, rebuked him in His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face﴾ [al-An'am: 52].

[Page 174]

This indicates that Muhammad (ﷺ) undertook a sin.
The answer: The driving away mentioned in this verse is to be understood as absolute driving away in a permanent sense, while the driving away mentioned in the event concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) was a reduction for specific times, for the sake of preserving benefits.

The fourth issue: al-Jubba'i (a Mu'tazili theologian) argued that intercession before Allah to ward off punishment is not permissible, using the saying of Noah (peace be upon him): ﴿who would protect me from Allah if I drove them away?﴾ Its meaning is: if this driving away were forbidden, then who would protect me from Allah? That is, who would deliver me from His punishment? And if intercession were permissible, it would be permissible for Noah (peace be upon him) as well, and then his statement ﴿who would protect me from Allah﴾ would be invalid. Know that this argument resembles their argument on this issue by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48], up to His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48]. The answer given there is the answer to this statement.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 34:**

The Almighty said: ﴿They said, "O Noah, you have disputed with us and multiplied our disputation. So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿He said, "Only Allah will bring it to you, if He wills, and you will not escape."﴾ ﴿And my counsel will not benefit you, if I wished to advise you, if Allah intends to lead you astray. He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned."﴾

On this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** When the disbelievers raised that doubt and Noah, peace be upon him, answered it with correct and fitting replies, the disbelievers raised two statements against Noah:

The first: they described him with excessive disputation, saying, "O Noah, you have disputed with us and multiplied our disputation." This shows that he, peace be upon him, had multiplied the debate with them. That debate was only about establishing monotheism (tawhid), prophethood, and the Return (ma'ad). This shows that argument in establishing proofs and removing doubts is the craft of the prophets, and that imitation (taqlid), ignorance, and persistence in falsehood are the craft of the disbelievers.

The second: they asked to hasten the punishment he had threatened them with, saying, ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful.﴾ Then he, peace be upon him, answered this with a correct reply, saying, ﴿Only Allah will bring it to you, if He wills, and you will not escape.﴾ The meaning is that the sending down of punishment is not up to me; it is the creation of Allah the Exalted. He does it if He wills, as He wills. When He intends to send down punishment, no one can make Him helpless, that is, no one can prevent Him from it. The one who is "unable to be overcome" (mu'jiz) is the one who does what he wants while the desire of another cannot be carried out, so he is described as having "made him helpless." Thus His saying, ﴿and you will not escape﴾ means you have no way to do what He wills. So what Allah the Exalted wills of punishment cannot be prevented from Him if He intends to send it down upon you. It has been said that its meaning is: "and you will not be able to prevent it," and it has been said: "and you will not be preserved," and it has been said: "and you will not outrun Him to escape." These statements are close in meaning.

Know that when Noah, peace be upon him, had answered their doubts, he concluded the speech with a decisive conclusion, saying, ﴿And my counsel will not benefit you, if I wished to advise you﴾, that is: if Allah intends to lead you astray, then my counsel will by no means benefit you. Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from this verse that Allah the Exalted may indeed will disbelief from the servant, and that when He wills it from him, the emergence of faith from him is impossible. They said: Noah, peace be upon him, said, ﴿And my counsel will not benefit you, if I wished to advise you, if Allah intends to lead you astray﴾, and the implication is: "My counsel will not benefit you if Allah intends to lead you astray and mislead you." This is clear in support of our position.

As for the Mu'tazila, they said: the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that if Allah the Exalted wills to lead the people astray, they will not benefit from the counsel of the Messenger. This is granted, for we know that if Allah the Exalted wills to lead a servant astray, the counsel of advisers will not benefit him. But why do you say that He, the Exalted, intended this misguidance? The dispute has arisen only about this. Rather, we say: Noah, peace be upon him, mentioned this statement only to indicate that He, the Exalted, did not lead them astray, but rather delegated the choice to them. Its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: he, peace be upon him, made clear that if He, the Exalted, willed to lead them astray, there would remain no benefit in counsel. If there were no benefit in it, He would not have commanded him to advise the disbelievers. The Muslims are unanimous that he, peace be upon him, was commanded to call the disbelievers and advise them. So we know that this counsel is not devoid of benefit. And when it is not devoid of benefit, it is necessarily established that He, the Exalted, did not lead them astray. Thus this becomes a proof for us from this aspect.

The second: if the ruling were established against them that Allah the Exalted had led them astray, this would become an excuse for them for not bringing faith, and Noah would be cut off in his debate with them. This is because they would say to him: "You have conceded that Allah led us astray, so there remains no benefit in your counsel or in our earnestness and striving. If you claim that Allah the Exalted has led us astray, you have made us excused, so it is not incumbent upon us to accept this call." Thus it is established that if the matter were as the opponent says, this would become a proof for the disbelievers against Noah, peace be upon him. And it is known that Noah, peace be upon him, could not have said a statement by which he would be silenced, rendered obligated, and unable to establish the proof of Allah the Exalted. Thus it is established by what we have mentioned that this verse does not support the statement of the Mujabbira (the determinists, those who hold that human beings are compelled). Then they (the Mu'tazila) mentioned some interpretations:

The first: those disbelievers were determinists, and they used to say that their disbelief was by the will of Allah the Exalted. At this point Noah, peace be upon him, said: his counsel will not benefit them, if the matter is as they claimed. An example of this is when a man punishes his son for his sin, and the son says, "I cannot do other than what I am doing." The father says, "Then my counsel and my rebuke will not benefit you." It is not meant that he confirms what the son said, but rather that he is denying it.

The second: al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿He leads you astray﴾ is: He punishes you. The meaning is: my counsel will not benefit you today when the punishment has descended upon you, and you believe at that time, because faith is not accepted when punishment descends. My counsel benefits you only if you believe before witnessing the punishment.

The third: al-Jubba'i said: error (ghiwaya) is failure in seeking, as evidenced by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So they will meet error (ghayy)﴾ [Maryam: 59], that is, a failure in the good of the Hereafter. The poet said:

*"Whoever goes astray will not lack one who blames him for his error."*

The fourth: when a person persists in disbelief and persists in it, Allah the Exalted withholds from him the favors (lutf) and leaves him to himself. This resembles the situation where He wills to lead him astray, and for this reason it is good to say that Allah the Exalted led him astray. This is the sum of the Mu'tazila's statements on this matter. The answer to such statements we have mentioned many times and in various ways, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

**The second issue:** His saying, ﴿And my counsel will not benefit you, if I wished to advise you, if Allah intends to lead you astray﴾ is a conditional consequence (jaza') dependent on a condition, followed by another condition. This requires that the condition placed later in wording be prior in existence. This is because when a man says to his wife, "You are divorced if you enter the house," the understanding is that this divorce is a consequence of that entry. When he then mentions another condition after it, such as saying, "if you eat the bread," the meaning is that the attachment of that consequence to the first condition is conditional upon the fulfillment of this second condition, and the condition is prior to the conditioned in existence. So, according to this, if the second condition is fulfilled, the consequence becomes attached to the first condition. But if the condition mentioned second is not fulfilled, the consequence is not attached to the first condition. This is the verification of this construction. For this reason the jurists (fuqaha') said: the condition placed later in wording is prior in meaning, and the condition placed earlier in wording is later in meaning.

Know that when Noah, peace be upon him, had established these meanings, he said, ﴿He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned﴾, and this is the utmost of warning. That is: He is your God who created you and nurtured you, and He has power over your essences and your attributes before death, at death, and after death; your return is to Him. This conveys the utmost degree of warning.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 35–36:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it." Say: "If I have invented it, then upon me is my crime, and I am innocent of what you commit."﴾

Know that the meaning of "iftarahu" (he invented it) is that he fabricated it and made it up, and brought it from his own self. The pronoun "ha" (it) refers to the revelation that he conveyed to them. As for His saying, ﴿upon me is my crime﴾: the "ijram" (crime) is the seeking out and acquisition of forbidden things. This is an instance of the omission of a modifier (hadhf al-mudaf), since the meaning is: "upon me is the punishment of my crime." There is another omission in the verse, namely that the meaning is: "If I have invented it, then upon me is the punishment of my offence; and if I am truthful and you have denied me, then upon you is the punishment for that denial." However, He omitted this remainder because the context indicates it, as in His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during periods of the night﴾ [Az-Zumar: 9], where He did not mention the remainder. As for His saying, ﴿and I am innocent of what you commit﴾, it means: I am innocent of the punishment for your crime. Most commentators hold that this is part of Noah's speech, peace be upon him, and this verse occurs in the story of Muhammad ﷺ in the course of relating the account of Noah. Their view is very far-fetched. Also, His saying, ﴿If I have invented it, then upon me is my crime﴾ does not indicate that he was in doubt; rather it is a statement made in a manner of denial when despairing of acceptance.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it was revealed to Noah: "None of your people will believe except those who have already believed, so do not be distressed by what they have been doing."﴾

In this are several issues:

First issue: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: When this came from Allah the Exalted, he invoked against his people and said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ [Nuh: 26]. His saying, ﴿so do not be distressed﴾ means: do not grieve. Abu Zayd said: "ibta'sa al-rajulu" means the man was afflicted with something he disliked. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"Whatever Allah apportions, accept it without being distressed by it, and sit honoured, with a comfortable mind."

Meaning: not grieving and not disliking.

Second issue: Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) argued from this verse for the soundness of their view on qada' (divine decree) and qadar (predestination). They said: He, the Exalted, informed about His people that they would not believe after that. So if their faith were to occur, it would either be with this report remaining true and this knowledge remaining knowledge, or with this report turning into falsehood and this knowledge turning into ignorance. The first is evidently invalid, because the existence of faith together with the report about non-belief being true, and with the knowledge of non-belief being present at the time faith exists, is a combination of two contradictories. The second is also invalid, because the report of Allah turning into a lie and the knowledge of Allah turning into ignorance is impossible. Since the occurrence of faith from them must be in one of these two forms, and each of them has been established as impossible, the occurrence of faith from them is impossible, even though they were commanded to it. Moreover, the people were commanded to believe, and part of faith is affirming the truth of all that Allah the Exalted has reported. Among it is His saying: ﴿that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾. It follows that they were commanded to believe that they would never believe at all, and that is the imposition of a combination of two contradictories. The explanation of this argument has been discussed in this book many times and in various ways.

Third issue: The Mu'tazila differed as to whether it is permissible for Allah the Exalted to send down the punishment of annihilation upon a people for whom it was known that among them there would be someone who believes, or whose offspring would include someone who believes. Some said that it is not permissible. They argued from what Allah the Exalted related of Noah, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ ﴿Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except a wicked disbeliever﴾ [Nuh: 26–27]. This indicates that the sending down of the punishment of annihilation upon them was only good from Him, the Exalted, because He knew that none of them would believe, nor would any of their offspring believe. The judge (al-Qadi) said, and many of our scholars said: such an act from Allah the Exalted is permissible, even if some of them would believe. As for Noah's saying, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ [Nuh: 26], it indicates that he only asked this because it was known that they would mislead His servants and would not beget except a wicked disbeliever. This indicates that the ruling was based on the combination of these two causes together. Also, there is no evidence in it that, had these two not occurred, the destruction could not have been sent down. The closer view is that Noah, peace be upon him, out of his intense love for their faith, had asked his Lord to spare them; so He informed him that none of them would believe, in order that the love which had settled in his heart would depart from it. That is why He said afterwards: ﴿so do not be distressed by what they have been doing﴾, meaning: do not grieve over that, nor be troubled, and do not think that there is humiliation in it; for the religion is mighty, even if the number of those who hold to it is small, and falsehood is abased, even if the number of those who uphold it is large.

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿And make the ark under Our eyes and by Our inspiration, and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged. Indeed, they are to be drowned.﴾

Know that His statement, ﴿Indeed, none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ (11:36), indicates that Noah (peace be upon him) was informed that He would punish and destroy them. He could have punished them in various ways, so God informed him that He would punish them by this kind, which is drowning. Since the means by which deliverance from drowning is achieved is the construction of a ship, God commanded him to prepare and build the ship. God inspired him to make it in the shape of the breast of a bird (ju'ju' al-ta'ir).

If it is asked: is God's statement, ﴿Make the ark﴾, a command of obligation (amr ijab) or a command of permission (amr ibaha)?

We say: the more apparent view is that it is a command of obligation, because there is no way for him to preserve his own life and the lives of others from destruction except by this means, and preserving the self from destruction is obligatory, and whatever an obligation cannot be fulfilled without is itself obligatory. It is possible, however, that this command was not one of obligation but of permission, and it is like a person taking a house for himself to dwell in and live in.

As for His statement, ﴿under Our eyes﴾, it cannot be taken in its apparent sense, for several reasons:

First: it would imply that God has many eyes. This contradicts the apparent meaning of His statement, ﴿so that you may be made under My eye﴾ (20:39).

Second: it would imply that Noah makes that ark by means of those eyes, as one says, "I cut with the knife" and "I wrote with the pen." It is known that this is false.

Third: it has been established by definitive rational proofs that God is exalted above having organs, limbs, parts, and components. Therefore, it is necessary to resort to ta'wil (figurative interpretation). This has several aspects:

The first: the meaning of ﴿under Our eyes﴾ is: under the eye of the angel who was instructing him how to make the ship. It is said, "So-and-so is an eye upon so-and-so," meaning he has been appointed over him to watch closely over his affairs and his eye is never turned away from him.

The second: whoever has great care for something places his eye upon it. Since placing the eye upon a thing is a cause of intensifying caution and care, the eye was used as a kinayah (metonymy) for caution. For this reason the exegetes said: its meaning is "by Our protecting you with the protection of one who sees you and has the power to repel harm from you." The summary of the matter is that his undertaking the work of the ship is conditioned on two things:

One: that his enemies not prevent him from that work.

The second: that he knows how the ship should be assembled and constructed and how harm can be averted from it. His statement, ﴿and by Our inspiration﴾, points to the fact that God inspires him how the ship should be made so that the desired outcome is achieved.

* * *

As for His statement, ﴿and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged. Indeed, they are to be drowned﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: it means, "Do not ask Me to delay the punishment from them, for I have decided this judgment concerning them." When Noah (peace be upon him) knew this, he afterward supplicated against them and said: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dweller﴾ (71:26).

The second: ﴿do not address Me﴾ regarding hastening that punishment upon those who have wronged, for since I have decreed that this punishment descend at a specific time, hastening it is impossible.

The third: by "those who have wronged" is meant his wife and his son Kan'an.
