Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 38–39:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he was constructing the ship, and whenever a group of the chiefs of his people passed by him, they mocked him. He said, "If you mock us, then indeed we mock you just as you mock."﴾ ﴿"And you will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and upon whom will descend an enduring punishment."﴾

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he was constructing the ship﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: Regarding His saying: ﴿And he was constructing the ship﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: It is a narration of a past state; that is, at that time it was true of him that he was constructing the ship.

The second: The estimated meaning is: "And he began constructing the ship," and it is abbreviated to His saying: ﴿And he was constructing the ship﴾.

Page 179
The second issue: They mentioned many statements concerning the description of the ship:

The first of them: Noah, peace be upon him, made the ship over two years, and it was said: over four years. Its length was three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height in the sky thirty cubits. It was made of teak wood, and he made for it three decks. He carried in the lowest deck the wild beasts, the predatory animals and the creeping things; in the middle deck the animals and the cattle; and in the upper deck he sat, he and those who were with him, along with what they needed of provisions. And he carried with him the body of Adam, peace be upon him.

The second: Al-Hasan said: its length was one thousand two hundred cubits and its width six hundred cubits.

Know that such discussions do not please me, because they are matters for which there is absolutely no need to know, and no benefit is connected to knowing them at all, and delving into them is of the category of superfluities, especially with the certainty that there is nothing here that indicates the correct side. What we know is that it was of such spaciousness that it could contain the believers among his people and what they needed, and the pairs of every living creature; because this measure is mentioned in the Qur'an, whereas beyond that measure nothing is mentioned.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whenever a group of the chiefs of his people passed by him, they mocked him﴾, there are two interpretations of "al-mala'" (the chiefs/notables): it is said: a group; and it is said: a stratum of their nobles and elders. They differed concerning what they mocked him for, and there are several aspects:

The first of them: They used to say: "O Noah, you used to claim the messengership of God, Exalted, and after that you became a carpenter."

The second: They used to say to him: "If you were truthful in your claim, your God would make you independent of this arduous work."

The third: They had not seen a ship before that, and did not know how it could be used, so they were amazed at him and mocked him.

The fourth: That ship was large, and he was building it in a place very far from water, and they used to say: "There is no water here, and you cannot transport it to the great rivers and to the seas," so they counted that as folly and madness.

The fifth: When his period with the people lengthened, and he warned them of drowning, and they had witnessed nothing of that meaning, neither news nor trace, their assumption came to dominate that he was lying in that statement; so when he occupied himself with building the ship, they inevitably mocked him. All these aspects are possible.

Then, exalted is He, related of him that he used to say: ﴿If you mock us, then indeed we mock you just as you mock﴾, and in it there are aspects:

The first: The estimated meaning: "If you mock us at this moment, then we mock you with a mockery like your mockery when drowning befalls you in the world and disgrace in the Hereafter."

The second: "If you judge us to be ignorant regarding what we are doing, then we judge you to be ignorant regarding what you are upon of disbelief and exposing yourselves to the anger of God, Exalted, and His punishment; so you are more deserving of mockery than we are."

The third: "If you deem us foolish, then we deem you foolish, and your deeming us foolish is uglier and more severe; because you do not deem others foolish except out of ignorance of the reality of the matter and deception by outward appearance, as is the habit of children and the ignorant."

If it is said: Mockery is among the effects of sins, so how is that befitting for the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them?

We say: God, Exalted, named the retaliation "mockery," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And you will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him"﴾, that is: "And you will soon know who is more deserving of mockery and who has the better outcome." And in His saying: ﴿who will receive﴾ there are two aspects:

The first: That it be an interrogative in the sense of "which," as if it were said: "You will soon know which of us will receive a punishment," and according to this aspect, the position of "man" (who) is nominative, as the subject of the beginning.

The second: That it be in the sense of "alladhi" (the one who), and it is in the accusative position. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and upon whom will descend an enduring punishment﴾, that is: it is obligatory for him and will alight upon him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 38–39:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he was constructing the ship, and whenever a group of the chiefs of his people passed by him, they mocked him. He said, "If you mock us, then indeed we mock you just as you mock."﴾ ﴿"And you will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and upon whom will descend an enduring punishment."﴾

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he was constructing the ship﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: Regarding His saying: ﴿And he was constructing the ship﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: It is a narration of a past state; that is, at that time it was true of him that he was constructing the ship.

The second: The estimated meaning is: "And he began constructing the ship," and it is abbreviated to His saying: ﴿And he was constructing the ship﴾.

Page 179
The second issue: They mentioned many statements concerning the description of the ship:

The first of them: Noah, peace be upon him, made the ship over two years, and it was said: over four years. Its length was three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height in the sky thirty cubits. It was made of teak wood, and he made for it three decks. He carried in the lowest deck the wild beasts, the predatory animals and the creeping things; in the middle deck the animals and the cattle; and in the upper deck he sat, he and those who were with him, along with what they needed of provisions. And he carried with him the body of Adam, peace be upon him.

The second: Al-Hasan said: its length was one thousand two hundred cubits and its width six hundred cubits.

Know that such discussions do not please me, because they are matters for which there is absolutely no need to know, and no benefit is connected to knowing them at all, and delving into them is of the category of superfluities, especially with the certainty that there is nothing here that indicates the correct side. What we know is that it was of such spaciousness that it could contain the believers among his people and what they needed, and the pairs of every living creature; because this measure is mentioned in the Qur'an, whereas beyond that measure nothing is mentioned.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whenever a group of the chiefs of his people passed by him, they mocked him﴾, there are two interpretations of "al-mala'" (the chiefs/notables): it is said: a group; and it is said: a stratum of their nobles and elders. They differed concerning what they mocked him for, and there are several aspects:

The first of them: They used to say: "O Noah, you used to claim the messengership of God, Exalted, and after that you became a carpenter."

The second: They used to say to him: "If you were truthful in your claim, your God would make you independent of this arduous work."

The third: They had not seen a ship before that, and did not know how it could be used, so they were amazed at him and mocked him.

The fourth: That ship was large, and he was building it in a place very far from water, and they used to say: "There is no water here, and you cannot transport it to the great rivers and to the seas," so they counted that as folly and madness.

The fifth: When his period with the people lengthened, and he warned them of drowning, and they had witnessed nothing of that meaning, neither news nor trace, their assumption came to dominate that he was lying in that statement; so when he occupied himself with building the ship, they inevitably mocked him. All these aspects are possible.

Then, exalted is He, related of him that he used to say: ﴿If you mock us, then indeed we mock you just as you mock﴾, and in it there are aspects:

The first: The estimated meaning: "If you mock us at this moment, then we mock you with a mockery like your mockery when drowning befalls you in the world and disgrace in the Hereafter."

The second: "If you judge us to be ignorant regarding what we are doing, then we judge you to be ignorant regarding what you are upon of disbelief and exposing yourselves to the anger of God, Exalted, and His punishment; so you are more deserving of mockery than we are."

The third: "If you deem us foolish, then we deem you foolish, and your deeming us foolish is uglier and more severe; because you do not deem others foolish except out of ignorance of the reality of the matter and deception by outward appearance, as is the habit of children and the ignorant."

If it is said: Mockery is among the effects of sins, so how is that befitting for the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them?

We say: God, Exalted, named the retaliation "mockery," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And you will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him"﴾, that is: "And you will soon know who is more deserving of mockery and who has the better outcome." And in His saying: ﴿who will receive﴾ there are two aspects:

The first: That it be an interrogative in the sense of "which," as if it were said: "You will soon know which of us will receive a punishment," and according to this aspect, the position of "man" (who) is nominative, as the subject of the beginning.

The second: That it be in the sense of "alladhi" (the one who), and it is in the accusative position. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and upon whom will descend an enduring punishment﴾, that is: it is obligatory for him and will alight upon him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when Our command came and the oven gushed forth, We said: "Load therein of every kind two mates, and your family, except him against whom the word has already gone forth, and those who believe." And none believed with him except a few.﴾

Regarding the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: (ḥattā, "until") is the particle after which a statement begins; it is introduced upon the conditional and consequent clause, and it stands as the endpoint (ghāyah) of His saying: ﴿and he was making the ark﴾, meaning: he kept making it until the time of the appointed moment came.

The second issue: The word "command" in His saying, ﴿when Our command came﴾, may have two meanings:

The first: that He, exalted, makes clear that nothing comes to be except by the command of God, exalted, as He said: ﴿Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40]. So this is what is meant.

The second: that the "command" here means the punishment that was promised.

The third issue: Concerning the "oven" (tannūr) there are two opinions:

One of them: it is the oven in which bread is baked.

The second: it is other than that. As for the first, that it is the oven in which bread is baked, this is the view of a great group of exegetes, such as Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḥasan, and Mujāhid. Among these, they differed: some said it was the oven of Noah, peace be upon him; it was said it belonged to Adam; al-Ḥasan said: it was an oven of stone, and it belonged to Eve, until it passed to Noah, peace be upon him. They differed about its location. Al-Shaʿbi said it was in the vicinity of Kufa, and it is reported from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, that it was in the mosque of Kufa. He said: seventy prophets have prayed in it. It was also said: it was in Syria, at a place called ʿAyn Wardān, and this is the view of Muqātil. It was said: the oven gushed forth in India. It was also said that his wife used to bake in that oven, and she informed him of the water coming out of that oven, so he immediately busied himself with placing those things in the ship.

The second opinion: the "oven" does not mean an oven for bread. On this basis, there are several statements:

The first: the water burst forth from the surface of the earth, as He said: ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with pouring water, and caused the earth to burst forth with springs, and the waters met for a matter already decreed﴾ [al-Qamar: 11]. And the Arabs call the surface of the earth a "tannūr."

The second: the oven is the most noble place on earth and its highest location, and water was brought forth from that place so that this would be a miracle for him. Also the meaning is that when the water sprang from the high parts of the earth and from elevated places, they were likened in their height to ovens.

The third: ﴿and the oven gushed forth﴾ means the dawn rose; this is reported from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him.

The fourth: ﴿and the oven gushed forth﴾ may mean that the matter intensified, as one says: "the battle grew hot" (ḥamiya al-waṭīs). The meaning of the verse is: when you see the matter intensifying and the water increasing, save yourself and those with you by going to the ship.

If it is said: which of these statements is the most correct?

We say: the basic principle is to take speech in its literal sense, and the word tannūr is literally applied to the place where bread is baked, so it is necessary to apply the word to that. There is no impossibility in reason in saying that the water first sprang forth from a specific place, and that place was an oven.

If it is said: the "oven" is mentioned with the definite article (al-), and this is only used for a previously known, specific thing familiar to the listener, and there is no oven on earth of this description; therefore it must be taken to mean: when you see the water's springing intensify and the matter grow strong, save yourself and those with you.

We say: it is not far-fetched to say that this oven belonged to Noah, peace be upon him, either that it was the oven of Adam or Eve, or that it was an oven which God, exalted, designated for Noah, peace be upon him, and informed him: when you see the water boiling, know that the matter has happened. On this basis, there is no need to turn the speech away from its apparent meaning.

The fourth issue: The meaning of (fāra) is to gush out with force and intensity, by analogy with the boiling of a pot when the fire is strong. There is no doubt that the oven itself does not boil over; rather, the water boiled up from the oven. And what is related, that the boiling of the oven was a sign of the people's destruction, is not impossible, since this is a momentous event, and God, exalted, had promised the believers deliverance; so He must set for them a sign by which they would recognize the appointed time. Thus it is not far-fetched that this state was made a sign of the occurrence of this event.

* * *

The fifth issue: Al-Layth said: "tannūr" is a word common to every language, and its keeper is a tannār. Al-Azhari said: this shows that a noun may be non-Arabic, and then the Arabs arabicize it so it becomes Arabic. The evidence for this is that the original form is tannār, and "tannūr" is not known in Arabic speech before this. A parallel is what entered Arabic speech from foreign speech: dībāj, dīnār, sundus, and istabraq; when the Arabs spoke these words, they became Arabic.

Know that when the oven gushed forth, at that point God, exalted, commanded him to load three kinds of things into the ship.

The first: His saying: ﴿We said: "Load therein of every kind two mates"﴾. Al-Akhfash said: you say that "the two" (al-ithnān) are a pair (zawjān). God, exalted, said: ﴿And of everything We created two mates﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 49]. So the heaven is a mate, the earth is a mate, winter is a mate, summer is a mate, day is a mate, and night is a mate. And you say of a woman: she is a mate (zawj), and he is her mate. God, exalted, said: ﴿and created of it its mate﴾ [al-Nisa: 1], meaning the woman. And He said: ﴿and that He created the two mates, the male and the female﴾ [al-Najm: 45]. Thus it is established that one may be called a mate. Among what proves this is His saying: ﴿eight mates: of sheep two, and of goats two﴾ ﴿and of camels two, and of cattle two﴾.

Having understood this, we say: "two mates" is an expression for any two things, one of which is male and the other female. The meaning is: every two things that are of this kind, load two of them into the ship, one male and the other female. Therefore Hafs read ﴿min kullin﴾ with tanwīn, and they intended: load two mates from every thing, the male being a mate and the female being a mate. It cannot be said against this: two mates are only two; so what is the benefit of His saying ﴿two mates, two﴾? We say: this is like His saying: ﴿Do not take two gods, two﴾ [al-Nahl: 51], and His saying: ﴿one blast﴾ [al-Haqqah: 13]. As for the well-known reading, this question does not arise. They differed as to whether anything other than animals is included in His saying ﴿two mates, two﴾. We say: as for animals, they are included, since His saying ﴿of every kind two mates, two﴾ encompasses all animals. As for plants, the wording does not indicate them, but according to the context of the situation it is not far-fetched, because people need plants in all their kinds. It is related in narrations from Ibn Masʿud, may God be pleased with him, that he said: Noah, peace be upon him, could not carry the lion until fever was cast upon it; for Noah, peace be upon him, said: "My Lord, from where shall I feed the lion when I carry it?" God, exalted, said: "I shall keep it occupied from food." So God, exalted, sent fever upon it. Such sayings are better left aside; for the elephant's need for food is greater, and it has no fever.

The second: among the things which God commanded Noah, peace be upon him, to load into the ship:

صفحة ١٨٢

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and your family, except him against whom the word has already gone forth﴾. They said: they were seven: Noah, peace be upon him, and his three sons, namely Sam, Ham, and Japheth, and each of them had a wife; and it was also said: they were eight, these together with Noah's wife, peace be upon him.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿except him against whom the word has already gone forth﴾, the intended ones are his son and his wife, and they were disbelievers, against whom God, exalted, had decreed destruction.

If it is said: man is more noble than all animals; so what is the reason that the beginning was made with mention of the animals?

We say: man is rational, and by his reason he is as one compelled to avert the causes of destruction from himself, so there is no need to exhort him at length; unlike the striving to save the rest of the animals. For this reason the beginning was made with it.

Know that our companions argued with His saying: ﴿except him against whom the word has already gone forth﴾ to establish binding decree and necessary destiny. They said: because His saying ﴿the word has already gone forth against him﴾ indicates that everyone against whom the word has gone forth does not change from his state; it is like His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The happy one is he who is made happy in his mother's womb, and the wretched one is he who is made wretched in his mother's womb."

The third kind of those things is His saying: ﴿and those who believe﴾. They said: they were eighty. Muqatil said: in the region of Mosul there is a village called "the village of the Eighty"; it was so named because these people, when they came out of the ship, built it, and so it took this name. And they mentioned figures more and less than this, and that is something for which there is no way to knowledge; except that God, exalted, described them as few, in His saying: ﴿and none believed with him except a few﴾.

If it is said: since those who believed with him and entered the ship were a group, why was it not said "qalīlūn" (few, plural), as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, these are a small band, few﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 54]?

We say: both wordings are permissible, and the implied sense here is: "none believed with him except a small company (nafar qalīl)." As for what is related, that Iblis entered the ship, this is far-fetched; for he is of the jinn, and he is a fiery or airy body, and how would drowning affect him? Also, the Book of God does not indicate it, and no sound report has come concerning it; so the better course is to leave aside discussion of it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 41:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he said, "Embark therein; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾

As for His saying ﴿And he said﴾, meaning: Nuh (peace be upon him) said to his people: ﴿Embark﴾. Al-rukub (riding) is being raised above the back of a thing, and from it come riding an animal, riding a ship, and riding the sea. Anything that rises above something has ridden it; one says: "The debt rode him" (rakibahu al-dayn). Al-Layth said: The Arabs call one who boards a ship "rakib al-safinah" (rider of the ship). As for al-rukban and al-rakb, they are those who ride beasts and camels. Al-Wahidi said: The particle "fi" in His saying ﴿Embark therein﴾ cannot be connected to the verb of riding, because one says "rakibtu al-safinah" (I rode the ship) and one does not say "rakibtu fi al-safinah" (I rode in the ship). Rather, the proper reading is that the object of "embark" is omitted, and the sense is: "Embark upon the water in the ship." Also, it is possible that the benefit of this addition is that He commanded them to be inside the hull of the ship, not on its back; for had He said "ur-kabuha" (embark it), they would have imagined that He commanded them to be on the back of the ship.

Page 183
As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim read "majrāhā" with a fatha on the mim, and the others read it with a damma on the mim. They agreed that in "murṣāhā" the mim is with a damma. The author of al-Kashshaf said: Mujahid read "mujrīhā wa-mursīhā" in the form of the active participle, in the genitive case as two epithets of Allah, the Exalted. Al-Wahidi said: al-majra is a verbal noun like al-ijra' (causing to run), and similar to it is His saying: ﴿a blessed descent (munzalan mubarakan)﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 29] and ﴿cause me to enter a sound entrance and cause me to exit a sound exit﴾ [al-Isra': 80]. As for the one who reads "majrāhā" with a fatha on the mim, it is also a verbal noun like al-jary (running). The proponent of this reading argued with His saying: ﴿and it runs with them﴾ [Hud: 42]; had it been "mujrāhā" it would have been "wa-hiya tujarriihim". The argument of the one who reads with a damma on the mim is that "jarat bihim" and "ajratahum" are close in meaning; so when He says ﴿tajri bihim﴾ [Hud: 42] it is as if He said "tujarrihim". As for al-mursa, it too is a verbal noun like al-irsa'. One says: "rasa al-shay'u yarsu" when a thing becomes firm, and "arsahu ghayruhu" when another makes it firm. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and the mountains He set firm﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 32]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means, it runs in the name of Allah and by His power, and it anchors in the name of Allah and by His power. It was said: when he wished it to run with them he would say "in the name of Allah is its course", and it would run; and when he wished it to anchor he would say "in the name of Allah is its anchorage", and it would anchor.

The second issue: They mentioned several possibilities for the governing element (ʿamil al-iʿrab) of "in the name of Allah":

The first: "Embark, in the name of Allah."

The second: "Begin, in the name of Allah."

The third: "In the name of Allah is its running and its anchoring."

It was said: it set sail on the first day of Rajab, and it was said: on the tenth of Rajab; six months passed, and it came to rest on al-Judi on the tenth day of Muharram.

The third issue: The verse has two possibilities:

The first possibility: that the whole of His saying ﴿And he said, "Embark therein; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage"﴾ is one single statement, and the sense is: "And he said, 'Embark therein, in the name of its course and its anchorage,'" meaning that riding should be accompanied by this remembrance.

The second possibility: that they are two statements, and the sense is: Nuh (peace be upon him) commanded them to embark, then informed them that its course and its anchorage are nothing but by the name of Allah, His command and His power.

The first meaning indicates that a person should not begin any matter unless, at the time of beginning it, he is mindful of the name of Allah, the Exalted, with the sacred remembrances, so that by the blessing of that remembrance it becomes a cause for the completion of that aim.

The second meaning indicates that when he boarded the ship, he informed the people that the ship is not itself the cause of attaining salvation; rather, what is obligatory is to bind one's resolve and hang one's heart upon the grace of Allah, the Exalted. He informed them that He, the Exalted, is the One who causes the ship to run and anchor, so beware of relying upon the ship; rather, your reliance must be upon the grace of Allah, for He is the One who causes it to run and anchor. Thus, on the first reading Nuh (peace be upon him) at the time of boarding the ship was in the station of remembrance, and on the second reading he was in the station of reflection, disavowing might and power, setting aside the means, and his heart immersed in the light of the majesty of the Causer of causes.

Know that when a person reflects in seeking the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, through proof and argument, it is as if he has sat in the ship of contemplation and reflection, while the waves of darkness and misguidance have risen over those mountains and climbed to the summits of the peaks.

When the ship of thought and deliberation begins to move, there must be his reliance upon Allah, the Exalted, and his supplication to Allah, the Exalted,

Page 184
and it must be with the tongue of the heart and the gaze of the intellect. He says: "In the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage," until the ship of his thought reaches the shore of salvation and he is delivered from the waves of misguidance.
* * *
As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, there is a question concerning it: that time was the time of destruction and the manifestation of subjugation, so how is this remembrance fitting for it?
Its answer: Perhaps the people who boarded the ship believed about themselves that we were saved only by the blessing of our knowledge; so Allah, the Exalted, alerted them with this statement to remove that conceit from them, for a person is never free of kinds of lapses and the darknesses of desires, and in all states he is in need of the help, grace and benevolence of Allah, and that He be merciful in His punishment and forgiving of His sins.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 42–43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains. And Noah called to his son, who was apart, "O my son, board with us and do not be with the disbelievers."﴾ ﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." Noah said, "There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for whom He has mercy." And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned.﴾

Know that in His saying: ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains﴾ there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿with them through waves﴾ is connected to an omitted element, and the implied meaning is: "And he said, 'Board it,' so they boarded it, saying, 'In the name of Allah,' and it sailed with them through waves like mountains."

The second issue: Huge waves arise only when strong, violent, stormy winds occur. This indicates that at that time there were violent, severe winds, and the purpose of this is to show the intensity of the terror and dread.

The third issue: Sailing through the waves means that the ship moves within the waves, and this necessitates drowning. So the meaning is that when the waves surrounded the ship from all sides, that ship was likened to one moving within those waves.

Then Allah, exalted is He, related that he called to his son, and in this are issues:

The first issue: They differed over whether he was truly his son, and there are opinions on this:

The first opinion: He was his son in reality. The evidence for this is that Allah, exalted is He, explicitly stated it, saying: ﴿And Noah called to his son﴾, and Noah also explicitly stated it, saying: ﴿O my son﴾. Turning this word away from its literal sense to mean that he raised him, and thus applying the name "son" to him for this reason, is turning the speech from its literal meaning to its metaphorical meaning without necessity, and that is not permissible. Those who opposed this apparent meaning opposed it only because they found it unlikely that the son of a prophet, who is infallible, would be a disbeliever. But this is far-fetched, for it is established that the father of our Messenger (ﷺ) was a disbeliever, and the father of Abraham (peace be upon him) was a disbeliever by the explicit text of the Qur'an; so likewise here. Then, those who hold this opinion differed over the following: when he (peace be upon him) said, ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ [Nuh: 26], how then did he call to him despite his disbelief?

صفحة ١٨٥
They answered this in several ways:
The first: He used to feign agreement with his father, so Noah thought he was a believer, and therefore he called to him; had it not been so, he would not have loved his salvation.

The second: He (peace be upon him) knew that he was a disbeliever, but he thought that when he witnessed the drowning and the great terrors, he would accept faith; so his saying ﴿O my son, board with us﴾ became like an indication that he asked him to believe, and this was reinforced by his saying ﴿and do not be with the disbelievers﴾, meaning: follow them in disbelief, and board with us.

The third: Perhaps the compassion of fatherhood moved him to that call, and what preceded in His saying ﴿except for one against whom the word has already gone forth﴾ was like something general, so perhaps he (peace be upon him) allowed that he might not be among those included in it.

The second opinion: He was the son of his wife, and this is the view of Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir and the view of al-Hasan al-Basri. It is narrated that 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) recited: "And Noah called to her son," with the pronoun referring to his wife. Muhammad ibn 'Ali and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr recited "ibnah" with a fatha on the ha', meaning "ibnaha" (her son), but they dispensed with the alif by the fatha. Qatadah said: I asked al-Hasan about it, and he said: "By Allah, he was not his son." I said: "Allah related from him that he said: ﴿Indeed, my son is of my family﴾ [Hud: 45], and you say he was not his son?" He said: "He did not say: 'He is from me,' but he said: 'from my family,' and this indicates my view."

The third opinion: He was born on his bed to someone other than his lawful father (illegitimate). Those who hold this view argue by the saying of Allah, exalted is He, concerning the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot: ﴿but they betrayed them﴾. This is a vile opinion, and the status of the prophets must be safeguarded from this disgrace, especially since it contradicts the explicit text of the Qur'an. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿but they betrayed them﴾ [At-Tahrim: 10], there is nothing in it indicating that this betrayal occurred through the cause they mentioned. It was said to Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father): "What was that betrayal?" He said: "The wife of Noah used to say, 'My husband is mad,' and the wife of Lot used to point people to his guests when they came to him." Then the decisive proof against the falsehood of this view is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women; and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women﴾ [An-Nur: 26], and also His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or an idolatress, and the fornicatress is not married except by a fornicator or an idolater; and that has been made unlawful to the believers﴾ [An-Nur: 3]. In sum, we have shown that the truth is what was stated in the first opinion.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and he was apart﴾, know that "ma'zil" in the language means: a place cut off from others, and its root is from 'azl, which is removal and distancing. One says: "I was apart from such-and-such," meaning in a place from which it has been separated.

Know that His saying ﴿and he was apart﴾ does not indicate apart from what, so for this reason they mentioned several possibilities:

The first: He was apart from the ship, because he thought the mountain would prevent him from drowning.

The second: He was apart from his father, his brothers, and his people.

The third: He was apart from the disbelievers, as if he had separated himself from them, so Noah (peace be upon him) thought that this was only because he loved to part from them.

As for His saying: ﴿O my son, board with us and do not be with the disbelievers﴾, we say: Hafs, from 'Asim, recited "Ya buntayya" with a fatha on the ya' throughout the Qur'an, while the rest recited with a kasra. Abu 'Ali said: The correct form is the kasra, because the lam of "ibn" is a ya' or a waw; when you form the diminutive, you add the diminutive ya', so it becomes necessary to restore the deleted lam, otherwise the diminutive ya' would have to take the vowels of i'rab (case endings), but it does not take them, because if it were vowelled it would necessarily change as all long vowel letters change when they are letters of i'rab, such as "'asa" and "qafa"; and if it changed, its indication of diminutive would be nullified. Then you add a possessive to yourself, and three ya's gather:

The first of them is for the diminutive.
The second is the lam of the verb.
The third is the one for the possessive.

You say: "This is buneyy." When you call him, there are two options: retaining the ya'

صفحة ١٨٦
and deleting it. The preferred option is to delete the possessive ya' and keep the kasra as an indication of it, as in "ya ghulam." Whoever recited "ya buntayya" with a fatha on the ya' intended the possessive as well, just as the one who recited with a kasra intended it, but he replaced the kasra with a fatha and the ya' with an alif for lightness, so it became "ya buntaya," as the poet said:

"O daughter of my uncle, do not blame me and go to sleep,"

then he deleted the alif for lightness.

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, related from Noah (peace be upon him) that he invited him to board the ship, He related from his son that he said: ﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water.﴾ This indicates that the son was persisting in disbelief, insisting upon it, and denying his father regarding what he reported. At this point Noah (peace be upon him) said: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for whom He has mercy.﴾ There is an issue here: the one whom Allah has mercy upon is protected, so how is it proper to make an exception of the protected from the protector, which is his saying: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah﴾? They gave many answers to this:

The first answer: Allah, exalted is He, said before this verse: ﴿And he said, "Board it; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ So He made clear that He is Merciful and that by His mercy He delivers those who boarded the ship from the calamity of drowning.

Knowing this, we say: when Noah's son said: "﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water,﴾" Noah (peace be upon him) said: "You are mistaken. ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for whom He has mercy.﴾" The meaning is: except that One of whom I mentioned that by His mercy He delivers these from drowning. So the verse's implied sense becomes: "There is no protector today from the punishment of Allah except Allah, the Merciful." Its implied sense is: "There is no escape from Allah except to Allah," and this is like his (peace be upon him) saying in his supplication: "And I seek refuge in You from You." This interpretation is most excellent.

The second answer, which is what the author of Hall al-'Uqad mentioned: this exception is made from an implied element which is in the status of what is spoken, because the meaning of the speech clearly indicates it. The implied sense is: "There is no protector today for anyone from the command of Allah, except whom He has mercy upon." This is like your saying: "We do not strike anyone today except Zayd," for its implied sense is: "Do not strike anyone except Zayd," but he left out the explicit mention of it because the speech indicates it. So it is the same here.

The third answer: the interpretation is that His saying ﴿There is no protector﴾ means "no one possessing protection," as they say: "ramih" and "laban," meaning "one possessing a spear" and "one possessing milk." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿from a gushing water﴾ [At-Tariq: 6] and ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 21], meaning the same as what we mentioned. So here too: the protector is one who possesses protection, and thus includes the protected, and then the exception of His saying ﴿except whom He has mercy upon﴾ from it is correct.

The fourth answer: His saying ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah except whom He has mercy upon﴾ means by "except whom He has mercy upon" himself; for Noah and his company are those whom Allah, exalted is He, singled out with His mercy, and the meaning is: "There is no protector for you except Allah," in the sense that through Him Allah's mercy is attained, just as the giving of life was attributed to Jesus (peace be upon him) in His saying: ﴿and I give life to the dead﴾ [Al 'Imran: 49], because the giving of life occurred through his supplication.

The fifth answer: His saying ﴿except whom He has mercy upon﴾ is a disconnected exception, and the meaning is: "But whom Allah has mercy upon is protected." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾ [An-Nisa: 157]. Then He, exalted is He, made clear by His saying ﴿and the wave came between them﴾, that is, because of this interposition he was excluded from being addressed by Noah, ﴿and he was among the drowned.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 42–43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains. And Noah called to his son, who was apart, "O my son, board with us and do not be with the disbelievers."﴾ ﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." Noah said, "There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for whom He has mercy." And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned.﴾

Know that in His saying: ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains﴾ there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿with them through waves﴾ is connected to an omitted element, and the implied meaning is: "And he said, 'Board it,' so they boarded it, saying, 'In the name of Allah,' and it sailed with them through waves like mountains."

The second issue: Huge waves arise only when strong, violent, stormy winds occur. This indicates that at that time there were violent, severe winds, and the purpose of this is to show the intensity of the terror and dread.

The third issue: Sailing through the waves means that the ship moves within the waves, and this necessitates drowning. So the meaning is that when the waves surrounded the ship from all sides, that ship was likened to one moving within those waves.

Then Allah, exalted is He, related that he called to his son, and in this are issues:

The first issue: They differed over whether he was truly his son, and there are opinions on this:

The first opinion: He was his son in reality. The evidence for this is that Allah, exalted is He, explicitly stated it, saying: ﴿And Noah called to his son﴾, and Noah also explicitly stated it, saying: ﴿O my son﴾. Turning this word away from its literal sense to mean that he raised him, and thus applying the name "son" to him for this reason, is turning the speech from its literal meaning to its metaphorical meaning without necessity, and that is not permissible. Those who opposed this apparent meaning opposed it only because they found it unlikely that the son of a prophet, who is infallible, would be a disbeliever. But this is far-fetched, for it is established that the father of our Messenger (ﷺ) was a disbeliever, and the father of Abraham (peace be upon him) was a disbeliever by the explicit text of the Qur'an; so likewise here. Then, those who hold this opinion differed over the following: when he (peace be upon him) said, ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant﴾ [Nuh: 26], how then did he call to him despite his disbelief?

صفحة ١٨٥
They answered this in several ways:
The first: He used to feign agreement with his father, so Noah thought he was a believer, and therefore he called to him; had it not been so, he would not have loved his salvation.

The second: He (peace be upon him) knew that he was a disbeliever, but he thought that when he witnessed the drowning and the great terrors, he would accept faith; so his saying ﴿O my son, board with us﴾ became like an indication that he asked him to believe, and this was reinforced by his saying ﴿and do not be with the disbelievers﴾, meaning: follow them in disbelief, and board with us.

The third: Perhaps the compassion of fatherhood moved him to that call, and what preceded in His saying ﴿except for one against whom the word has already gone forth﴾ was like something general, so perhaps he (peace be upon him) allowed that he might not be among those included in it.

The second opinion: He was the son of his wife, and this is the view of Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir and the view of al-Hasan al-Basri. It is narrated that 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) recited: "And Noah called to her son," with the pronoun referring to his wife. Muhammad ibn 'Ali and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr recited "ibnah" with a fatha on the ha', meaning "ibnaha" (her son), but they dispensed with the alif by the fatha. Qatadah said: I asked al-Hasan about it, and he said: "By Allah, he was not his son." I said: "Allah related from him that he said: ﴿Indeed, my son is of my family﴾ [Hud: 45], and you say he was not his son?" He said: "He did not say: 'He is from me,' but he said: 'from my family,' and this indicates my view."

The third opinion: He was born on his bed to someone other than his lawful father (illegitimate). Those who hold this view argue by the saying of Allah, exalted is He, concerning the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot: ﴿but they betrayed them﴾. This is a vile opinion, and the status of the prophets must be safeguarded from this disgrace, especially since it contradicts the explicit text of the Qur'an. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿but they betrayed them﴾ [At-Tahrim: 10], there is nothing in it indicating that this betrayal occurred through the cause they mentioned. It was said to Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father): "What was that betrayal?" He said: "The wife of Noah used to say, 'My husband is mad,' and the wife of Lot used to point people to his guests when they came to him." Then the decisive proof against the falsehood of this view is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women; and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women﴾ [An-Nur: 26], and also His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or an idolatress, and the fornicatress is not married except by a fornicator or an idolater; and that has been made unlawful to the believers﴾ [An-Nur: 3]. In sum, we have shown that the truth is what was stated in the first opinion.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿and he was apart﴾, know that "ma'zil" in the language means: a place cut off from others, and its root is from 'azl, which is removal and distancing. One says: "I was apart from such-and-such," meaning in a place from which it has been separated.

Know that His saying ﴿and he was apart﴾ does not indicate apart from what, so for this reason they mentioned several possibilities:

The first: He was apart from the ship, because he thought the mountain would prevent him from drowning.

The second: He was apart from his father, his brothers, and his people.

The third: He was apart from the disbelievers, as if he had separated himself from them, so Noah (peace be upon him) thought that this was only because he loved to part from them.

As for His saying: ﴿O my son, board with us and do not be with the disbelievers﴾, we say: Hafs, from 'Asim, recited "Ya buntayya" with a fatha on the ya' throughout the Qur'an, while the rest recited with a kasra. Abu 'Ali said: The correct form is the kasra, because the lam of "ibn" is a ya' or a waw; when you form the diminutive, you add the diminutive ya', so it becomes necessary to restore the deleted lam, otherwise the diminutive ya' would have to take the vowels of i'rab (case endings), but it does not take them, because if it were vowelled it would necessarily change as all long vowel letters change when they are letters of i'rab, such as "'asa" and "qafa"; and if it changed, its indication of diminutive would be nullified. Then you add a possessive to yourself, and three ya's gather:

The first of them is for the diminutive.
The second is the lam of the verb.
The third is the one for the possessive.

You say: "This is buneyy." When you call him, there are two options: retaining the ya'

صفحة ١٨٦
and deleting it. The preferred option is to delete the possessive ya' and keep the kasra as an indication of it, as in "ya ghulam." Whoever recited "ya buntayya" with a fatha on the ya' intended the possessive as well, just as the one who recited with a kasra intended it, but he replaced the kasra with a fatha and the ya' with an alif for lightness, so it became "ya buntaya," as the poet said:

"O daughter of my uncle, do not blame me and go to sleep,"

then he deleted the alif for lightness.

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, related from Noah (peace be upon him) that he invited him to board the ship, He related from his son that he said: ﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water.﴾ This indicates that the son was persisting in disbelief, insisting upon it, and denying his father regarding what he reported. At this point Noah (peace be upon him) said: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for whom He has mercy.﴾ There is an issue here: the one whom Allah has mercy upon is protected, so how is it proper to make an exception of the protected from the protector, which is his saying: ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah﴾? They gave many answers to this:

The first answer: Allah, exalted is He, said before this verse: ﴿And he said, "Board it; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ So He made clear that He is Merciful and that by His mercy He delivers those who boarded the ship from the calamity of drowning.

Knowing this, we say: when Noah's son said: "﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water,﴾" Noah (peace be upon him) said: "You are mistaken. ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for whom He has mercy.﴾" The meaning is: except that One of whom I mentioned that by His mercy He delivers these from drowning. So the verse's implied sense becomes: "There is no protector today from the punishment of Allah except Allah, the Merciful." Its implied sense is: "There is no escape from Allah except to Allah," and this is like his (peace be upon him) saying in his supplication: "And I seek refuge in You from You." This interpretation is most excellent.

The second answer, which is what the author of Hall al-'Uqad mentioned: this exception is made from an implied element which is in the status of what is spoken, because the meaning of the speech clearly indicates it. The implied sense is: "There is no protector today for anyone from the command of Allah, except whom He has mercy upon." This is like your saying: "We do not strike anyone today except Zayd," for its implied sense is: "Do not strike anyone except Zayd," but he left out the explicit mention of it because the speech indicates it. So it is the same here.

The third answer: the interpretation is that His saying ﴿There is no protector﴾ means "no one possessing protection," as they say: "ramih" and "laban," meaning "one possessing a spear" and "one possessing milk." Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿from a gushing water﴾ [At-Tariq: 6] and ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [Al-Haqqah: 21], meaning the same as what we mentioned. So here too: the protector is one who possesses protection, and thus includes the protected, and then the exception of His saying ﴿except whom He has mercy upon﴾ from it is correct.

The fourth answer: His saying ﴿There is no protector today from the command of Allah except whom He has mercy upon﴾ means by "except whom He has mercy upon" himself; for Noah and his company are those whom Allah, exalted is He, singled out with His mercy, and the meaning is: "There is no protector for you except Allah," in the sense that through Him Allah's mercy is attained, just as the giving of life was attributed to Jesus (peace be upon him) in His saying: ﴿and I give life to the dead﴾ [Al 'Imran: 49], because the giving of life occurred through his supplication.

The fifth answer: His saying ﴿except whom He has mercy upon﴾ is a disconnected exception, and the meaning is: "But whom Allah has mercy upon is protected." A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾ [An-Nisa: 157]. Then He, exalted is He, made clear by His saying ﴿and the wave came between them﴾, that is, because of this interposition he was excluded from being addressed by Noah, ﴿and he was among the drowned.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 44:

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وقِيلَ ياأرْضُ ابْلَعِي ماءَكِ ويا سَماءُ أقْلِعِي وغِيضَ الماءُ وقُضِيَ الأمْرُ واسْتَوَتْ عَلى الجُودِيِّ وقِيلَ بُعْدًا لِلْقَوْمِ الظّالِمِينَ﴾

Know that the purpose of this speech is another description of the event of the Flood. The sense is that when the matter of the Flood came to its end, it was said such-and-such. ﴿And it was said: O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold!﴾ It is said: "bala'a al-ma'a yabla'uhu balʿan" (he drank the water) when he drinks it, and "ibtala'a al-ta'ama ibtila'an" (he swallowed the food) when he does not chew it. The people of the language (the lexicographers) said: the standard form is "bali'a" with a kasra on the lam, and "yabla'u" with a fatha on it. ﴿And O sky, withhold!﴾ It is said: "aqla'a al-rajulu ʿan ʿamalihi" (the man desisted from his work) when he stopped it, and "aqla'at al-sama'u ba'da ma matarat" (the sky cleared after it had rained) when it held back. ﴿And the water subsided﴾: it is said "ghaada al-ma'u yaghidu ghaydan wa maghadan" (the water decreased) when it diminished, and "ghidtuhu ana" (I caused it to diminish). This belongs to the pattern of "fa'ala al-shay'u" (the thing did) and "fa'altuhu ana" (I did it), like "jabara al-ʿazmu wa jabartuhu" (the bone was set and I set it), "faghara al-fammu wa faghartuhu" (the mouth gaped and I made it gape), "dalaʿa al-lisanu wa dalaʿtuhu" (the tongue protruded and I made it protrude), and "naqasa al-shay'u wa naqastuhu" (the thing decreased and I decreased it). So His saying ﴿and the water subsided﴾ means it decreased, and nothing of it remained.

Know that this verse contains many expressions, each of which points to the greatness of God the Exalted and the loftiness of His majesty:

The first: His saying "(wa-qīla)" (and it was said). This is because it indicates that He, glorified be He, is in such majesty, loftiness and greatness that whenever "qīla" (it was said) is mentioned, the intellect turns to none but Him, and thought directs itself only to the fact that the one who speaks is He alone. This is an alert, from this aspect, that it is established in minds that there is no ruler over the worlds and no disposer of the upper world and the lower world except Him.

The second: His saying ﴿O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold!﴾ Sense perception shows the greatness, strength and power of these bodies. When the intellect perceives the existence of a being that overpowers these bodies, dominates them, and disposes of them as He wills and desires, this becomes a cause for the rational faculty to stand upon the perfection of God's majesty, the height of His dominion, and the perfection of His power and will.

The third: The sky and the earth are inanimate things, so His saying ﴿O earth﴾ and ﴿O sky﴾ suggests, outwardly, that His command and obligation take effect upon inanimate things. At this point the imagination judges that since the command is so with them, His command is all the more binding upon rational beings. My intention is not that God commands inanimate things, for that is false. Rather, the meaning is that directing the form of command, outwardly, toward these strong and powerful inanimate things fully establishes in the imagination a kind of His greatness and majesty.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿And the matter was decided﴾, the meaning is that what He decreed and determined in eternity is a decree that is firm and definitive. It came as an alert that everything God the Exalted has decreed occurs at its appointed time, that there is no repeller of His decree, and no obstacle to the execution of His judgment on His earth and His sky.

If it is said: How is it fitting for God's wisdom to drown children because of the crime of the disbelievers?

We answer: The response to this is from two aspects.

The first: Many of the exegetes say that God rendered the wombs of their women barren forty years before the drowning, so that only those who had reached the age of forty were drowned.

One may say: If the matter were as you have mentioned, that would be a wondrous and overpowering sign. And it is unlikely, along with its manifestness, that they would remain steadfast in disbelief. Furthermore, grant that you have mentioned what you have mentioned; what then is your position on the destruction of the birds and the beasts, although no obligation whatsoever rests upon them?

The second response, and it is the truth, is that there is no objection to God the Exalted in His acts: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya: 23]. As for the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school of theology), they say that God drowned the children and the animals, and this runs parallel to His permission for the slaughter of these beasts and for their use in harsh and strenuous labors.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and it settled upon al-Judi﴾, the meaning is: the ship settled upon a mountain in the Jazirah (the region of upper Mesopotamia) called al-Judi. That mountain was a low-lying mountain, so the ship's settling upon it was a sign that the source of that water had ended. That settling took place on the day of ʿAshura.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿And it was said: away with the wrongdoing people﴾, there are two views concerning it:

The first: that it is from the speech of God the Exalted. He said this to them by way of curse and expulsion.

The second: that it is from the speech of Noah, peace be upon him, and his companions. This is because the one who is usually saved from a terrifying matter, through the gathering of a people of oppressors, when they are destroyed and he is saved from among them, says words like this. Also, it is in the manner of supplication against them, so attributing it to human speech is more fitting.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 45–47:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges."﴾ ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, his deeds are unrighteous. So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers."﴾

In this passage there are two issues:

The first issue: Know that regarding His saying ﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family﴾, we have already mentioned the disagreement over whether he was truly his son or not, so we will not repeat it. Then Allah the Exalted mentioned that He said: ﴿O Noah, indeed he is not of your family.﴾ Know that since it has been established by evidence that he was his son, the saying ﴿indeed he is not of your family﴾ must be interpreted in one of two ways:

The first: that the intended meaning is that he is not of the people of your religion.

The second: the intended meaning is that he is not of your family whom I promised to save along with you. The two views are close in meaning.

The second issue: This verse indicates that what matters is kinship of religion, not kinship of lineage. In this case, kinship of lineage was present in its strongest form, but since kinship of religion was absent, Allah the Exalted indeed negated him in the most emphatic terms, namely His saying: ﴿indeed he is not of your family.﴾

* * *

Then He said: ﴿indeed, his deeds are unrighteous.﴾ Al-Kisa'i read "ʿamila" in the form of the past-tense verb, and "ghayra" with a fatha. The meaning is: your son did an unrighteous deed, that is, he associated partners with Allah and denied the truth. The word "ghayra" is in the accusative because it is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun. The rest of the readers read "ʿamalun" with a damma and tanwin, and in it there are two views:

The first: the pronoun in His saying "innahu" refers to the request, meaning that this request is an unrighteous deed, namely his saying: ﴿indeed my son is of my family and indeed Your promise is true﴾, because seeking the salvation of a disbeliever after the firm judgment had already been issued that He would save none of them is a false request.

The second: this pronoun refers to the son. On this reading, describing him as an unrighteous deed has several aspects:

The first: when a man's deeds and benevolence are abundant, it is said of him that he is knowledge, generosity, and bounty. Likewise here, since the son of Noah frequently undertook false deeds, he was judged to be, in himself, a false deed.

The second: the intended meaning is that he is one possessing an unrighteous deed, and the noun was deleted because the context indicates it.

The third: some have said that the meaning of His saying ﴿indeed he is an unrighteous deed﴾ is that he is the son of fornication, and this view is categorically false.

Then Allah the Exalted said to Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant.﴾ On this there are two issues:

The first issue: Those who have criticized the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, have argued from this verse in several respects:

The first aspect: the reading "ʿamalun" with damma and tanwin is a mutawatir reading, so it is muhkam (clear), and this requires that the pronoun in His saying ﴿indeed he is an unrighteous deed﴾ refers either to the son of Noah or to that request. The view that it refers to the son of Noah is not complete except by supposing an implied element, which is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it is not permissible to resort to it except in case of necessity, and there is no necessity here. For if we judge that the pronoun refers to the earlier request, we have dispensed with this pronoun. So it is established that this pronoun refers to this request, and the meaning becomes that this request is an unrighteous deed, that is, your saying "indeed my son is of my family" in seeking his salvation is an unrighteous deed, and that shows that this request was a sin and a disobedience.

The second aspect: His saying ﴿So do not ask Me﴾ is a prohibition to him from asking, and what is mentioned earlier is his saying ﴿indeed my son is of my family﴾. This indicates that He forbade him from that request, so that request was a sin and a disobedience.

The third aspect: His saying ﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾ indicates that that request had proceeded not from knowledge, and speaking without knowledge is a sin, due to the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 169].

The fourth aspect: the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿Indeed, I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ indicates that that request was pure ignorance, and this indicates the utmost reproach and the extreme of rebuke. Also, using ignorance as a metaphor for sin is well known in the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿they do evil in ignorance﴾ [an-Nisa': 17], and Allah the Exalted said, relating about Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant.﴾

The fifth aspect: Noah, peace be upon him, acknowledged his commission of sin and disobedience in this station, for he said: ﴿My Lord, indeed I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge. And unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers.﴾ His acknowledgment of this indicates that he was a sinner.

The sixth aspect in holding to this verse: this verse indicates that Noah called upon his Lord seeking the deliverance of his son from drowning, and the earlier verse, namely His saying ﴿And Noah called out to his son﴾ [Hud: 42], and his saying ﴿O my son, board with us﴾ [Hud: 42], indicate that he, peace be upon him, sought agreement from his son. We say: either it is said that the seeking of this matter from Allah preceded his seeking it from the son, or it was the reverse. The first is false, for if the seeking of this matter from Allah, the Exalted, had preceded his seeking it from the son, then he would have heard from Allah that He would not deliver that son from drowning, and that He, the Exalted, had forbidden him from that request. After this, how could he say to him: ﴿O my son, board with us and do not be with the disbelievers﴾ [Hud: 42]? As for if we say that this request to the son came first, then he had heard from the son his saying: ﴿I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water﴾ [Hud: 43], and his disbelief became apparent by this. How then could he ask Allah to deliver him? Also, Allah the Exalted informed that when Noah sought this of him and he refused, he became among the drowned. How then could he ask Allah to deliver him from drowning after he had become among the drowned?

So this verse, through these six aspects, indicates the occurrence of disobedience from Noah, peace be upon him.

Know that since the many proofs have established the obligation of exempting the prophets, peace be upon them, from sins, it is necessary to interpret these mentioned aspects as the abandonment of what is better and more perfect, and "the good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near." **The second issue:** When they came out, God promised him safety first, and then blessing second. As for the promise of safety, it may carry two meanings:

The first: God Most High stated in the preceding verse that Noah, peace be upon him, repented of his lapse and humbled himself before God Most High, saying: ﴿And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers.﴾ This humbling is the very same humbling that God Most High related of Adam, peace be upon him, when he repented of his lapse, namely His words: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers.﴾ (al-A'raf 7:23). So Noah, peace be upon him, needed to be given good news by God Most High of safety from threat and warning. When it was said to him, ﴿O Noah, descend with peace from Us,﴾ he attained security from all the hardships connected with religion.

The second: Since that flood was general over the whole earth, when Noah, peace be upon him, came out of the ship, he knew that there was nothing on the earth of what is useful, of plants and animals. So he was like one who fears: how will he live? How will he meet all his needs for food and drink? When God Most High said, ﴿descend with peace from Us,﴾ that fear left him, because this indicates the attainment of safety from calamities, and that is not possible except with security and abundance of provision. Then, when God Most High promised him safety, He followed it by promising him blessing. Blessing (*barakah*) is an expression for lastingness, permanence, stability, and the attainment of hope. From it comes *buruk al-ibil* (the kneeling of camels), and from it *birkah* (a pool), because water remains settled in it, and from it *tabaraka* (blessed is He), meaning His glorification is established. Then the exegetes differed in explaining this lastingness and permanence.

The first view: God Most High made Noah the father of mankind, because all who survived were of his offspring. On this basis, whoever holds this view says: when Noah came out of the ship, everyone who was with him who was not from his descendants died, and offspring came only from his descendants. So all creation is from his offspring and descendants. Others said: no one was in Noah's ship, peace be upon him, except those from his lineage and descendants. Under either assumption, all creation was born only from him and from his children. The proof for this is God Most High's words: ﴿And We made his descendants the ones who remain.﴾ (al-Saffat 37:77). Thus it is established that Noah, peace be upon him, was the "lesser Adam." This is what is meant by the blessings which God promised him.

The second view: When God Most High promised him safety from calamities, He promised him that the causes of safety, comfort and ease would continue to increase, be stable and firmly established. Then, when God Most High honoured him with safety and blessing, He afterward described the condition of those who were with him, saying: ﴿and upon nations from those who are with you.﴾ They differed about what is meant by this, in three views. Some understood it as referring to those peoples who were saved with him, and made them nations and groups, because at that time there was no human on the whole earth except them; for this reason He made them nations. Others said: rather, what is meant is "from those with you" in terms of offspring and generation. They argued that the proof for this is that only those who believed were with him, and God Most High has decreed that they are few, in His words: ﴿And none believed with him except a few.﴾ (Hud 11:40). Others said: what is meant by this is the totality of those present with him together with those who would be born after that.

The preferred view is the second: the "min" (from) in His words ﴿from those who are with you﴾ indicates the starting point, and the meaning is: "and upon nations arising from those who are with you."

Know that God Most High divided those nations arising from those who were with him into two categories:

One: those whom He joined with Noah in the arrival of God's peace and blessings to them, and they are the people of faith.

The second: nations He described as those whom He would grant enjoyment for a period in this world, and then in the Hereafter a painful punishment will touch them. So God Most High decreed that the nations arising from those who were with Noah, peace be upon him, must necessarily divide into believer and disbelieving. The exegetes said: every believing man and believing woman until the Day of Resurrection entered into that safety, and every disbelieving man and disbelieving woman until the Day of Resurrection entered into that enjoyment and that punishment.

Then the people of verification (*ahl al-tahqiq*) said: God Most High only magnified Noah's station by bringing safety and blessings to him, because He said ﴿with peace from Us.﴾ This indicates that the truthful (*siddiqun*) do not rejoice in a favour merely because it is a favour, but they rejoice in a favour insofar as it is from the Truth. In reality their joy is in the Truth, their seeking is for the Truth, and their turning is toward the Truth. This is a noble station which none knows except the elect of God Most High. For joy in safety and blessing insofar as they are safety and blessing is one thing, and joy in safety and blessing insofar as they are from the Truth is another. The first is the portion of the general mass of creation; the second is the portion of those brought near (*muqarrabun*). For this reason one of them said: whoever prefers knowledge (*irfan*) for the sake of knowledge has spoken with the second [view]; but whoever prefers knowledge not for the sake of knowledge, but for the sake of the Known, has plunged into the depths of arrival.

As for the people of punishment, in describing their condition He said: ﴿and nations We will grant enjoyment, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them.﴾ So He decreed that He would give them a share of the enjoyment of this world, and this indicates the baseness of this world. For when God Most High mentioned the condition of the believers, He did not mention at all whether He would give them this world or not; but when He mentioned the condition of the disbelievers, He mentioned that He would give them this world. This is a great reminder of the baseness of bodily happinesses and an encouragement toward spiritual stations.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 49:

Page 8

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is among the tidings of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew them before this. So be patient; indeed, the good outcome is for the righteous.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the story of Noah, peace be upon him, in detail, He said: "That" (tilka), i.e., those verses which We have mentioned and those details which We have explained, "is among the tidings of the unseen" (min anba'i al-ghayb), i.e., among the reports which were hidden from creation. So His saying "That" (tilka) is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), "among the tidings of the unseen" is the predicate (khabar), "which We reveal to you" is a second predicate, and what follows it is also a third predicate.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Neither you nor your people knew them﴾, and the meaning is: you did not know this story, and indeed your people did not know it either. The parallel to this is that you say to a person: "You do not know this matter, neither you nor the people of your town."

If it is said: Was not the story of the Flood of Noah, peace be upon him, well known among the people of knowledge?

We say: That story was well known in its general outline, but the detailed points mentioned were not known.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So be patient; indeed, the good outcome is for the righteous.﴾ The meaning is: O Muhammad, be patient, you and your people, over the harm of these disbelievers, just as Noah and his people were patient over the harm of those disbelievers. This contains an indication that the outcome of patience is victory, triumph, joy and happiness, just as it was for Noah, peace be upon him, and his people.

If someone says: He, exalted is He, mentioned this story in Surah Yunus, and then He repeated it here once more. What is the benefit of this repetition?

We say: A single story may be benefited from in several respects. In the first surah, the disbelievers were hastening the descent of the punishment, so He mentioned the story of Noah to explain that his people denied him because the punishment did not appear, and then in the end it did appear; similarly in the case of Muhammad, ﷺ. In this surah, He mentioned this story because the disbelievers were excessive in causing distress. So Allah mentioned this story to show that the disbelievers' undertaking of harm and distress existed in the time of Noah, but when he, peace be upon him, was patient, he attained conquest and victory; so be (like that), O Muhammad, so that you may attain the goal. And since the way of benefiting from this story differs in each surah, its repetition is not devoid of benefit.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 50–51:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And to 'Ad, their brother Hud. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. You are not but fabricators."﴾ ﴿"O my people, I do not ask you for any reward for it. My reward is only from the One who originated me. Then will you not reason?"﴾

Know that this is the second story among the narratives that Allah the Exalted mentions in this surah. Know also that this is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon His saying: ﴿And We had certainly sent Noah﴾ [Hud: 25], and the implied meaning is: "And We had certainly sent to 'Ad their brother Hud." His saying "Hud" is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan).

Know that He, the Exalted, described Hud as their brother, and it is known that this brotherhood was not one of religion but of lineage, because Hud was a man from the tribe of 'Ad, and this tribe was a tribe of the Arabs, and they were in the region of Yemen. A parallel to this is what is said to a man, "O brother of Tamim" or "O brother of Sulaym," and what is meant is: a man from them.

If it is said: He, the Exalted, said about the son of Noah: ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family﴾, thereby making clear that kinship by lineage is of no benefit when kinship in religion is not attained. Here, however, He established this brotherhood despite the difference in religion. So what is the difference between the two?

We say: The purpose of this speech is to win over the people of Muhammad ﷺ, because his people used to find it strange, despite him being one of their own tribe, that he should be a messenger to them from Allah. So Allah the Exalted mentioned that Hud was one of 'Ad, and that Salih was one of Thamud, to remove this strangeness.

Know that He, the Exalted, related of Hud, peace be upon him, that he called his people to various kinds of obligations.

The first kind: he called them to monotheism, saying: ﴿O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. You are not but fabricators.﴾ There is a question here: how did he call them to worship Allah the Exalted before establishing the proof for the existence of God the Exalted?

We say: The indications of the existence of Allah the Exalted are manifest, and they are the signs of the horizons and of the selves. Rarely is there found in the world a group that denies the existence of God the Exalted. That is why Allah the Exalted said, describing the disbelievers: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ [Luqman: 25]

The author of this book, Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him and conclude his life with goodness, said: I entered the lands of India and saw those disbelievers unanimous in acknowledging the existence of God, and most of the lands of the Turks are likewise. The matter at issue is the worship of idols, for it is a calamity that has spread over most parts of the earth. The situation was the same in ancient times, meaning the time of Noah, Hud and Salih, peace be upon them. These prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, used to prevent them from worshipping idols. So His saying "Worship Allah" means: do not worship other than Allah. The evidence for this is that He said immediately after it: ﴿you have no deity other than Him﴾, and that indicates that the intended purpose of this speech is to prevent them from occupying themselves with worshipping idols.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿you have no deity other than Him﴾, "other than Him" (ghayruhu) has been read in the nominative (raf') as an adjective upon the place (mahall) of the prepositional phrase, and has been read in the genitive (jarr) as an adjective upon the wording (lafz).
* * *
Then He said: ﴿You are not but fabricators﴾, meaning: you are lying in your saying that these idols are fit to be worshipped, or in your saying that they deserve worship. And how could this not be a lie and a fabrication, when they are inanimate objects with no sense and no perception, and it is the human being who assembled and shaped them? How is it fitting for the human being who made them to worship them, and to place his forehead upon the dust in veneration of them! Then, when he, peace be upon him, guided them to monotheism and prevented them from worshipping idols, he said: ﴿O my people, I do not ask you for any reward for it. My reward is only from the One who originated me﴾, and this is the very thing that Noah, peace be upon him, had said. That is because when the call to Allah the Exalted is purified of the taint of greed, its effect upon the heart is strong.

Then He said: ﴿Then will you not reason?﴾, meaning: will you not reason that I am correct in forbidding the worship of idols? That is because the knowledge of the soundness of this prohibition is, as it were, implanted in the primary intuitions of the intellects.
