Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 52:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord and then turn to Him in repentance; He will send down the sky upon you in abundance and increase you in strength upon your strength, and do not turn away as criminals.﴾

Know that this is the second type of the obligations which Hud (peace be upon him) mentioned to his people. That is because in the first position he called them to monotheism (tawhid), and in this position he called them to seek forgiveness (istighfar) and then to repentance (tawbah). The difference between them has already been explained at the beginning of this surah. Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: "Seek forgiveness" means ask Him to forgive you what preceded of your shirk, and then "turn to Him in repentance" after that by regret for what has passed and by resolve not to return to the like of it. Then he (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, whenever you do that, God Exalted will multiply blessings for you and strengthen you to benefit from those blessings." This is the ultimate of what is sought from felicities, for if blessings are not present, benefiting from them is impossible; and if they are present but something prevents the living being from benefiting from them, the purpose is likewise not achieved. But when blessings are abundant and complete power to benefit from them is attained, then the utmost of happiness and joy is achieved. So His saying, ﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundance﴾ is a reference to the multiplication of blessings, because the source of the arrival of blessings is the suitable rains. And His saying, ﴿and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾ is a reference to the perfection of the powers by which it is possible to benefit from that blessing. There is no doubt that this phrase comprises the glad tidings of attaining felicities, and that increase beyond it is impossible according to clear reason. A rational person must reflect upon these subtleties so as to know the hidden secrets in this noble Book. As for the exegetes, they said: this people had been distinguished in this world by two kinds of perfection:

The first: their orchards and fields were in the utmost of goodness and delight. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Iram, of the pillars, the like of which has not been created in the lands﴾ [al-Fajr: 7].

The second: they were at the utmost of strength and might; therefore they said: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat: 15]. Since this people took pride over all creation in these two matters, Hud (peace be upon him) promised them that if they abandoned the worship of idols and occupied themselves with seeking forgiveness and repentance, God Exalted would strengthen their condition in these two desired matters and increase them in them by many degrees. It is also related that when God Exalted sent Hud (peace be upon him) to them, they denied him, and God withheld rain from them for years and made the wombs of their women barren. Hud said to them: "If you believe in God, God will revive your lands and grant you wealth and children." That is His saying: ﴿He will send down the sky upon you in abundance﴾. Al-midrar means one that gives much milk, and it is of the forms of intensification. His saying: ﴿and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾ — they interpreted this strength as wealth and children, and vigor in the limbs, because all of that is what a person is strengthened by.

If it is said: the upshot of the discourse is that Hud (peace be upon him) said: "If you occupy yourselves with worship of God Exalted, the doors of worldly goods will be opened for you," and the matter is not so, because he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Affliction is reserved for the prophets, then the friends of God, then the best and then the next best." How then is the reconciliation of these two? Moreover, the custom of the Qur'an has been to encourage acts of obedience by means of the arrangement of worldly and otherworldly goods upon them. As for encouraging obedience for the sake of worldly goods being arranged upon it, that is not fitting for the Qur'an; rather it is a method mentioned in the Torah.

The answer: since he greatly emphasized encouragement toward otherworldly felicities, he did not neglect also encouraging the good of this world to a sufficient degree.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿and do not turn away as criminals﴾, its meaning is: do not turn away from me and from what I call you to and encourage you toward, being criminals, that is, persisting in your crimes and sins.

Qur'an 11:53–59 and the commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O Hud, you have not brought us any clear proof, and we will not abandon our gods on your word, nor will we believe you."﴾ ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil.﴾ He said, "I call God to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free of what you associate ﴿besides Him. So scheme against me all together, then give me no respite.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have put my trust in God, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock. Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path."﴾

Know that when Exalted God related what Hud, peace be upon him, said to the people, He also related what the people said to him, and they were several things:

The first: their saying, ﴿You have not brought us any clear proof﴾, i.e., any argument. The "bayyinah" (clear proof) is so named because it makes the truth clear from falsehood. It is known that he, peace be upon him, had displayed miracles, but the people, out of their ignorance, denied them and claimed that he had brought no miracle at all.

The second: their saying, ﴿Nor will we abandon our gods on your word﴾. This too is weak, because they used to acknowledge that the one who benefits and harms is God Exalted, and that the idols neither benefit nor harm. When this is the case, it becomes evident by the immediate judgment of reason that worshipping them is not permissible. Their abandoning of their gods would not come about merely from his saying, but from the judgment of reflective reason and the immediate sense of the soul.

The third: their saying, ﴿Nor will we believe you﴾. This indicates persistence, blind imitation, and obstinate denial.

The fourth: their saying, ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾. It is said: "i'tarahu kadha" (it seized him and befell him) when it overcame him and afflicted him. The meaning is: you insulted our gods, so they made you mad and corrupted your mind. Then Exalted God mentioned that when they said this, Hud, peace be upon him, said: ﴿I call God to witness, and bear witness yourselves that I am free of what you associate﴾ ﴿besides Him﴾, and this is clear.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So scheme against me all together, then give me no respite.﴾ This is similar to what Noah, peace be upon him, said to his people: ﴿So resolve upon your affair with your associates﴾ [Yunus: 71], up to His saying: ﴿and give me no respite﴾.
Know that this is an overpowering miracle, for when one man confronts a great people and says to them: "Exert yourselves in your enmity toward me and in what necessitates harming me, and do not delay," he would not say this unless he was certain from God Exalted that He would protect him and guard him from the plotting of enemies.

Then He said: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock.﴾ Al-Azhari said: In the language of the Arabs, the "nasiyah" (forelock) is the place where hair grows at the front of the head, and the hair growing there is called a forelock by the name of its place.
Know that when the Arabs described a person as humbled and submissive, they would say: "The forelock of so-and-so is only in the hand of so-and-so," meaning that he obeys him, because whoever you seize by the forelock you have subdued. When they took a captive and wished to release him and show him favor, they would cut his forelock, so that this would be a sign of his subjugation. Thus the Qur'an addressed them in terms they understood. So His saying, ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ means: there is no living being but that it is under His subjugation and power, and submissive to His decree and destiny.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾, and in it there are several interpretations:
The first: when He said, ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾, this indicated lofty power and great dominion, so He followed it with His saying, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾, meaning: although He is capable over them, He does not wrong them, and He does not act toward them except in what is the truth, the justice, and the correct. The Mu'tazilah said: His saying, ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾ indicates monotheism (tawhid), and His saying, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾ indicates justice ('adl). So it is established that religion is only complete through monotheism and justice.

The second: when He mentioned that His sovereignty had subdued all creation, He followed it with His saying, ﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾, meaning that nothing hidden is concealed from Him, and no fugitive escapes Him. He mentioned the straight path, by which He means the road that no one has a way except upon it, as He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14].

The third: that the intended meaning of ﴿Indeed, my Lord﴾ is that it indicates the straight path, i.e., it urges or leads you to it through invitation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 60:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But if they turn away, then I have already conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you. And my Lord will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿But if they turn away﴾ means: "But if you turn away" (in fact, the verb is tatawallaw, with the second ta' elided). There are two interpretations of it.

The first: the sense of the speech is: "If you turn away, I will not be blamed for any shortcoming in conveying [the message], and you were veiled (from the truth)." It is as if he says: "You are the ones who persisted in denial."

The second: ﴿But if they turn away, then I have already conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you.﴾

* * *
Then He said: ﴿And my Lord will replace you with another people﴾, meaning: He will create after you one who is more obedient to God than you. This is an indication of the descent of the punishment of annihilation. ﴿And you will not harm Him at all﴾, meaning: your destruction does not diminish His dominion in any way.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things.﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations:
The first: He is Guardian over the deeds of the servants until He recompenses them for them.

[Page 13]

The second: He protects me from your evil and your plotting.

The third: He is Guardian over every thing: He preserves it from destruction when He wills, and destroys it when He wills.

﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a harsh punishment.﴾ ﴿And that was ʿAd, who denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾ ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, ʿAd disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with ʿAd, the people of Hud.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿When Our command came﴾ means: Our punishment. That was what descended upon them of the furious wind, with which God punished them for seven nights and eight days, entering into their nostrils and exiting from their rears, throwing them down upon the earth on their faces, until they became like the trunks of hollow palm trees.

If it is asked: How does this wind affect their destruction?

We answer: It is possible that this was due to its intense heat, or its intense cold, or the intensity of its force, so that it snatches living beings from the earth and then dashes them down upon the ground. All of this is possible.

* * *
As for His saying ﴿We saved Hud﴾, know that it is permissible for a calamity to befall both the believer and the disbeliever together; in that case that calamity is a mercy upon the believer and a punishment upon the disbeliever. As for the punishment that descends upon those who deny the prophets, peace be upon them, it is necessary in God's wisdom, Exalted is He, that He save the believer from it; were it not so, it would not be known that it was a punishment for their disbelief. For this reason God, Exalted is He, said here: ﴿We saved Hud and those who believed with him.﴾
* * *
As for His saying ﴿by mercy from Us﴾, there are several interpretations:
The first: He intended that no one is saved, however much he strives in faith and righteous deeds, except by a mercy from God.

The second: What is meant by mercy is that He guided them to faith in God and righteous deeds.

The third: He showed them mercy at that time and distinguished them from the disbelievers in the punishment.

* * *
As for His saying ﴿and We saved them from a harsh punishment﴾, the meant first salvation is salvation from the punishment of this world, and the second salvation is from the punishment of the Resurrection. He described it as "harsh" only to alert that the punishment which befell them after their death, in comparison to the punishment in which they fell, was a harsh punishment. The meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and We saved them﴾ is: We decreed that they do not deserve that harsh punishment and do not fall into it.

Know that when Exalted is He mentioned the story of ʿAd, He addressed the people of Muhammad (ﷺ), saying: ﴿And that was ʿAd﴾. This is an indication toward their graves and their traces, as if He, Exalted is He, said: Travel through the earth, look at them, and take heed. Then He gathered their attributes, and then mentioned the outcome of their affairs in this world and the Hereafter. As for their attributes, they are three:

The first attribute: His saying ﴿who denied the signs of their Lord﴾. What is meant is: they denied the indication of the miracles to the truth, or the denial [of the indication] of created things to the existence of the Wise Creator, if it is established that they were heretics.

The second attribute: His saying ﴿disobeyed His messengers﴾. The reason for it is that whoever disobeys one messenger has disobeyed all the messengers, due to His saying: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285]. It has also been said: no messenger was sent to them except Hud, peace be upon him.

The third attribute: His saying ﴿and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant﴾. The meaning is that the base people used to imitate their leaders in their saying: ﴿This is none but a human like yourselves﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24]. What is meant by the "tyrant" is the arrogant, the rebellious, the obstinate, the defiant, the contrarian, and the one who contends and opposes.

Know that when Exalted is He mentioned their attributes, after that He mentioned their conditions, saying: ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning: the curse was made to accompany them, following them and attending them in this world and the Hereafter. The meaning of "curse" (la'nah) is distance from the mercy of God, Exalted is He, and from every good.

Then, Exalted is He, explained the original cause of the descent of these hateful conditions upon them, saying: ﴿Unquestionably, ʿAd disbelieved in their Lord.﴾ It has been said: He meant "disbelieved in their Lord" with the preposition bi- elided. It has also been said: disbelief is denial, so the sense is: "Unquestionably, ʿAd denied their Lord." And it has been said: it is of the category of eliding the annexed term, meaning: they disbelieved the blessing of their Lord.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿Unquestionably, away with ʿAd, the people of Hud.﴾ Regarding this there are two questions:

The first question: Curse means distance. So when He said ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection﴾, what is the benefit of His saying ﴿Unquestionably, away with ʿAd﴾?

The answer: repetition with two different expressions indicates the utmost emphasis.

The second question: What is the benefit of His saying ﴿the people of Hud﴾?

The answer: ʿAd were two ʿAds. The first, the ancient one, are the people of Hud; the second are Iram of the pillars (Iram dhat al-ʿImad). So this was mentioned to remove confusion. The second answer: excessive explicitness in specification indicates greater emphasis.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 11, verses 61–62:**

God's words: ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship God; you have no god other than Him. He produced you from the earth and settled you in it. So seek His forgiveness, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive."﴾ ﴿They said: "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? Indeed, we are in disquieting doubt about what you call us to."﴾

Know that this is the third story among the stories mentioned in this surah, the story of Salih with Thamud. Its structure is like the structure in the story of Hud, except that here, when he commanded them to monotheism, he mentioned two proofs in confirming it.

The first proof is His saying: ﴿He produced you from the earth﴾. In this there are two aspects.

The first aspect: all of them are created from the loins of Adam, and he was created from the earth. I say: this is correct, but there is another aspect closer than this one. That is because a human being is created from semen and from menstrual blood. Semen is only generated from blood, and blood is only generated from foods, and these foods are either animal or vegetable. Animals are in the same condition as humans, so everything must ultimately end at plants. It is evident that plants are generated from the earth. Thus it is established that He, exalted is He, produced us from the earth.

The second aspect: the word "min" ("from") means, in the sense of its implication, "He produced you in the earth." This is weak, because whenever it is possible to take the speech in its apparent meaning, there is no need to turn it away from that. As for the explanation of how the generation of a human from the earth indicates the existence of the Creator, we have explained it many times.

The second proof is His saying: ﴿and settled you in it﴾. In this there are three aspects.

The first: He made you its inhabitants (ʿummār). They said: the kings of Persia had greatly increased in digging rivers and planting trees, so they naturally obtained long lifespans. A prophet from among the prophets of their time asked his Lord about the cause of those lifespans. God, exalted is He, revealed to him: "They developed My lands, so My servants lived in them."

Mu'awiya began to revive a piece of land near the end of his life. It was said to him: "What motivated you to this?" He said: "Only the saying of the one who said:

The young man is not a young man if he is not a source of light,
and there are no traces of him upon the earth."

The second: He, exalted is He, prolonged your lives in it. The derivation of ﴿istaʿmarakum﴾ is from "ʿumr" (lifespan), like "istabqākum" is from "baqāʾ" (remaining).

The third: it is derived from ʿumrā (a gift of use for the lifetime of the recipient, i.e., a life-estate), meaning He made it yours for the duration of your lives. When you die, it passes to others.

Know that the fact that the earth is receptive to beneficial constructions for humans, and that humans are capable of them, is a great indication of the existence of the Creator. Its outcome returns to what God mentioned in another verse, His saying: ﴿And He who decreed and then guided﴾ [al-A'la: 3]. This is because the coming into being of a human, along with the fact that there has been produced in his essence the guiding intellect and the power to perform appropriate actions, indicates the existence of a wise Creator. And the earth's being described with attributes that correspond to benefits and agree with advantages also indicates the existence of a wise Creator.

As for His saying: ﴿So seek His forgiveness, then turn to Him﴾, its explanation has already preceded.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is near﴾, it means He is near by knowledge and hearing. ﴿Responsive﴾ means He answers the supplication of those in need, by His bounty and mercy.

Then God explained that Salih, peace be upon him, when he established these proofs, ﴿they said: "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this."﴾ In this there are several aspects:

The first: since he was a man of strong intellect and strong judgment, and was from their tribe, their hope was strong that he would support their religion, strengthen their creed, and confirm their path. That is because whenever an excellent man arises among a people, they hope for him in this respect.

The second: some of them said: the meaning is that you used to show compassion to our poor, help our weak, and visit our sick. So our hope in you was strong, that you were among the helpers and the beloved. How then have you shown enmity and hatred? Then they added to this speech a great expression of astonishment at his saying: ﴿Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped?﴾ The purpose of this speech was to hold fast to the way of imitation (taqlid) and the obligation of following the fathers and predecessors. A similar astonishment is what God, exalted is He, related about the disbelievers of Mecca when they said: ﴿"Has he made the gods one god? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!"﴾ [Sad: 5]. Then they said: ﴿"And indeed, we are in doubt about what you call us to, [a doubt that is] disquieting."﴾ Doubt (shakk) is that a person remains hesitating between negation and affirmation, and "disquieting" (murib) is the one about whom evil is suspected. So His saying ﴿"we are in doubt"﴾ means that the correctness of his statement had not been preponderant in their belief, and His saying ﴿"disquieting"﴾ means that the corruption of his statement had become preponderant in their belief. This is an exaggeration in discrediting his speech.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 63–64:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself, then who will support me against Allah if I disobey Him? You would add nothing to me but loss."﴾

Know that His saying, ﴿if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾, came with the particle of doubt (ḥarf al-shakk), although he was in complete certainty regarding his matter. However, addressing the opponent in this manner is closer to acceptance. It is as though he said: "Suppose that I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and that I am truly a prophet, and consider that if I follow you and disobey my Lord in His commands, then who will prevent me from the punishment of Allah? You would add nothing to me under this supposition but loss." There are two opinions concerning the explanation of this word:

The first: under this supposition, you would cause my deeds to be lost and nullified.

The second: the meaning is: "You add nothing to me by what you say to me and what you compel me to, except that I would make you lose" — that is, I would attribute loss to you and say to you, "You are losers." The first view is closer, because His saying, ﴿who will support me against Allah if I disobey Him﴾, is like an indication that he meant: if I follow you in the disbelief you are upon, to which you have called me, I would increase only in loss regarding the religion, and so I would become one of the ruined losers.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 65:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you, so leave her to eat upon Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you.﴾ ﴿But they hamstrung her, so he said: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."﴾

Know that the custom regarding one who claims prophethood among a people who worship idols is that he begins with the call to worship Allah, then follows it with the claim of prophethood. It is inevitable that they ask him for a miracle. As for Salih (peace be upon him), it is related that his people went out to a festival of theirs, and they asked him to bring them a sign and to bring forth for them, from a particular rock that they pointed to, a she-camel. So Salih called upon his Lord, and the she-camel came forth as they had asked.

Know that this she-camel was a miracle in several respects:

The first: that Allah, exalted is He, created her from the rock.

The second: that Allah, exalted is He, created her inside the mountain, then split the mountain open for her.

The third: that Allah, exalted is He, created her pregnant without a male.

The fourth: that He created her in that form all at once, without birth.

The fifth: what is reported, that she had a day of drinking, and the whole people had another day of drinking.

The sixth: that there came from her a great quantity of milk, sufficient for a great multitude. Each of these aspects is a strong miracle. The Qur'an does not contain, beyond the fact that that she-camel was a sign and a miracle, an explanation of in which of these respects she was a miracle; this is not explained in it.

Page 17
Then He said: ﴿So leave her to eat upon Allah's earth﴾. The meaning is that he (peace be upon him) lifted from the people the burden of her upkeep, so she became, along with being a sign for them, beneficial to them and not harmful to them, because they used to benefit from her milk. It is reported that he (peace be upon him) feared for her from them when he witnessed their persistence in disbelief, for the adversary does not love the proof of his opponent to appear, but strives to hide it and nullify it with the utmost possible effort. For this reason he feared that they would proceed to kill her; therefore he took precaution and said: ﴿and do not touch her with harm﴾, and he threatened them that if they touched her with harm, there would be a near punishment. That is a severe warning to them against proceeding to kill her. Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear that despite this they hamstrung her and slaughtered her. It is possible that they hamstrung her to nullify that proof, or because she narrowed the water-drinking for the people, or because they desired her fat and flesh. His saying: ﴿lest a near punishment seize you﴾ refers to the third day, which is his saying: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes﴾. Then Allah, exalted is He, made clear that the people hamstrung her, so at that point Salih (peace be upon him) said to them: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days﴾. The meaning of enjoyment (tamattu') is delighting in benefits and pleasures that are perceived by the senses, and since enjoyment is attained only by the living, it was used to express life. His saying: ﴿in your homes﴾ has two interpretations:

The first: that by "home" is meant the land, and lands are called diyar because one dwells (yudar) in them, that is, one acts freely in them; it is said: Diyar Bakr, meaning their lands.

The second: that by the dwellings is meant the worldly life. His saying: ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾ means: not a lie. The verbal noun may come in the form of the passive participle, as in "majlud" (flogged) and "ma'qul" (understood), and ﴿by whichever of you is the afflicted (maftun)﴾. It has also been said: "not denied in it." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: When Allah, exalted is He, granted them those three days, He had indeed encouraged them toward faith; for when they hamstrung the she-camel, Salih (peace be upon him) warned them of the descent of punishment. They said: "And what is the sign of that?" He said: "On the first day your faces will become yellow, on the second red, and on the third black; then punishment will come to you on the fourth day." When they saw their faces had blackened, they became certain of the punishment, so they took precaution and prepared themselves for the punishment. Then the fourth day dawned upon them, and it was the Shout, the thunderbolt, and the punishment.

If it is said: How is it conceivable that these signs appeared among them, corresponding exactly to what Salih (peace be upon him) said, and yet they remained persistent in disbelief?

We say: As long as the indications have not reached the degree of certainty and conviction, their continuing in disbelief is not impossible; but when they become certain and definitive, the matter has reached the limit of compulsion, and faith at that time is not accepted.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 66–68:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that Day. Indeed your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty.﴾ ﴿And the cry seized those who had wronged, so they became, in their homes, prostrate corpses.﴾ ﴿As if they had never flourished therein. Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!﴾

Know that a verse like this has already passed in the story of 'Ad. His saying, ﴿and from the disgrace of that Day﴾, contains several issues.

**The first issue:** The wa' in His saying ﴿and from the disgrace﴾ is the wa' of conjunction (wāw al-ʿaṭf), and there are two views on it.

The first: the intended meaning is, "We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, from the punishment that descended upon his people, and from the disgrace that clung to them, and whose shame remained recorded and attributed to them." This is because the meaning of *khizy* (disgrace) is a defect whose scandal becomes apparent and at which one is ashamed. So what was omitted was omitted, relying on the indication of what remains.

The second: the intended meaning is, "We saved Salih by mercy from Us, and We saved them from the disgrace of that Day."

**The second issue:** Al-Kisa'i, and Nafi' in the transmission of Warsh and Qalun, and one of the transmissions from al-A'mash, read *yawmi'idhin* (يَوْمَئِذٍ) with a fatha on the mim, and in al-Ma'arij, *"ʿadhābi yawmaʾidhin"* (ﷻ, al-Ma'arij 11). The rest read it with a kasra on the mim in both places. 

Whoever reads with a fatha, it is on the basis that *yawm* is in an idafa (construct) to *idh* (إذْ), and that *idh* is indeclinable (mabni). An element annexed to an indeclinable element may be made indeclinable as well. Do you not see that the annexed element acquires definiteness and indefiniteness from what it is annexed to? So it is the same here.

As for the kasra on *idh*, the reason is that it is annexed to a full sentence consisting of a subject and predicate. You say, "I came to you when (*idh*) the sun was rising." When it is cut off from the annexed element, it receives nunation (tanwin, the addition of a final -n sound) so that the nunation indicates that. Then the dhal is given a kasra because of its sukun and the sukun of the nunation.

As for the reading with a kasra, it is on the basis that *khizy* is annexed to *yawm*. Its being annexed to an indeclinable element does not require that it be indeclinable, because this idafa is not obligatory.

**The third issue:** *Khizy* is great humiliation, to the point that it reaches the limit of scandal. For this reason, God, exalted is He, said concerning those who wage war: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world﴾ (al-Ma'idah 33). God, exalted is He, named that punishment *khizy* only because it is a lasting scandal by which their likes take warning. Then He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty﴾. That was fitting, because He, exalted is He, made clear that He brought that punishment upon the disbeliever and protected the people of faith from it. This distinction is valid only from one who is capable, who can overpower the natures of things, so that the same thing is a trial and punishment with respect to one person, and comfort and sweet provision with respect to another person.

Then He, exalted is He, clarified that matter, saying: ﴿And the cry seized those who had wronged﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** He said ﴿seized﴾ and did not say "I seized," because the *ṣayḥah* (cry) is taken to be a shouting. Also, a separator was placed between the verb and the feminine noun, so the separator served as a substitute for the feminine marker (*tāʾ al-taʾnīth*), and there are precedents for this already mentioned.

**The second issue:** They mentioned two views on the *ṣayḥah*. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the intended meaning is the thunderbolt (*ṣāʿiqah*). The second: the *ṣayḥah* is a great, terrifying cry, which they heard, and by it they all died. So they became, in the morning, dead and prostrate in their houses and dwellings. *Juthum* (جُثُومٌ) means their falling upon their faces. It is said that God commanded Jibril (peace be upon him) to cry out to them with that cry by which they died. It is also possible that God created it. Shouting (*ṣiyāḥ*) only occurs as a sound arising in a throat and mouth, and likewise screaming (*ṣurākh*). If it is from God's action, then He created it in the throat of an animal; and if it is the action of Jibril (peace be upon him), then it arose in his mouth and throat. The evidence for this is that the sound of thunder is greater than any cry, yet it is not called by that name, nor is it called a scream.

If it is said: What is the cause of the cry being something that causes death?

We say: There are several reasons. The first of them:

That a great cry occurs only when there is a strong cause that makes the air undulate, and that strong undulation may sometimes reach a person's eardrum and tear the membrane of the brain, thus causing death.

The second: that it is an awe-inspiring thing, so great awe arises at its occurrence, and psychological conditions, when they become strong, cause death.

The third: that when a great cry arises from the clouds, it must be accompanied by an intense, burning lightning, and that is the thunderbolt (*ṣāʿiqah*) which Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, mentioned.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they became, in their homes, prostrate﴾. *Juthum* is stillness. It is said of birds when they spend the night in their nests: they have settled (*jathamat*). Then the Arabs applied this word to what does not move because of death. So God, exalted is He, described these destroyed ones as having become still at the moment of destruction, until it was as if they had never been alive. His saying ﴿as if they had never flourished therein﴾ means as if they had never existed. *Maghna* (المَغْنى) is the place where a living person dwells; it is said: "So-and-so dwelt (*ghaniya*) in such-and-such a place" when he stayed there.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!﴾ Hamzah and Hafs, from 'Asim, read *"alā inna thamūda"* without nunation throughout the Qur'an, while the rest read *thamūda* with nunation (tanwin). Both *li-thamūda* and *li-thamūdin* are read with ṣarf (declension, i.e., inflection with nunation as a triptote). Ṣarf is for going to the living group, or to the greatest ancestor. Its prohibition (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf) is due to definiteness and feminine gender, considering the meaning of "tribe" (*qabīlah*).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 66–68:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that Day. Indeed your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty.﴾ ﴿And the cry seized those who had wronged, so they became, in their homes, prostrate corpses.﴾ ﴿As if they had never flourished therein. Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!﴾

Know that a verse like this has already passed in the story of 'Ad. His saying, ﴿and from the disgrace of that Day﴾, contains several issues.

**The first issue:** The wa' in His saying ﴿and from the disgrace﴾ is the wa' of conjunction (wāw al-ʿaṭf), and there are two views on it.

The first: the intended meaning is, "We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, from the punishment that descended upon his people, and from the disgrace that clung to them, and whose shame remained recorded and attributed to them." This is because the meaning of *khizy* (disgrace) is a defect whose scandal becomes apparent and at which one is ashamed. So what was omitted was omitted, relying on the indication of what remains.

The second: the intended meaning is, "We saved Salih by mercy from Us, and We saved them from the disgrace of that Day."

**The second issue:** Al-Kisa'i, and Nafi' in the transmission of Warsh and Qalun, and one of the transmissions from al-A'mash, read *yawmi'idhin* (يَوْمَئِذٍ) with a fatha on the mim, and in al-Ma'arij, *"ʿadhābi yawmaʾidhin"* (ﷻ, al-Ma'arij 11). The rest read it with a kasra on the mim in both places. 

Whoever reads with a fatha, it is on the basis that *yawm* is in an idafa (construct) to *idh* (إذْ), and that *idh* is indeclinable (mabni). An element annexed to an indeclinable element may be made indeclinable as well. Do you not see that the annexed element acquires definiteness and indefiniteness from what it is annexed to? So it is the same here.

As for the kasra on *idh*, the reason is that it is annexed to a full sentence consisting of a subject and predicate. You say, "I came to you when (*idh*) the sun was rising." When it is cut off from the annexed element, it receives nunation (tanwin, the addition of a final -n sound) so that the nunation indicates that. Then the dhal is given a kasra because of its sukun and the sukun of the nunation.

As for the reading with a kasra, it is on the basis that *khizy* is annexed to *yawm*. Its being annexed to an indeclinable element does not require that it be indeclinable, because this idafa is not obligatory.

**The third issue:** *Khizy* is great humiliation, to the point that it reaches the limit of scandal. For this reason, God, exalted is He, said concerning those who wage war: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world﴾ (al-Ma'idah 33). God, exalted is He, named that punishment *khizy* only because it is a lasting scandal by which their likes take warning. Then He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty﴾. That was fitting, because He, exalted is He, made clear that He brought that punishment upon the disbeliever and protected the people of faith from it. This distinction is valid only from one who is capable, who can overpower the natures of things, so that the same thing is a trial and punishment with respect to one person, and comfort and sweet provision with respect to another person.

Then He, exalted is He, clarified that matter, saying: ﴿And the cry seized those who had wronged﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** He said ﴿seized﴾ and did not say "I seized," because the *ṣayḥah* (cry) is taken to be a shouting. Also, a separator was placed between the verb and the feminine noun, so the separator served as a substitute for the feminine marker (*tāʾ al-taʾnīth*), and there are precedents for this already mentioned.

**The second issue:** They mentioned two views on the *ṣayḥah*. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the intended meaning is the thunderbolt (*ṣāʿiqah*). The second: the *ṣayḥah* is a great, terrifying cry, which they heard, and by it they all died. So they became, in the morning, dead and prostrate in their houses and dwellings. *Juthum* (جُثُومٌ) means their falling upon their faces. It is said that God commanded Jibril (peace be upon him) to cry out to them with that cry by which they died. It is also possible that God created it. Shouting (*ṣiyāḥ*) only occurs as a sound arising in a throat and mouth, and likewise screaming (*ṣurākh*). If it is from God's action, then He created it in the throat of an animal; and if it is the action of Jibril (peace be upon him), then it arose in his mouth and throat. The evidence for this is that the sound of thunder is greater than any cry, yet it is not called by that name, nor is it called a scream.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 69–71 (part 1 of 2):

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Our messengers certainly came to Ibrahim with the good news. They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace," and he did not delay before bringing a roasted calf.﴾ ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he disliked them and felt fear of them. They said, "Do not fear. We have been sent to the people of Lut."﴾ ﴿And his wife was standing, so she laughed, and We gave her the good news of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub.﴾

Know that this is the fourth story among the stories mentioned in this surah. Here there are several issues.

The first issue: The grammarians said: the word "qad" (certainly) has entered here, because the listener to the stories of the prophets (peace be upon them) expects one story after another, and "qad" is used to express expectation. The lam entered "la-qad" to emphasize the report. The word ﴿messengers﴾ is plural, and its minimum is three. So this indicates with certainty the occurrence of three. As for more than this number, there is no way to establish it except by another proof. They agreed that the principal one among them was Jibril (peace be upon him). Then the reports differed. It was said: Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him with twelve angels in the form of youths who are at the peak of beauty. Al-Dahhak said: they were nine. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: they were three: Jibril, Mikail, and Israfil (peace be upon them), and they are the ones Allah mentioned in the surah "adh-Dhariyat" in His saying: ﴿Has there come to you the report of the honored guests of Ibrahim?﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 24], and in al-Hijr: ﴿And inform them about the guests of Ibrahim﴾ [al-Hijr: 51].

The second issue: They differed about the meaning of "al-bushra" (the good news) in two ways:
The first: that the meaning is what Allah gave him as good news afterwards, in His saying: ﴿So We gave her the good news of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub.﴾
The second: that the meaning is that he gave Ibrahim (peace be upon him) the good news of the safety of Lut and the destruction of his people.

Page 20

As for His saying: ﴿They said, "Salaman." He said, "Salam."﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "qalu silmun, qala silmun" with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam, without an alif. In "adh-Dhariyat" it is similar. Al-Farra' said: there is no difference between the two readings, just as they say "hill" and "halal," and "haram" and "haram." This is because in the exegesis it is reported that when they came, they greeted him. Abu Ali al-Farisi said: it is possible that "silm" is the opposite of enmity and war, as if when they refrained from taking what he had offered them, he disliked them and felt fear of them, so he said: "I am at peace, and I am not at war or enmity, so do not refrain from eating my food as one refrains from eating the food of an enemy." This view, in my opinion, is far-fetched, because according to this assumption, Ibrahim's speaking with this expression should have been after bringing the food. However, the Qur'an indicates that this speech occurred before the food was brought, because He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They said, "Salaman." He said, "Salam." And he did not delay before bringing a roasted calf﴾, and the fa' indicates sequence, so this shows that his bringing that roasted calf came after the mention of the greeting.

The second issue: ﴿Qalu salaman﴾ its estimated meaning is: "We greet you with a greeting." He said: "Salam," its estimated meaning is: "My matter is peace," meaning: I do not intend anything other than safety and reconciliation. Al-Wahidi said: it is possible that the meaning is: "Salam 'alaykum" (peace be upon you), so he brought it in the nominative case as a report of their statement as they said it, and the predicate was omitted, just as it was omitted in His saying: ﴿So patience is beautiful﴾ [Yusuf: 18]. Such omission is only good when the intended meaning is known after the omission, and here the intended meaning is known, so the omission is indeed good. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿So overlook them and say, "Salam"﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 89], with the predicate omitted.

Know that some of them greeted others only out of regard for the permission mentioned in His saying: ﴿Do not enter houses other than your houses until you seek permission and greet their people﴾ [an-Nur: 27].

The third issue: Most often "Salam 'alaykum" is used without alif and lam, because it carries the meaning of supplication, so it is like their saying: "Good is before you."

If it is said: How is it permissible to make an indefinite noun the subject (mubtada')?
We say: When the indefinite noun is qualified (mawsufa), it is permissible to make it the subject. So when you say "Salam 'alaykum," the indefiniteness in this position indicates completeness and perfection, as if it were said: "A complete, perfect peace be upon you." Its parallel is our saying "Salam 'alayka," and His saying: ﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord"﴾ [Maryam: 47], and His saying: ﴿"Peace," a word from a Lord, Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58], ﴿Peace upon Nuh among the worlds﴾ [as-Saffat: 79], ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 23–24]. As for His saying: ﴿And peace upon those who follow guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47], this is also permissible, and what is meant by it is the essence and reality.

I say: His saying "Salam 'alaykum" [ar-Ra'd: 24] is more complete than saying "as-salamu 'alaykum," because the indefiniteness in "Salam 'alaykum" [ar-Ra'd: 24] indicates perfection, emphasis, and completeness. As for the word "as-salam," it indicates only the reality (mahiyya). Al-Akhfash said: among the Arabs there are those who say "Salam 'alaykum," stripping the word "salam" of alif, lam, and tanwin. The reason for this is that frequency of use permitted this lightening. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So he did not delay before bringing a roasted calf.﴾ They said: Ibrahim had stayed fifteen nights without a guest coming to him, so he was distressed by this. Then the angels came to him, and he saw guests the like of whom he had never seen, so he hurried and brought a roasted calf. So His saying: ﴿he did not delay in bringing it, a roasted calf﴾ means: he did not delay in bringing it, rather he hastened in it. Or the estimated meaning is: his bringing it did not delay. The "'ijl" (calf) is the young of a cow.

As for "hanidh": it is that which is roasted in a pit in the ground with heated stones. This is well known as the practice of the people of the desert. Its original form is "mahnudh" (roasted), just as it is said "tabikh" and "matbukh" (cooked). It was also said: "hanidh" is that whose fat drips, and it is said: "hanadhat al-faras" when you put the saddle cloth on the horse until it drips with sweat.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching toward it﴾, meaning toward the calf. Al-Farra' said: toward the food, and that is the calf. ﴿he disliked them﴾, meaning he found them strange (ankaraha). It is said: "nakiraho," "ankarahu," and "istankarahu" (all meaning he disliked it).

Know that the guests only refrained from the food because they were angels, and angels do not eat or drink. They came to him in the form of guests so that they would be in a state he loves, for he was extremely fond of hospitality. As for Ibrahim (peace be upon him), we say: either it is said that he (peace be upon him) did not know they were angels, but rather believed they were human, or it is said that he knew they were angels. On the first possibility, the cause of his fear is two matters:

One of them: that he would dwell in a remote part of the land far from people, so when they refrained from eating, he feared they intended him some harm. The second: that one who is not known, when he arrives and food is presented to him, if he eats, security is achieved, and if he does not eat, fear is produced.

As for the second possibility, namely that he knew they were the angels of Allah, the cause of his fear on this supposition is also two matters:

One of them: that he feared their descent was for a matter that Allah disapproved of for him.
The second: that he feared their descent was to punish his people.

If it is said: Which of these two possibilities is closer and more apparent?

We say: As for the one who says that he did not know they were the angels of Allah, he may argue with several matters:

One of them: that he hastened to bring the food, and had he known they were angels, he would not have done that.
The second: that when he saw them refraining from eating, he feared them, and had he known they were angels, he would not have inferred evil from their refraining from eating.
The third: that he saw them at first in the form of humans, and that does not indicate that they were angels.

As for the one who says he knew this, he argues by His saying: ﴿Do not fear. We have been sent to the people of Lut﴾, and this is only said to one who knows them but does not know for what cause they were sent. Then the Exalted explained that the angels removed that fear from him, so they said: ﴿Do not fear. We have been sent to the people of Lut﴾, and its meaning is: we have been sent with punishment to the people of Lut, because he (Allah) omitted it, the proof for it being established in another surah, which is His saying: ﴿We have been sent to a people who are criminals﴾ [al-Hijr: 58], ﴿to send upon them stones﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 33].

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And his wife was standing﴾, meaning Sarah, daughter of Azar ibn Bahura, the paternal cousin of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). His saying "standing" (qa'ima): it was said that she was standing behind the curtain listening to the messengers, for perhaps she too was afraid. It was also said: she was standing serving the guests while Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was sitting with them. This interpretation is confirmed by the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-imra'atuhu qa'ima wa-huwa qa'id" (And his wife was standing while he was sitting).

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So she laughed, and We gave her the good news of Ishaq﴾. They differed about the laughing in two views. Some of them took it to be laughter itself, and some of them took this word to have another meaning apart from laughter. As for those who took it to be laughter itself, they differed about why she laughed, and they mentioned several reasons:

The first: al-Qadi said: that cause must necessarily be a cause mentioned in this verse, and that is nothing other than that she rejoiced at the removal of that fear from Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when the angels said: ﴿Do not fear. We have been sent to the people of Lut﴾, and her joy grew because of his joy at the removal of his fear. In such a state a person may laugh. In general, her laughing was because of the angels' saying to Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿Do not fear﴾, so it was like good news, and it was said to her: "We make this good news into two good tidings." Just as good news came through the removal of fear, good news has also come through the birth of the child you have been seeking from the beginning of your life until this time. This interpretation is extremely good.

The second: It is possible that she was greatly outraged at the people of Lut, because of their disbelief and their evil deeds. When they showed that they had come to destroy them, joy came upon her and she laughed.

The third: Al-Suddi said: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said to them: "Will you not eat?" They said: "We do not eat food except for a price." He said: "Its price is that you mention the name of Allah, the Exalted, at its beginning and praise Him at its end." Then Jibril said to Mikail (peace be upon them both): "It is right for a man like this to be taken by his Lord as a close friend (khalil)." So his wife laughed out of joy at this speech.

The fourth: Sarah said to Ibrahim (peace be upon him): "Send for your brother's son and take him to yourself, for Allah, the Exalted, does not leave his people until He punishes them." So when this speech was finished, the angels entered upon Ibrahim (peace be upon him). When they informed him that they had only come to destroy the people of Lut, their statement agreed with hers, so she laughed from the intensity of her joy at the agreement between her speech and the speech of the angels.

We have been sent to the people of Lut﴾, and its meaning is: we have been sent with punishment to the people of Lut, because he (Allah) omitted it, the proof for it being established in another surah, which is His saying: ﴿We have been sent to a people who are criminals﴾ [al-Hijr: 58], ﴿to send upon them stones﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 33].

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And his wife was standing﴾, meaning Sarah, daughter of Azar ibn Bahura, the paternal cousin of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). His saying "standing" (qa'ima): it was said that she was standing behind the curtain listening to the messengers, for perhaps she too was afraid. It was also said: she was standing serving the guests while Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was sitting with them. This interpretation is confirmed by the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-imra'atuhu qa'ima wa-huwa qa'id" (And his wife was standing while he was sitting).

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So she laughed, and We gave her the good news of Ishaq﴾. They differed about the laughing in two views. Some of them took it to be laughter itself, and some of them took this word to have another meaning apart from laughter. As for those who took it to be laughter itself, they differed about why she laughed, and they mentioned several reasons:

The first: al-Qadi said: that cause must necessarily be a cause mentioned in this verse, and that is nothing other than that she rejoiced at the removal of that fear from Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when the angels said: ﴿Do not fear. We have been sent to the people of Lut﴾, and her joy grew because of his joy at the removal of his fear. In such a state a person may laugh. In general, her laughing was because of the angels' saying to Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿Do not fear﴾, so it was like good news, and it was said to her: "We make this good news into two good tidings." Just as good news came through the removal of fear, good news has also come through the birth of the child you have been seeking from the beginning of your life until this time. This interpretation is extremely good.

The second: It is possible that she was greatly outraged at the people of Lut, because of their disbelief and their evil deeds. When they showed that they had come to destroy them, joy came upon her and she laughed.

The third: Al-Suddi said: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said to them: "Will you not eat?" They said: "We do not eat food except for a price." He said: "Its price is that you mention the name of Allah, the Exalted, at its beginning and praise Him at its end." Then Jibril said to Mikail (peace be upon them both): "It is right for a man like this to be taken by his Lord as a close friend (khalil)." So his wife laughed out of joy at this speech.

The fourth: Sarah said to Ibrahim (peace be upon him): "Send for your brother's son and take him to yourself, for Allah, the Exalted, does not leave his people until He punishes them." So when this speech was finished, the angels entered upon Ibrahim (peace be upon him). When they informed him that they had only come to destroy the people of Lut, their statement agreed with hers, so she laughed from the intensity of her joy at the agreement between her speech and the speech of the angels.

The fifth: When the angels informed Ibrahim (peace be upon him) that they were from the angels and not from humans, and that they had only come to destroy the people of Lut, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) asked them for a miracle indicating that they were from the angels. They called upon their Lord to bring the roasted calf back to life, so that roasted calf leapt from the place where it had been placed to its pasture. Ibrahim's wife, who was standing, laughed when she saw that roasted calf leap from its place.

The sixth: She laughed in wonder that a people had been overtaken by punishment while they were heedless.

The seventh: It is not far-fetched to say that they gave her the good news of the birth of a child in general, and she laughed, either out of astonishment, for it is said that at that time she was about ninety-some years old and Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was a hundred years old; or out of joy. Then, when she laughed, Allah the Exalted gave her the good news that this child would be Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub.

The eighth: She laughed because she marvelled at Ibrahim's (peace be upon him) fear of three persons while he had with him his retinue and servants.

The ninth: This is by way of inversion (taqdim and ta'khir), and the meaning is: "and his wife was standing, so We gave her the good news of Ishaq, and she laughed out of joy because of that good news." The laughing has been placed first, though its meaning comes later.

The tenth: The meaning of ﴿fa-dahikat﴾ is: she menstruated. This is related from Mujahid and Ikrimah, who said: ﴿fa-dahikat﴾ means she menstruated, at her joy at being safe from fear. So when her menstruation appeared, she was given the good news of the birth of a child. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda denied that "dahikat" can mean "haydat" (menstruated). Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: If these linguists did not know this usage, others did know it. Al-Layth related concerning this verse that ﴿fa-dahikat﴾ means "tamithat" (she menstruated). Al-Azhari related from some of them that its origin is from "dihak al-tal'a" (the laughing of the spathe of a palm), and it is said: "the spathe laughed" when it split open.

Know that all these aspects are additional, and the correct view is only the first.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾. Concerning this there are two issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and Hafs, from 'Asim, read "Ya'qub" in the accusative (naṣb), and the rest read it in the nominative (raf'). As for the reading in the accusative, the sense is: "We gave her the good news of Ishaq, and after Ishaq We granted her Ya'qub." As for the reading in the nominative, the sense is: "And after Ishaq, Ya'qub is born, or is existent."

The second issue: Concerning the word "wara'" (after/behind) there are two opinions:
The first, which is the view of most scholars, is that its meaning is "after," i.e., after Ishaq comes Ya'qub. This is the apparent meaning.
The second: that "al-wara'" means a grandchild (son of a son). It is related from al-Sha'bi that he was asked, "This is your son?" and he said, "Yes, from the wara'," and he was his grandson. This view, in my opinion, is highly strained, and the wording seems to reject it.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 11, verses 72–73**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this my husband is an old man? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing."﴾ ﴿They said, "Do you wonder at the command of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious."﴾

**Issues concerning the verse:**

**The first issue:** Al-Farra' said: The original form of *al-wayl* (woe) is *way*, which means disgrace (*al-khizy*). It is said, "Way for so-and-so," meaning, "Disgrace upon him." So His saying *waylaka* means, "Disgrace upon you." Sibawayh said: *Waylun* is a warning (*zajr*) to one who has come close to destruction, and *waylun* is for one who has fallen into it. Al-Khalil said: I have not heard in its pattern anything but *wayhun*, *wayka*, and *wayha*, and these words are close in meaning. As for His saying ﴿O woe to me!﴾ (*ya waylata*), some said that this alif is the alif of *al-nudba* (lamenting). The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: The alif in *waylata* is substituted for the *ya'* of possession in *ya waylati*, and likewise in *ya lahafa* and *ya 'ajaba*. Then the alif and the fatha were substituted for the *ya'* and the kasra, because the fatha and the alif are lighter than the *ya'* and the kasra.

As for His saying ﴿Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this my husband is an old man﴾, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr read *a-ālidu* with a hamza and a madda. The rest read it with two hamzas and no madda.

**The second issue:** Someone might say: She marvelled at the power of Allah the Exalted, and marvelling at the power of Allah the Exalted necessitates disbelief. The proof of the first premise is in three aspects:

First: His saying the Exalted, reporting her, in the context of wonder: ﴿Shall I give birth while I am an old woman﴾.

Second: His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is an astonishing thing﴾.

Third: The saying of the angels to her: ﴿Do you wonder at the command of Allah?﴾.

As for the proof that marvelling at the power of Allah the Exalted necessitates disbelief: this wonder indicates her ignorance of the power of Allah the Exalted, and that necessitates disbelief.

The answer: She only marvelled according to custom and habit, not according to power. For if a truthful informant told a Muslim man that Allah the Exalted would turn this mountain into pure gold, there is no doubt that he would marvel, looking at the customary circumstances, not because he denied the power of Allah the Exalted over that.

**The third issue:** His saying ﴿and this my husband is an old man (*shaykhan*)﴾. Know that *shaykhan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: This is one of the subtleties and obscurities of grammar. The word *hadha* is for pointing, so His saying ﴿and this my husband is an old man﴾ is as if it were said: "My husband is pointed to while being in the state of being an old man," and the purpose is to define this particular state, which is old age.

**The fourth issue:** Some read *wa-hādhā baʿlī shaykhun* (with *shaykhun* in the nominative) as being the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is my husband, and he is an old man"; or *baʿlī* is an apposition (*badal*) to the subject, and *shaykhun* is the predicate; or both of them are predicates. Then the Exalted related that the angels said: ﴿Do you wonder at﴾

[p. 24]

﴿the command of Allah?﴾ The meaning is that they marvelled at her marvelling. Then they said: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house﴾. The purpose of this statement is to mention what removes that wonder. Its implied meaning is: Indeed, the mercy of Allah upon you is abundant, and His blessings for you are continuous and successive, and they are prophethood, overwhelming miracles, and divine success in great goods. So when you see that Allah has broken customs in singling you out with these lofty and exalted honours, and in manifesting extraordinary events and producing clear signs and miracles, how is it fitting for you to marvel?

As for His saying ﴿O people of the house﴾, it is a praise for them. It is in the accusative either as a vocative (*nida'*) or as a specification (*ikhtisas*). Then they confirmed that with their saying: ﴿Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious﴾. *Al-Hamid* is the one who is praised, the one whose acts are praised, and *al-Majid* is the glorious (*al-majid*), the one who possesses nobility and generosity. Among the praiseworthy acts is conveying the obedient servant to his desire and his request, and among the kinds of bounty and generosity is that the seeker is not prevented from what he seeks. So when it is known that He the Exalted is capable over all things, and that He is Praiseworthy and Glorious, how can this wonder remain in reality? Thus it is established that the purpose of mentioning these words is the removal of the wonder.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 74–75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the fear had left Abraham and the good news had come to him, he began to plead with Us concerning the people of Lot.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, compassionate, and repentant.﴾

Know that this is the fifth story, the story of Lot, peace be upon him. Know that al-Ra'w (fear) is al-khawf (fear), which is what he felt as apprehension (khifah) when he disapproved of his guests. The meaning is: when the fear had gone and joy had come about through the arrival of the good news of a son, he began to plead with Us concerning the people of Lot. The answer (jawab) to "lamma" (when) is his saying "akhadha" (he began), but it has been omitted from the wording because the context indicates it. It has also been said that its estimated form is: "When fear had left Abraham, he pleaded with Us."

Know that His saying ﴿yujadiluna﴾ (he pleads with Us) means he pleads with Our messengers.

If it is said: if this pleading was with Allah, Exalted is He, then it is audacity toward Allah, and audacity toward Allah is among the greatest sins; and because the purpose of this pleading was to remove that judgment, this indicates that he was not content with the decree of Allah, Exalted is He, and that he disbelieved. And if this pleading was with the angels, it is also strange; because the purpose of this pleading was that they should leave off destroying the people of Lot. If he believed that they were pleading about this destruction of their own accord, this is an ill opinion of them; and if he believed that they had come by the command of Allah, then this pleading implies that he was asking them to oppose the command of Allah, Exalted is He, and this is objectionable.

The answer is in two respects:

The first respect, which is the general answer: He, exalted is He, praised him right after this verse, saying: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, compassionate, and repentant.﴾ Had this pleading been among the sins, what indicates great praise would not have been mentioned after it.

The second respect, which is the detailed answer: the purpose of this pleading was Abraham's effort to delay the punishment from them. This is established in several ways:

The first way: the angels said: ﴿Indeed, We are going to destroy the people of this town﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 31]. Abraham said: "Tell me, if there were fifty righteous believers in it, would you destroy it?" They said: "No." He said: "Forty?" They said: "No." He said: "Thirty?" They said: "No." And so on until he reached ten. They said: "No." He said: "Tell me, if there were a single Muslim in it, would you destroy it?" They said: "No." At that point he said: "Indeed, in it is Lot." Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned this in Surat al-'Ankabut, saying: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with the good news, they said: Indeed, we are going to destroy the people of this town; indeed, its people have been wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿He said: Indeed, in it is Lot. They said: We know best who is in it; we will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is of those who remain behind.﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 31–32].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed for them and felt helpless regarding them, and they said: Do not fear and do not grieve; indeed, we will save you and your family, except your wife﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 33]. Thus it is clear from this that Abraham's pleading concerning the people of Lot was only because of Lot's residence among them.

The second way: It may be said that he, peace be upon him, was inclined that they should be reached by Allah's mercy through the delay of the punishment from them, hoping that they might perhaps embrace faith and repent of their sins. Perhaps those pleadings occurred because Abraham was saying that the command of Allah had come to bring the punishment, and an absolute command does not necessarily require immediacy, but admits of delay; so wait a further period. The angels were saying that an absolute command admits of immediacy, and there were indications there pointing to immediacy. Then each of them began to establish his position with the well-known arguments, and so the pleading took place for this reason. This second way is, in my view, the one relied upon.

The third way in the answer: Perhaps Abraham, peace be upon him, asked about the wording of that command, and that command was conditioned by a condition, so they differed over whether that condition had been met among that people or not, and the pleading took place because of this. In sum, we see scholars in our time pleading with one another when holding to the texts, and that does not entail discrediting any one of them; so it is likewise here.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, compassionate, and repentant.﴾ This is a great praise from Allah, Exalted is He, of Abraham. As for al-Halim (the forbearing), it is the one who does not hasten to requite others, but takes his time with them, so he postpones and pardons; and whoever is of this character loves this manner from others. This is as if it were an indication that his pleading was concerning a matter connected with forbearance and the delay of punishment. Then there was added to this what is related to forbearance, namely His saying: ﴿awwah, munib﴾ (compassionate, repentant); because whoever practices forbearance toward others will groan (yata'awwah) when he witnesses hardships reaching others. So when he saw the coming of the angels to destroy the people of Lot, his grief over that became great, and he began to lament over it; therefore Allah, Exalted is He, described him with this attribute. He also described him as munib (repentant), because whoever shows such great compassion for others will turn back, repent, and return to Allah to remove that punishment from them. Or it may be said: whoever does not accept that others fall into hardships, it is more fitting that he not accept that he himself fall into them; and there is no way to safeguard oneself from falling into the punishment of Allah except through repentance and turning back; so it is obligatory that one whose condition is this be munib.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 76–77:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Ibrahim, turn away from this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, there will reach them a punishment that cannot be turned back.﴾ ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lut, he was distressed for them and felt powerless to protect them, and said, "This is a trying day."﴾
