**Al-Razi's commentary on the verse of Surah Hud (11:78–80):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿His people came rushing towards him, and before that they had been doing evil deeds. He said: "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me regarding my guests. Is there not among you a single man of right judgement?"﴾ ﴿They said: "You know well that we have no right to your daughters, and you know well what we want."﴾ ﴿He said: "If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar."﴾

Concerning this, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** When the angels entered the house of Lut (peace be upon him), his wife, that evil old woman, went off and told his people: "Some people have entered our house whose faces I have never seen to be finer, whose clothes are cleaner, and whose scent is more pleasant than theirs." Then ﴿his people came rushing towards him﴾, meaning they hastened. Allah the Exalted made clear that their hastening was probably in pursuit of the wicked deed, by His saying: ﴿and before that they had been doing evil deeds﴾. It is related that the people entered the house of Lut and wanted to enter the room in which Jibril (peace be upon him) was. Jibril (peace be upon him) placed his hand on the door, so they could not open it until they broke it. Then he wiped their eyes with his hand, and they became blind. They said: "O Lut, you have brought sorcerers upon us and you have stirred up turmoil."

The lexicographers have two opinions regarding ﴿yuhra'una﴾ (they come rushing):

The first opinion: This is one of those cases in which the form of the active verb is used in the form of the passive, with no known agent, like: "Fulan was addicted (ulli'a) to the matter," "Zayd was made to tremble (ur'ida)," and "Amr was made proud (zuhiya)" from *al-zahw* (pride).

The second opinion: It is not permissible for an agent to be expressed in the passive form, and in these verbs the agent has been omitted. So the interpretation of "ulli'a Zayd" is that his nature made him addicted, and "ur'ida al-rajul" means his anger made him tremble, and "zuhiya Amr" means his wealth made him proud. "Uhri'a" means that fear or greed made him rush. They also differed: some said *al-ihrā'* is hastening with trembling, while others said it is a fierce running.

As for His saying: ﴿He said: "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you"﴾, there are two views. Qatadah said: the intended meaning is his own daughters by his loins. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the intended meaning is the women of his community, because they are daughters in themselves, and they are related to him through following him and accepting his call. The grammarians said: slight relationship suffices for a good ascription, because he was a prophet to them, so he was like a father to them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab, 6), and he is a father to them. This view is, in my opinion, the preferred one, and several points support it:

The first: For a man to offer his daughters to the rabble and the wicked is an improbable matter, unbecoming to people of honour, so how much more so for the greatest of the prophets?

The second: He said: ﴿these are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾, and his daughters by his loins would not suffice for a great crowd, whereas the women of his community are sufficient for everyone.

The third: It is soundly reported that he had two daughters, Zanta and Za'ura. Applying the word "daughters" to two girls is not permissible, because it is established that the minimum plural is three. As for those who hold the first view, they agree that he (peace be upon him) did not call the people to fornication with women, but rather that he called them to marry them. Regarding this there are two views:

One: He called them to marry them on condition that they first accept faith.

The second: It was permissible in his law to marry a believing woman to an unbeliever, and this was also the case at the beginning of Islam, as evidenced by the fact that he (ﷺ) married his daughter Zaynab to Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi', who was a polytheist, and he married his daughter to Utba ibn Abi Lahab. Then this was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e. naskh, abrogation) by His saying: ﴿and do not marry polytheist women until they believe﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 221), and by His saying: ﴿and do not marry off polytheist men until they believe﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 221).

They also differed. Most of them said: he had two daughters, and on this assumption he expressed the two with the plural form, as in His saying: ﴿if he has brothers﴾ (Surah al-Nisa', 11), and ﴿for your hearts have inclined﴾ (Surah al-Tahrim, 4). It was also said that they were more than two.

As for His saying: ﴿they are purer for you﴾, there are two issues in it:

[Page 28]

**The first issue:** The apparent sense of His saying ﴿they are purer for you﴾ requires that the act they were seeking be pure, and it is known that it is corrupt. Furthermore, there is no purity in a man's marriage; rather this is like our saying "Allah is greatest," meaning that He is great. Also, consider His saying: ﴿Is that better as a welcome, or the tree of zaqqum?﴾ (Surah al-Saffat, 62), and there is no good in it. When Abu Sufyan said: "Hubal is high," or "Uhud is high," the Prophet said: "Allah is higher and more majestic," and there is no comparison between Allah and an idol.

**The second issue:** It is narrated from Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, al-Hasan, and Isa ibn Umar that they read ﴿hunna atharu lakum﴾ with the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, indicating the state of the subject), as we mentioned regarding His saying: ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾. However, most grammarians agreed that this is an error. They said: if ﴿these are my daughters, they are purer﴾ were read this way, it would be like His saying: ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾, but the word *hunna* ("they") has come in between, and that prevents making *atharu* ("purer") a *ḥāl*. They elaborated on this at length.

Then He said: ﴿so fear Allah and do not disgrace me regarding my guests﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Abu 'Amr and Nafi' read ﴿wa-la tukhzūnī﴾ with the *yā'* (the first person pronoun) kept in, according to the original form, while the rest omit it for lightness and because the kasra indicates it.

**The second issue:** Regarding the expression ﴿la tukhzūnī﴾ there are two aspects:

The first: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "Do not shame me regarding my guests," meaning that if they attacked his guests with what is hateful, disgrace would befall him.

The second: "Do not disgrace me regarding my guest," that is, do not embarrass me before them, because the host of a guest is bound to feel shame at every ugly act that reaches the guest. It is said: "al-rajul khaziya" when he felt shy.

**The third issue:** Here "the guest" (*al-ḍayf*) stands in place of "the guests" (*al-aḍyāf*), just as "the child" (*al-ṭifl*) stands in place of "the children" (*al-aṭfāl*), as in His saying: ﴿or the children who have not yet attained knowledge of hidden parts of women﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 31). It is also permissible for *al-ḍayf* to be a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), in which case there is no need for it to be pluralized, as one says "men fasting" (*rijāl ṣawwam*). Then He said: ﴿Is there not among you a single man of right judgement?﴾ Concerning this there are two views:

The first: "*Rashīd*" means "one who guides," that is, one who speaks the truth and turns these rabble away from my guests.

The second: "*Rashīd*" means "one who is guided," and the meaning is: Is there not among you a man whom Allah the Exalted has guided to righteousness, and made happy with rectitude and right guidance, so that he would prevent this ugly act? The first is preferable.

\* \* \*

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They said: "You know well that we have no right to your daughters"﴾, and concerning this there are several aspects:

The first: "We have no need or desire for your daughters." The reasoning is that whoever is in need of something is as if he has some kind of right to it; therefore for this reason the negation of right is used as a metaphor for the negation of need.

The second: We let the word stand on its apparent meaning, so we say: its meaning is that they are not wives for us, and we have no right to them whatsoever, nor does our nature incline towards them. So how could they stand in place of the act we desire? This is an allusion to the wicked act.

The third: "We have no right to your daughters" because you invited us to marry them on condition of faith, and we will not respond to you in that, so we have no right to them. Then Allah the Exalted related that Lut, on hearing these words, said: ﴿If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar.﴾ Concerning this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** The answer to "law" (*law*, "if only") is omitted, because the context indicates it. The intended meaning is: "I would have prevented you and strongly repelled you." A parallel is His saying: ﴿if only a Qur'an had been such that mountains could be set in motion by it﴾ (Surah al-Ra'd, 31), and His saying: ﴿if only you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ (Surah al-An'am, 27). Al-Wahidi said: the answer is omitted here because the mind goes to many kinds of prevention and repulsion.

[Page 29]

**The second issue:** ﴿If only I had strength against you﴾, that is, if only I had something by which I could be strengthened against you. Calling the cause of strength "strength" is permissible, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Prepare against them whatever you can of strength and of horses held ready﴾ (Surah al-Anfal, 60), and the intended meaning there is weapons. Others said: it means the ability to repel them. As for His saying ﴿or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾, the intended meaning is a fortified, impregnable place, likening it to the strong rock of a mountain.

If it is asked: what is the point here in conjoining a verb to a noun (*ʿaṭf al-fiʿl ʿalā al-ism*)?

We answer: the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: it has been read as ﴿aw āwiya﴾ with the accusative, by implying *an* (that), as if it were said: "If only I had strength against you, or [that] I could take refuge."

Know that His saying ﴿If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾ requires that each of these two statements be understood as having an independent purpose. There are several explanations:

The first: What is meant by ﴿If only I had strength against you﴾ is that he himself be capable of repelling them, and that he be empowered, either by himself or by the help of others, to subdue and discipline them.

And what is meant by ﴿or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾ is that he would have no power to repel them, but he could find a fortress to shelter in, so that he would be safe from their evil by means of it.

The third: When he witnessed the folly of the people and their daring in bad conduct, he wished for the attainment of a powerful strength to repel them. Then he corrected himself and said: "Rather, the better course is that I take refuge in a mighty pillar," which is clinging to the protection of Allah the Exalted. According to this interpretation, His saying ﴿or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾ is a separate statement not connected to what precedes it, and by this way there is no need for conjoining a verb to a noun. For this reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Lut; he used to take refuge in a mighty pillar."

If it is asked: what is the point here in conjoining a verb to a noun (*ʿaṭf al-fiʿl ʿalā al-ism*)?

We answer: the author of *al-Kashshaf* said: it has been read as ﴿aw āwiya﴾ with the accusative, by implying *an* (that), as if it were said: "If only I had strength against you, or [that] I could take refuge."

Know that His saying ﴿If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾ requires that each of these two statements be understood as having an independent purpose. There are several explanations:

The first: What is meant by ﴿If only I had strength against you﴾ is that he himself be capable of repelling them, and that he be empowered, either by himself or by the help of others, to subdue and discipline them.

And what is meant by ﴿or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾ is that he would have no power to repel them, but he could find a fortress to shelter in, so that he would be safe from their evil by means of it.

The third: When he witnessed the folly of the people and their daring in bad conduct, he wished for the attainment of a powerful strength to repel them. Then he corrected himself and said: "Rather, the better course is that I take refuge in a mighty pillar," which is clinging to the protection of Allah the Exalted. According to this interpretation, His saying ﴿or could take refuge in a mighty pillar﴾ is a separate statement not connected to what precedes it, and by this way there is no need for conjoining a verb to a noun. For this reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Lut; he used to take refuge in a mighty pillar."

[Page 27]

**Al-Razi's commentary on the verse of Surah Hud (11:78–80):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿His people came rushing towards him, and before that they had been doing evil deeds. He said: "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me regarding my guests. Is there not among you a single man of right judgement?"﴾ ﴿They said: "You know well that we have no right to your daughters, and you know well what we want."﴾ ﴿He said: "If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a mighty pillar."﴾

Concerning this, there are several issues:

**The first issue:** When the angels entered the house of Lut (peace be upon him), his wife, that evil old woman, went off and told his people: "Some people have entered our house whose faces I have never seen to be finer, whose clothes are cleaner, and whose scent is more pleasant than theirs." Then ﴿his people came rushing towards him﴾, meaning they hastened. Allah the Exalted made clear that their hastening was probably in pursuit of the wicked deed, by His saying: ﴿and before that they had been doing evil deeds﴾. It is related that the people entered the house of Lut and wanted to enter the room in which Jibril (peace be upon him) was. Jibril (peace be upon him) placed his hand on the door, so they could not open it until they broke it. Then he wiped their eyes with his hand, and they became blind. They said: "O Lut, you have brought sorcerers upon us and you have stirred up turmoil."

The lexicographers have two opinions regarding ﴿yuhra'una﴾ (they come rushing):

The first opinion: This is one of those cases in which the form of the active verb is used in the form of the passive, with no known agent, like: "Fulan was addicted (ulli'a) to the matter," "Zayd was made to tremble (ur'ida)," and "Amr was made proud (zuhiya)" from *al-zahw* (pride).

The second opinion: It is not permissible for an agent to be expressed in the passive form, and in these verbs the agent has been omitted. So the interpretation of "ulli'a Zayd" is that his nature made him addicted, and "ur'ida al-rajul" means his anger made him tremble, and "zuhiya Amr" means his wealth made him proud. "Uhri'a" means that fear or greed made him rush. They also differed: some said *al-ihrā'* is hastening with trembling, while others said it is a fierce running.

As for His saying: ﴿He said: "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you"﴾, there are two views. Qatadah said: the intended meaning is his own daughters by his loins. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the intended meaning is the women of his community, because they are daughters in themselves, and they are related to him through following him and accepting his call. The grammarians said: slight relationship suffices for a good ascription, because he was a prophet to them, so he was like a father to them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab, 6), and he is a father to them. This view is, in my opinion, the preferred one, and several points support it:

The first: For a man to offer his daughters to the rabble and the wicked is an improbable matter, unbecoming to people of honour, so how much more so for the greatest of the prophets?

The second: He said: ﴿these are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾, and his daughters by his loins would not suffice for a great crowd, whereas the women of his community are sufficient for everyone.

The third: It is soundly reported that he had two daughters, Zanta and Za'ura. Applying the word "daughters" to two girls is not permissible, because it is established that the minimum plural is three. As for those who hold the first view, they agree that he (peace be upon him) did not call the people to fornication with women, but rather that he called them to marry them. Regarding this there are two views:

One: He called them to marry them on condition that they first accept faith.

The second: It was permissible in his law to marry a believing woman to an unbeliever, and this was also the case at the beginning of Islam, as evidenced by the fact that he (ﷺ) married his daughter Zaynab to Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi', who was a polytheist, and he married his daughter to Utba ibn Abi Lahab. Then this was abrogated (*nusikha*, i.e. naskh, abrogation) by His saying: ﴿and do not marry polytheist women until they believe﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 221), and by His saying: ﴿and do not marry off polytheist men until they believe﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 221).

They also differed. Most of them said: he had two daughters, and on this assumption he expressed the two with the plural form, as in His saying: ﴿if he has brothers﴾ (Surah al-Nisa', 11), and ﴿for your hearts have inclined﴾ (Surah al-Tahrim, 4). It was also said that they were more than two.

As for His saying: ﴿they are purer for you﴾, there are two issues in it:

[Page 28]

**The first issue:** The apparent sense of His saying ﴿they are purer for you﴾ requires that the act they were seeking be pure, and it is known that it is corrupt. Furthermore, there is no purity in a man's marriage; rather this is like our saying "Allah is greatest," meaning that He is great. Also, consider His saying: ﴿Is that better as a welcome, or the tree of zaqqum?﴾ (Surah al-Saffat, 62), and there is no good in it. When Abu Sufyan said: "Hubal is high," or "Uhud is high," the Prophet said: "Allah is higher and more majestic," and there is no comparison between Allah and an idol.

**The second issue:** It is narrated from Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, al-Hasan, and Isa ibn Umar that they read ﴿hunna atharu lakum﴾ with the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative, indicating the state of the subject), as we mentioned regarding His saying: ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾. However, most grammarians agreed that this is an error. They said: if ﴿these are my daughters, they are purer﴾ were read this way, it would be like His saying: ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾, but the word *hunna* ("they") has come in between, and that prevents making *atharu* ("purer") a *ḥāl*. **The second issue:** Regarding the expression ﴿la tukhzūnī﴾ there are two aspects:

The second: "Do not disgrace me regarding my guest," that is, do not embarrass me before them, because the host of a guest is bound to feel shame at every ugly act that reaches the guest. It is said: "al-rajul khaziya" when he felt shy.

**The third issue:** Here "the guest" (*al-ḍayf*) stands in place of "the guests" (*al-aḍyāf*), just as "the child" (*al-ṭifl*) stands in place of "the children" (*al-aṭfāl*), as in His saying: ﴿or the children who have not yet attained knowledge of hidden parts of women﴾ (Surah al-Nur, 31). It is also permissible for *al-ḍayf* to be a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), in which case there is no need for it to be pluralized, as one says "men fasting" (*rijāl ṣawwam*). Then He said: ﴿Is there not among you a single man of right judgement?﴾ Concerning this there are two views:

The first: "*Rashīd*" means "one who guides," that is, one who speaks the truth and turns these rabble away from my guests.

The second: "*Rashīd*" means "one who is guided," and the meaning is: Is there not among you a man whom Allah the Exalted has guided to righteousness, and made happy with rectitude and right guidance, so that he would prevent this ugly act? The first is preferable.

\* \* \*

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 81–82:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They said, "O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So travel with your family during a portion of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife. Indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them. Indeed, their appointment is the morning. Is not the morning near?"﴾.

Know that the words of Allah the Exalted, reporting about Lot (peace be upon him) that he said: ﴿If only I had against you some strength or could take refuge in a strong support﴾, indicate that he was in extreme distress and grief, because of the boldness of those rabble in doing what would bring disgrace regarding his guests. When the angels saw that state, they gave him glad tidings of several kinds:

The first: that they are the messengers of Allah.

The second: that the disbelievers will not reach what they intended.

The third: that Allah will destroy them.

The fourth: that Allah will save him and his family from that punishment.

The fifth: that your support is strong, and your helper is Allah the Exalted. Thus he received these glad tidings. It is narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) said to him: "Indeed your people will never reach you, so open the door." They entered, and Jibril (peace be upon him) struck their faces with his wing and obliterated their eyes, blinding them, so they could no longer recognize the way nor find their houses. This is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And they had already sought to seduce him away from his guests, so We obliterated their eyes﴾ [al-Qamar: 37]. The meaning of His saying: ﴿they will never reach you﴾ is: with evil or harm, for We shall prevent them from that.

Then He said: ﴿So travel with your family﴾. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "fa-sri" with a connected (waṣl) alif, while the rest read it with a cut (qat') alif. Both are dialectal forms: it is said "saraytu bi'l-layl" and "asraytu", and Hassan recited:

"They traveled to you, and she had not been traveling [before]"

He brought both forms. Whoever reads with the cut alif has as his proof the saying of Allah, glorified and exalted: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night (asra bi-'abdihi)﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Whoever reads with the connected alif has as his proof His saying: ﴿And by the night when it passes (idha yasri)﴾ [al-Fajr: 4]. Al-Sura means travel at night; it is said "sara yasri" when one travels by night, and "asra bi-fulan" when someone is made to travel by night. Al-qit' min al-layl is a portion of it, and it is like al-qit'a (a piece). The meaning is: depart by night so that you may get ahead of the descent of the punishment whose appointment is the morning. Nafi' ibn al-Azraq said to Abdullah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Inform me about the saying of Allah, ﴿during a portion of the night﴾." He said: "It is the last part of the night, before dawn." Qatada said: "After a part of the night." Others said: "It is the middle of the night, for at that time it was cut into two halves."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and let none of you look back﴾. He forbade those with him from looking back (al-iltifat). Al-iltifat is a person's looking at what is behind him. The apparent meaning is that they had in the town wealth, goods and friends, so the angels commanded them to leave and abandon those things, not turning to them at all. The intended meaning is the severing of the heart from those things. It may also mean turning away, as in His saying: ﴿They said, "Have you come to us to turn us away (litaltifana)?"﴾ [Yunus: 78], i.e., to turn us away. On this interpretation, the meaning of ﴿and let none of you look back﴾ is the prohibition of lagging behind.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿except your wife﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "illa imra'atuka" with a nominative ending (raf'), while the rest read it with an accusative ending (nasb). Al-Wahidi said: whoever reads with the accusative, which is the preferred reading, has made her an exception from "your family", meaning: "So travel with your family, except your wife." What confirms the soundness of this reading is that in the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it is "fa-asri bi-ahlika illa imra'ataka", where he omitted the phrase "and let none of you look back" from this place. As for those who read with the nominative, the sense is: "and let none of you look back, except your wife."

If it is said: this reading necessitates that she was commanded to look back, because when one says, "Let none of you stand up except Zayd," it is a command to Zayd to stand up.

Abu Bakr al-Anbari answered this, saying: the meaning of "illa" here is the disjunctive exception (al-istithna' al-munqati'), in the sense of: "let none of you look back, but your wife does look back, so what befalls them will befall her." When this exception is disjunctive, her looking back is an act of disobedience. What we have mentioned is reinforced by what is narrated from Qatada, that he said: she was with Lot when he left the town, and when she heard of this punishment she turned back and said: "O my people!" So a stone struck her and destroyed her.

Know that the reading with the nominative is stronger, because the reading with the accusative prevents her from leaving with his family. But on this interpretation the exception is from "the family", as if he had commanded Lot to leave with his family and abandon this woman, for she is destroyed along with those who are destroyed. As for the reading with the accusative, it is stronger in another respect, namely that with the accusative reading the exception remains connected, whereas with the nominative reading the exception becomes disjunctive.

Then Allah the Exalted made clear that they said: ﴿Indeed, what strikes them will strike her.﴾ The meaning is that the same punishment that struck them will strike her. Then they said: ﴿Indeed, their appointment is the morning.﴾ It is narrated that when they said to Lot (peace be upon him): "Indeed their appointment is the morning," he said: "I wish it were sooner than that, rather now." They said: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ The exegetes said: when Lot (peace be upon him) heard this speech, he went out with his family during the night.

**[Page 32]**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon it stones of hardened clay, layered, marked from your Lord. And they are not far from the wrongdoers.﴾

There are several issues in the verse.

**The first issue: the "command" (al-amr).** There are two views.

The first view is that the command here means what is the opposite of prohibition. This is supported by several considerations.

The first: the word *amr* has this meaning as its real (ḥaqīqa) meaning, and its other meanings are figurative (majāz), in order to avoid homonymy (ishtirāk).

The second: the command cannot be taken here to mean the punishment. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest﴾, and this "making" is the punishment. So this verse shows that the command is a condition (sharṭ) and the punishment is the consequence (jazā'), and the condition is other than the consequence. Therefore this command is other than the punishment. Everyone who holds this view says that it is the command that is the opposite of prohibition.

The third: God, exalted is He, said before this verse: ﴿We were sent to the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 70]. This indicates that they were commanded by God, exalted is He, to go to the people of Lot and to bring this punishment to them.

Having understood this, we say: God, exalted is He, commanded a group of angels to overturn those cities at a specified time. When that time came, they proceeded to carry out that act. So His saying ﴿When Our command came﴾ refers to that assignment.

If it is said: if the matter were so, it would have been necessary to say: "When Our command came, they made its highest part its lowest," because the act proceeded from those who were commanded.

We answer: this does not follow according to our school, because the act of the servant is the act of God, exalted is He, according to us. Also, what occurred from them occurred by the command of God, exalted is He, and by His power. So it is not remote to attribute it to God, Mighty and Majestic; for just as an act may rightly be attributed to the one who directly performs it, it may also rightly be attributed to the cause.

The second view: the intended meaning of the command here is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Naḥl: 40]. The explanation of that command has already been given.

The third view: the intended meaning of the command is the punishment. On this interpretation, an ellipsis (iḍmār) is required, and the meaning is: "When the time of Our punishment came, We made its highest part its lowest."

**The second issue: the description of that punishment.** You should know that God, exalted is He, described that punishment in this verse with two kinds of description.

The first: His saying: ﴿We made its highest part its lowest﴾. It is narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) inserted one of his wings beneath the cities of the people of Lot, uprooted them, and ascended with them to the heavens, until the people of the heavens heard the braying of donkeys, the barking of dogs, and the crowing of roosters. No jar was overturned for them, and no vessel was upset for them. Then he turned them over in one single motion and struck them down upon the earth.

You should know that this act was an overpowering miracle (muʿjiza qāhira) in two respects.

One of them: uprooting the earth and raising it up to near the heavens is an act that breaks ordinary custom (khāriq li-l-ʿādāt).

The second: striking it from that great distance upon the earth in such a way that the other surrounding villages were not moved at all, and the calamity did not reach Lot (peace be upon him) and his household, despite their nearness to that place, is also an overpowering miracle.

The second: His saying: ﴿and We rained upon it stones of hardened clay﴾. The scholars differ about *sijjīl* in several respects.

The first: it is a Persian word that has been Arabicized (muʿarrab), and its origin is *sankil*, and it is a thing composed of stone and clay, on condition that it be extremely hard. Al-Azhari said: when the Arabs Arabicized it, it became Arabic, and the Arabs Arabicized many words, such as *dībāj* (brocade), *dīwān* (register), and *istabraq* (silk brocade).

The second: *sijjīl* is like *sajl*, which is a large bucket.

The third: *sijjīl* means hard stones.

The fourth: it is "sent down upon them," from *asjaltuhu*, when you send it, and it is a *faʿīl* form from it.

The fifth: from *asjaltuhu*, meaning I gave it, its sense being: like a gift in abundance. It has also been said: names of those to be punished were written upon them.

The sixth: it is from *sijill*, which is a register (kitāb). Its sense is: from what is written in eternity, meaning God decreed that He would punish them with them. And *sijjīl* is taken from *sajl*, which is a large bucket, because it contains many rulings. It has also been said that it is taken from *musājala*, which is boasting (mufākhara).

The seventh: *min sijjīl* means "from Jahannam," with the *nūn* changed to *lām*.

The eighth: it is from the lowest heaven, and it is called *sijjīl* according to Abu Zayd.

The ninth: *sijjīl* is clay, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿stones of clay﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 33]. This is the view of ʿIkrima and Qatada. Al-Hasan said: the origin of the stone was clay, but it became hard with the passage of time.

The tenth: *sijjīl* is the place of the stones, and they are specific mountains. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from mountains in which is hail﴾ [al-Nūr: 43].

You should know that He, exalted is He, described those stones with attributes:

The first attribute: that they are of *sijjīl*, which has already been mentioned.

The second attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿layered (manḍūd)﴾. Al-Wahidi said: it is a passive participle from *naḍd*, which is the placing of one thing upon another. Concerning it there are several views:

The first: those stones were, in their descent, some above others, and this was expressed in an emphatic manner.

The second: every stone, the parts within it are layered, some upon others, and joined to one another.

The third: God, exalted is He, had created them in their mines and layered some of them upon others, and prepared them for the destruction of the wrongdoers.

You should know that His saying ﴿manḍūd﴾ is an attribute of *sijjīl*.

The third attribute: *musawwama* (marked). This attribute is an attribute of the stones, and its meaning is "marked." The discussion of it has already passed in the explanation of His saying: ﴿and the marked (musawwama) horses﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 14]. They differed about the manner of that mark, in several views:

The first: al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: upon them were the likenesses of signet rings.

The second: Ibn Salih said: I saw among them, with Umm Hani, stones in which there were red lines in the form of onyx (jiz').

The third: Ibn Juraij said: upon them was a sign which the stones of the earth do not share, and which indicates that God, exalted is He, created them only for punishment.

The fourth: al-Rabiʿ said: upon every stone was written the name of the one it was to be cast at.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿from your Lord﴾, meaning: in His treasuries, which no one disposes of except Him.

Then He said: ﴿And they are not far from the wrongdoers﴾. By this He means the disbelievers of Makkah, and the purpose is that He casts them with these stones. It is narrated from Anas that he said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked Jibril (peace be upon him) about this," and he said: "It refers to the wrongdoers of your community. There is no wrongdoer among them except that he is in the path of a stone that falls upon him from one hour to another."

It has also been said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿and it﴾ refers to the cities. That is: those cities in which this event occurred are not far from the disbelievers of Makkah. This is because those cities were in al-Sham, and it is near Makkah.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 84–86:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. And do not diminish from the measure and the scale. Indeed, I see you in prosperity, and indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day."﴾ ﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice, and do not deprive the people of their due and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption.﴾ ﴿What remains [with you] from Allah is better for you, if you are [truly] believers. And I am not a guardian over you.﴾

Know that this is the sixth of the stories mentioned in this surah. Know also that Madyan (Madyan) is the name of a son of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and then it became the name of the tribe. Many of the exegetes (mufassirun) hold that Madyan is the name of a city built by Madyan ibn Ibrahim (peace be upon him). The meaning according to this reading is: "And We sent [to] the people of Madyan," so the word "the people" (al-ahl) has been omitted.

Know that we have explained that the prophets (peace be upon them) begin, at the outset, by calling to monotheism (tawhid). Therefore Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) said: ﴿you have no deity other than Him﴾. Then, after calling to monotheism, they proceed to what is more important and then to what is more important still. Since the customary practice of the people of Madyan was cheating in the measure and the scale, he called them to abandon this habit, and said: ﴿And do not diminish from the measure and the scale﴾. Diminishing in this has two aspects:

The first: that the giving (of the measure) is from their side, so they reduce its quantity.

The second: that they have the taking, so they take more than what is due, and this entails the diminishing of the right of another. In both cases, diminution occurs in the right of another. Then he said: ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾, and in this there are two views:

The first: that he warned them of the rise of prices and the loss of blessing if they did not repent; it is as if he said: "Abandon this cheating, or else Allah will remove from you what good and comfort you have."

The second: that the meaning is that Exalted Allah has brought you abundant good, wealth, cheapness and plenty, so you have no need for this cheating. Then he said: ﴿And indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day﴾, and concerning this there are several discussions:

The first discussion: Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "I fear" means "I know that the punishment of an all-encompassing Day will occur." Others said: rather, what is meant is fear, because they may abandon that practice out of dread that punishment will befall them; and since this warning was ongoing, what is attained is conjecture (zann), not certainty (ilm).

The second discussion: He, Exalted, threatened them with a punishment that would encompass them such that none would escape from it. The word "all-encompassing" (muhit) is, outwardly, a description of the Day, but in meaning it is a description of the punishment; and this is a well-known figurative usage, like His saying: ﴿This is a distressful day﴾ [Hud: 77].

Page 34
The third discussion: they differed about what is meant by this punishment. Some said: it is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, because it is the Day established for the encompassing of punishment upon those who are punished. Some said: rather, it includes the punishment of this world and the Hereafter. Some said: rather, what is meant is the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal) in this world, as in the case of all the other prophets. The closest view is that every punishment is included in it, and the encompassing of punishment around them is like the encompassing of a circle around what is inside it, so that it reaches them from every side; and this is an intensification in the threat, like His saying: ﴿and its fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Then he said: ﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice﴾.

If it is said: repetition occurred in this verse in three ways, for he first said: ﴿And do not diminish from the measure and the scale﴾, then he said: ﴿give full measure and weight﴾, which is the very same as the first; then he said: ﴿and do not deprive the people of their due﴾, which is the very same as what preceded. So what is the benefit of this repetition?

We say: there are several aspects to it:

The first aspect: the people were persisting in that practice, so in forbidding it there was need for emphasis and insistence, and repetition conveys emphasis and intensity of concern and attention.

The second aspect: his saying ﴿And do not diminish from the measure and the scale﴾ is a prohibition against diminishing, while his saying ﴿give full measure and weight﴾ is a command to give what is just, and prohibition of the opposite of a thing is distinct from a command to it. It is not open to a speaker to say: the prohibition of the opposite of a thing is a command to it. So repetition would be necessary from this aspect. We reply: the answer is from two aspects:

The first: He, Exalted, combined the command to a thing with the prohibition of its opposite for emphasis, as you say: "Maintain your kinship ties and do not cut them off," and this combination indicates the utmost emphasis.

The second: We say: we do not grant that the command is as you described; for it is permissible that He forbids diminishing and also forbids the very principle of dealing, so He, Exalted, forbade diminishing and commanded the giving of what is due, in order to show that He, Exalted, did not forbid transactions and did not prohibit sales; rather He forbade only cheating. This is because a group of people say that transactions cannot be free of cheating and withholding of rights, so transactions would be entirely forbidden; to dispel this illusion, He, Exalted, forbade cheating in the first verse and commanded full giving in the other. As for His third saying, ﴿and do not deprive the people of their due﴾, it is not a repetition; for He, Exalted, restricted the prohibition in the preceding verse to diminution in the measure and the scale, and then He generalized the ruling to all things. Thus it is clear from this explanation that they are not repeated; rather, each carries an additional benefit.

The third aspect: He, Exalted, said in the first verse: ﴿And do not diminish from the measure and the scale﴾, and in the second He said: ﴿give full measure and weight﴾. Giving in full (iyfa') is an expression for bringing it in a manner of completeness and perfection, and this is not attained except by giving an amount beyond what is due. For this reason the jurists said: He, Exalted, commanded the washing of the face, and this is not attained except by washing a part of the parts of the head. The conclusion is: in the first verse He, Exalted, forbade diminution, and in the second He commanded the giving of an amount of excess; and certainty and assurance of discharging the obligation are not attained except by giving that excess. It is as if He, Exalted, first forbade a person's striving to make another's property deficient so that he might gain that excess, and in the second commanded striving to diminish one's own property so as to exit the obligation with certainty.

His saying ﴿with justice﴾ means with fairness, and its meaning is the command to give what is due in such a way that certainty of having discharged the obligation is attained with it; so the command to give an excess beyond that is not implied. Then He said: ﴿and do not deprive the people of their due﴾; and "deprivation" (bakhs) is diminution in all things. We have stated that the first verse indicated the prohibition of diminution

Page 35
in the measure and the scale, and this verse indicates the prohibition of diminution in all things. Then He said: ﴿and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾.

If it is said: "'Athw" means complete corruption, so His saying ﴿and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾ runs in the manner of saying: "and do not corrupt on the earth, being corrupters."

We say: there are several views on this:

The first: whoever strives to bring harm to another has caused that other to strive to bring harm to him; so His saying ﴿and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾ means: "do not strive to corrupt the interests of others," for that in reality is your striving to corrupt the interests of yourselves.

The second: what is meant by His saying ﴿and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾ is the interests of your worldly life and your Hereafter.

The third: "and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption of the interests of the religions."

Then He said: ﴿What remains [with you] from Allah is better for you﴾. It was recited as "taqiyyat Allah," and it is His piety and His watchfulness that turns one away from sins. Then we say: the meaning is: what Allah has left for you of lawful gain after giving full measure and weight is better than deprivation and cheating; that is, the lawful wealth that remains for you is better than that excess gained by way of deprivation and cheating. Al-Hasan said: "baqiyyat Allah" means: the obedience to Allah is better for you than that small amount, because the reward of obedience remains forever. Qatadah said: "your portion from your Lord is better for you." I say: what is meant by this remainder is either the wealth that remains for one in this world, or the reward of Allah, or His being pleased with him, and all of these are better than the amount gained by cheating. As for lasting wealth: when people know a person for truthfulness, trustworthiness and distance from treachery, they rely upon him and return to him in all their dealings, so the door of provision is opened for him; and when they know him for treachery and deceit, they turn away from him and do not deal with him at all, so the doors of provision are narrowed for him. As for taking this remainder as reward, the matter is clear, for all of this world perishes and passes away, while Allah's reward is enduring. As for taking it as attaining the pleasure of Exalted Allah, the matter in it is clear. Thus it is established by this proof that the remainder of Allah is better. Then He said: ﴿if you are [truly] believers﴾. He made faith a condition for it being good for them only because, if they are believers who acknowledge reward and punishment, they know that striving to attain reward and to guard against punishment is better for them than striving for that small amount.

Know that what is conditioned upon a condition is absent when the condition is absent. Thus this verse indicates outwardly that whoever does not refrain from this cheating is not a believer.

Then Exalted Allah said: ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾, and concerning this there are two views:

The first: the meaning is: I have advised you and guided you to good, ﴿and I am not a guardian over you﴾, that is, I have no power to prevent you from this ugly action.

Some said: rather, it includes the punishment of this world and the Hereafter. Some said: rather, what is meant is the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal) in this world, as in the case of all the other prophets. The closest view is that every punishment is included in it, and the encompassing of punishment around them is like the encompassing of a circle around what is inside it, so that it reaches them from every side; and this is an intensification in the threat, like His saying: ﴿and its fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Then he said: ﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight in justice﴾.

If it is said: repetition occurred in this verse in three ways, for he first said: ﴿And do not diminish from the measure and the scale﴾, then he said: ﴿give full measure and weight﴾, which is the very same as the first; then he said: ﴿and do not deprive the people of their due﴾, which is the very same as what preceded. So what is the benefit of this repetition?

We say: there are several aspects to it:

The first aspect: the people were persisting in that practice, so in forbidding it there was need for emphasis and insistence, and repetition conveys emphasis and intensity of concern and attention.

The second aspect: his saying ﴿And do not diminish from the measure and the scale﴾ is a prohibition against diminishing, while his saying ﴿give full measure and weight﴾ is a command to give what is just, and prohibition of the opposite of a thing is distinct from a command to it. It is not open to a speaker to say: the prohibition of the opposite of a thing is a command to it. So repetition would be necessary from this aspect. We reply: the answer is from two aspects:

The first: He, Exalted, combined the command to a thing with the prohibition of its opposite for emphasis, as you say: "Maintain your kinship ties and do not cut them off," and this combination indicates the utmost emphasis.

The second: We say: we do not grant that the command is as you described; for it is permissible that He forbids diminishing and also forbids the very principle of dealing, so He, Exalted, forbade diminishing and commanded the giving of what is due, in order to show that He, Exalted, did not forbid transactions and did not prohibit sales; rather He forbade only cheating. This is because a group of people say that transactions cannot be free of cheating and withholding of rights, so transactions would be entirely forbidden; to dispel this illusion, He, Exalted, forbade cheating in the first verse and commanded full giving in the other. As for His third saying, ﴿and do not deprive the people of their due﴾, it is not a repetition; for He, Exalted, restricted the prohibition in the preceding verse to diminution in the measure and the scale, and then He generalized the ruling to all things. Thus it is clear from this explanation that they are not repeated; rather, each carries an additional benefit.

The third aspect: He, Exalted, said in the first verse: ﴿And do not diminish from the measure and the scale﴾, and in the second He said: ﴿give full measure and weight﴾. Giving in full (iyfa') is an expression for bringing it in a manner of completeness and perfection, and this is not attained except by giving an amount beyond what is due. For this reason the jurists said: He, Exalted, commanded the washing of the face, and this is not attained except by washing a part of the parts of the head. The conclusion is: in the first verse He, Exalted, forbade diminution, and in the second He commanded the giving of an amount of excess; and certainty and assurance of discharging the obligation are not attained except by giving that excess. It is as if He, Exalted, first forbade a person's striving to make another's property deficient so that he might gain that excess, and in the second commanded striving to diminish one's own property so as to exit the obligation with certainty.

His saying ﴿with justice﴾ means with fairness, and its meaning is the command to give what is due in such a way that certainty of having discharged the obligation is attained with it; so the command to give an excess beyond that is not implied. Then He said: ﴿and do not deprive the people of their due﴾; and "deprivation" (bakhs) is diminution in all things. We have stated that the first verse indicated the prohibition of diminution

Page 35
in the measure and the scale, and this verse indicates the prohibition of diminution in all things. Then He said: ﴿and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾.

If it is said: "'Athw" means complete corruption, so His saying ﴿and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾ runs in the manner of saying: "and do not corrupt on the earth, being corrupters."

We say: there are several views on this:

The first: whoever strives to bring harm to another has caused that other to strive to bring harm to him; so His saying ﴿and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾ means: "do not strive to corrupt the interests of others," for that in reality is your striving to corrupt the interests of yourselves.

The second: what is meant by His saying ﴿and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption﴾ is the interests of your worldly life and your Hereafter.

The third: "and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption of the interests of the religions."

Then He said: ﴿What remains [with you] from Allah is better for you﴾. It was recited as "taqiyyat Allah," and it is His piety and His watchfulness that turns one away from sins. Then we say: the meaning is: what Allah has left for you of lawful gain after giving full measure and weight is better than deprivation and cheating; that is, the lawful wealth that remains for you is better than that excess gained by way of deprivation and cheating. Al-Hasan said: "baqiyyat Allah" means: the obedience to Allah is better for you than that small amount, because the reward of obedience remains forever. Qatadah said: "your portion from your Lord is better for you." I say: what is meant by this remainder is either the wealth that remains for one in this world, or the reward of Allah, or His being pleased with him, and all of these are better than the amount gained by cheating. As for lasting wealth: when people know a person for truthfulness, trustworthiness and distance from treachery, they rely upon him and return to him in all their dealings, so the door of provision is opened for him; and when they know him for treachery and deceit, they turn away from him and do not deal with him at all, so the doors of provision are narrowed for him. As for taking this remainder as reward, the matter is clear, for all of this world perishes and passes away, while Allah's reward is enduring. As for taking it as attaining the pleasure of Exalted Allah, the matter in it is clear. Thus it is established by this proof that the remainder of Allah is better. Then He said: ﴿if you are [truly] believers﴾. He made faith a condition for it being good for them only because, if they are believers who acknowledge reward and punishment, they know that striving to attain reward and to guard against punishment is better for them than striving for that small amount.

Know that what is conditioned upon a condition is absent when the condition is absent. Thus this verse indicates outwardly that whoever does not refrain from this cheating is not a believer.

* * *

Then Exalted Allah said: ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾, and concerning this there are two views:

The first: the meaning is: I have advised you and guided you to good, ﴿and I am not a guardian over you﴾, that is, I have no power to prevent you from this ugly action.

The second: he had indicated earlier that engaging in deprivation and cheating entails the loss of Allah's blessing; so he said: ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾, meaning: if you do not abandon this ugly action, Allah's blessings will depart from you, and I am not able to preserve them for you in that state.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 87:

Page 36

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we should leave what our fathers worshipped, or that we should not do with our wealth what we wish? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning."﴾

There are several issues (masa'il) in this verse:

The first issue: Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from ʿAsim recited "aṣalātuka" (أصلاتك) without a waw. The rest recited "aṣalawātuka" (أصلواتك) in the plural.

The second issue: Know that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, commanded them with two things: monotheism (tawhid) and refraining from defrauding (bakhs). The people objected to his command regarding these two kinds of obedience. So his saying, ﴿that we should leave what our fathers worshipped﴾, is an indication that he commanded them to monotheism, and his saying, ﴿or that we should not do with our wealth what we wish﴾, is an indication that he commanded them to abandon defrauding.

As for the first, they indicated in it an adherence to the way of blind imitation (taqlid), because they considered it far-fetched that he should command them to abandon the worship of what their fathers used to worship, meaning: how can we abandon the path we took from our fathers and forebears? That is adherence to pure imitation.

The third issue: concerning the word "ṣalāh" (prayer), there are two opinions here:

The first: what is meant by it is religion and faith, because prayer is the most prominent emblem of religion, so they used the mention of prayer as a metaphor (kinayah) for religion. Or we may say: the root of ṣalāh is from following (ittiba'), and from it is derived the "muṣalli" among horses, which follows the leader, because its head is at the "ṣilwayy" of the leader, which are the two sides of the thighs. The meaning is: your religion commands you with this.

The second: that what is meant by it is these specific acts. It is narrated that Shu'ayb used to pray much, and when his people saw him praying, they winked at one another and laughed. By their saying, "does your prayer command you," they intended mockery and derision. Just as when you see a fool who studies books and then utters corrupt speech, and it is said to him, "this is from studying those books," in a spirit of ridicule and derision, so too here.

If it is said: the construction of the verse is: "Do your prayers command you that we should not do with our wealth what we wish?" and they only mentioned this statement as a form of denial, yet they did not deny that they were free to do with their wealth as they wished. How then is the interpretation?

We say: there are two aspects to this:

The first: the construction is: "Do your prayers command you that we should leave what our fathers worshipped, and that we should leave doing what we wish?" According to this, his saying, ﴿or that we should do﴾ is conjoined to what is in his saying, ﴿what our fathers worshipped﴾.

The second: that the prayer is made to command and forbid. The construction is: "Do your prayers command you to leave the worship of idols, and forbid you that we should do with our wealth what we wish?" Ibn Abi ʿAblah recited: "aw an tafʿala fi amwalina ma tashaʾ" (أو أن تفعل في أموالنا ما تشاء) with the second-person ta' in both places, which is what he used to command them: to abandon cheating and defrauding, to be content with lawful little, and that this is better than abundant unlawful gain.

Then He, exalted, said, relating about them: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning.﴾ In this there are several aspects:

The first aspect: the meaning is: "Indeed, you are the foolish, the ignorant," but they reversed this as a form of mockery and derision toward him, just as it is said to a miser who is base: "If Hatim saw you, he would prostrate to you."

The second aspect: the meaning is: you are described, in your own estimation and in the estimation of your people, as forbearing and discerning.

The third aspect: he, peace be upon him, was well known among them as forbearing and discerning. So when he commanded them to part from their way, they said to him: "Indeed, you are the forbearing, the discerning, known for your way in this matter; how can you forbid us from a religion we found our fathers and forebears upon?" The intent is to deem such an act far-fetched from one described as forbearing and discerning. And this aspect is the most correct of the aspects.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 88–90:

﴿He said, "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me good provision from Himself, [then how could I betray Him?] And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from. I intend only reform, as far as I am able. My success is only through Allah. Upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn back."﴾ ﴿"And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to incur what befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih. And the people of Lot are not far from you."﴾ ﴿"And seek forgiveness from your Lord, then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving."﴾

There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: Know that He, exalted is He, related what Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) said in reply to their statements. The first is his saying: ﴿Tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me good provision from Himself,﴾ and in it there are several aspects:

The first: His saying ﴿if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ refers to what Allah gave him of knowledge, guidance, religion and prophethood. His saying ﴿and He has given me good provision from Himself﴾ refers to the lawful wealth Allah gave him, for it is related that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) had much wealth.

Know that the answer to the conditional particle ﴿in﴾ (if) is omitted, and the implied meaning is: since Allah has given me all the spiritual blessings, which is the clear evidence, and the physical blessings, which are wealth and good provision, how could it befit me, with this great favour, to betray His revelation and to oppose His command and prohibition? This answer closely corresponds to what came before, because they had said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾. How then could it befit you, with your forbearance and your rectitude, to forbid us from the religion of our fathers? It is as if he said: I only undertook this action because the blessings of Allah upon me are many, and He has commanded me with this conveyance and message. How, then, could it befit me, with the abundance of Allah's blessings upon me, to oppose His command and His obligation?

The second: The meaning may be that it is as if he said: Since it is established for me that devoting worship to other than Allah, and engaging in cheating and short-measuring, are reprehensible deeds, and I am a man who intends to reform your affairs, and I do not need your wealth, because Allah has given me good provision, how could it befit me, in these circumstances, to betray the revelation of Allah and His judgment?

The third: His saying ﴿if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ means the miracle that he possessed. His saying ﴿and He has given me good provision from Himself﴾ means that he does not ask them for any reward or payment, and this is what all the prophets said: ﴿I do not ask you any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:109].

The second issue: His saying ﴿and He has given me good provision from Himself﴾ indicates that this provision came only from Allah, by His help, and that acquisition (kasb) has no role in it. This contains an admonition that honour is from Allah, and humiliation is from Allah. And since everything is from Allah, I do not care about your opposition, nor do I rejoice in your agreement; I am only to establish the religion of Allah and to clarify the laws of Allah.

As for the second of the answers that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) gave: his saying ﴿and I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf said: It is said: "Fulan opposed me to such-and-such" (khalafani ila kadha) when he intends it while you turn away from it, and "Fulan opposed me from it" (khalafani 'anhu) when he turns away from it while you intend it. A man meets you coming back from the water, and you ask him about his companion, and he says: "He opposed me to the water," meaning that he has gone to it coming (as one who arrives), while I am going away from it returning (as one who departs). From this is His saying ﴿and I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from﴾, meaning: I do not intend to get ahead of you to your desires which I forbid you from, in order to monopolize them without you. This is the explanation of the linguistic sense. As for the verification of the statement: the people admitted that he is forbearing and rightly guided, and that indicates perfection of intellect, and perfection of intellect moves its possessor to choose the more correct and more beneficial path. So it is as if he (peace be upon him) said to them: Since you have acknowledged the perfection of my intellect, know that what my intellect has chosen for myself must be the most correct and most beneficial path. The call to the oneness of Allah and abandoning short-measuring and diminishing (of the rights of others) comes back to two parts: reverence for the command of Allah, and compassion for the creation of Allah. I am persistent in both of them, never abandoning them in any circumstance at all. So since you have acknowledged to me forbearance and rectitude and you see that I do not abandon this way, know that this way is the best of ways and the most noble of religions and laws.

As for the third of the aspects that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) mentioned: it is his saying ﴿I intend only reform, as far as I am able﴾. The meaning is: I intend only to reform you through my admonition and advice. His saying ﴿as far as I am able﴾ has several aspects:

The first: that it is an adverbial expression of time (zarf), and the implied meaning is: for the duration of my ability to reform, and as long as I am able to do it, I spare no effort in it.

The second: that it is a substitute (badal) for "reform", i.e., the extent to which I am able of it.

The third: that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), i.e., I intend only to reform what I am able to reform.

Know that the purpose of this statement is that the people had acknowledged that he is forbearing and rightly guided, and they acknowledged this only because he was well known among the people for this attribute. So it is as if he (peace be upon him) said to them: You know from my condition that I strive only for reform and for removing corruption and discord. So when I order you to monotheism and to abandoning harming people, know that it is a true religion, and that my aim in it is not to cause discord or to stir up strife. For you know that I detest that path, and I revolve only around what brings about reconciliation and righteousness to the extent of my capacity. That is conveying and warning. As for compelling obedience, I have no power over it. Then he (peace be upon him) confirmed this by his saying: ﴿My success is only through Allah. Upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn back.﴾ And by this he showed that his reliance and his trust in carrying out all righteous deeds is upon the success and guidance of Allah.

Know that his saying (peace be upon him) "I rely" is an allusion to pure monotheism, because his saying "I rely" implies restriction (hasr), namely that a person should not rely upon anyone except Allah. How could it be otherwise, since everything other than the Truth, glorified is He, is possible in its essence, perishing in its essence, and does not come into being except by His bringing it into existence and His creating it? When this is so, reliance is not permissible except upon Allah, and the greatest level of knowledge of the origin is what we have mentioned. As for his saying ﴿and to Him I turn back﴾, it is an allusion to knowledge of the return (ma'ad), and it also implies restriction, because his saying ﴿and to Him I turn back﴾ indicates that there is no return for creation except to Allah. And it is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that whenever Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was mentioned, he would say: "That is the orator of the prophets," because of the excellence of his discourse among his people.

As for the fourth of the aspects that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) mentioned, it is his saying:

[p. 39]
﴿And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to incur that which befell...﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Jarama" (to incur/earn) is like "kasaba" (to earn) in its transitivity, sometimes to one object and sometimes to two objects. It is said: "jarama dhanban wa kasabahu" (he committed a sin and earned it), and "jarrama-hu dhanban wa kassaba-hu iyyahu" (he caused him to commit a sin and to earn it). From it is His saying: ﴿Let not my opposition cause you to incur the striking (of the punishment)﴾, meaning: let not my opposition earn for you the attainment of the punishment. Ibn Kathir read "yujarrimannakum" with a damma on the yā' (ye), from "ajramtuhu dhanban," when you make him one who commits it, i.e., one who earns it. This is transmitted from "jarama" which is transitive to one object. On this basis there is no difference between "jaramtuhu dhanban" and "ajramtuhu iyyahu," and the two readings are equivalent in meaning, with no difference between them, except that the well-known reading is more eloquent in wording, just as "kassaba-hu malan" is more eloquent than "akssaba-hu."

Having known this, we say: the meaning of the verse is: let not your enmity toward me earn for you the punishment of extermination in this world, like what befell the people of Noah (peace be upon him) by drowning, and the people of Hud by the barren wind, and the people of Salih by the earthquake, and the people of Lot by the sinking of the earth.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and the people of Lot are not far from you﴾, in it there are two aspects:

The first: that the meaning is the negation of distance in place, because the land of the people of Lot (peace be upon him) is near Madyan.

The second: that the meaning is the negation of distance in time, because the destruction of the people of Lot (peace be upon him) is the nearest of the destructions known to people in the time of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him). On these two interpretations, nearness in place and in time gives greater knowledge and complete awareness of the conditions. So it is as if he says: take heed from their conditions, and beware of opposing Allah and contending with Him, lest there descend upon you the like of that punishment.

If it is said: why did He say ﴿and the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ when the proper form would have been "bi-ba'idin" (plural)?

The author of al-Kashshaf answered it in two ways:

The first: that the implied meaning is: their destruction is not a far thing.

The second: that it is permissible that the masculine and feminine be treated alike in "near", "far", "much" and "little", because they come in the pattern of verbal nouns such as "al-sahil" (neighing) and "al-nahiq" (braying) and the like.

As for the fifth of the aspects that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) mentioned, it is his saying: ﴿And seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ for worshipping idols, ﴿then repent to Him﴾ from short-measuring and diminishing, ﴿indeed my Lord is Merciful﴾ to His friends, ﴿and Loving﴾. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: "al-Wadud" among the names of Allah, exalted is He, means the one who loves His servants, from the expression "waddadtu al-rajul awadduhu" (I loved the man). And al-Azhari said in the book "Sharh Asma' Allah Ta'ala" (Explanation of the Names of Allah, exalted is He): It is also permissible that "wadud" is an intensive form (fa'ul) in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), like "rukub" and "halub," and its meaning is that His righteous servants love Him and hold Him dear because of the abundance of His bounty and kindness to creation.

Know that this order which Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) observed in mentioning these five aspects is a subtle arrangement. For he first showed that the manifestation of clear evidence to him and the abundance of Allah's blessing upon him, outwardly and inwardly, prevents him from betraying the revelation of Allah, and restrains him from negligence in His obligations. Second, he showed that he is persistent in acting upon this call, and if it were false he would not have occupied himself with it, given your acknowledgment that he is forbearing and rightly guided. Third, he showed its soundness by another way, which is that he was known for bringing about the causes of righteousness and concealing the causes of strife. So if this call were false he would not have occupied himself with it. Then, when he showed the soundness of his way, he pointed to the removal of opposition and said: it is not fitting that my enmity toward you should lead you to a doctrine and religion by which you fall into severe punishment from Allah, as the nations of the earlier prophets fell into it. Then, when he had established the soundness of his own doctrine by these proofs, he returned to affirming what he had mentioned first, namely monotheism and the prohibition of short-measuring, by his saying: ﴿then repent to Him﴾. Then he showed them that the prior disbelief and disobedience on their part should not prevent them from faith and obedience, because He is Merciful and Loving, who accepts faith and repentance from the disbeliever and the wicked, for His mercy and His love for them require that. And this argument is in the utmost perfection.

The first: that it is an adverbial expression of time (zarf), and the implied meaning is: for the duration of my ability to reform, and as long as I am able to do it, I spare no effort in it.

The second: that it is a substitute (badal) for "reform", i.e., the extent to which I am able of it.

The third: that it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), i.e., I intend only to reform what I am able to reform.

Know that the purpose of this statement is that the people had acknowledged that he is forbearing and rightly guided, and they acknowledged this only because he was well known among the people for this attribute. So it is as if he (peace be upon him) said to them: You know from my condition that I strive only for reform and for removing corruption and discord. So when I order you to monotheism and to abandoning harming people, know that it is a true religion, and that my aim in it is not to cause discord or to stir up strife. For you know that I detest that path, and I revolve only around what brings about reconciliation and righteousness to the extent of my capacity. That is conveying and warning. As for compelling obedience, I have no power over it. Then he (peace be upon him) confirmed this by his saying: ﴿My success is only through Allah. Upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn back.﴾ And by this he showed that his reliance and his trust in carrying out all righteous deeds is upon the success and guidance of Allah.

Know that his saying (peace be upon him) "I rely" is an allusion to pure monotheism, because his saying "I rely" implies restriction (hasr), namely that a person should not rely upon anyone except Allah. How could it be otherwise, since everything other than the Truth, glorified is He, is possible in its essence, perishing in its essence, and does not come into being except by His bringing it into existence and His creating it? When this is so, reliance is not permissible except upon Allah, and the greatest level of knowledge of the origin is what we have mentioned. As for his saying ﴿and to Him I turn back﴾, it is an allusion to knowledge of the return (ma'ad), and it also implies restriction, because his saying ﴿and to Him I turn back﴾ indicates that there is no return for creation except to Allah. And it is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that whenever Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was mentioned, he would say: "That is the orator of the prophets," because of the excellence of his discourse among his people.

As for the fourth of the aspects that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) mentioned, it is his saying:

[p. 39]
﴿And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to incur that which befell...﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Jarama" (to incur/earn) is like "kasaba" (to earn) in its transitivity, sometimes to one object and sometimes to two objects. It is said: "jarama dhanban wa kasabahu" (he committed a sin and earned it), and "jarrama-hu dhanban wa kassaba-hu iyyahu" (he caused him to commit a sin and to earn it). Ibn Kathir read "yujarrimannakum" with a damma on the yā' (ye), from "ajramtuhu dhanban," when you make him one who commits it, i.e., one who earns it.
