* * *

As for His saying ﴿and the people of Lot are not far from you﴾, in it there are two aspects:

The first: that the meaning is the negation of distance in place, because the land of the people of Lot (peace be upon him) is near Madyan.

The second: that the meaning is the negation of distance in time, because the destruction of the people of Lot (peace be upon him) is the nearest of the destructions known to people in the time of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him). On these two interpretations, nearness in place and in time gives greater knowledge and complete awareness of the conditions. So it is as if he says: take heed from their conditions, and beware of opposing Allah and contending with Him, lest there descend upon you the like of that punishment.

If it is said: why did He say ﴿and the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ when the proper form would have been "bi-ba'idin" (plural)?

The author of al-Kashshaf answered it in two ways:

The first: that the implied meaning is: their destruction is not a far thing.

The second: that it is permissible that the masculine and feminine be treated alike in "near", "far", "much" and "little", because they come in the pattern of verbal nouns such as "al-sahil" (neighing) and "al-nahiq" (braying) and the like.

As for the fifth of the aspects that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) mentioned, it is his saying: ﴿And seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ for worshipping idols, ﴿then repent to Him﴾ from short-measuring and diminishing, ﴿indeed my Lord is Merciful﴾ to His friends, ﴿and Loving﴾. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: "al-Wadud" among the names of Allah, exalted is He, means the one who loves His servants, from the expression "waddadtu al-rajul awadduhu" (I loved the man). And al-Azhari said in the book "Sharh Asma' Allah Ta'ala" (Explanation of the Names of Allah, exalted is He): It is also permissible that "wadud" is an intensive form (fa'ul) in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), like "rukub" and "halub," and its meaning is that His righteous servants love Him and hold Him dear because of the abundance of His bounty and kindness to creation.

Know that this order which Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) observed in mentioning these five aspects is a subtle arrangement. For he first showed that the manifestation of clear evidence to him and the abundance of Allah's blessing upon him, outwardly and inwardly, prevents him from betraying the revelation of Allah, and restrains him from negligence in His obligations. Second, he showed that he is persistent in acting upon this call, and if it were false he would not have occupied himself with it, given your acknowledgment that he is forbearing and rightly guided. Third, he showed its soundness by another way, which is that he was known for bringing about the causes of righteousness and concealing the causes of strife. So if this call were false he would not have occupied himself with it. Then, when he showed the soundness of his way, he pointed to the removal of opposition and said: it is not fitting that my enmity toward you should lead you to a doctrine and religion by which you fall into severe punishment from Allah, as the nations of the earlier prophets fell into it. Then, when he had established the soundness of his own doctrine by these proofs, he returned to affirming what he had mentioned first, namely monotheism and the prohibition of short-measuring, by his saying: ﴿then repent to Him﴾. Then he showed them that the prior disbelief and disobedience on their part should not prevent them from faith and obedience, because He is Merciful and Loving, who accepts faith and repentance from the disbeliever and the wicked, for His mercy and His love for them require that. And this argument is in the utmost perfection.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 88–90:

﴿He said, "O my people, tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me good provision from Himself, [then how could I betray Him?] And I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from. I intend only reform, as far as I am able. My success is only through Allah. Upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn back."﴾ ﴿"And O my people, let not my opposition cause you to incur what befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih. And the people of Lot are not far from you."﴾ ﴿"And seek forgiveness from your Lord, then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving."﴾

There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: Know that He, exalted is He, related what Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) said in reply to their statements. The first is his saying: ﴿Tell me, if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has given me good provision from Himself,﴾ and in it there are several aspects:

The first: His saying ﴿if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ refers to what Allah gave him of knowledge, guidance, religion and prophethood. His saying ﴿and He has given me good provision from Himself﴾ refers to the lawful wealth Allah gave him, for it is related that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) had much wealth.

Know that the answer to the conditional particle ﴿in﴾ (if) is omitted, and the implied meaning is: since Allah has given me all the spiritual blessings, which is the clear evidence, and the physical blessings, which are wealth and good provision, how could it befit me, with this great favour, to betray His revelation and to oppose His command and prohibition? This answer closely corresponds to what came before, because they had said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾. How then could it befit you, with your forbearance and your rectitude, to forbid us from the religion of our fathers? It is as if he said: I only undertook this action because the blessings of Allah upon me are many, and He has commanded me with this conveyance and message. How, then, could it befit me, with the abundance of Allah's blessings upon me, to oppose His command and His obligation?

The second: The meaning may be that it is as if he said: Since it is established for me that devoting worship to other than Allah, and engaging in cheating and short-measuring, are reprehensible deeds, and I am a man who intends to reform your affairs, and I do not need your wealth, because Allah has given me good provision, how could it befit me, in these circumstances, to betray the revelation of Allah and His judgment?

The third: His saying ﴿if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ means the miracle that he possessed. His saying ﴿and He has given me good provision from Himself﴾ means that he does not ask them for any reward or payment, and this is what all the prophets said: ﴿I do not ask you any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:109].

The second issue: His saying ﴿and He has given me good provision from Himself﴾ indicates that this provision came only from Allah, by His help, and that acquisition (kasb) has no role in it. This contains an admonition that honour is from Allah, and humiliation is from Allah. So it is as if he (peace be upon him) said to them: Since you have acknowledged the perfection of my intellect, know that what my intellect has chosen for myself must be the most correct and most beneficial path. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 91:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and we see you as weak among us. Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty against us."﴾

Know that when he (peace be upon him) went far in explanation and clarification, they answered him with corrupt words. The first is their saying: ﴿"O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say"﴾. On this there are several questions.

The first question: someone may ask, "He (peace be upon him) was addressing them in their own tongue, so why did they say ﴿we do not understand﴾?" The scholars gave several kinds of answers.

The first: the meaning is "we do not grasp much of what you say," because they did not turn their understanding toward him, owing to their intense aversion to his speech. This is like His saying: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts veils, lest they understand it﴾ [al-An'am: 25].

The second: they did understand him in their hearts, but they gave his words no weight, so they said this in a tone of contempt, as a man says to his companion when he pays no heed to what he says, "I do not know what you are saying."

The third: these proofs he presented did not convince them of the soundness of monotheism, prophethood, resurrection, and the obligation to abandon injustice and theft. So their saying ﴿we do not understand﴾ means: we did not recognize the soundness of the proofs you mentioned for these demands.

The second question: some people said that fiqh (jurisprudence, understanding) is a term for a specific science, namely knowing the speaker's purpose in his speech. They based this on this verse, His saying ﴿we do not understand much of what you say﴾, where He attached fiqh to speech. Then it became a term for a particular kind of religious sciences. Others said it is a term for understanding in general. It is said: "So-and-so was given fiqh in religion," meaning understanding. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whomever Allah wills good for, He gives him understanding (yufaqqihhu) in religion," meaning He makes him understand its interpretation.

The second kind of thing they mentioned is their saying: ﴿and we see you as weak among us﴾. On this there are two views.

The first: he is the weak one who cannot prevent the people from himself.

The second: "weak" in the dialect of Himyar means blind. Know that this view is weak, for several reasons.

The first: it abandons the apparent meaning without evidence.

The second: His saying ﴿among us﴾ refutes this view. Do you not see that if He had said, "we see you as blind among us," it would have been wrong, because a blind man is blind among them and among others?

The third: after this they said ﴿Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾, so they denied him the strength they had attributed to his clan. Since the strength they attributed to the clan means support, the strength they denied him must also mean support. Those who took the word to mean weakness of sight probably did so because it is a cause of weakness.

Know that our companions (the Ash'aris) permit blindness for the prophets, but this expression cannot be used as evidence for this meaning, for the reason we have stated.

As for the Mu'tazila (a theological school), they disagreed about it. Some of them said it is not permissible, because the prophet is one who must perform acts of worship, and blindness prevents him from avoiding impurities, and because it impairs the possibility of his being a judge or a witness. So it is even more fitting that it should bar him from prophethood. But discussion of this does not suit this verse, because we have shown that the verse contains no indication of this meaning.

The third kind of thing they mentioned is their saying: ﴿Were it not for your clan, we would have stoned you﴾. On this there are two questions.

Page 41
The first question: the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: a rahṭ (clan) is from three to ten, and it is said up to seven. His clan was of their religion. They said: were it not for the respect due to your clan among us because they follow our religion, we would have stoned you. The purpose of this statement is that they made clear he had no respect among them and no standing in their hearts, and that they did not kill him only out of regard for his clan.

The second question: in the language, rajm means throwing. This may be with stones when intending to kill. Since this stoning was a cause of killing, they called killing "rajm." It may also be by speech, which is slander, as in His saying ﴿stoning in the unseen﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], and His saying ﴿and they hurl (yaqdhifuna) at him from a distant place﴾ [Saba': 53]. It may also be by cursing and reviling, as in His saying ﴿the accursed (al-rajim) Satan﴾ [Al 'Imran: 36]. And it may be by driving away, as in His saying ﴿missiles against the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5].

Having known this, the verse has two meanings:

The first: ﴿we would have stoned you﴾ means we would have killed you.

The second: we would have reviled and expelled you.

The fourth kind of thing they mentioned is their saying: ﴿and you are not mighty against us﴾. Its meaning is that since you are not mighty over us, it was easy for us to proceed to kill you and harm you.

Know that all these points they raised do not refute what Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) established by way of proofs and clear evidence. Rather, they are on the level of answering argument and proof with insult and foolishness.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 92–93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah? And you have put Him behind your backs [as something cast aside]. Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do.﴾ ﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am [also] acting. You will learn who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and who is a liar. And watch; indeed, I am with you a watcher.﴾

Know that when the disbelievers threatened Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, with killing and harm, Allah the Exalted related what he said in this situation, and it consists of two kinds of speech.

The first kind: his saying, ﴿O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah? And you have put Him behind your backs [as something cast aside]. Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do.﴾ The meaning is: the people claimed that they refrained from harming him out of regard for his clan. So he said: You claim that you leave off killing me out of honor for my clan, while Allah the Exalted is more deserving that His command be followed. It is as if he is saying: your protecting me out of obedience to the command of Allah the Exalted is more fitting than your protecting me out of regard for the right of my clan.

* * *
As for his saying, ﴿and you have put Him behind your backs [as something cast aside]﴾, the meaning is: you have forgotten Him and made Him like a thing thrown behind the back, not heeded. The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: "al-Zhihri" is attributed to "al-zahr" (back), and the kasra is one of the changes of the relative form (nisba); its parallel is their saying in the relative form of "al-amss" (yesterday): "imsiyy" with a kasra on the hamza. And his saying, ﴿indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾, means that He is knowing of your conditions, so nothing of them is hidden from Him.

The second kind: his saying, ﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am [also] acting﴾. Al-makana (position) is the state by which its possessor is enabled to do his work. The meaning: act while being described with utmost capacity and power, and whatever is within your means and ability of bringing evils to me, then indeed I too am acting according to the measure of the power Allah the Exalted has given me.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿You will learn who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and who is a liar.﴾ In this there are two issues:

The first issue: one may ask: why did he not say "so you will learn" (fa-sawfa ta'lamun)?

The answer: including the fa' connects an apparent thing with a particle set for connection, whereas omitting the fa' makes it an answer to a presumed question. The presumed sense: when he said, ﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am [also] acting﴾, it is as if they said: "Then what will happen after that?" So he said: ﴿You will learn﴾. It is thus clear that omitting the particle fa' here is more complete in terms of awfulness and dread. Then he said: ﴿And watch; indeed, I am with you a watcher.﴾ The meaning: await the outcome; indeed I am with you a watcher, i.e., one awaiting. The raqib (watcher) is in the sense of al-raqib (one who watches), from raqaba him, like al-darib and al-sarim in the sense of al-darib (striker) and al-sarim (cutter); or in the sense of al-muraqib (one who observes), like al-'ashir and al-nadim; or in the sense of al-murtaqib (one who awaits), like al-faqir and al-rafi' in the sense of al-muftaqir (needy) and al-murtafi' (elevated).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 92–93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah? And you have put Him behind your backs [as something cast aside]. Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do.﴾ ﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am [also] acting. You will learn who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and who is a liar. And watch; indeed, I am with you a watcher.﴾

Know that when the disbelievers threatened Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, with killing and harm, Allah the Exalted related what he said in this situation, and it consists of two kinds of speech.

The first kind: his saying, ﴿O my people, is my clan more esteemed by you than Allah? And you have put Him behind your backs [as something cast aside]. Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do.﴾ The meaning is: the people claimed that they refrained from harming him out of regard for his clan. So he said: You claim that you leave off killing me out of honor for my clan, while Allah the Exalted is more deserving that His command be followed. It is as if he is saying: your protecting me out of obedience to the command of Allah the Exalted is more fitting than your protecting me out of regard for the right of my clan.

* * *
As for his saying, ﴿and you have put Him behind your backs [as something cast aside]﴾, the meaning is: you have forgotten Him and made Him like a thing thrown behind the back, not heeded. The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: "al-Zhihri" is attributed to "al-zahr" (back), and the kasra is one of the changes of the relative form (nisba); its parallel is their saying in the relative form of "al-amss" (yesterday): "imsiyy" with a kasra on the hamza. And his saying, ﴿indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾, means that He is knowing of your conditions, so nothing of them is hidden from Him.

The second kind: his saying, ﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am [also] acting﴾. Al-makana (position) is the state by which its possessor is enabled to do his work. The meaning: act while being described with utmost capacity and power, and whatever is within your means and ability of bringing evils to me, then indeed I too am acting according to the measure of the power Allah the Exalted has given me.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿You will learn who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and who is a liar.﴾ In this there are two issues:

The first issue: one may ask: why did he not say "so you will learn" (fa-sawfa ta'lamun)?

The answer: including the fa' connects an apparent thing with a particle set for connection, whereas omitting the fa' makes it an answer to a presumed question. The presumed sense: when he said, ﴿And O my people, act according to your position; indeed, I am [also] acting﴾, it is as if they said: "Then what will happen after that?" So he said: ﴿You will learn﴾. It is thus clear that omitting the particle fa' here is more complete in terms of awfulness and dread. Then he said: ﴿And watch; indeed, I am with you a watcher.﴾ The meaning: await the outcome; indeed I am with you a watcher, i.e., one awaiting. The raqib (watcher) is in the sense of al-raqib (one who watches), from raqaba him, like al-darib and al-sarim in the sense of al-darib (striker) and al-sarim (cutter); or in the sense of al-muraqib (one who observes), like al-'ashir and al-nadim; or in the sense of al-murtaqib (one who awaits), like al-faqir and al-rafi' in the sense of al-muftaqir (needy) and al-murtafi' (elevated).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 94–95:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and the blast seized those who had wronged, so they became prostrate in their homes﴾ ﴿as though they had never flourished therein. Unquestionably, the people of Madyan were removed [far away] just as Thamud were removed﴾.

Al-Kalbi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: Allah did not punish two nations with one punishment except the people of Shu'ayb and the people of Salih. As for the people of Salih, the blast seized them from beneath them, while the people of Shu'ayb were seized from above them. As for His saying, ﴿And when Our command came﴾, it may be that what is meant is: when the time of Our command came, [sent through] an angel of the angels with that blast. It may also be that what is meant by the command is the punishment. In either case, Allah informed that He saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by mercy from Him. In this there are two aspects:

The first: that He delivered him from that punishment purely by His mercy, as a reminder that everything that reaches the servant is nothing but by the grace and mercy of Allah.

The second: that what is meant by mercy is faith, obedience and all the other righteous deeds, and these too were only achieved by the enabling (tawfiq) of Allah, exalted is He. Then He described the manner of that punishment, saying: ﴿and the blast seized those who had wronged﴾. He mentioned "the blast" with the definite article (al-) to point to the previously known referent, namely the blast of Jibril, peace be upon him. ﴿So they became prostrate in their homes﴾. The jathim is one who remains fixed in its place and does not move from it. The meaning is that when Jibril, peace be upon him, cried out at them with that blast, the soul of each one of them departed, such that each fell dead in his place. ﴿As though they had never flourished therein﴾, i.e., as though they had never dwelt in their homes alive, going about and coming and going.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Unquestionably, the people of Madyan were removed [far away] just as Thamud were removed﴾. The explanation of this word has already been given before. He compared their condition to that of Thamud only because, as we have mentioned, He punished them with a punishment like the punishment of Thamud.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 96–99:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ ﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire, and wretched is the watering-place to which they are led﴾ ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. Wretched is the gift they are given﴾.

Know that this is the seventh of the stories which Allah, exalted is He, mentions in this surah, and it is the last of the stories of this surah. As for His saying: ﴿with Our signs and a clear authority﴾, there are several views:

The first: the intended meaning of the signs is the Torah together with the laws and rulings it contains, and the clear authority is the overwhelming, dazzling miracles. The implied meaning is: And We certainly sent Musa with laws, rulings and obligations, and We strengthened him with overwhelming miracles and dazzling proofs.

The second: the signs are the miracles and the clear proofs, as in His saying: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [Yunus: 68] and His saying: ﴿Allah has sent down no authority for it﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. On this interpretation there are two possibilities in the verse:

The first: these signs contain a clear authority for Musa regarding the truthfulness of his prophethood.

The second: the clear authority is intended to be the staff, because it is the most famous of them. This is because Allah gave Musa nine clear signs: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, a loss of fruits and lives. Some replaced the loss of fruits and lives with the mountain being lifted over them and the splitting of the sea.

They differed over why proof is called authority (sultan). Some of the verifiers said: because the possessor of proof overcomes one who has no proof when examined, just as a ruler (sultan) overcomes others; for this reason proof is described as an authority. Al-Zajjaj said: authority is proof, and authority was named sultan because it is the proof of Allah on His earth; its derivation is from al-salit, and al-salit is that by which one is illuminated, and from this oil is called salit. There is a third view: that sultan is derived from tasliṭ (empowerment), and scholars are sultans by virtue of their perfection in scholarly strength, and kings are sultans by virtue of the power and capacity they possess; yet the authority of scholars is more perfect and stronger than the authority of kings, because the authority of scholars does not accept abrogation or dismissal, whereas the authority of kings accepts both; and because the authority of kings follows the authority of scholars, and the authority of scholars is of the same kind as the authority of the prophets, while the authority of kings is of the same kind as the authority of the Pharaohs.

If it is said: If you take the signs mentioned in His saying ﴿with Our signs﴾ to mean miracles, and the authority to mean proofs, and the clear (mubin) also means that it is a cause of manifestation, then what is the difference between these three levels?

We say: "signs" (ayat) is a term for the common element among indications which give probability, and among proofs which give certainty. As for "authority" (sultan), it is a term for what gives certainty and conviction, except that it is a term for the common element among proofs which are confirmed by the senses and proofs which are not confirmed by the senses. As for the decisive proof which is confirmed by the senses, it is the clear authority. Since the miracles of Musa, peace be upon him, were of this kind, Allah therefore described them as a clear authority. Then He said: ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, meaning: We sent Musa with signs like these to Pharaoh and his chiefs, that is, his assembly. Then He said: ﴿but they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾. It may be that the intended meaning is his command to them to disbelieve in Musa and his miracles, and it may be that the intended meaning of "command" is the way and the affair.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾, that is, it did not guide to good. It is also said: rashid means one possessing rushd (right guidance).

Know that the distance of Pharaoh's path from rectitude was evident, because he was a materialist denying the Creator and the return. He used to say: there is no god for the world, and it is obligatory for the people of every land to occupy themselves with obedience to their ruler and servitude to him, for the sake of the welfare of the world; and he denied that rectitude lies in the worship and knowledge of Allah. Since he denied these two matters, he was entirely devoid of rectitude. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned his attribute and the attribute of his people, saying: ﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire﴾. Concerning this there are two discussions:

The first discussion, from the linguistic standpoint: it is said "qadama fulan fulanan" meaning "taqaddamahu" (he went ahead of him), and from it comes qadimat al-rajul (the forward-most part of a man), just as it is said "qadamahu" meaning "taqaddamahu", and from it comes muqaddimat al-jaysh (the vanguard of the army).

The second discussion, from the standpoint of meaning: Pharaoh was a leader to his people in error while they were in this world, and likewise their leader will go before them to the Fire while they follow him. Or it may be said: just as he went ahead of his people in this world and brought them into the sea and drowned them, so likewise he will go ahead of them on the Day of Resurrection and bring them into the Fire and burn them. It is also permissible that by His saying ﴿and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ He intends: his command was not righteous, with a praiseworthy outcome; and His saying ﴿He will go before his people﴾ is an explanation of that and a clarification of it, that is: how could his command be rightly guided when its outcome is thus?

If it is said: Why did He not say "He will go before his people and lead them into the Fire", but rather said "He will go before his people and led them into the Fire" in the past tense?

We say: because the past has occurred and entered existence, so there is absolutely no way to avert it; when the future is expressed with the past tense, it indicates the utmost emphasis. Then He said: ﴿and wretched is the watering-place to which they are led﴾. Concerning this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: the word "fire" (al-nar) is feminine, so it should have been said "wa-bi'sat al-wird al-mawrud"; but the word "wird" is masculine, so both masculine and feminine are permissible, as you say: "ni'ma al-manzil daruka" and "ni'mat al-manzil daruka"; whoever uses the masculine gives precedence to "al-manzil", and whoever uses the feminine follows the feminine "al-dar". This is how al-Wahidi said it.

The second discussion: "wird" may mean "wurud" (arrival), in which case it is a verbal noun, and it may mean "warid" (one who arrives), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ [Maryam: 86], and it may mean "the place arrived at", like the water to which one comes. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "al-wird al-mawrud" is that whose arrival has taken place; so Allah, exalted is He, compared Pharaoh to one who goes ahead of those coming to the water, and compared his followers to those coming to the water. Then He said: wretched is the watering-place to which they are brought, namely the Fire; because the watering-place is only intended for quenching thirst and cooling the hearts, and the Fire is its opposite.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection﴾. The meaning is that they were followed in this world by a curse, and also on the Day of Resurrection. Its meaning is that cursing from Allah, from the angels and from the prophets clings to them in this world and in the Hereafter and does not leave them. A parallel to this is His saying in Surah al-Qasas: ﴿And We made them follow in this world a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾ [al-Qasas: 42].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Wretched is the gift they are given﴾. Al-rifd is the gift, and its origin is that which helps one attain what is sought. Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, about His saying: ﴿Wretched is the gift they are given﴾. He said: it is curse after curse. Qatadah said: two curses from Allah, exalted is He, followed one after another upon them: a curse in this world and a curse in the Hereafter. And everything you make an aid to something, you have given it as a rifd.

Then He said: ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, meaning: We sent Musa with signs like these to Pharaoh and his chiefs, that is, his assembly. Then He said: ﴿but they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾. It may be that the intended meaning is his command to them to disbelieve in Musa and his miracles, and it may be that the intended meaning of "command" is the way and the affair.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾, that is, it did not guide to good. It is also said: rashid means one possessing rushd (right guidance).

Know that the distance of Pharaoh's path from rectitude was evident, because he was a materialist denying the Creator and the return. He used to say: there is no god for the world, and it is obligatory for the people of every land to occupy themselves with obedience to their ruler and servitude to him, for the sake of the welfare of the world; and he denied that rectitude lies in the worship and knowledge of Allah. Since he denied these two matters, he was entirely devoid of rectitude. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned his attribute and the attribute of his people, saying: ﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire﴾. Concerning this there are two discussions:

The first discussion, from the linguistic standpoint: it is said "qadama fulan fulanan" meaning "taqaddamahu" (he went ahead of him), and from it comes qadimat al-rajul (the forward-most part of a man), just as it is said "qadamahu" meaning "taqaddamahu", and from it comes muqaddimat al-jaysh (the vanguard of the army).

The second discussion, from the standpoint of meaning: Pharaoh was a leader to his people in error while they were in this world, and likewise their leader will go before them to the Fire while they follow him. Or it may be said: just as he went ahead of his people in this world and brought them into the sea and drowned them, so likewise he will go ahead of them on the Day of Resurrection and bring them into the Fire and burn them. It is also permissible that by His saying ﴿and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided﴾ He intends: his command was not righteous, with a praiseworthy outcome; and His saying ﴿He will go before his people﴾ is an explanation of that and a clarification of it, that is: how could his command be rightly guided when its outcome is thus?

If it is said: Why did He not say "He will go before his people and lead them into the Fire", but rather said "He will go before his people and led them into the Fire" in the past tense?

We say: because the past has occurred and entered existence, so there is absolutely no way to avert it; when the future is expressed with the past tense, it indicates the utmost emphasis. Then He said: ﴿and wretched is the watering-place to which they are led﴾. Concerning this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: the word "fire" (al-nar) is feminine, so it should have been said "wa-bi'sat al-wird al-mawrud"; but the word "wird" is masculine, so both masculine and feminine are permissible, as you say: "ni'ma al-manzil daruka" and "ni'mat al-manzil daruka"; whoever uses the masculine gives precedence to "al-manzil", and whoever uses the feminine follows the feminine "al-dar". This is how al-Wahidi said it.

The second discussion: "wird" may mean "wurud" (arrival), in which case it is a verbal noun, and it may mean "warid" (one who arrives), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ [Maryam: 86], and it may mean "the place arrived at", like the water to which one comes. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "al-wird al-mawrud" is that whose arrival has taken place; so Allah, exalted is He, compared Pharaoh to one who goes ahead of those coming to the water, and compared his followers to those coming to the water. Then He said: wretched is the watering-place to which they are brought, namely the Fire; because the watering-place is only intended for quenching thirst and cooling the hearts, and the Fire is its opposite.

* * *

Its meaning is that cursing from Allah, from the angels and from the prophets clings to them in this world and in the Hereafter and does not leave them. A parallel to this is His saying in Surah al-Qasas: ﴿And We made them follow in this world a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised﴾ [al-Qasas: 42].

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Wretched is the gift they are given﴾. Al-rifd is the gift, and its origin is that which helps one attain what is sought. Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, about His saying: ﴿Wretched is the gift they are given﴾. He said: it is curse after curse. Qatadah said: two curses from Allah, exalted is He, followed one after another upon them: a curse in this world and a curse in the Hereafter. And everything you make an aid to something, you have given it as a rifd.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 96–99:

Wretched is the gift they are given﴾.

Know that this is the seventh of the stories which Allah, exalted is He, mentions in this surah, and it is the last of the stories of this surah. As for His saying: ﴿with Our signs and a clear authority﴾, there are several views:

The first: the intended meaning of the signs is the Torah together with the laws and rulings it contains, and the clear authority is the overwhelming, dazzling miracles. The implied meaning is: And We certainly sent Musa with laws, rulings and obligations, and We strengthened him with overwhelming miracles and dazzling proofs.

The second: the signs are the miracles and the clear proofs, as in His saying: ﴿You have no authority for this﴾ [Yunus: 68] and His saying: ﴿Allah has sent down no authority for it﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. On this interpretation there are two possibilities in the verse:

The first: these signs contain a clear authority for Musa regarding the truthfulness of his prophethood.

The second: the clear authority is intended to be the staff, because it is the most famous of them. This is because Allah gave Musa nine clear signs: the staff, the hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, a loss of fruits and lives. Some replaced the loss of fruits and lives with the mountain being lifted over them and the splitting of the sea.

They differed over why proof is called authority (sultan). Some of the verifiers said: because the possessor of proof overcomes one who has no proof when examined, just as a ruler (sultan) overcomes others; for this reason proof is described as an authority. Al-Zajjaj said: authority is proof, and authority was named sultan because it is the proof of Allah on His earth; its derivation is from al-salit, and al-salit is that by which one is illuminated, and from this oil is called salit. There is a third view: that sultan is derived from tasliṭ (empowerment), and scholars are sultans by virtue of their perfection in scholarly strength, and kings are sultans by virtue of the power and capacity they possess; yet the authority of scholars is more perfect and stronger than the authority of kings, because the authority of scholars does not accept abrogation or dismissal, whereas the authority of kings accepts both; and because the authority of kings follows the authority of scholars, and the authority of scholars is of the same kind as the authority of the prophets, while the authority of kings is of the same kind as the authority of the Pharaohs.

If it is said: If you take the signs mentioned in His saying ﴿with Our signs﴾ to mean miracles, and the authority to mean proofs, and the clear (mubin) also means that it is a cause of manifestation, then what is the difference between these three levels?

We say: "signs" (ayat) is a term for the common element among indications which give probability, and among proofs which give certainty. As for "authority" (sultan), it is a term for what gives certainty and conviction, except that it is a term for the common element among proofs which are confirmed by the senses and proofs which are not confirmed by the senses. As for the decisive proof which is confirmed by the senses, it is the clear authority. Since the miracles of Musa, peace be upon him, were of this kind, Allah therefore described them as a clear authority. Then He said: ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, meaning: We sent Musa with signs like these to Pharaoh and his chiefs, that is, his assembly. Then He said: ﴿but they followed the command of Pharaoh﴾. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 100–101:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is some of the news of the towns which We relate to you. Some of them are still standing, and some are mown down.﴾ ﴿We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. And the gods they invoked besides Allah did not avail them anything when the command of your Lord came, and they added nothing to them but perdition.﴾

Know that when Exalted is He mentioned the stories of the earlier peoples, He said: ﴿That is some of the news of the towns which We relate to you.﴾ There are several benefits in mentioning them:

The first: The benefit of pure rational proof comes only to the perfectly endowed person, and that is extremely rare. But when you present the proofs and then reinforce them with the tales of the earlier peoples, the mention of these tales becomes like something that conveys those rational proofs to the intellects.

The second aspect: Exalted is He mixed into these tales the kinds of proofs that the Prophets, peace be upon them, held fast to, and He mentions the disputations of the disbelievers against those proofs and their doubts in rejecting them. Then He mentions, following both, the answers of the Prophets to them. Then He mentions, following that, that when they persisted and grew arrogant, they fell into the punishment of this world, and the curse and punishment remained upon them in this world and in the Hereafter. So the mention of these stories was a means of conveying the proofs and the answers to doubts to the hearts of the deniers, and a means of removing harshness and hardness from their hearts. Thus it is established that the best method of calling to Allah, Exalted is He, is what we have mentioned.

The third benefit: He, peace be upon him, used to relate these stories without studying books and without being a pupil of anyone, and that is a great miracle which indicates prophethood, as we have established.

The fourth benefit: Those who hear these stories become firmly convinced that the end of the truthful and the heretic, the agreeable and the hypocrite, is departure from this world and leaving it. However, the believer leaves this world with a beautiful praise in this world and a great reward in the Hereafter, while the disbeliever leaves this world with a curse in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. So when these tales are repeated upon the hearing, the heart must soften, the soul must submit, enmity must disappear, and fear must arise in the heart that drives it to reflection and reasoning. This is a noble discourse on the benefits of mentioning these stories.

As for His saying: ﴿That is some of the news of the towns﴾, there are several discussions:

The first discussion: His saying ﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative pointing to what is absent, and what is meant here is a pointing to these stories that have passed, though they are present; the answer to this has been given in His saying: ﴿This is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

The second discussion: The word "that" (dhalika) is used to point to the singular, the dual, and the plural, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68]. And it is also possible that what is meant is: that which we have mentioned is such and such.

The third discussion: The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿That﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿some of the news of the towns﴾ is the predicate (khabar), and ﴿We relate to you﴾ is a predicate after a predicate; i.e., that mentioned is some of the news of the towns related to you. Then he said: ﴿Some of them are still standing, and some are mown down.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿of them﴾ refers to the towns. He likened what remains of the traces and walls of the towns to crops standing on their stalks, and what has been effaced and withered to the mown harvest. The meaning is that of those towns, some of them have something remaining, and some of them have perished and no trace of them remains at all.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ On this there are several aspects:

The first: We did not wrong them by punishment and destruction, but they wronged themselves by disbelief and disobedience.

The second: What befell the people was not an injustice from Allah; rather it was justice and wisdom, because the people first wronged themselves by their daring to disbelief and sins, so they deserved from Allah that punishment on account of those deeds.

The third: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: He means: We did not diminish them of the bounty of this world and provision, but they diminished their own share, inasmuch as they belittled the rights of Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So the gods they invoked besides Allah did not avail them anything﴾, that is, those gods benefited them in nothing at all.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And they added nothing to them but perdition (tatbib).﴾ Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "but ruin (takhsir)." It is said: "tabba" when one suffers loss, and "tabbabahu" when another causes him to fall into loss. The meaning is that the disbelievers believed about the idols that they help in attaining benefits and repelling harms. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that when they were in need of a helper, they found nothing from them that could bring benefit or repel harm. Then, just as they did not find that, they found its opposite: that this belief removed from them the benefits of this world and the Hereafter, and brought upon them the harms of this world and the Hereafter. So that was among the greatest causes of loss.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 11, verses 102–104:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing. Indeed His seizure is painful and severe.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed.﴾ ﴿And We do not delay it except for a term numbered.﴾

Within the verse there are issues (masa'il):

**The first issue:** ʿĀṣim and al-Jaḥdarī read "إذ أخذ القرى" with one alif, while the rest read it with two alifs.

**The second issue:** Know that when God, exalted is He, informed His Messenger, peace be upon him, in His Book about what He had done to the peoples of the prophets who came before him, when they opposed the messengers and rejected them, with the punishment of total annihilation (istiʾṣāl), and He made clear that they had wronged themselves, so that punishment befell them in this world, He then said after that: ﴿Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing.﴾ Thus He made clear that His punishment is not limited to those who came before, but the case is the same in the seizing of all wrongdoers. His saying ﴿while they are wrongdoing﴾: the pronoun in it refers to "the towns," but in reality it refers to their people. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And how many a town did We shatter that had been wrongdoing﴾ [al-Anbiya: 11], and His saying: ﴿And how many a town did We destroy that had exulted in its livelihood﴾ [al-Qasas: 58].

Know that when God, exalted is He, had explained the manner of the seizing of the earlier nations, and then explained that He seizes all wrongdoers in that same manner, He followed it with something that adds emphasis and strength, saying: ﴿Indeed His seizure is painful and severe.﴾ So He described that punishment as painful and severe. There is no distress in this world except pain, and no intensification in this world or the Hereafter, nor in imagination or intellect, except the intensification of pain.

Know that this verse indicates that whoever commits an act of wrongdoing must make amends for it through repentance and turning back (to God), so that he does not fall into the seizing which God, exalted is He, described as painful and severe. And it should not be thought that these rulings are specific to those earlier peoples, because when He, exalted is He, recounted the conditions of the earlier peoples, He said: ﴿Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing.﴾ So He made clear that everyone who shares with those earlier peoples in doing what is not fitting must inevitably share with them in that painful and severe seizing.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter.﴾ Al-Qaffal said: The explanation of this statement is that it may be said: These people were punished in this world only because of their denial of the prophets and their association of partners with God. So if they were punished in this world for that, and this world is the abode of action, then being punished for it in the Hereafter, which is the abode of recompense, is more fitting.

Know that many of the exegetes who grasped this line of inquiry relied upon this interpretation. Yet it is weak, because according to this interpretation that al-Qaffal mentioned, the manifestation of the punishment of annihilation in this world would be evidence that the doctrine of the Resurrection, the raising of the dead, and their gathering is true and right.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires that knowledge that the Resurrection is true functions as a condition for deriving a lesson from the manifestation of the punishment of annihilation. This meaning is almost contrary to what al-Qaffal stated, because al-Qaffal makes knowledge of the punishment of annihilation the basis for knowledge that the Resurrection is true. Therefore what al-Qaffal stated is invalidated. The more correct view, in my opinion, is to say: knowledge that the Resurrection is true depends on knowledge that the one who governs the existence of these heavens and earths is a free-choosing agent, not a necessitating cause by its essence. As long as a person does not know that the God of the world is a free-choosing agent, capable of all possibilities, and that all the events occurring in the heavens and earths come about only through His bringing into being and His decree, he cannot take a lesson from the punishment of annihilation. This is because those who claim that the cause of the existence of this world is a necessitating cause by its essence, and not a free-choosing agent, claim that these events which appeared in the days of the prophets, such as drowning, burning, sinking into the earth, transformation, and the Cry, all happened only because of conjunctions of the stars and their connection with one another. If that is the case, then their occurrence is no evidence for the truthfulness of the prophets. But as for the one who believes in the Resurrection, that faith is not complete unless he believes that the God of the world is a free-choosing agent, and that He has knowledge of all particulars. If that is the case, it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the occurrence of these tremendous events and great happenings was caused by the God of the world creating and bringing them into being, and that they were not caused by the courses and conjunctions of the stars. Then he benefits from hearing these narratives and uses them as evidence for the truthfulness of the prophets. Thus the soundness of His saying is established: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter.﴾

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, mentioned the Hereafter, He described that Day with two attributes:

The first: it is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, meaning that the creation of the first and the last, all of them, will be assembled and brought together on that Day.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 11, verses 102–104:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing. Indeed His seizure is painful and severe.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed.﴾ ﴿And We do not delay it except for a term numbered.﴾

Within the verse there are issues (masa'il):

**The first issue:** ʿĀṣim and al-Jaḥdarī read "إذ أخذ القرى" with one alif, while the rest read it with two alifs.

**The second issue:** Know that when God, exalted is He, informed His Messenger, peace be upon him, in His Book about what He had done to the peoples of the prophets who came before him, when they opposed the messengers and rejected them, with the punishment of total annihilation (istiʾṣāl), and He made clear that they had wronged themselves, so that punishment befell them in this world, He then said after that: ﴿Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing.﴾ Thus He made clear that His punishment is not limited to those who came before, but the case is the same in the seizing of all wrongdoers. His saying ﴿while they are wrongdoing﴾: the pronoun in it refers to "the towns," but in reality it refers to their people. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And how many a town did We shatter that had been wrongdoing﴾ [al-Anbiya: 11], and His saying: ﴿And how many a town did We destroy that had exulted in its livelihood﴾ [al-Qasas: 58].

Know that when God, exalted is He, had explained the manner of the seizing of the earlier nations, and then explained that He seizes all wrongdoers in that same manner, He followed it with something that adds emphasis and strength, saying: ﴿Indeed His seizure is painful and severe.﴾ So He described that punishment as painful and severe. There is no distress in this world except pain, and no intensification in this world or the Hereafter, nor in imagination or intellect, except the intensification of pain.

Know that this verse indicates that whoever commits an act of wrongdoing must make amends for it through repentance and turning back (to God), so that he does not fall into the seizing which God, exalted is He, described as painful and severe. And it should not be thought that these rulings are specific to those earlier peoples, because when He, exalted is He, recounted the conditions of the earlier peoples, He said: ﴿Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are wrongdoing.﴾ So He made clear that everyone who shares with those earlier peoples in doing what is not fitting must inevitably share with them in that painful and severe seizing.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter.﴾ Al-Qaffal said: The explanation of this statement is that it may be said: These people were punished in this world only because of their denial of the prophets and their association of partners with God. So if they were punished in this world for that, and this world is the abode of action, then being punished for it in the Hereafter, which is the abode of recompense, is more fitting.

Know that many of the exegetes who grasped this line of inquiry relied upon this interpretation. Yet it is weak, because according to this interpretation that al-Qaffal mentioned, the manifestation of the punishment of annihilation in this world would be evidence that the doctrine of the Resurrection, the raising of the dead, and their gathering is true and right.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires that knowledge that the Resurrection is true functions as a condition for deriving a lesson from the manifestation of the punishment of annihilation. This meaning is almost contrary to what al-Qaffal stated, because al-Qaffal makes knowledge of the punishment of annihilation the basis for knowledge that the Resurrection is true. Therefore what al-Qaffal stated is invalidated. The more correct view, in my opinion, is to say: knowledge that the Resurrection is true depends on knowledge that the one who governs the existence of these heavens and earths is a free-choosing agent, not a necessitating cause by its essence. As long as a person does not know that the God of the world is a free-choosing agent, capable of all possibilities, and that all the events occurring in the heavens and earths come about only through His bringing into being and His decree, he cannot take a lesson from the punishment of annihilation. This is because those who claim that the cause of the existence of this world is a necessitating cause by its essence, and not a free-choosing agent, claim that these events which appeared in the days of the prophets, such as drowning, burning, sinking into the earth, transformation, and the Cry, all happened only because of conjunctions of the stars and their connection with one another. If that is the case, then their occurrence is no evidence for the truthfulness of the prophets. But as for the one who believes in the Resurrection, that faith is not complete unless he believes that the God of the world is a free-choosing agent, and that He has knowledge of all particulars. If that is the case, it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the occurrence of these tremendous events and great happenings was caused by the God of the world creating and bringing them into being, and that they were not caused by the courses and conjunctions of the stars. Then he benefits from hearing these narratives and uses them as evidence for the truthfulness of the prophets. Thus the soundness of His saying is established: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter.﴾

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. Among them will be the wretched and the happy.﴾ ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them there is groaning and wailing.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills. Indeed your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.﴾ ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills, a gift unceasing.﴾

In the verse there are issues (masa'il):

The first issue: Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamzah read ﴿ya'ti﴾ with the ya' omitted, while the rest read it with the ya'. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The omission of the ya' and making do with the kasrah in its place is common in the dialect of Hudhayl. Similar to it is their saying "la adri" (I do not know), related by al-Khalil and Sibawayh.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The subject of ya'ti is Allah, Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿Do they wait for anything but that Allah should come to them?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] and His saying: ﴿Or that your Lord should come?﴾ [al-An'am: 158], and this is supported by the reading of whoever read "wa ma yu'akhkhiruh" with the ya'. I say: I do not like this interpretation, because His saying: ﴿Do they wait for anything but that Allah should come to them?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] is related by Allah, Exalted, about certain peoples, and the apparent meaning is that they were the Jews, and that is not a proof. Likewise His saying: ﴿Or that your Lord should come?﴾ [al-An'am: 158]. But here it is the explicit speech of Allah, Exalted, and attributing the act of coming to Him is problematic.

If they say: What is your view of His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr: 22]?

We say: There are interpretations for that, and also it is explicit, so it cannot be repelled, and therefore abstaining from it is obligatory. Rather, the correct thing to say is that what is meant is: the Day when the awesome, terrifying, greatly magnified thing comes, and Allah, Exalted, is omitted from mention by His specification so that it would be more potent in instilling fear.

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The governing element for the accusative of the time-adverb is His saying ﴿la takallamu﴾ (will speak), or an implied "udhkur" (remember).

Page 49

As for His saying ﴿no soul will speak except by His permission﴾, there is an ellipsis in it, and the implied meaning is: no soul will speak on that Day except by the permission of Allah, Exalted.

If it is said: How can this verse be reconciled with other verses which seem to contradict it? Among them is His saying: ﴿On the Day every soul will come pleading for itself﴾ [al-Nahl: 111]; and among them is that they lie and swear by Allah concerning it, namely their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]; and among them is His saying: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24]; and among them is His saying: ﴿This is a Day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 35].

The answer is in two respects:

The first: Wherever a prohibition from speech occurs, it is to be understood as referring to the true and correct responses.

The second: That Day is a long day and has stations. In some of them they argue for themselves, in some of them they refrain from speech, and in some of them they are permitted and so they speak, and in some of them their mouths are sealed and their hands speak and their feet bear witness.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The pronoun in His saying ﴿Among them﴾ refers to the people of the standing place (of judgment). It is not mentioned because it is known, and because His saying ﴿no soul will speak except by His permission﴾ indicates it, since mention of mankind has already passed in His saying ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered﴾ [Hud: 103].

The second issue: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾ indicates that the people of the standing place do not go outside these two divisions.

If it is said: Are there not among mankind insane persons and children, who lie outside these two divisions?

We say: What is meant is those who are gathered from among those who are released for reckoning, and they do not go outside these two divisions.

If it is said: Al-Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) has argued with this verse against the view that the People of the Heights (al-A'raf) are neither in Paradise nor in Hell. What is your view on it?

We say: Since it is granted that children and insane persons lie outside these two divisions because they are not called to account, why is it not also permissible to say that the People of the Heights lie outside them too, because they also are not called to account, since Allah, Exalted, knows about their condition that their reward equals their punishment, so there is no benefit in reckoning them?

If it is said: Al-Qadi also argued from this verse that everyone who attends the arena of the Resurrection must have either an increased reward or an increased punishment. As for one whose reward equals his punishment, although that is possible rationally, this text indicates that it does not exist.

We say: The discussion concerning it is what has preceded: that the happy one is the one who is among the people of reward, and the wretched one is the one who is among the people of punishment. The singling out of these two divisions for mention does not indicate the negation of a third division. The proof of this is that most verses contain mention only of the believer and the disbeliever, and there is no mention in them of a third who is neither believer nor disbeliever, although al-Qadi affirmed it. So if the absence of mention of that third does not necessitate its non-existence, then likewise the mention of this third does not necessitate its non-existence.

Page 50

The third issue: Know that He, Exalted, has now judged some of the people of the Resurrection to be happy and some of them to be wretched. Whoever Allah has judged with a judgment, and that matter is known from him, it is impossible for him to be otherwise, for otherwise it would follow that the report of Allah, Exalted, would become false and His knowledge ignorance, and that is impossible. So it is established that the happy one does not turn into a wretched one, and the wretched one does not turn into a happy one. The statement of this proof has passed in this book countless times. It is related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When the words ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾ were revealed, I said: O Messenger of Allah, then upon what do we act: upon a matter already finished, or upon a matter not yet finished? He said: 'Upon a matter already finished, O 'Umar, the pens have dried with it, and the decrees have run with it; but each is made easy for that for which he was created.'"

The Mu'tazilah said: It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "Among them is the wretched one by his deed and the happy one by his deed."

We say: A decisive proof is not overturned by these reports. Moreover, there is no dispute that he became wretched only by his deed, and became happy only by his deed; but since that deed occurred by the decree and predestination of Allah, the proof we have mentioned remains valid.

Know that when He, Exalted, divided the people of the Resurrection into these two divisions, He explained the condition of each of them, saying: ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them there is groaning and wailing.﴾ In this there are issues:

The first issue: They have mentioned several views concerning the difference between the zafir (groaning) and the shahiq (wailing):

The first view: Al-Layth said: The zafir is when a man fills his chest while in severe distress with breath and does not exhale it, and the shahiq is when he exhales that breath. Al-Farra' said: It is said of a horse: he has a great zafrah, meaning a great belly. I say: When a person's grief becomes great, the spirit of his heart is confined within the interior of the heart. When the spirit is confined, the heat grows strong and becomes great, and at that point a person needs a strong breath in order to draw in much cold air, so that he may be able to cool that heat. For this reason, at that time, the drawing in of air into the interior of the body becomes great, and then his chest rises and his sides swell. And since the innate heat and the animal spirit are confined within the heart, coldness takes hold of the outer organs, so the instruments of breathing sometimes fail to push out that abundant air that has been inhaled, so that abundant air remains confined in the chest, and the person nearly suffocates from it. Then nature strives to expel that air. So, according to the analogy of the physicians' statement: the zafir is the drawing in of abundant air to cool the heat produced in the heart by the confinement of the spirit within it, and the shahiq is the expulsion of that air when nature strives to expel it. Each of these two states indicates severe distress and great grief.

The second view: On the difference between the zafir and the shahiq, some said: the zafir is like the beginning of the donkey's bray, while the shahiq is like the end of the donkey's bray.

The third view: Al-Hasan said: We have mentioned that the zafir signifies elevation. So we say: the zafir is the blaze of Hell, which raises them by its force, until when they reach the highest degrees of Hell and hope to get out of it, the angels strike them with iron maces and return them to the lowest level of Hell. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they are returned to it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. So their rising in the Fire is the zafir, and their descending again is the shahiq.

The fourth view: Abu Muslim said: The zafir is the breath that gathers in the chest during intense weeping, so that the breath is cut off, and the shahiq is what appears when distress and sorrow intensify, and perhaps a fainting follows them, and perhaps death results from it.

The fifth view: Abu al-'Aliyah said: The zafir is in the throat, and the shahiq is in the chest.

The sixth view: Some people said: The zafir is a strong sound, and the shahiq is a weak sound.

The seventh view: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: ﴿for them there is groaning and wailing﴾ means: regret, a high-pitched sigh, weeping that does not cease, and sorrow that is not relieved.

The eighth view: The zafir indicates strength, and the shahiq indicates weakness, according to what we have established by linguistic usage.

Having understood this, we say: It is not far-fetched that what is meant by the zafir is the intensity of their inclination toward the world of this life and toward bodily pleasures, and what is meant by the shahiq is their weakness in attaining happiness through the world of spirituals, and their perfection through divine lights and holy ascents.
