Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills.﴾ In it there are two issues:

The first issue: Some people said that the punishment of the disbelievers is discontinued and has an end. They argued with the Qur'an and with reason. As for the Qur'an, there are verses among which is this verse, and the argument from it is in two respects:

The first: He, Exalted, said: ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾. This text indicates that the duration of their punishment is equal to the duration of the continuance of the heavens and the earth. Then we agree that the duration of the continuance of the heavens and the earth is finite, so it follows that the duration of the punishment of the disbelievers is discontinued.

The second: His saying ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ is an exception from the duration of their punishment, and that indicates the cessation of that punishment during the time of this exception. Among what they also held onto is His saying, Exalted, in the surah "Asking one another" (al-Naba'): ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ [al-Naba': 23]; He, Exalted, made clear that their remaining in that punishment will be only for countable ages.

As for reason, there are two arguments:

The first: The disobedience of the disbeliever is finite, and to match a finite crime with a punishment that has no end is injustice, and that is not permissible.

The second: That punishment is harm devoid of benefit, and so it is ugly.

The proof that it is devoid of benefit is that this benefit does not return to Allah, Exalted, since He is exalted above benefit and harm; nor to that person being punished, since for him it is pure harm; nor to anyone else, since the people of Paradise are occupied with their own pleasures, so there is no benefit for them in delighting in the everlasting punishment of others. So it is established that that punishment is harm devoid of all aspects of benefit, and therefore it must not be permitted.

As for the great majority of the community, they agreed that the punishment of the disbeliever is everlasting, and at this point they needed to answer the argument from this verse. As for His saying ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, they mentioned two answers concerning it:

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 105–108 (part 2 of 3):**

The first view: they said the intended meaning is the heavens and earth of the Hereafter. They said the proof that there are a heaven and an earth in the Hereafter is His saying, ﴿On the Day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48], and His saying, ﴿And He has given us the land to inherit, [that] we may settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. Also, the people of the Hereafter must have something that bears them and shades them, and that is the earth and the heavens.

One may reply: a comparison (*tashbih*) is only apt and permissible when the state of the thing compared to is known and established, so that other things are compared to it to confirm the ruling for the thing being compared. The existence of the heavens and earth in the Hereafter is not known. Even if their existence were known, their enduring in a way that never perishes at all is not known. When the very existence of these two is unknown to most of creation, and their permanence is likewise unknown to most, then comparing the punishment of the wretched to them in permanence is a statement without benefit. At most, one could say: since the Qur'an establishes the existence of heavens and earth in the Hereafter, and establishes their permanence, it is obligatory to acknowledge this, and then the comparison is apt. But we say: since the way to establishing the permanence of the heavens and earth of the people of the Hereafter is revelation (*sam'*), and revelation has indicated the permanence of the punishment of the unbeliever, then the evidence that established the ruling in the original case (*asl*) is present in the same way in the branch case (*far'*). In this kind of case, they all agreed that *qiyas* (analogical reasoning) is void and the comparison is invalid. So too here.

The second answer: they said that the Arabs express permanence and eternity by saying, "as long as the heavens and the earth endure." Its parallel is also their saying, "as long as the night and day alternate," "as long as the sea surges," and "as long as the mountain stands." God addressed the Arabs in their customary speech. When they mention these things, on the basis of their belief that they remain forever, we know that these expressions, according to their custom, convey eternity and permanence free of cessation.

One may reply: Do you concede that the saying of the speaker, "abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure," prevents their remaining in existence after the heavens perish, or do you say that it does not indicate this meaning?

If it is the first, then the difficulty is unavoidable, because the text has indicated that the duration of their stay in the Fire must be equal to the duration of the heavens' survival, and it prevents their remaining in the Fire after the heavens perish. Then it is established that the heavens must perish, and at that point you are compelled to say that this punishment ends. If you say that this statement does not prevent their remaining in the Fire after the heavens and the earth perish, then you have no need for this answer at all. Thus it is established that this answer is void on both assumptions.

Know that the true answer, in my view, on this matter is something else: the established reading of the verse is that whenever the heavens and the earth are enduring, their being in the Fire remains. This indicates that whenever the condition is fulfilled, the conditioned thing is fulfilled, but it does not indicate that when the condition is absent, the conditioned thing is absent. Do you not see that we say: "If this is a human, then it is an animal." If we say, "But it is a human," it follows that it is an animal. But if we say, "But it is not a human," it does not follow that it is not an animal. For it is established in the science of logic (*mantiq*) that denying the consequent in a conditional does not yield any conclusion. So too here: when we say, "Whenever the heavens endure, their punishment endures," then if we say, "But the heavens are enduring," it follows that their punishment is present. But if we say, "But the heavens have not remained," it does not follow that the permanence of their punishment is absent.

If they say: then if the punishment is present whether or not the heavens remain, the comparison has no benefit left.

We say: rather, in it there is the greatest benefit, which is that it indicates the continuing of that torment age upon age, for a time whose length and extent the intellect cannot encompass. As for whether it will have an end or not, that is known from other proofs. This answer that I have established is a true answer, but only someone accustomed to rational sciences (*ma'qulat*) will understand it.

As for the second objection, namely the reliance on His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, they have mentioned several kinds of answers.

The first answer, which Ibn Qutayba, Ibn al-Anbari and al-Farra' mentioned, is this: they said: this is an exception which God made, but He does not in fact do it at all. It is like your saying: "By God, I will surely strike you, except if I see otherwise," while your resolve is to strike him. So too here. They elaborated at length in establishing this answer and in giving examples for it, but its essence is what we have mentioned.

One may reply: this is weak, because when he says, "I will surely strike you, except if I see otherwise," the meaning is: "I will strike you except when I judge that leaving off striking is better." This does not at all indicate whether this seeing has occurred or not. This is unlike His saying, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, whose meaning is the ruling of their abiding therein, except for the period which your Lord wills. Here the wording indicates that this willing has definitely occurred. So how can the analogy of this statement be drawn to that statement?

The second answer: it is said that the word ﴿illa﴾ (except) here is used with the meaning of *siwa* (other than). The meaning is that when He said, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, it was understood from it that they would be in the Fire for the entire period of the endurance of the heavens and earth of this world. Then He said, "other than" what exceeds that by an everlasting abiding, by His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾. The meaning is: except what your Lord wills of the additional period that has no end. So He first mentioned for their abiding a duration that the Arabs regard as the longest, then added to it the everlasting permanence that has no end.

The third answer: the intended meaning of this exception is the time of their standing at the place of reckoning (*mawqif*). It is as if He said: "As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, except the time of their standing for the reckoning, for at that time they will not be in the Fire." Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: the intended meaning is "except what your Lord wills," which is the state of their being in the grave (*qabr*), or the intended meaning is "except what your Lord wills" of the period of their lives in this world. These three statements are close in meaning: the sense is abiding therein for the measure of their stay in this world, or in the intermediate state (*barzakh*), or the measure of their standing for the reckoning, after which they go to the Fire.

The fourth answer: they said the exception refers back to His saying, ﴿for them therein is [heavy] sighing and wailing﴾. The explanation of this is that we say: His saying, ﴿for them therein is sighing and wailing﴾ together with ﴿abiding therein﴾ conveys that sighing and wailing occur along with abiding. When the exception enters upon this, there must occur a time in which this combined state does not occur. It is established in rational matters that just as a whole is negated by the negation of all its parts, so it is also negated by the negation of a single one of its parts. So when at the end they reach the state of becoming still, silent and extinguished, then they no longer have sighing and wailing, and one part of that whole is absent. At that point, that exception is valid without any need to rule that their being in the Fire ceases.

The fifth answer: that this exception be understood to mean that the people of punishment will not always be in the Fire, but may be moved to the cold, the frigid zone (*zamharir*), and other kinds of punishment, and this suffices for the validity of this exception.

The sixth answer: some people said: this exception indicates the exclusion of the people of monotheism (*tawhid*) from the Fire. This is because His saying, ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire﴾, indicates that the whole class of the wretched is subject to this ruling. Then His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, requires that this ruling not remain upon that whole group, and it suffices for the removal of the ruling of abiding from the whole that it be removed from some of them. So it is necessary that the ruling of abiding not remain for some of the wretched. Since it is established that abiding is obligatory for the disbelievers, it must be said: those from whom the ruling of abiding is removed are the sinners among the people of prayer (*ahl al-salah*). This is a strong argument in this matter.

If it is said: this answer is only determined when all the other answers you have mentioned are invalid, so what is the evidence for their invalidity? Furthermore, a similar exception is mentioned concerning the blessed, for He said: ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills — a gift uninterrupted﴾.

[Page 54]

We say: by this answer we have shown that this verse does not indicate the cessation of the threat against the disbelievers. Then, if we want to use this verse as evidence for the validity of our position that God brings the sinners among the people of prayer out of the Fire...

We say: as for taking the word ﴿illa﴾ to mean *siwa* (other than), it is a departure from the apparent meaning. As for taking the exception to refer to the state of the life of this world, the intermediate state, and the place of standing, that too is far-fetched, because the exception came from abiding in the Fire, and it is known that abiding in the Fire is a mode of being in the Fire. Before one is in the Fire, abiding in the Fire is impossible; and if abiding has not occurred, the excepted thing has not occurred, and the exception is impossible. As for his saying that the exception refers to the sighing and wailing, this too abandons the apparent meaning. So there remains for the verse no valid interpretation except this one which we have mentioned.

As for his saying that the intended meaning of the exception is its transfer from the Fire to the zamharir, we say: if that were the case, it would be necessary that punishment by the zamharir not occur except after the period of the heavens and earth has ended. But the sound reports indicate that the transfer from the Fire to the zamharir and vice versa occurs many times each day. So this answer is refuted.

As for his saying that a similar exception is present concerning the blessed, we say: the community (*umma*) has agreed (*ijma'*, consensus) that it is impossible to say that anyone enters Paradise and then leaves it for the Fire. Because of this consensus, we needed to interpret that exception according to one of those interpretations. But as for this verse, this consensus has not occurred, so it is necessary to apply it to its apparent meaning. This is the complete discussion of this verse.

* * *

Know that when He mentioned this exception, He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Accomplisher of what He intends﴾. This fits well with this verse if we take the exception as bringing the sinners out of the Fire. It is as if He says: "I displayed domination and power, then I displayed forgiveness and mercy, because I am the Accomplisher of what I intend, and no one has any right of judgment over Me at all."

Then He said: ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

The first issue: Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read *su'idu* (سُعِدُوا) with a *damma* on the *sin*, while the rest read it with a *fatha*. The *damma* is permissible because it is derived by dropping the augment from *as'ada* (to make happy), and because *sa'ida* (to be happy) is intransitive while *as'ada* is transitive. *Sa'ida* and *as'ada* have the same meaning, and from this comes *al-mas'ud* (the fortunate), which is among the names of men.

The second issue: the exception in the matter of the blessed must be interpreted according to one of the aspects mentioned earlier, and here there is another aspect, namely that it may happen to some of them that they are raised from Paradise to the Throne and to the lofty dwellings which only God Most High knows. God Most High said: ﴿God has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence; and approval from God is greater﴾ [al-Tawba: 72]. As for His saying, ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: *jadhdha yajudhdhu jadhdhan* means he cut it off. And "God cut off their root" (*jadha Allahu dabirahum*). So His saying, ﴿uninterrupted﴾ means not cut off. Its parallel is His saying concerning the description of the bliss of Paradise: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 33].

Second issue: know that when God, exalted is He, stated explicitly in this verse that the intended meaning of this exception is not that this state is discontinuous, then, since He singled out this place with this clarification and did not mention the same in the case of the wretched, this indicates that the intended meaning of that exception is discontinuity. This is the complete discussion of this verse.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. Among them will be the wretched and the happy.﴾ ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them there is groaning and wailing.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills. Indeed your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.﴾ ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills, a gift unceasing.﴾

In the verse there are issues (masa'il):

The first issue: Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamzah read ﴿ya'ti﴾ with the ya' omitted, while the rest read it with the ya'. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The omission of the ya' and making do with the kasrah in its place is common in the dialect of Hudhayl. Similar to it is their saying "la adri" (I do not know), related by al-Khalil and Sibawayh.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The subject of ya'ti is Allah, Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿Do they wait for anything but that Allah should come to them?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] and His saying: ﴿Or that your Lord should come?﴾ [al-An'am: 158], and this is supported by the reading of whoever read "wa ma yu'akhkhiruh" with the ya'. I say: I do not like this interpretation, because His saying: ﴿Do they wait for anything but that Allah should come to them?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] is related by Allah, Exalted, about certain peoples, and the apparent meaning is that they were the Jews, and that is not a proof. Likewise His saying: ﴿Or that your Lord should come?﴾ [al-An'am: 158]. But here it is the explicit speech of Allah, Exalted, and attributing the act of coming to Him is problematic.

If they say: What is your view of His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr: 22]?

We say: There are interpretations for that, and also it is explicit, so it cannot be repelled, and therefore abstaining from it is obligatory. Rather, the correct thing to say is that what is meant is: the Day when the awesome, terrifying, greatly magnified thing comes, and Allah, Exalted, is omitted from mention by His specification so that it would be more potent in instilling fear.

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The governing element for the accusative of the time-adverb is His saying ﴿la takallamu﴾ (will speak), or an implied "udhkur" (remember).

Page 49

As for His saying ﴿no soul will speak except by His permission﴾, there is an ellipsis in it, and the implied meaning is: no soul will speak on that Day except by the permission of Allah, Exalted.

If it is said: How can this verse be reconciled with other verses which seem to contradict it? Among them is His saying: ﴿On the Day every soul will come pleading for itself﴾ [al-Nahl: 111]; and among them is that they lie and swear by Allah concerning it, namely their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]; and among them is His saying: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24]; and among them is His saying: ﴿This is a Day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 35].

The answer is in two respects:

The first: Wherever a prohibition from speech occurs, it is to be understood as referring to the true and correct responses.

The second: That Day is a long day and has stations. In some of them they argue for themselves, in some of them they refrain from speech, and in some of them they are permitted and so they speak, and in some of them their mouths are sealed and their hands speak and their feet bear witness.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The pronoun in His saying ﴿Among them﴾ refers to the people of the standing place (of judgment). It is not mentioned because it is known, and because His saying ﴿no soul will speak except by His permission﴾ indicates it, since mention of mankind has already passed in His saying ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered﴾ [Hud: 103].

The second issue: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾ indicates that the people of the standing place do not go outside these two divisions.

If it is said: Are there not among mankind insane persons and children, who lie outside these two divisions?

We say: What is meant is those who are gathered from among those who are released for reckoning, and they do not go outside these two divisions.

If it is said: Al-Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) has argued with this verse against the view that the People of the Heights (al-A'raf) are neither in Paradise nor in Hell. What is your view on it?

We say: Since it is granted that children and insane persons lie outside these two divisions because they are not called to account, why is it not also permissible to say that the People of the Heights lie outside them too, because they also are not called to account, since Allah, Exalted, knows about their condition that their reward equals their punishment, so there is no benefit in reckoning them?

If it is said: Al-Qadi also argued from this verse that everyone who attends the arena of the Resurrection must have either an increased reward or an increased punishment. As for one whose reward equals his punishment, although that is possible rationally, this text indicates that it does not exist.

We say: The discussion concerning it is what has preceded: that the happy one is the one who is among the people of reward, and the wretched one is the one who is among the people of punishment. The singling out of these two divisions for mention does not indicate the negation of a third division. The proof of this is that most verses contain mention only of the believer and the disbeliever, and there is no mention in them of a third who is neither believer nor disbeliever, although al-Qadi affirmed it. So if the absence of mention of that third does not necessitate its non-existence, then likewise the mention of this third does not necessitate its non-existence.

Page 50

The third issue: Know that He, Exalted, has now judged some of the people of the Resurrection to be happy and some of them to be wretched. Whoever Allah has judged with a judgment, and that matter is known from him, it is impossible for him to be otherwise, for otherwise it would follow that the report of Allah, Exalted, would become false and His knowledge ignorance, and that is impossible. So it is established that the happy one does not turn into a wretched one, and the wretched one does not turn into a happy one. The statement of this proof has passed in this book countless times. It is related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When the words ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾ were revealed, I said: O Messenger of Allah, then upon what do we act: upon a matter already finished, or upon a matter not yet finished? He said: 'Upon a matter already finished, O 'Umar, the pens have dried with it, and the decrees have run with it; but each is made easy for that for which he was created.'"

The Mu'tazilah said: It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "Among them is the wretched one by his deed and the happy one by his deed."

We say: A decisive proof is not overturned by these reports. Moreover, there is no dispute that he became wretched only by his deed, and became happy only by his deed; but since that deed occurred by the decree and predestination of Allah, the proof we have mentioned remains valid.

Know that when He, Exalted, divided the people of the Resurrection into these two divisions, He explained the condition of each of them, saying: ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them there is groaning and wailing.﴾ In this there are issues:

The first issue: They have mentioned several views concerning the difference between the zafir (groaning) and the shahiq (wailing):

The first view: Al-Layth said: The zafir is when a man fills his chest while in severe distress with breath and does not exhale it, and the shahiq is when he exhales that breath. Al-Farra' said: It is said of a horse: he has a great zafrah, meaning a great belly. I say: When a person's grief becomes great, the spirit of his heart is confined within the interior of the heart. When the spirit is confined, the heat grows strong and becomes great, and at that point a person needs a strong breath in order to draw in much cold air, so that he may be able to cool that heat. For this reason, at that time, the drawing in of air into the interior of the body becomes great, and then his chest rises and his sides swell. And since the innate heat and the animal spirit are confined within the heart, coldness takes hold of the outer organs, so the instruments of breathing sometimes fail to push out that abundant air that has been inhaled, so that abundant air remains confined in the chest, and the person nearly suffocates from it. Then nature strives to expel that air. So, according to the analogy of the physicians' statement: the zafir is the drawing in of abundant air to cool the heat produced in the heart by the confinement of the spirit within it, and the shahiq is the expulsion of that air when nature strives to expel it. Each of these two states indicates severe distress and great grief.

The second view: On the difference between the zafir and the shahiq, some said: the zafir is like the beginning of the donkey's bray, while the shahiq is like the end of the donkey's bray.

The third view: Al-Hasan said: We have mentioned that the zafir signifies elevation. So we say: the zafir is the blaze of Hell, which raises them by its force, until when they reach the highest degrees of Hell and hope to get out of it, the angels strike them with iron maces and return them to the lowest level of Hell. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they are returned to it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. So their rising in the Fire is the zafir, and their descending again is the shahiq.

The fourth view: Abu Muslim said: The zafir is the breath that gathers in the chest during intense weeping, so that the breath is cut off, and the shahiq is what appears when distress and sorrow intensify, and perhaps a fainting follows them, and perhaps death results from it.

The fifth view: Abu al-'Aliyah said: The zafir is in the throat, and the shahiq is in the chest.

The sixth view: Some people said: The zafir is a strong sound, and the shahiq is a weak sound.

The seventh view: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: ﴿for them there is groaning and wailing﴾ means: regret, a high-pitched sigh, weeping that does not cease, and sorrow that is not relieved.

The eighth view: The zafir indicates strength, and the shahiq indicates weakness, according to what we have established by linguistic usage.

Having understood this, we say: It is not far-fetched that what is meant by the zafir is the intensity of their inclination toward the world of this life and toward bodily pleasures, and what is meant by the shahiq is their weakness in attaining happiness through the world of spirituals, and their perfection through divine lights and holy ascents.

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills.﴾ In it there are two issues:

The first issue: Some people said that the punishment of the disbelievers is discontinued and has an end. They argued with the Qur'an and with reason. As for the Qur'an, there are verses among which is this verse, and the argument from it is in two respects:

The first: He, Exalted, said: ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾. This text indicates that the duration of their punishment is equal to the duration of the continuance of the heavens and the earth. Then we agree that the duration of the continuance of the heavens and the earth is finite, so it follows that the duration of the punishment of the disbelievers is discontinued.

The second: His saying ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ is an exception from the duration of their punishment, and that indicates the cessation of that punishment during the time of this exception. Among what they also held onto is His saying, Exalted, in the surah "Asking one another" (al-Naba'): ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ [al-Naba': 23]; He, Exalted, made clear that their remaining in that punishment will be only for countable ages.

As for reason, there are two arguments:

The first: The disobedience of the disbeliever is finite, and to match a finite crime with a punishment that has no end is injustice, and that is not permissible.

The second: That punishment is harm devoid of benefit, and so it is ugly.

The proof that it is devoid of benefit is that this benefit does not return to Allah, Exalted, since He is exalted above benefit and harm; nor to that person being punished, since for him it is pure harm; nor to anyone else, since the people of Paradise are occupied with their own pleasures, so there is no benefit for them in delighting in the everlasting punishment of others. So it is established that that punishment is harm devoid of all aspects of benefit, and therefore it must not be permitted.

As for the great majority of the community, they agreed that the punishment of the disbeliever is everlasting, and at this point they needed to answer the argument from this verse. As for His saying ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, they mentioned two answers concerning it:

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 105–108 (part 2 of 3):**

The first view: they said the intended meaning is the heavens and earth of the Hereafter. They said the proof that there are a heaven and an earth in the Hereafter is His saying, ﴿On the Day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48], and His saying, ﴿And He has given us the land to inherit, [that] we may settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. Also, the people of the Hereafter must have something that bears them and shades them, and that is the earth and the heavens.

One may reply: a comparison (*tashbih*) is only apt and permissible when the state of the thing compared to is known and established, so that other things are compared to it to confirm the ruling for the thing being compared. The existence of the heavens and earth in the Hereafter is not known. Even if their existence were known, their enduring in a way that never perishes at all is not known. When the very existence of these two is unknown to most of creation, and their permanence is likewise unknown to most, then comparing the punishment of the wretched to them in permanence is a statement without benefit. At most, one could say: since the Qur'an establishes the existence of heavens and earth in the Hereafter, and establishes their permanence, it is obligatory to acknowledge this, and then the comparison is apt. But we say: since the way to establishing the permanence of the heavens and earth of the people of the Hereafter is revelation (*sam'*), and revelation has indicated the permanence of the punishment of the unbeliever, then the evidence that established the ruling in the original case (*asl*) is present in the same way in the branch case (*far'*). In this kind of case, they all agreed that *qiyas* (analogical reasoning) is void and the comparison is invalid. So too here.

The second answer: they said that the Arabs express permanence and eternity by saying, "as long as the heavens and the earth endure." Its parallel is also their saying, "as long as the night and day alternate," "as long as the sea surges," and "as long as the mountain stands." God addressed the Arabs in their customary speech. When they mention these things, on the basis of their belief that they remain forever, we know that these expressions, according to their custom, convey eternity and permanence free of cessation.

One may reply: Do you concede that the saying of the speaker, "abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure," prevents their remaining in existence after the heavens perish, or do you say that it does not indicate this meaning?

If it is the first, then the difficulty is unavoidable, because the text has indicated that the duration of their stay in the Fire must be equal to the duration of the heavens' survival, and it prevents their remaining in the Fire after the heavens perish. Then it is established that the heavens must perish, and at that point you are compelled to say that this punishment ends. If you say that this statement does not prevent their remaining in the Fire after the heavens and the earth perish, then you have no need for this answer at all. Thus it is established that this answer is void on both assumptions.

Know that the true answer, in my view, on this matter is something else: the established reading of the verse is that whenever the heavens and the earth are enduring, their being in the Fire remains. This indicates that whenever the condition is fulfilled, the conditioned thing is fulfilled, but it does not indicate that when the condition is absent, the conditioned thing is absent. Do you not see that we say: "If this is a human, then it is an animal." If we say, "But it is a human," it follows that it is an animal. But if we say, "But it is not a human," it does not follow that it is not an animal. For it is established in the science of logic (*mantiq*) that denying the consequent in a conditional does not yield any conclusion. So too here: when we say, "Whenever the heavens endure, their punishment endures," then if we say, "But the heavens are enduring," it follows that their punishment is present. But if we say, "But the heavens have not remained," it does not follow that the permanence of their punishment is absent.

If they say: then if the punishment is present whether or not the heavens remain, the comparison has no benefit left.

We say: rather, in it there is the greatest benefit, which is that it indicates the continuing of that torment age upon age, for a time whose length and extent the intellect cannot encompass. As for whether it will have an end or not, that is known from other proofs. This answer that I have established is a true answer, but only someone accustomed to rational sciences (*ma'qulat*) will understand it.

As for the second objection, namely the reliance on His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, they have mentioned several kinds of answers.

The first answer, which Ibn Qutayba, Ibn al-Anbari and al-Farra' mentioned, is this: they said: this is an exception which God made, but He does not in fact do it at all. It is like your saying: "By God, I will surely strike you, except if I see otherwise," while your resolve is to strike him. So too here. They elaborated at length in establishing this answer and in giving examples for it, but its essence is what we have mentioned.

One may reply: this is weak, because when he says, "I will surely strike you, except if I see otherwise," the meaning is: "I will strike you except when I judge that leaving off striking is better." This does not at all indicate whether this seeing has occurred or not. This is unlike His saying, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, whose meaning is the ruling of their abiding therein, except for the period which your Lord wills. Here the wording indicates that this willing has definitely occurred. So how can the analogy of this statement be drawn to that statement?

The second answer: it is said that the word ﴿illa﴾ (except) here is used with the meaning of *siwa* (other than). The meaning is that when He said, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, it was understood from it that they would be in the Fire for the entire period of the endurance of the heavens and earth of this world. Then He said, "other than" what exceeds that by an everlasting abiding, by His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾. The meaning is: except what your Lord wills of the additional period that has no end. So He first mentioned for their abiding a duration that the Arabs regard as the longest, then added to it the everlasting permanence that has no end.

The third answer: the intended meaning of this exception is the time of their standing at the place of reckoning (*mawqif*). It is as if He said: "As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, except the time of their standing for the reckoning, for at that time they will not be in the Fire." Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: the intended meaning is "except what your Lord wills," which is the state of their being in the grave (*qabr*), or the intended meaning is "except what your Lord wills" of the period of their lives in this world. These three statements are close in meaning: the sense is abiding therein for the measure of their stay in this world, or in the intermediate state (*barzakh*), or the measure of their standing for the reckoning, after which they go to the Fire.

The fourth answer: they said the exception refers back to His saying, ﴿for them therein is [heavy] sighing and wailing﴾. The explanation of this is that we say: His saying, ﴿for them therein is sighing and wailing﴾ together with ﴿abiding therein﴾ conveys that sighing and wailing occur along with abiding. When the exception enters upon this, there must occur a time in which this combined state does not occur. It is established in rational matters that just as a whole is negated by the negation of all its parts, so it is also negated by the negation of a single one of its parts. So when at the end they reach the state of becoming still, silent and extinguished, then they no longer have sighing and wailing, and one part of that whole is absent. At that point, that exception is valid without any need to rule that their being in the Fire ceases.

The fifth answer: that this exception be understood to mean that the people of punishment will not always be in the Fire, but may be moved to the cold, the frigid zone (*zamharir*), and other kinds of punishment, and this suffices for the validity of this exception.

The sixth answer: some people said: this exception indicates the exclusion of the people of monotheism (*tawhid*) from the Fire. This is because His saying, ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire﴾, indicates that the whole class of the wretched is subject to this ruling. Then His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, requires that this ruling not remain upon that whole group, and it suffices for the removal of the ruling of abiding from the whole that it be removed from some of them. So it is necessary that the ruling of abiding not remain for some of the wretched. Since it is established that abiding is obligatory for the disbelievers, it must be said: those from whom the ruling of abiding is removed are the sinners among the people of prayer (*ahl al-salah*). This is a strong argument in this matter.

If it is said: this answer is only determined when all the other answers you have mentioned are invalid, so what is the evidence for their invalidity? Furthermore, a similar exception is mentioned concerning the blessed, for He said: ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills — a gift uninterrupted﴾.

[Page 54]

We say: by this answer we have shown that this verse does not indicate the cessation of the threat against the disbelievers. Then, if we want to use this verse as evidence for the validity of our position that God brings the sinners among the people of prayer out of the Fire...

We say: as for taking the word ﴿illa﴾ to mean *siwa* (other than), it is a departure from the apparent meaning. As for taking the exception to refer to the state of the life of this world, the intermediate state, and the place of standing, that too is far-fetched, because the exception came from abiding in the Fire, and it is known that abiding in the Fire is a mode of being in the Fire. Before one is in the Fire, abiding in the Fire is impossible; and if abiding has not occurred, the excepted thing has not occurred, and the exception is impossible. As for his saying that the exception refers to the sighing and wailing, this too abandons the apparent meaning. So there remains for the verse no valid interpretation except this one which we have mentioned.

As for his saying that the intended meaning of the exception is its transfer from the Fire to the zamharir, we say: if that were the case, it would be necessary that punishment by the zamharir not occur except after the period of the heavens and earth has ended. But the sound reports indicate that the transfer from the Fire to the zamharir and vice versa occurs many times each day. So this answer is refuted.

As for his saying that a similar exception is present concerning the blessed, we say: the community (*umma*) has agreed (*ijma'*, consensus) that it is impossible to say that anyone enters Paradise and then leaves it for the Fire. Because of this consensus, we needed to interpret that exception according to one of those interpretations. But as for this verse, this consensus has not occurred, so it is necessary to apply it to its apparent meaning. This is the complete discussion of this verse.

* * *

Know that when He mentioned this exception, He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Accomplisher of what He intends﴾. This fits well with this verse if we take the exception as bringing the sinners out of the Fire. It is as if He says: "I displayed domination and power, then I displayed forgiveness and mercy, because I am the Accomplisher of what I intend, and no one has any right of judgment over Me at all."

Then He said: ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

The first issue: Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read *su'idu* (سُعِدُوا) with a *damma* on the *sin*, while the rest read it with a *fatha*. The *damma* is permissible because it is derived by dropping the augment from *as'ada* (to make happy), and because *sa'ida* (to be happy) is intransitive while *as'ada* is transitive. *Sa'ida* and *as'ada* have the same meaning, and from this comes *al-mas'ud* (the fortunate), which is among the names of men.

The second issue: the exception in the matter of the blessed must be interpreted according to one of the aspects mentioned earlier, and here there is another aspect, namely that it may happen to some of them that they are raised from Paradise to the Throne and to the lofty dwellings which only God Most High knows. God Most High said: ﴿God has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence; and approval from God is greater﴾ [al-Tawba: 72]. As for His saying, ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: *jadhdha yajudhdhu jadhdhan* means he cut it off. And "God cut off their root" (*jadha Allahu dabirahum*). So His saying, ﴿uninterrupted﴾ means not cut off. Its parallel is His saying concerning the description of the bliss of Paradise: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 33].

Second issue: know that when God, exalted is He, stated explicitly in this verse that the intended meaning of this exception is not that this state is discontinuous, then, since He singled out this place with this clarification and did not mention the same in the case of the wretched, this indicates that the intended meaning of that exception is discontinuity. This is the complete discussion of this verse.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. Among them will be the wretched and the happy.﴾ ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them there is groaning and wailing.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills. Indeed your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.﴾ ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills, a gift unceasing.﴾

In the verse there are issues (masa'il):

The first issue: Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamzah read ﴿ya'ti﴾ with the ya' omitted, while the rest read it with the ya'. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The omission of the ya' and making do with the kasrah in its place is common in the dialect of Hudhayl. Similar to it is their saying "la adri" (I do not know), related by al-Khalil and Sibawayh.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The subject of ya'ti is Allah, Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿Do they wait for anything but that Allah should come to them?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] and His saying: ﴿Or that your Lord should come?﴾ [al-An'am: 158], and this is supported by the reading of whoever read "wa ma yu'akhkhiruh" with the ya'. I say: I do not like this interpretation, because His saying: ﴿Do they wait for anything but that Allah should come to them?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] is related by Allah, Exalted, about certain peoples, and the apparent meaning is that they were the Jews, and that is not a proof. Likewise His saying: ﴿Or that your Lord should come?﴾ [al-An'am: 158]. But here it is the explicit speech of Allah, Exalted, and attributing the act of coming to Him is problematic.

If they say: What is your view of His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr: 22]?

We say: There are interpretations for that, and also it is explicit, so it cannot be repelled, and therefore abstaining from it is obligatory. Rather, the correct thing to say is that what is meant is: the Day when the awesome, terrifying, greatly magnified thing comes, and Allah, Exalted, is omitted from mention by His specification so that it would be more potent in instilling fear.

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The governing element for the accusative of the time-adverb is His saying ﴿la takallamu﴾ (will speak), or an implied "udhkur" (remember).

Page 49

As for His saying ﴿no soul will speak except by His permission﴾, there is an ellipsis in it, and the implied meaning is: no soul will speak on that Day except by the permission of Allah, Exalted.

If it is said: How can this verse be reconciled with other verses which seem to contradict it? Among them is His saying: ﴿On the Day every soul will come pleading for itself﴾ [al-Nahl: 111]; and among them is that they lie and swear by Allah concerning it, namely their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]; and among them is His saying: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24]; and among them is His saying: ﴿This is a Day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 35].

The answer is in two respects:

The first: Wherever a prohibition from speech occurs, it is to be understood as referring to the true and correct responses.

The second: That Day is a long day and has stations. In some of them they argue for themselves, in some of them they refrain from speech, and in some of them they are permitted and so they speak, and in some of them their mouths are sealed and their hands speak and their feet bear witness.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The pronoun in His saying ﴿Among them﴾ refers to the people of the standing place (of judgment). It is not mentioned because it is known, and because His saying ﴿no soul will speak except by His permission﴾ indicates it, since mention of mankind has already passed in His saying ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered﴾ [Hud: 103].

The second issue: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾ indicates that the people of the standing place do not go outside these two divisions.

If it is said: Are there not among mankind insane persons and children, who lie outside these two divisions?

We say: What is meant is those who are gathered from among those who are released for reckoning, and they do not go outside these two divisions.

If it is said: Al-Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) has argued with this verse against the view that the People of the Heights (al-A'raf) are neither in Paradise nor in Hell. What is your view on it?

We say: Since it is granted that children and insane persons lie outside these two divisions because they are not called to account, why is it not also permissible to say that the People of the Heights lie outside them too, because they also are not called to account, since Allah, Exalted, knows about their condition that their reward equals their punishment, so there is no benefit in reckoning them?

If it is said: Al-Qadi also argued from this verse that everyone who attends the arena of the Resurrection must have either an increased reward or an increased punishment. As for one whose reward equals his punishment, although that is possible rationally, this text indicates that it does not exist.

We say: The discussion concerning it is what has preceded: that the happy one is the one who is among the people of reward, and the wretched one is the one who is among the people of punishment. The singling out of these two divisions for mention does not indicate the negation of a third division. The proof of this is that most verses contain mention only of the believer and the disbeliever, and there is no mention in them of a third who is neither believer nor disbeliever, although al-Qadi affirmed it. So if the absence of mention of that third does not necessitate its non-existence, then likewise the mention of this third does not necessitate its non-existence.

Page 50

The third issue: Know that He, Exalted, has now judged some of the people of the Resurrection to be happy and some of them to be wretched. Whoever Allah has judged with a judgment, and that matter is known from him, it is impossible for him to be otherwise, for otherwise it would follow that the report of Allah, Exalted, would become false and His knowledge ignorance, and that is impossible. So it is established that the happy one does not turn into a wretched one, and the wretched one does not turn into a happy one. The statement of this proof has passed in this book countless times. It is related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When the words ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾ were revealed, I said: O Messenger of Allah, then upon what do we act: upon a matter already finished, or upon a matter not yet finished? He said: 'Upon a matter already finished, O 'Umar, the pens have dried with it, and the decrees have run with it; but each is made easy for that for which he was created.'"

The Mu'tazilah said: It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "Among them is the wretched one by his deed and the happy one by his deed."

We say: A decisive proof is not overturned by these reports. Moreover, there is no dispute that he became wretched only by his deed, and became happy only by his deed; but since that deed occurred by the decree and predestination of Allah, the proof we have mentioned remains valid.

Know that when He, Exalted, divided the people of the Resurrection into these two divisions, He explained the condition of each of them, saying: ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them there is groaning and wailing.﴾ In this there are issues:

The first issue: They have mentioned several views concerning the difference between the zafir (groaning) and the shahiq (wailing):

The first view: Al-Layth said: The zafir is when a man fills his chest while in severe distress with breath and does not exhale it, and the shahiq is when he exhales that breath. Al-Farra' said: It is said of a horse: he has a great zafrah, meaning a great belly. I say: When a person's grief becomes great, the spirit of his heart is confined within the interior of the heart. When the spirit is confined, the heat grows strong and becomes great, and at that point a person needs a strong breath in order to draw in much cold air, so that he may be able to cool that heat. For this reason, at that time, the drawing in of air into the interior of the body becomes great, and then his chest rises and his sides swell. And since the innate heat and the animal spirit are confined within the heart, coldness takes hold of the outer organs, so the instruments of breathing sometimes fail to push out that abundant air that has been inhaled, so that abundant air remains confined in the chest, and the person nearly suffocates from it. Then nature strives to expel that air. So, according to the analogy of the physicians' statement: the zafir is the drawing in of abundant air to cool the heat produced in the heart by the confinement of the spirit within it, and the shahiq is the expulsion of that air when nature strives to expel it. Each of these two states indicates severe distress and great grief.

The second view: On the difference between the zafir and the shahiq, some said: the zafir is like the beginning of the donkey's bray, while the shahiq is like the end of the donkey's bray.

The third view: Al-Hasan said: We have mentioned that the zafir signifies elevation. So we say: the zafir is the blaze of Hell, which raises them by its force, until when they reach the highest degrees of Hell and hope to get out of it, the angels strike them with iron maces and return them to the lowest level of Hell. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they are returned to it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. So their rising in the Fire is the zafir, and their descending again is the shahiq.

The fourth view: Abu Muslim said: The zafir is the breath that gathers in the chest during intense weeping, so that the breath is cut off, and the shahiq is what appears when distress and sorrow intensify, and perhaps a fainting follows them, and perhaps death results from it.

The fifth view: Abu al-'Aliyah said: The zafir is in the throat, and the shahiq is in the chest.

The sixth view: Some people said: The zafir is a strong sound, and the shahiq is a weak sound.

The seventh view: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: ﴿for them there is groaning and wailing﴾ means: regret, a high-pitched sigh, weeping that does not cease, and sorrow that is not relieved.

The eighth view: The zafir indicates strength, and the shahiq indicates weakness, according to what we have established by linguistic usage.

Having understood this, we say: It is not far-fetched that what is meant by the zafir is the intensity of their inclination toward the world of this life and toward bodily pleasures, and what is meant by the shahiq is their weakness in attaining happiness through the world of spirituals, and their perfection through divine lights and holy ascents.

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills.﴾ In it there are two issues:

The first issue: Some people said that the punishment of the disbelievers is discontinued and has an end. They argued with the Qur'an and with reason. As for the Qur'an, there are verses among which is this verse, and the argument from it is in two respects:

The first: He, Exalted, said: ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾. This text indicates that the duration of their punishment is equal to the duration of the continuance of the heavens and the earth. Then we agree that the duration of the continuance of the heavens and the earth is finite, so it follows that the duration of the punishment of the disbelievers is discontinued.

The second: His saying ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ is an exception from the duration of their punishment, and that indicates the cessation of that punishment during the time of this exception. Among what they also held onto is His saying, Exalted, in the surah "Asking one another" (al-Naba'): ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ [al-Naba': 23]; He, Exalted, made clear that their remaining in that punishment will be only for countable ages.

As for reason, there are two arguments:

The first: The disobedience of the disbeliever is finite, and to match a finite crime with a punishment that has no end is injustice, and that is not permissible.

The second: That punishment is harm devoid of benefit, and so it is ugly.

The proof that it is devoid of benefit is that this benefit does not return to Allah, Exalted, since He is exalted above benefit and harm; nor to that person being punished, since for him it is pure harm; nor to anyone else, since the people of Paradise are occupied with their own pleasures, so there is no benefit for them in delighting in the everlasting punishment of others. So it is established that that punishment is harm devoid of all aspects of benefit, and therefore it must not be permitted.

As for the great majority of the community, they agreed that the punishment of the disbeliever is everlasting, and at this point they needed to answer the argument from this verse. As for His saying ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, they mentioned two answers concerning it:

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 105–108 (part 2 of 3):**

The first view: they said the intended meaning is the heavens and earth of the Hereafter. They said the proof that there are a heaven and an earth in the Hereafter is His saying, ﴿On the Day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48], and His saying, ﴿And He has given us the land to inherit, [that] we may settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. Also, the people of the Hereafter must have something that bears them and shades them, and that is the earth and the heavens.

One may reply: a comparison (*tashbih*) is only apt and permissible when the state of the thing compared to is known and established, so that other things are compared to it to confirm the ruling for the thing being compared. The existence of the heavens and earth in the Hereafter is not known. Even if their existence were known, their enduring in a way that never perishes at all is not known. When the very existence of these two is unknown to most of creation, and their permanence is likewise unknown to most, then comparing the punishment of the wretched to them in permanence is a statement without benefit. At most, one could say: since the Qur'an establishes the existence of heavens and earth in the Hereafter, and establishes their permanence, it is obligatory to acknowledge this, and then the comparison is apt. But we say: since the way to establishing the permanence of the heavens and earth of the people of the Hereafter is revelation (*sam'*), and revelation has indicated the permanence of the punishment of the unbeliever, then the evidence that established the ruling in the original case (*asl*) is present in the same way in the branch case (*far'*). In this kind of case, they all agreed that *qiyas* (analogical reasoning) is void and the comparison is invalid. So too here.

The second answer: they said that the Arabs express permanence and eternity by saying, "as long as the heavens and the earth endure." Its parallel is also their saying, "as long as the night and day alternate," "as long as the sea surges," and "as long as the mountain stands." God addressed the Arabs in their customary speech. When they mention these things, on the basis of their belief that they remain forever, we know that these expressions, according to their custom, convey eternity and permanence free of cessation.

One may reply: Do you concede that the saying of the speaker, "abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure," prevents their remaining in existence after the heavens perish, or do you say that it does not indicate this meaning?

If it is the first, then the difficulty is unavoidable, because the text has indicated that the duration of their stay in the Fire must be equal to the duration of the heavens' survival, and it prevents their remaining in the Fire after the heavens perish. Then it is established that the heavens must perish, and at that point you are compelled to say that this punishment ends. If you say that this statement does not prevent their remaining in the Fire after the heavens and the earth perish, then you have no need for this answer at all. Thus it is established that this answer is void on both assumptions.

Know that the true answer, in my view, on this matter is something else: the established reading of the verse is that whenever the heavens and the earth are enduring, their being in the Fire remains. This indicates that whenever the condition is fulfilled, the conditioned thing is fulfilled, but it does not indicate that when the condition is absent, the conditioned thing is absent. Do you not see that we say: "If this is a human, then it is an animal." If we say, "But it is a human," it follows that it is an animal. But if we say, "But it is not a human," it does not follow that it is not an animal. For it is established in the science of logic (*mantiq*) that denying the consequent in a conditional does not yield any conclusion. So too here: when we say, "Whenever the heavens endure, their punishment endures," then if we say, "But the heavens are enduring," it follows that their punishment is present. But if we say, "But the heavens have not remained," it does not follow that the permanence of their punishment is absent.

If they say: then if the punishment is present whether or not the heavens remain, the comparison has no benefit left.

We say: rather, in it there is the greatest benefit, which is that it indicates the continuing of that torment age upon age, for a time whose length and extent the intellect cannot encompass. As for whether it will have an end or not, that is known from other proofs. This answer that I have established is a true answer, but only someone accustomed to rational sciences (*ma'qulat*) will understand it.

As for the second objection, namely the reliance on His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, they have mentioned several kinds of answers.

The first answer, which Ibn Qutayba, Ibn al-Anbari and al-Farra' mentioned, is this: they said: this is an exception which God made, but He does not in fact do it at all. It is like your saying: "By God, I will surely strike you, except if I see otherwise," while your resolve is to strike him. So too here. They elaborated at length in establishing this answer and in giving examples for it, but its essence is what we have mentioned.

One may reply: this is weak, because when he says, "I will surely strike you, except if I see otherwise," the meaning is: "I will strike you except when I judge that leaving off striking is better." This does not at all indicate whether this seeing has occurred or not. This is unlike His saying, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, whose meaning is the ruling of their abiding therein, except for the period which your Lord wills. Here the wording indicates that this willing has definitely occurred. So how can the analogy of this statement be drawn to that statement?

The second answer: it is said that the word ﴿illa﴾ (except) here is used with the meaning of *siwa* (other than). The meaning is that when He said, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, it was understood from it that they would be in the Fire for the entire period of the endurance of the heavens and earth of this world. Then He said, "other than" what exceeds that by an everlasting abiding, by His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾. The meaning is: except what your Lord wills of the additional period that has no end. So He first mentioned for their abiding a duration that the Arabs regard as the longest, then added to it the everlasting permanence that has no end.

The third answer: the intended meaning of this exception is the time of their standing at the place of reckoning (*mawqif*). It is as if He said: "As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, except the time of their standing for the reckoning, for at that time they will not be in the Fire." Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: the intended meaning is "except what your Lord wills," which is the state of their being in the grave (*qabr*), or the intended meaning is "except what your Lord wills" of the period of their lives in this world. These three statements are close in meaning: the sense is abiding therein for the measure of their stay in this world, or in the intermediate state (*barzakh*), or the measure of their standing for the reckoning, after which they go to the Fire.

The fourth answer: they said the exception refers back to His saying, ﴿for them therein is [heavy] sighing and wailing﴾. The explanation of this is that we say: His saying, ﴿for them therein is sighing and wailing﴾ together with ﴿abiding therein﴾ conveys that sighing and wailing occur along with abiding. When the exception enters upon this, there must occur a time in which this combined state does not occur. It is established in rational matters that just as a whole is negated by the negation of all its parts, so it is also negated by the negation of a single one of its parts. So when at the end they reach the state of becoming still, silent and extinguished, then they no longer have sighing and wailing, and one part of that whole is absent. At that point, that exception is valid without any need to rule that their being in the Fire ceases.

The fifth answer: that this exception be understood to mean that the people of punishment will not always be in the Fire, but may be moved to the cold, the frigid zone (*zamharir*), and other kinds of punishment, and this suffices for the validity of this exception.

The sixth answer: some people said: this exception indicates the exclusion of the people of monotheism (*tawhid*) from the Fire. This is because His saying, ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire﴾, indicates that the whole class of the wretched is subject to this ruling. Then His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, requires that this ruling not remain upon that whole group, and it suffices for the removal of the ruling of abiding from the whole that it be removed from some of them. So it is necessary that the ruling of abiding not remain for some of the wretched. Since it is established that abiding is obligatory for the disbelievers, it must be said: those from whom the ruling of abiding is removed are the sinners among the people of prayer (*ahl al-salah*). This is a strong argument in this matter.

If it is said: this answer is only determined when all the other answers you have mentioned are invalid, so what is the evidence for their invalidity? Furthermore, a similar exception is mentioned concerning the blessed, for He said: ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills — a gift uninterrupted﴾.

As for taking the exception to refer to the state of the life of this world, the intermediate state, and the place of standing, that too is far-fetched, because the exception came from abiding in the Fire, and it is known that abiding in the Fire is a mode of being in the Fire. Before one is in the Fire, abiding in the Fire is impossible; and if abiding has not occurred, the excepted thing has not occurred, and the exception is impossible. As for his saying that the exception refers to the sighing and wailing, this too abandons the apparent meaning. So there remains for the verse no valid interpretation except this one which we have mentioned.

As for his saying that the intended meaning of the exception is its transfer from the Fire to the zamharir, we say: if that were the case, it would be necessary that punishment by the zamharir not occur except after the period of the heavens and earth has ended. As for his saying that a similar exception is present concerning the blessed, we say: the community (*umma*) has agreed (*ijma'*, consensus) that it is impossible to say that anyone enters Paradise and then leaves it for the Fire. Because of this consensus, we needed to interpret that exception according to one of those interpretations. But as for this verse, this consensus has not occurred, so it is necessary to apply it to its apparent meaning. This is the complete discussion of this verse.

This fits well with this verse if we take the exception as bringing the sinners out of the Fire. It is as if He says: "I displayed domination and power, then I displayed forgiveness and mercy, because I am the Accomplisher of what I intend, and no one has any right of judgment over Me at all."
