Then He said: ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

The first issue: Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read *su'idu* (سُعِدُوا) with a *damma* on the *sin*, while the rest read it with a *fatha*. The *damma* is permissible because it is derived by dropping the augment from *as'ada* (to make happy), and because *sa'ida* (to be happy) is intransitive while *as'ada* is transitive. *Sa'ida* and *as'ada* have the same meaning, and from this comes *al-mas'ud* (the fortunate), which is among the names of men.

The second issue: the exception in the matter of the blessed must be interpreted according to one of the aspects mentioned earlier, and here there is another aspect, namely that it may happen to some of them that they are raised from Paradise to the Throne and to the lofty dwellings which only God Most High knows. God Most High said: ﴿God has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence; and approval from God is greater﴾ [al-Tawba: 72]. As for His saying, ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: *jadhdha yajudhdhu jadhdhan* means he cut it off. And "God cut off their root" (*jadha Allahu dabirahum*). So His saying, ﴿uninterrupted﴾ means not cut off. Its parallel is His saying concerning the description of the bliss of Paradise: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 33].

Second issue: know that when God, exalted is He, stated explicitly in this verse that the intended meaning of this exception is not that this state is discontinuous, then, since He singled out this place with this clarification and did not mention the same in the case of the wretched, this indicates that the intended meaning of that exception is discontinuity. This is the complete discussion of this verse.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. Among them will be the wretched and the happy.﴾ ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them there is groaning and wailing.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills. Indeed your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.﴾ ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills, a gift unceasing.﴾

In the verse there are issues (masa'il):

The first issue: Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamzah read ﴿ya'ti﴾ with the ya' omitted, while the rest read it with the ya'. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The omission of the ya' and making do with the kasrah in its place is common in the dialect of Hudhayl. Similar to it is their saying "la adri" (I do not know), related by al-Khalil and Sibawayh.

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The subject of ya'ti is Allah, Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿Do they wait for anything but that Allah should come to them?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] and His saying: ﴿Or that your Lord should come?﴾ [al-An'am: 158], and this is supported by the reading of whoever read "wa ma yu'akhkhiruh" with the ya'. I say: I do not like this interpretation, because His saying: ﴿Do they wait for anything but that Allah should come to them?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210] is related by Allah, Exalted, about certain peoples, and the apparent meaning is that they were the Jews, and that is not a proof. Likewise His saying: ﴿Or that your Lord should come?﴾ [al-An'am: 158]. But here it is the explicit speech of Allah, Exalted, and attributing the act of coming to Him is problematic.

If they say: What is your view of His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes﴾ [al-Fajr: 22]?

We say: There are interpretations for that, and also it is explicit, so it cannot be repelled, and therefore abstaining from it is obligatory. Rather, the correct thing to say is that what is meant is: the Day when the awesome, terrifying, greatly magnified thing comes, and Allah, Exalted, is omitted from mention by His specification so that it would be more potent in instilling fear.

The third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The governing element for the accusative of the time-adverb is His saying ﴿la takallamu﴾ (will speak), or an implied "udhkur" (remember).

Page 49

As for His saying ﴿no soul will speak except by His permission﴾, there is an ellipsis in it, and the implied meaning is: no soul will speak on that Day except by the permission of Allah, Exalted.

If it is said: How can this verse be reconciled with other verses which seem to contradict it? Among them is His saying: ﴿On the Day every soul will come pleading for itself﴾ [al-Nahl: 111]; and among them is that they lie and swear by Allah concerning it, namely their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]; and among them is His saying: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat: 24]; and among them is His saying: ﴿This is a Day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted to offer excuses﴾ [al-Mursalat: 35].

The answer is in two respects:

The first: Wherever a prohibition from speech occurs, it is to be understood as referring to the true and correct responses.

The second: That Day is a long day and has stations. In some of them they argue for themselves, in some of them they refrain from speech, and in some of them they are permitted and so they speak, and in some of them their mouths are sealed and their hands speak and their feet bear witness.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: The pronoun in His saying ﴿Among them﴾ refers to the people of the standing place (of judgment). It is not mentioned because it is known, and because His saying ﴿no soul will speak except by His permission﴾ indicates it, since mention of mankind has already passed in His saying ﴿That is a Day for which mankind will be gathered﴾ [Hud: 103].

The second issue: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾ indicates that the people of the standing place do not go outside these two divisions.

If it is said: Are there not among mankind insane persons and children, who lie outside these two divisions?

We say: What is meant is those who are gathered from among those who are released for reckoning, and they do not go outside these two divisions.

If it is said: Al-Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) has argued with this verse against the view that the People of the Heights (al-A'raf) are neither in Paradise nor in Hell. What is your view on it?

We say: Since it is granted that children and insane persons lie outside these two divisions because they are not called to account, why is it not also permissible to say that the People of the Heights lie outside them too, because they also are not called to account, since Allah, Exalted, knows about their condition that their reward equals their punishment, so there is no benefit in reckoning them?

If it is said: Al-Qadi also argued from this verse that everyone who attends the arena of the Resurrection must have either an increased reward or an increased punishment. As for one whose reward equals his punishment, although that is possible rationally, this text indicates that it does not exist.

We say: The discussion concerning it is what has preceded: that the happy one is the one who is among the people of reward, and the wretched one is the one who is among the people of punishment. The singling out of these two divisions for mention does not indicate the negation of a third division. The proof of this is that most verses contain mention only of the believer and the disbeliever, and there is no mention in them of a third who is neither believer nor disbeliever, although al-Qadi affirmed it. So if the absence of mention of that third does not necessitate its non-existence, then likewise the mention of this third does not necessitate its non-existence.

Page 50

The third issue: Know that He, Exalted, has now judged some of the people of the Resurrection to be happy and some of them to be wretched. Whoever Allah has judged with a judgment, and that matter is known from him, it is impossible for him to be otherwise, for otherwise it would follow that the report of Allah, Exalted, would become false and His knowledge ignorance, and that is impossible. So it is established that the happy one does not turn into a wretched one, and the wretched one does not turn into a happy one. The statement of this proof has passed in this book countless times. It is related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When the words ﴿Among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾ were revealed, I said: O Messenger of Allah, then upon what do we act: upon a matter already finished, or upon a matter not yet finished? He said: 'Upon a matter already finished, O 'Umar, the pens have dried with it, and the decrees have run with it; but each is made easy for that for which he was created.'"

The Mu'tazilah said: It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "Among them is the wretched one by his deed and the happy one by his deed."

We say: A decisive proof is not overturned by these reports. Moreover, there is no dispute that he became wretched only by his deed, and became happy only by his deed; but since that deed occurred by the decree and predestination of Allah, the proof we have mentioned remains valid.

Know that when He, Exalted, divided the people of the Resurrection into these two divisions, He explained the condition of each of them, saying: ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them there is groaning and wailing.﴾ In this there are issues:

The first issue: They have mentioned several views concerning the difference between the zafir (groaning) and the shahiq (wailing):

The first view: Al-Layth said: The zafir is when a man fills his chest while in severe distress with breath and does not exhale it, and the shahiq is when he exhales that breath. Al-Farra' said: It is said of a horse: he has a great zafrah, meaning a great belly. I say: When a person's grief becomes great, the spirit of his heart is confined within the interior of the heart. When the spirit is confined, the heat grows strong and becomes great, and at that point a person needs a strong breath in order to draw in much cold air, so that he may be able to cool that heat. For this reason, at that time, the drawing in of air into the interior of the body becomes great, and then his chest rises and his sides swell. And since the innate heat and the animal spirit are confined within the heart, coldness takes hold of the outer organs, so the instruments of breathing sometimes fail to push out that abundant air that has been inhaled, so that abundant air remains confined in the chest, and the person nearly suffocates from it. Then nature strives to expel that air. So, according to the analogy of the physicians' statement: the zafir is the drawing in of abundant air to cool the heat produced in the heart by the confinement of the spirit within it, and the shahiq is the expulsion of that air when nature strives to expel it. Each of these two states indicates severe distress and great grief.

The second view: On the difference between the zafir and the shahiq, some said: the zafir is like the beginning of the donkey's bray, while the shahiq is like the end of the donkey's bray.

The third view: Al-Hasan said: We have mentioned that the zafir signifies elevation. So we say: the zafir is the blaze of Hell, which raises them by its force, until when they reach the highest degrees of Hell and hope to get out of it, the angels strike them with iron maces and return them to the lowest level of Hell. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it, they are returned to it﴾ [al-Sajdah: 20]. So their rising in the Fire is the zafir, and their descending again is the shahiq.

The fourth view: Abu Muslim said: The zafir is the breath that gathers in the chest during intense weeping, so that the breath is cut off, and the shahiq is what appears when distress and sorrow intensify, and perhaps a fainting follows them, and perhaps death results from it.

The fifth view: Abu al-'Aliyah said: The zafir is in the throat, and the shahiq is in the chest.

The sixth view: Some people said: The zafir is a strong sound, and the shahiq is a weak sound.

The seventh view: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: ﴿for them there is groaning and wailing﴾ means: regret, a high-pitched sigh, weeping that does not cease, and sorrow that is not relieved.

The eighth view: The zafir indicates strength, and the shahiq indicates weakness, according to what we have established by linguistic usage.

Having understood this, we say: It is not far-fetched that what is meant by the zafir is the intensity of their inclination toward the world of this life and toward bodily pleasures, and what is meant by the shahiq is their weakness in attaining happiness through the world of spirituals, and their perfection through divine lights and holy ascents.

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills.﴾ In it there are two issues:

The first issue: Some people said that the punishment of the disbelievers is discontinued and has an end. They argued with the Qur'an and with reason. As for the Qur'an, there are verses among which is this verse, and the argument from it is in two respects:

The first: He, Exalted, said: ﴿as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾. This text indicates that the duration of their punishment is equal to the duration of the continuance of the heavens and the earth. Then we agree that the duration of the continuance of the heavens and the earth is finite, so it follows that the duration of the punishment of the disbelievers is discontinued.

The second: His saying ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ is an exception from the duration of their punishment, and that indicates the cessation of that punishment during the time of this exception. Among what they also held onto is His saying, Exalted, in the surah "Asking one another" (al-Naba'): ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ [al-Naba': 23]; He, Exalted, made clear that their remaining in that punishment will be only for countable ages.

As for reason, there are two arguments:

The first: The disobedience of the disbeliever is finite, and to match a finite crime with a punishment that has no end is injustice, and that is not permissible.

The second: That punishment is harm devoid of benefit, and so it is ugly.

The proof that it is devoid of benefit is that this benefit does not return to Allah, Exalted, since He is exalted above benefit and harm; nor to that person being punished, since for him it is pure harm; nor to anyone else, since the people of Paradise are occupied with their own pleasures, so there is no benefit for them in delighting in the everlasting punishment of others. So it is established that that punishment is harm devoid of all aspects of benefit, and therefore it must not be permitted.

As for the great majority of the community, they agreed that the punishment of the disbeliever is everlasting, and at this point they needed to answer the argument from this verse. As for His saying ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, they mentioned two answers concerning it:

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 105–108 (part 2 of 3):**

The first view: they said the intended meaning is the heavens and earth of the Hereafter. They said the proof that there are a heaven and an earth in the Hereafter is His saying, ﴿On the Day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾ [Ibrahim: 48], and His saying, ﴿And He has given us the land to inherit, [that] we may settle in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. Also, the people of the Hereafter must have something that bears them and shades them, and that is the earth and the heavens.

One may reply: a comparison (*tashbih*) is only apt and permissible when the state of the thing compared to is known and established, so that other things are compared to it to confirm the ruling for the thing being compared. The existence of the heavens and earth in the Hereafter is not known. Even if their existence were known, their enduring in a way that never perishes at all is not known. When the very existence of these two is unknown to most of creation, and their permanence is likewise unknown to most, then comparing the punishment of the wretched to them in permanence is a statement without benefit. At most, one could say: since the Qur'an establishes the existence of heavens and earth in the Hereafter, and establishes their permanence, it is obligatory to acknowledge this, and then the comparison is apt. But we say: since the way to establishing the permanence of the heavens and earth of the people of the Hereafter is revelation (*sam'*), and revelation has indicated the permanence of the punishment of the unbeliever, then the evidence that established the ruling in the original case (*asl*) is present in the same way in the branch case (*far'*). In this kind of case, they all agreed that *qiyas* (analogical reasoning) is void and the comparison is invalid. So too here.

The second answer: they said that the Arabs express permanence and eternity by saying, "as long as the heavens and the earth endure." Its parallel is also their saying, "as long as the night and day alternate," "as long as the sea surges," and "as long as the mountain stands." God addressed the Arabs in their customary speech. When they mention these things, on the basis of their belief that they remain forever, we know that these expressions, according to their custom, convey eternity and permanence free of cessation.

One may reply: Do you concede that the saying of the speaker, "abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure," prevents their remaining in existence after the heavens perish, or do you say that it does not indicate this meaning?

If it is the first, then the difficulty is unavoidable, because the text has indicated that the duration of their stay in the Fire must be equal to the duration of the heavens' survival, and it prevents their remaining in the Fire after the heavens perish. Then it is established that the heavens must perish, and at that point you are compelled to say that this punishment ends. If you say that this statement does not prevent their remaining in the Fire after the heavens and the earth perish, then you have no need for this answer at all. Thus it is established that this answer is void on both assumptions.

Know that the true answer, in my view, on this matter is something else: the established reading of the verse is that whenever the heavens and the earth are enduring, their being in the Fire remains. This indicates that whenever the condition is fulfilled, the conditioned thing is fulfilled, but it does not indicate that when the condition is absent, the conditioned thing is absent. Do you not see that we say: "If this is a human, then it is an animal." If we say, "But it is a human," it follows that it is an animal. But if we say, "But it is not a human," it does not follow that it is not an animal. For it is established in the science of logic (*mantiq*) that denying the consequent in a conditional does not yield any conclusion. So too here: when we say, "Whenever the heavens endure, their punishment endures," then if we say, "But the heavens are enduring," it follows that their punishment is present. But if we say, "But the heavens have not remained," it does not follow that the permanence of their punishment is absent.

If they say: then if the punishment is present whether or not the heavens remain, the comparison has no benefit left.

We say: rather, in it there is the greatest benefit, which is that it indicates the continuing of that torment age upon age, for a time whose length and extent the intellect cannot encompass. As for whether it will have an end or not, that is known from other proofs. This answer that I have established is a true answer, but only someone accustomed to rational sciences (*ma'qulat*) will understand it.

As for the second objection, namely the reliance on His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, they have mentioned several kinds of answers.

The first answer, which Ibn Qutayba, Ibn al-Anbari and al-Farra' mentioned, is this: they said: this is an exception which God made, but He does not in fact do it at all. It is like your saying: "By God, I will surely strike you, except if I see otherwise," while your resolve is to strike him. So too here. They elaborated at length in establishing this answer and in giving examples for it, but its essence is what we have mentioned.

One may reply: this is weak, because when he says, "I will surely strike you, except if I see otherwise," the meaning is: "I will strike you except when I judge that leaving off striking is better." This does not at all indicate whether this seeing has occurred or not. This is unlike His saying, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾, whose meaning is the ruling of their abiding therein, except for the period which your Lord wills. Here the wording indicates that this willing has definitely occurred. So how can the analogy of this statement be drawn to that statement?

The second answer: it is said that the word ﴿illa﴾ (except) here is used with the meaning of *siwa* (other than). The meaning is that when He said, ﴿abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, it was understood from it that they would be in the Fire for the entire period of the endurance of the heavens and earth of this world. Then He said, "other than" what exceeds that by an everlasting abiding, by His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾. The meaning is: except what your Lord wills of the additional period that has no end. So He first mentioned for their abiding a duration that the Arabs regard as the longest, then added to it the everlasting permanence that has no end.

The third answer: the intended meaning of this exception is the time of their standing at the place of reckoning (*mawqif*). It is as if He said: "As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, except the time of their standing for the reckoning, for at that time they will not be in the Fire." Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: the intended meaning is "except what your Lord wills," which is the state of their being in the grave (*qabr*), or the intended meaning is "except what your Lord wills" of the period of their lives in this world. These three statements are close in meaning: the sense is abiding therein for the measure of their stay in this world, or in the intermediate state (*barzakh*), or the measure of their standing for the reckoning, after which they go to the Fire.

The fourth answer: they said the exception refers back to His saying, ﴿for them therein is [heavy] sighing and wailing﴾. The explanation of this is that we say: His saying, ﴿for them therein is sighing and wailing﴾ together with ﴿abiding therein﴾ conveys that sighing and wailing occur along with abiding. When the exception enters upon this, there must occur a time in which this combined state does not occur. It is established in rational matters that just as a whole is negated by the negation of all its parts, so it is also negated by the negation of a single one of its parts. So when at the end they reach the state of becoming still, silent and extinguished, then they no longer have sighing and wailing, and one part of that whole is absent. At that point, that exception is valid without any need to rule that their being in the Fire ceases.

The fifth answer: that this exception be understood to mean that the people of punishment will not always be in the Fire, but may be moved to the cold, the frigid zone (*zamharir*), and other kinds of punishment, and this suffices for the validity of this exception.

The sixth answer: some people said: this exception indicates the exclusion of the people of monotheism (*tawhid*) from the Fire. This is because His saying, ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire﴾, indicates that the whole class of the wretched is subject to this ruling. Then His saying, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾, requires that this ruling not remain upon that whole group, and it suffices for the removal of the ruling of abiding from the whole that it be removed from some of them. So it is necessary that the ruling of abiding not remain for some of the wretched. Since it is established that abiding is obligatory for the disbelievers, it must be said: those from whom the ruling of abiding is removed are the sinners among the people of prayer (*ahl al-salah*). This is a strong argument in this matter.

If it is said: this answer is only determined when all the other answers you have mentioned are invalid, so what is the evidence for their invalidity? Furthermore, a similar exception is mentioned concerning the blessed, for He said: ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills — a gift uninterrupted﴾.

[Page 54]

We say: by this answer we have shown that this verse does not indicate the cessation of the threat against the disbelievers. Then, if we want to use this verse as evidence for the validity of our position that God brings the sinners among the people of prayer out of the Fire...

We say: as for taking the word ﴿illa﴾ to mean *siwa* (other than), it is a departure from the apparent meaning. As for taking the exception to refer to the state of the life of this world, the intermediate state, and the place of standing, that too is far-fetched, because the exception came from abiding in the Fire, and it is known that abiding in the Fire is a mode of being in the Fire. Before one is in the Fire, abiding in the Fire is impossible; and if abiding has not occurred, the excepted thing has not occurred, and the exception is impossible. As for his saying that the exception refers to the sighing and wailing, this too abandons the apparent meaning. So there remains for the verse no valid interpretation except this one which we have mentioned.

As for his saying that the intended meaning of the exception is its transfer from the Fire to the zamharir, we say: if that were the case, it would be necessary that punishment by the zamharir not occur except after the period of the heavens and earth has ended. But the sound reports indicate that the transfer from the Fire to the zamharir and vice versa occurs many times each day. So this answer is refuted.

As for his saying that a similar exception is present concerning the blessed, we say: the community (*umma*) has agreed (*ijma'*, consensus) that it is impossible to say that anyone enters Paradise and then leaves it for the Fire. Because of this consensus, we needed to interpret that exception according to one of those interpretations. But as for this verse, this consensus has not occurred, so it is necessary to apply it to its apparent meaning. This is the complete discussion of this verse.

* * *

Know that when He mentioned this exception, He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Accomplisher of what He intends﴾. This fits well with this verse if we take the exception as bringing the sinners out of the Fire. It is as if He says: "I displayed domination and power, then I displayed forgiveness and mercy, because I am the Accomplisher of what I intend, and no one has any right of judgment over Me at all."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿As for those who were made happy, they will be in Paradise, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾. Concerning this there are two issues.

The first issue: Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read *su'idu* (سُعِدُوا) with a *damma* on the *sin*, while the rest read it with a *fatha*. The *damma* is permissible because it is derived by dropping the augment from *as'ada* (to make happy), and because *sa'ida* (to be happy) is intransitive while *as'ada* is transitive. *Sa'ida* and *as'ada* have the same meaning, and from this comes *al-mas'ud* (the fortunate), which is among the names of men.

The second issue: the exception in the matter of the blessed must be interpreted according to one of the aspects mentioned earlier, and here there is another aspect, namely that it may happen to some of them that they are raised from Paradise to the Throne and to the lofty dwellings which only God Most High knows. God Most High said: ﴿God has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence; and approval from God is greater﴾ [al-Tawba: 72]. As for His saying, ﴿a gift uninterrupted﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: *jadhdha yajudhdhu jadhdhan* means he cut it off. And "God cut off their root" (*jadha Allahu dabirahum*). So His saying, ﴿uninterrupted﴾ means not cut off. Its parallel is His saying concerning the description of the bliss of Paradise: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 33].

Second issue: know that when God, exalted is He, stated explicitly in this verse that the intended meaning of this exception is not that this state is discontinuous, then, since He singled out this place with this clarification and did not mention the same in the case of the wretched, this indicates that the intended meaning of that exception is discontinuity. This is the complete discussion of this verse.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 109–111:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So be not in doubt about what these worship. They worship only as their fathers worshipped before. And indeed, We will give them their full portion without reduction.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, had explained the accounts of the idol-worshippers and then followed them with the conditions of the wretched and the conditions of the blessed, He explained to the Messenger, upon him be peace, the conditions of the disbelievers among his people. He said: ﴿So be not in doubt﴾. The meaning is: "So do not be," but He dropped the nun (ن) because of frequent usage. Also, when the nun falls at the end of an utterance, nothing remains of it when pronounced except mere nasalization (ghunnah), so they dropped it without hesitation. The meaning is: "So do not be in doubt about the state of what they worship, that it neither harms nor benefits."

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They worship only as their fathers worshipped before﴾. The meaning is that they resembled their fathers in clinging to ignorance and blind imitation (taqlid).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And indeed, We will give them their full portion without reduction﴾. It may be that the meaning is: "We will give them their portion," that is, what is due to them of punishment. It may also be that the meaning is: even though they disbelieved and turned away from the truth, We will give them their portion of provision and worldly goods. It may also be that the meaning is: We will give them their portion of the removal of excuse, the removal of impediments, the manifestation of proofs, the sending of messengers, and the sending down of books. It is also possible that all of these are intended.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book, but it was disputed over. And were it not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them. And indeed, they are in disquieting doubt about it﴾. ﴿And indeed, all of them—your Lord will surely pay them in full for their deeds. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 112–113:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded, and [so too] those who have turned back with you, and do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged, lest you be touched by the Fire, and you have not, other than Allah, any allies; then you would not be helped.﴾

Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when the Exalted had extensively explained the promise and the threat, He said to His Messenger: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾

صفحة 57
This word is comprehensive of everything related to beliefs and deeds, whether it is specific to him or relates to conveying the revelation and explaining the laws. There is no doubt that remaining upon true uprightness (istiqamah) is extremely difficult, and I will give an example that brings the difficulty of this meaning close to the sound intellect: the straight line that separates the shadow from the light is a single part that does not admit division in breadth, yet the very substance of that line is something that cannot be distinguished by the senses from its two ends; for when the edge of the shadow draws near to the edge of the light, the one is confused with the other in perception, so the senses do not succeed in apprehending that very line in such a way that it is distinguished from everything else.

When you have understood this in the example, then understand its counterpart in all the chapters of servitude. The first of them is the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and attaining this knowledge in a manner that keeps the servant preserved, on the side of affirmation, from likening (tashbih) and, on the side of negation, from denial of attributes (ta'til), is in the utmost difficulty. Consider likewise all the stations of knowledge within yourself. Furthermore, the irascible faculty and the appetitive faculty each have two extremes, excess and deficiency, and both are blameworthy, while the dividing line is the mean between them, such that one does not incline toward either side; standing upon it is difficult, and acting upon it is more difficult. Thus it is established that knowing the straight path is in the utmost difficulty, even if it is known, so remaining upon it and acting by it is more difficult. Since this station is in the utmost difficulty, it is no wonder that Ibn Abbas said: "No verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the whole Qur'an that was harder or more burdensome upon him than this verse." For this reason he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Hud and its sisters have grayed me." And it is narrated from some of them who said: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream, and I said to him: 'It is narrated from you that you said: Hud and its sisters have grayed me?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'And by which verse?' He said: 'By His saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾.'"

The second issue: Know that this verse is a great principle in the Shari'ah. For the Qur'an, when it came with the command concerning the acts of wudu' arranged in sequence in its wording, it became obligatory to observe the order in them, because of His saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾. And when the command came concerning zakah to pay camels from camels and cattle from cattle, it became obligatory to observe this; and likewise the ruling in everything for which the command of Allah, the Exalted, came. In my view, it is not permissible to specify a text by analogy (qiyas), because when the general wording of the text indicated a ruling, it became obligatory to judge by its implication, because of His saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾; and acting by analogy is a deviation from it. Then He said: ﴿and [so too] those who have turned back with you﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: Al-Wahidi said: "Man (من)" is in the place of nominative case in several respects:

The first: that it is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the hidden pronoun in His saying ﴿So be upright﴾, and the connection by the preposition (with you) replaced the need to emphasize it with an attached pronoun in the validity of the conjunction; that is, "So be upright, you and they."

The second: that it is a conjunction upon the pronoun in "you have been commanded (umirta)."

The third: that it is an inceptive (ibtida') on the supposition: "and those who have turned back with you, so let them be upright."

The second issue: The disbeliever and the sinner are obligated to return from disbelief and sin, so in that state their occupation with uprightness is not valid. As for the one who has repented from disbelief and sin, it is valid for him to occupy himself with uprightness upon the paths of the religion of Allah, the Exalted, and remaining upon the way of the servitude of Allah, the Exalted. Then He said: ﴿and do not transgress﴾. The meaning of transgression (tughyan) is that one exceeds the measure. Ibn Abbas said: "He means: be humble before Allah, the Exalted, and do not be arrogant toward anyone." It was also said: "Do not transgress regarding the Qur'an, so that you make lawful its unlawful and make unlawful its lawful." It was said: "Do not go beyond what you have been commanded and what has been set as a limit for you." It was said: "Do not deviate from the way of thanking Him and humbling yourselves to Him when His blessings upon you are great." The more preferable view is that all of these are included in it. Then He said: ﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged﴾. Ruku' (rukun, inclining) is the settling upon a thing and leaning toward it through love; its opposite is aversion from it. The common readers recited it with a fatha on the ta and the kaf, and the past tense of this is rakina (like ʿalima).

صفحة 58
There is another dialect: rakana yarkanu. Al-Azhari said: "It is not eloquent." The verification scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said: the prohibited ruku' is approval of what the wrongdoers are upon of wrongdoing, and beautifying that course and adorning it in their eyes and in the eyes of others, and sharing with them in any of those matters. As for associating with them to repel a harm or to bring about an immediate benefit, this does not fall under ruku'. The meaning of His saying ﴿lest you be touched by the Fire﴾ is: if you incline toward them, this is the consequence of inclining. Then He said: ﴿and you have not, other than Allah, any allies﴾, meaning: you have no allies who will deliver you from the punishment of Allah.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿then you would not be helped﴾, and the intended meaning is: you will not find anyone who will help you from that event.
Know that Allah, the Exalted, has decreed that whoever inclines toward the wrongdoers, the Fire must touch him; and if this is so, then what is the state of the wrongdoer himself?

صفحة 57
This word is comprehensive of everything related to beliefs and deeds, whether it is specific to him or relates to conveying the revelation and explaining the laws. There is no doubt that remaining upon true uprightness (istiqamah) is extremely difficult, and I will give an example that brings the difficulty of this meaning close to the sound intellect: the straight line that separates the shadow from the light is a single part that does not admit division in breadth, yet the very substance of that line is something that cannot be distinguished by the senses from its two ends; for when the edge of the shadow draws near to the edge of the light, the one is confused with the other in perception, so the senses do not succeed in apprehending that very line in such a way that it is distinguished from everything else.

When you have understood this in the example, then understand its counterpart in all the chapters of servitude. The first of them is the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and attaining this knowledge in a manner that keeps the servant preserved, on the side of affirmation, from likening (tashbih) and, on the side of negation, from denial of attributes (ta'til), is in the utmost difficulty. Consider likewise all the stations of knowledge within yourself. Furthermore, the irascible faculty and the appetitive faculty each have two extremes, excess and deficiency, and both are blameworthy, while the dividing line is the mean between them, such that one does not incline toward either side; standing upon it is difficult, and acting upon it is more difficult. Thus it is established that knowing the straight path is in the utmost difficulty, even if it is known, so remaining upon it and acting by it is more difficult. Since this station is in the utmost difficulty, it is no wonder that Ibn Abbas said: "No verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the whole Qur'an that was harder or more burdensome upon him than this verse." For this reason he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Hud and its sisters have grayed me." And it is narrated from some of them who said: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream, and I said to him: 'It is narrated from you that you said: Hud and its sisters have grayed me?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'And by which verse?' He said: 'By His saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾.'"

The second issue: Know that this verse is a great principle in the Shari'ah. For the Qur'an, when it came with the command concerning the acts of wudu' arranged in sequence in its wording, it became obligatory to observe the order in them, because of His saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾. And when the command came concerning zakah to pay camels from camels and cattle from cattle, it became obligatory to observe this; and likewise the ruling in everything for which the command of Allah, the Exalted, came. In my view, it is not permissible to specify a text by analogy (qiyas), because when the general wording of the text indicated a ruling, it became obligatory to judge by its implication, because of His saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾; and acting by analogy is a deviation from it. Then He said: ﴿and [so too] those who have turned back with you﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: Al-Wahidi said: "Man (من)" is in the place of nominative case in several respects:

The first: that it is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the hidden pronoun in His saying ﴿So be upright﴾, and the connection by the preposition (with you) replaced the need to emphasize it with an attached pronoun in the validity of the conjunction; that is, "So be upright, you and they."

The second: that it is a conjunction upon the pronoun in "you have been commanded (umirta)."

The third: that it is an inceptive (ibtida') on the supposition: "and those who have turned back with you, so let them be upright."

The second issue: The disbeliever and the sinner are obligated to return from disbelief and sin, so in that state their occupation with uprightness is not valid. As for the one who has repented from disbelief and sin, it is valid for him to occupy himself with uprightness upon the paths of the religion of Allah, the Exalted, and remaining upon the way of the servitude of Allah, the Exalted. Then He said: ﴿and do not transgress﴾. The meaning of transgression (tughyan) is that one exceeds the measure. Ibn Abbas said: "He means: be humble before Allah, the Exalted, and do not be arrogant toward anyone." It was also said: "Do not transgress regarding the Qur'an, so that you make lawful its unlawful and make unlawful its lawful." It was said: "Do not go beyond what you have been commanded and what has been set as a limit for you." It was said: "Do not deviate from the way of thanking Him and humbling yourselves to Him when His blessings upon you are great." The more preferable view is that all of these are included in it. Then He said: ﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged﴾. Ruku' (rukun, inclining) is the settling upon a thing and leaning toward it through love; its opposite is aversion from it. The common readers recited it with a fatha on the ta and the kaf, and the past tense of this is rakina (like ʿalima).

صفحة 58
There is another dialect: rakana yarkanu. Al-Azhari said: "It is not eloquent." The verification scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said: the prohibited ruku' is approval of what the wrongdoers are upon of wrongdoing, and beautifying that course and adorning it in their eyes and in the eyes of others, and sharing with them in any of those matters. As for associating with them to repel a harm or to bring about an immediate benefit, this does not fall under ruku'. The meaning of His saying ﴿lest you be touched by the Fire﴾ is: if you incline toward them, this is the consequence of inclining. Then He said: ﴿and you have not, other than Allah, any allies﴾, meaning: you have no allies who will deliver you from the punishment of Allah.
* * *
Then He said: ﴿then you would not be helped﴾, and the intended meaning is: you will not find anyone who will help you from that event.
Know that Allah, the Exalted, has decreed that whoever inclines toward the wrongdoers, the Fire must touch him; and if this is so, then what is the state of the wrongdoer himself?

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 114–115:

God's words: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove misdeeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ ﴿And be patient, for indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾

Know that when God commanded him to uprightness (istiqamah), He followed it with the command to pray, which indicates that the greatest act of worship after faith in God is the prayer. There are several issues in this verse.

**The first issue:** I have seen in some books of al-Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani that the Khawarij (a early sect) used this verse to prove that the only obligatory prayers are the Fajr and the 'Isha', for two reasons.

**The first reason:** They are performed at the two ends of the day, and God has commanded the establishment of the prayer at the two ends of the day, so this amount must be sufficient.

If it is said: God's words ﴿and in the early hours of the night﴾ require other prayers.

We reply: We do not accept this. The two ends of the day are described as being "early hours of the night," for whatever is not day is night. The most that can be said is that this requires the coordination of an attribute with what it describes, but this is common in the Qur'an and in poetry.

**The second reason:** God said ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove misdeeds﴾, and this suggests that whoever prays at the two ends of the day, their establishment is an expiation for every sin other than them. So even if it is said that the other prayers are obligatory, the establishment of these two must be an expiation for neglecting the other prayers. Know that this view is invalid by the consensus (ijma') of the community, so it should not be considered.

**The second issue:** There are many opinions on the interpretation of the two ends of the day. The closest view is that the prayers established at the two ends of the day are the Fajr and the 'Asr. This is because one end of the day is the rising of the sun, and the other end of it is the setting of the sun. So the first end is the Fajr prayer, and the second end cannot be the Maghrib prayer, because it is included under God's words ﴿and in the early hours of the night﴾. Therefore the second end must be understood as the 'Asr prayer.

Once you know this, the verse is evidence for the view of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, that performing the Fajr prayer while it is still bright (al-tanwir) is better, and that delaying the 'Asr is better. This is because the apparent meaning of this verse indicates the obligation of establishing the prayer at the two ends of the day, and we have shown that the two ends of the day are the first time of the sunrise and the second time of its setting. The community agrees that establishing the prayer at those times without necessity is not legally permitted. So acting on the apparent meaning of this verse is impossible, and it must be understood figuratively, meaning: establish the prayer at the time that is close to the two ends of the day. This is because what is close to a thing may be given its name. Given this, whatever time is closer to the sunrise and to its setting is closer to the apparent meaning of the words. Establishing the Fajr prayer at the time of brightness (al-tanwir) is closer to the time of sunrise than establishing it in the darkness before dawn (al-taghlis). Likewise, establishing the 'Asr prayer when the shadow of everything becomes twice its length is closer to the time of sunset than establishing it when the shadow of everything becomes equal to its length. A figurative meaning, the closer it is to the reality, the more preferable it is to interpret the word by it. Thus it is established that the apparent meaning of this verse strengthens the view of Abu Hanifa on these two matters.

* * *

As for God's words ﴿and in the early hours of the night﴾, they require the command to establish the prayer during three portions (zulaf) of the night, because the least plural is three, and the Maghrib and 'Isha' have two times. So the ruling on the obligation of the witr (odd-numbered prayer) must be applied, so that three portions arise in which the prayer must be performed. Since the obligation of the witr is established for the Prophet ﷺ, it is obligatory for others too, because of God's words ﴿and follow him﴾. A verse exactly parallel to this one is His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130]. So what is before the rising of the sun is the Fajr prayer, and what is before its setting is the 'Asr prayer.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and from the hours of the night, glorify Him﴾, which is similar to His words ﴿and in the early hours of the night﴾.

**The third issue:** The exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning a man who came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "What do you say about a man who did with a forbidden woman everything a man does with his wife except intercourse?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Let him perform ablution well, then let him stand and pray." So God revealed this verse. It was asked of the Prophet ﷺ: "Is this specific to him?" He said: "Rather, it is for people in general."

As for His words ﴿in the early hours of the night﴾, al-Layth said: a zulfah of the night is a portion from the beginning of the night, and its plural is zulaf. Al-Wahidi said: the root of the word is from zulfa, and zulfa means nearness. It is said: "I brought him near (azlaftuhu), so he drew near (izdalafa)," meaning I brought him close so he came close.

**The fourth issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf (a work of Qur'anic exegesis by al-Zamakhshari) said: it has been read as zulufan with two damma vowels, and as zulfan with a sukun on the lam, and as zulfa (ﷺ) in the pattern of qurba (nearness). So zulaf is the plural of zulfah, like zulam being the plural of zulmah. Zulf with sukun is like busrah and busr, and zulufu with two dammas is like yusrun in yusr. Zulfa has the meaning of zulfah, just as qurba has the meaning of qurbah, and it is what comes near to the end of the day from the night. It was also said in explaining His words ﴿and in the early hours of the night﴾: and near (qurban) to the night. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove misdeeds﴾, and on this there are two issues.

**The first issue:** There are two opinions concerning the interpretation of "good deeds."

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is that the five prayers are expiations for other sins, on condition of avoiding the major sins.

The second: It is narrated from Mujahid that the good deeds are the servant's saying: "Glory be to God, praise be to God, there is no god but God, and God is greatest."

**The second issue:** Those who argue that disobedience does not harm one who has faith use this verse. This is because faith is the noblest, most exalted and most excellent of good deeds, and the verse indicates that good deeds remove misdeeds. So faith, which is the highest of good deeds in rank, removes disbelief, which is the highest rank of disobedience. If this is so, then it is more appropriate that it overcomes the misdeed that is lower in rank. And if it does not result in the complete removal of punishment, then it at least results in the removal of the everlasting, perpetual torment.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ His words ﴿That﴾ refer to His words ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾ up to the end of the verses. ﴿A reminder for those who remember﴾ means an admonition for those who take heed and guidance for those who seek guidance.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And be patient, for indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ It was said: [be patient] upon the prayer. This is like His words: ﴿And enjoin your family to the prayer, and be steadfast in it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 116:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why were there not among the generations before you people of virtue (ulu baqiyyah) who would forbid corruption on earth, except a few of those whom We rescued from among them? But those who did wrong pursued the luxury in which they had been given ease, and they were criminals.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that the earlier nations were struck by the punishment of annihilation (adhab al-isti'sal), He explained that the cause of this was two matters:

The first cause: there was no group among them who would forbid corruption on earth. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why were there not among the generations﴾. The meaning is: "Why was there not" (fahalla kana). It is related from al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, the grammarian) that he said: "Every instance of the word 'lawla' (why not) in the Qur'an means 'halla' (why not), except the one in al-Saffat."

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "This narration from him is not sound, as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He, in other than al-Saffat: ﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord reached him, he would have been cast out onto the barren land﴾ [al-Qalam: 49] ﴿And had it not been for believing men﴾ [al-Fath: 25] ﴿And had We not strengthened you, you would almost have inclined toward them a little﴾ [al-Isra': 74]." And His saying: ﴿people of virtue (ulu baqiyyah)﴾ means people of excellence and goodness. Excellence and generosity are called baqiyyah, because a man keeps back from what he gives out the best and most excellent of it. So this word became a figure of speech for goodness, and it is said: "So-and-so is of the baqiyyah of the people," meaning of their best. From this is their saying: "In the corners are hidden things, and among men are remnants (baqaya)." It is also possible that baqiyyah carries the meaning of baqwa (remaining), as taqiyyah carries the meaning of taqwa, meaning: "Why was there not among them one with self-preservation and guarding of themselves from the wrath of Allah, exalted is He?" It is also read ﴿ulu buqyah﴾ on the pattern of luqyah, from baqqahu yubaqqihi, when one watches over him and waits for him, and the baqiyyah is the single instance of its verbal noun. The meaning is: "Why was there not among them people of watchfulness and fear of the vengeance of Allah, exalted is He?"

Then He said: ﴿except a few﴾. It is not possible to make this a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), because on this reading it would be an encouragement to the people of virtue to forbid corruption, except the few of the saved among them. As you say: "Why did your people not recite the Qur'an, except the righteous among them?" — you mean to exclude the righteous from those urged to recite the Qur'an. Having established this, we say that it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), and the sense is: "But a few of those whom We rescued from the generations did forbid corruption, while the rest were abandoning the prohibition."

The second cause for the descent of the punishment of annihilation is His saying: ﴿But those who did wrong pursued the luxury in which they had been given ease﴾. Tarruf is blessing, and a child is called mutraf when his body is pampered, and the mutraf is one whom blessing and abundance of livelihood have made insolent. By "those who did wrong" He means those who abandoned forbidding evil deeds, that is, they did not concern themselves with what is a great pillar of the pillars of the religion, namely enjoining good and forbidding evil. They pursued the seeking of desires and pleasures and occupied themselves with obtaining positions of leadership. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of al-Ju'fi, read ﴿wa-ittaba'a alladhina zalamu ma atrafu﴾, meaning: they pursued what was forbidden, which they had been given ease in. Then He said: ﴿and they were criminals﴾, and its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 117–119:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers.﴾ ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will not cease to differ.﴾ ﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy. And for that He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together."﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, clarified that He destroys the people of the towns only through injustice, and there are several interpretations of this.

The first interpretation: the meaning of injustice here is polytheism (shirk). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13]. The meaning is that He does not destroy the people of the towns merely because they are polytheists, if they are righteous in their dealings with one another. The summary is that the punishment of annihilation (ʿadhab al-istiʾṣal) does not descend because a people hold belief in shirk and disbelief, but it descends only when they do evil in their dealings and strive in harm and injustice. For this reason the jurists (fuqahaʾ) said: the rights of God, the Exalted, are founded on leniency and tolerance, while the rights of the servants are founded on strictness and stinginess. It is said in a report: "Dominion endures with disbelief, but does not endure with injustice." Thus the meaning of the verse, ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly﴾, is: He does not destroy them merely for their shirk if they are righteous, dealing with one another with uprightness and rectitude. This is the interpretation of the People of the Sunnah of this verse. They said: the evidence for it is that the people of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu‘ayb were struck by the punishment of annihilation only when God, the Exalted, related of them their harm to people and their injustice to creation.

The second interpretation, which the Mu‘tazilah prefer: if He had destroyed them while they were reformers, He would not be exalted above injustice; therefore He does not do that, but He destroys them only because of the evil of their deeds.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community﴾. The Mu‘tazilah interpret this verse as the will of compulsion and coercion, and the discussion of this has already passed.
* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But they will not cease to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy﴾. The intended meaning is the divergence of people in religions, morals and actions.

Know that there is no way to exhaust the doctrines of the world in this place. Whoever wishes that should consult our book which we named "al-Riyad al-Mawniqah." However, we mention here a comprehensive division of the doctrines, so we say: people are of two groups. Among them are those who acknowledge sensory knowledge, such as our knowledge that fire is hot and the sun is luminous, and self-evident knowledge, such as our knowledge that negation and affirmation cannot coincide; and among them are those who deny both. The deniers are the Sophists (al-Sufsata’iyyah), and the affirmers are the vast majority of the people of the world. They are two groups:

Among them are those who concede that those self-evident truths can be combined so that theoretical scientific conclusions are drawn from them, and among them are those who deny this—and they are those who also deny reflection upon knowledge, and they are few. The first are the vast majority of the people of the

صفحة ٦٢
world, and they are two groups:
Among them are those who attribute no principle at all to this corporeal world, and they are the fewest; and among them are those who attribute to it a principle. These are two groups: among them are those who say that this principle is necessitated by its essence—and they are the majority of the philosophers of this era—and among them are those who say that it is a free, choosing agent, and they are the majority of the people of the world. Then these are two groups:

Among them are those who say that He has not sent any messenger to the servants, and among them are those who say that He has sent messengers. The first are the Brahmins, and the second category are the adherents of revealed laws and religions: they are the Muslims, Christians, Jews and Magians. Within each of these communities there are differences without limit or count, the intellects are in turmoil, the objectives are obscure, and the disputes of illusion and imagination are unending. And since it was fitting for Hippocrates to say in the art of medicine: "Life is short, the art is long, judgment is difficult, and experience is perilous," it is all the more fitting to mention it in these lofty matters and obscure investigations.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verses 117–119:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers.﴾ ﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will not cease to differ.﴾ ﴿Except those upon whom your Lord has mercy. And for that He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind all together."﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, clarified that He destroys the people of the towns only through injustice, and there are several interpretations of this.

The first interpretation: the meaning of injustice here is polytheism (shirk). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13]. The meaning is that He does not destroy the people of the towns merely because they are polytheists, if they are righteous in their dealings with one another. The summary is that the punishment of annihilation (ʿadhab al-istiʾṣal) does not descend because a people hold belief in shirk and disbelief, but it descends only when they do evil in their dealings and strive in harm and injustice. For this reason the jurists (fuqahaʾ) said: the rights of God, the Exalted, are founded on leniency and tolerance, while the rights of the servants are founded on strictness and stinginess. It is said in a report: "Dominion endures with disbelief, but does not endure with injustice." Thus the meaning of the verse, ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly﴾, is: He does not destroy them merely for their shirk if they are righteous, dealing with one another with uprightness and rectitude. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 11, verse 120:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We relate to you from the news of the messengers that with which We strengthen your heart. And there has come to you in this the truth, an admonition, and a reminder for the believers.﴾

[Page 64]

Know that when Allah the Exalted mentioned the many stories in this surah, He mentioned in this verse two kinds of benefit.

The first benefit: strengthening the heart in conveying the message, in patience, and in bearing harm. This is because when a person is tested with a trial and a calamity, if he sees that someone shares it with him, it lightens on his heart, as it is said: "When a calamity becomes general, it becomes light." So when the Messenger hears these stories and knows that the condition of all the prophets, may God's blessings be upon them, along with their followers was like this, it becomes easy for him to bear the harm from his people, and he is able to be patient with it.

The second benefit is His saying: ﴿And there has come to you in this the truth, and an admonition, and a reminder for the believers.﴾

Regarding His saying: ﴿in this﴾ there are several views:

First: in this surah.

Second: in this verse.

Third: in this world. This is distant and not fitting to this place.

Know that restricting the coming of the truth to this surah does not necessarily mean that the condition of the other surahs is different in this respect, since it is possible that the truth mentioned in this surah is more complete in its state than what is mentioned in the other surahs. Even if there were nothing in it except His saying: ﴿So be upright as you have been commanded﴾, the matter would be as we have mentioned. Then He made clear that three things came in this surah: the truth, the admonition, and the reminder.

As for the truth: it is an indication of the proofs that point to the oneness of God, justice, and prophethood.

As for the reminder: it is an indication of guidance toward lasting good deeds.

As for the admonition: it is an indication of turning away from the world and of the ugliness of its conditions in the Hereafter, and of reminding of the happiness and misery that are there. This is because the soul came from that world, but due to its absorption in love of the body in this world, it forgot the conditions of that world. So divine speech reminds it of the conditions of that world, and for this reason it is correct to apply the word "reminder" to it.

Then here is another wondrous subtlety: divine knowledge necessarily requires a receptor and a cause that moves it. Its receptor is the heart, and if the heart is not fully prepared to accept those divine knowledges and holy manifestations, benefit from hearing the proofs will not be achieved. For this reason Allah the Exalted put first the mention of the reform of the heart, which is the strengthening of the heart. Then, when He mentioned the good condition of the receptor, He followed it with the mention of the cause, which is the coming of this surah containing the truth, the admonition, and the reminder. This order is of the utmost nobility and majesty.

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, had reached the utmost in giving warning and admonition, in encouragement and intimidation, He followed this by saying to the Messenger: ﴿And say to those who do not believe﴾, whom these clear proofs did not affect: ﴿Act according to your position; indeed, we are acting.﴾ This is exactly what Allah, exalted is He, related about Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, that he said to his people. The meaning is: do everything you are able to do against me of evil, for we too are acting. As for His saying ﴿Act﴾, although its form is that of a command, what is intended by it is a threat, like His saying, exalted is He, to Iblis: ﴿And incite whomever you can among them with your voice, and gather against them your cavalry and your infantry﴾ [al-Isra: 64], and like His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. And ﴿wait﴾ for what Satan promises you of abandonment, for we are waiting for what the Most Merciful has promised us of kinds of forgiveness and goodness. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: ﴿And wait﴾ for destruction, "for we are waiting for punishment for you."

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned a noble, lofty conclusion, comprehensive of all noble and sanctified aims, saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾

Know that the totality of what man needs to know consists of three matters: the past, the present, and the future. As for the past, it is that he knows the existent that was existent before him, and that existent which preceded him is the One who brought him from non-existence into existence, and that is Allah, exalted and sanctified is He.

Know that the reality of the essence of God and the true nature of His identity are not known to humans at all; what is known to humans are His attributes. His attributes are of two kinds: attributes of majesty (jalal) and attributes of honor (ikram). As for the attributes of majesty, they are negations (salbiyyat), like our saying: He is not a substance, nor a body, nor such and such. These negations, in reality, are not attributes of perfection, because negations are non-existence, and pure non-existence and mere negation contain no perfection. Thus our saying "He is not seized by drowsiness nor sleep" only conveys perfection because it indicates all-encompassing, perpetual knowledge free from change; were it not so, the absence of sleep would indicate no perfection at all. Do you not see that the dead and inanimate objects are not seized by drowsiness nor sleep! And His saying: ﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾ [al-An'am: 14] conveys only majesty, perfection and greatness, because His saying ﴿but is not fed﴾ [al-An'am: 14] indicates that He is necessarily existent in His essence, free of need for food and drink, indeed free of need for everything other than Him. Thus it is established that the attributes of perfection, might and exaltedness are the affirmative attributes (sifat thubutiyyah), and the most noble of the affirmative attributes that indicate perfection and majesty are two: knowledge and power. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, described His essence in this verse with these two, in the context of glorification, praise and laudation.

As for the attribute of knowledge, it is His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾ What is meant is that His knowledge penetrates all universals and particulars, the non-existent and the existent, the present and the absent. The full explanation and elaboration of this word's indication of the utmost perfection is what we mentioned in the commentary on His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him﴾ [al-An'am: 59]. As for the attribute of power, it is His saying: ﴿And to Him the whole matter will be returned.﴾ What is meant is that the return of all things is to Him, and this is only so if He is the source and origin of all things; and the One who is the origin of all possible beings and to whom all created and existent things return, is of great power, of penetrating will, a subduer of non-existence through existence and attainment, and an overpowerer of it through strength, action and perfection. These two attributes are what is mentioned in explaining the majesty of the origin and describing its grandeur.

The second level of the levels that a person must be knowledgeable of is: that he know what is important for him during the time of his life in this world, and that is none other than the perfecting of the soul through spiritual knowledge and sacred manifestations. This level has a beginning and an end. As for its beginning, it is occupation with bodily and spiritual acts of worship. As for bodily acts of worship, the best of movements is

[Page 66]
prayer (salah), the most complete of stillnesses is fasting (sawm), and the most beneficial of righteousness is charity (sadaqah).

As for spiritual worship, it is thought (fikr) and reflection upon the wonders of Allah's craftsmanship in the dominion of the heavens and the earth, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191]. As for the end of this level, it is ceasing from the means to their Causer, cutting off regard from all possible and originated things, directing the pupil of the intellect to the light of the world of majesty, and the spirit's immersion in the lights of the world of greatness. Whoever reaches this rank sees everything other than Him hastening, bewildered, in the courtyard of His greatness, perishing and passing away in the annihilation of the radiance of His names.

The summary of the matter: the first of the degrees of the journey to Allah, exalted is He, is servitude to Allah, and its last is trust in Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿So worship Him and rely upon Him.﴾

The third level of the important levels for every doer is knowledge of the future, that is, that he knows how his condition will become after the end of this bodily life, and whether his deeds have an effect on happiness and misery. To this the saying of the Exalted refers: (﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.﴾) The intended meaning is that He does not waste the acts of obedience of the obedient, nor neglect the states of the rebellious and denying; this will be by their being presented at the station of the Resurrection, being reckoned for the smallest speck and the tiniest thing, and being reproached for the small and the great, then the outcome results in a group in Paradise and a group in the Blaze. Thus it becomes clear that this verse is sufficient in pointing to all the lofty aims and sacred purposes, and that beyond it there is for the intellects no higher ascent, nor for thoughts any ultimate end. And Allah is the Guide to what is right.

The surah is completed by the praise and help of Allah. And it was found in the handwriting of the author, may Allah be pleased with him, in the copy from which this was transcribed: the tafsir of this surah was completed before dawn on the night of Monday in the month of Rajab, which Allah concluded with goodness and blessing, in the year six hundred and one. I had a son of righteous conduct who died in a foreign land in the prime of his youth, and my heart was like one burning for that reason. So I beseech Allah, my brothers in religion and my partners in the pursuit of certainty, and everyone who looks into this book and benefits from it, to remember that youth with mercy and forgiveness, and to remember this poor one with supplication, saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy; indeed You are the Bestower﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8]. And may Allah send blessings upon the best of His creation, Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
